Tatpar Quick Commerce: What Chennai Cannot Launch Without

Bengaluru — Wednesday, 30 September 2026

At 8:40 on a humid Wednesday morning, Aanya Deshmukh, vice-president of product at Tatpar Quick Commerce, stood before a whiteboard in the Koramangala office with a marker in one hand and a printed backlog in the other. The backlog ran to forty-two tickets, every one tagged "P0 — must have" by the team that had raised it. By Friday evening she had to hand founder and chief executive Rohan Sabharwal a locked list of what would ship on launch day, so the board could be told on Monday that Chennai was on track. She could not ship everything demanded, and she could not ship nothing. Somewhere between the two was a decision she had six weeks left to make.

Company background

Tatpar Quick Commerce was founded in Bengaluru in 2021 on a simple promise: groceries at the door within ten minutes. It built its business the way rivals Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart had — small, densely packed "dark stores" stocked for speed, tuned by a demand-forecasting model. By September 2026 Tatpar ran 236 dark stores across Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi-NCR, Hyderabad and Pune, handled roughly 3.4 lakh orders a day at ₹410 average order value, and ran at an annualised revenue rate near ₹1,900 crore. A Series C that March had brought in $140 million (about ₹1,170 crore), anchored by a Dubai-based fund whose partner sat on Tatpar's board and had, in the fundraising deck, been shown Chennai live before Diwali. Zepto and Blinkit already ran dark stores there; Swiggy Instamart had entered that summer. Tatpar was arriving late to a market its rivals had already begun to season.

The situation

Fourteen dark stores were leased and fitting out across T. Nagar, Anna Nagar, Velachery and Adyar. What remained was the app: catalogue, checkout, delivery logic and store tooling adapted for a city whose addressing, language and packaging rules differed from anywhere Tatpar had launched before. Engineering committed 24 engineers across Bengaluru and Pune, with a code freeze on 24 October ahead of the Diwali-week launch. Netting out on-call and review time, Karan Bhatia put usable capacity at 540 developer-days across three sprints, shown in Exhibit 1. Against that, the "Chennai Launch v1" backlog totalled an estimated 980 developer-days — 1.8 times what the team could build, and every requesting team believed its ask belonged on day one.

Aanya had watched this pattern before. Every function touching the launch — legal, design, support, growth — had reasonable grounds for urgency, each from a different city with a different idea of what "launch" meant. She called a workshop for Thursday, spanning the Bengaluru morning, Berlin's afternoon, Singapore's evening and, near midnight, New Jersey. Its purpose was not to rank the tickets by how much anyone wanted them, but to ask one question of each: would the release fail without it. That test, not the loudness of the request, would decide the must-have list.

The people

Karan Bhatia — Head of Engineering, Pune. Karan had watched two prior launches slip because "must have" quietly grew to mean "everything anyone asked for." He wanted a list his 24 engineers could actually deliver by the freeze, with margin for a new state's surprises.
Marta Hoffmann — Lead Product Designer, Berlin. Marta argued a sixth-city launch, arriving after three rivals, needed to feel like an event, not a copy of Hyderabad. She pressed for Chennai-themed onboarding and a Marina Beach loading animation.
Priya Raman — Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Priya brought ticket data from Hyderabad and Pune: 22 percent of week-one support contacts concerned addresses the app could not locate, worse in Chennai's older neighbourhoods, where street names carry Tamil variants and many homes lack a visible door number.
Robert Fein — Global Head of Growth, New Jersey. Robert managed Tatpar's Dubai-based board investor and needed a growth story for the board. He wanted WhatsApp order-sharing and an upgraded referral programme live at launch, arguing growth depended on customers inviting customers from day one.

Source: Tatpar engineering programme plan, September 2026.

Exhibit 2 lists six representative tickets, each carrying its "must have" tag, its effort, and its cost at Tatpar's blended rate of roughly ₹9,000 per developer-day.

Every row was defensible, yet none of it fit inside 540 developer-days. The workshop ran each ticket through one test — not "would this help," which everything passed, but "does the release fail without it on day one." Note the address ticket. Priya's data justified urgency, not the full ₹4.14 lakh revamp. The workshop split it: a ₹1.08 lakh minimum fix flagging undeliverable addresses before checkout was a must; the fuller, pleasanter revamp was a should. That distinction — the smallest change that prevents failure, not the fullest version of the request — was, in Karan's words, "the whole exercise in one line."

The options

Option A: Lock the must-have list at 512 developer-days

Aanya ships only what Exhibit 3 classifies as Must, leaving a 28-day buffer. Should items — the address revamp, the return flow — move to a fast-follow release two weeks later. Marta's launch loses its distinct identity, and Robert has no growth story for the board. The upside is a release Karan's team can actually deliver, tested, by the freeze.

Option B: Hire in extra capacity for the highest-value Should items

Aanya brings in four contract engineers for six weeks at ₹90,000 a week each — about ₹21.6 lakh — adding close to 120 developer-days, enough for the address revamp and return flow alongside the must list. The risk is ramp-up: new contractors typically lose 15–20 percent of their time to onboarding, with no guarantee four can be hired and made productive inside two weeks.

Option C: Delay the Chennai launch by three weeks, past Diwali

Aanya asks Rohan to move the launch to late November, giving the team runway to build should- and could-items without adding headcount. The cost is the festival window: order volumes run near 2.3 times normal through Diwali week, worth close to ₹14 crore in Chennai alone, plus three weeks for Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart to deepen their lead in a city Tatpar has not yet entered.

Questions for discussion

  1. Why did every ticket being defensible make prioritisation harder, not easier?
  2. Apply Aanya's test to the address-fix ticket and to Robert's WhatsApp referral ticket. Why the different buckets, despite both having a plausible case?
  3. What does splitting the address ticket into a "minimum fix" and "full revamp" reveal about what a must-have requires?
  4. Which option should Aanya recommend, and what would you tell Marta and Robert about the items left off the list?

A note for the learner

MoSCoW exists because "priority" is a word every stakeholder can claim without giving anything up. Left unchecked, a backlog like Tatpar's simply relabels every request "must have," and prioritisation becomes negotiation by volume. The method forces one falsifiable question onto each item: does the release fail — legally, operationally, or at a transaction — without this. The test is not about value or effort; it collapses both into a single gate that enthusiasm alone cannot pass. A regulatory display, or a step without which orders cannot be picked, passes it regardless of how quietly it was raised; a brand animation or growth feature fails it regardless of how loudly it was argued, however good it may later prove.

The address ticket carries the second lesson: a must-have is not the fullest version of a request but the smallest version that prevents failure. Tatpar did not need the ₹4.14 lakh revamp to avoid failed deliveries — a ₹1.08 lakh validation step sufficed. Conflating "ship something here" with "ship the whole ask" is how must-have lists balloon back past capacity.

A well-reasoned answer recommends Option A: lock the must-have list at 512 developer-days, inside the 540-day capacity, with a genuine buffer for a new state's unknowns. Option B stakes the launch on a ramp-up Karan cannot guarantee in two weeks; if it slips, Tatpar loses both scope and schedule. Option C trades a sizeable festival opportunity, and ground to three live competitors, for scope that does not need Diwali timing. The defensible message to Marta and Robert is not that their requests were wrong, but that a must-have list exists so a launch can happen at all — and a fast-follow release, sequenced and communicated clearly, is where their work belongs next.
exp20v2-prio.moscow:
Delivery & Technology · Prioritisation & Decision-Making

MoSCoW and Must-Have Analysis

On the morning of 14 September 2026, Priyanka Deshmukh, VP of Product at Iravati Freight Networks, a Pune-based dispatch and load-matching platform used by roughly 340 trucking fleets across western India, sat in a glass-walled meeting room with a spreadsheet she had come to dread. It listed 41 engineering tickets, all tagged for Dispatch 4.0, the release her team had promised the board would ship by 1 December. The date was not arbitrary: from 1 January 2027, the GST Network's revised e-way bill rules would require every consignment above ₹50,000 to carry a dynamically generated QR code linked in real time to the invoice, and Iravati's three largest customers, together worth ₹6.2 crore of annual recurring revenue, had said plainly that they would switch to a compliant competitor if the platform was not ready with enough runway to test it. Rohan Bhatia, her engineering lead, had already told her the 41 tickets represented roughly 96 developer-weeks of work. Her team, after subtracting festival leave and an unavoidable infrastructure migration, had 54 developer-weeks before the deadline. The wrong choice would either blow the compliance date or ship a release so stripped down it solved nobody's problem. Priyanka needed a way to decide, in a single afternoon and in front of a founder who wanted everything, what the release could not ship without.

The idea

MoSCoW sorts a list of candidate features or fixes into exactly four categories — Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have this time — defined not by how good an idea is but by what happens to the release if the item is left out. It was devised in 1994 by Dai Clegg, a consultant at Oracle UK, as part of a broader delivery method called DSDM (Dynamic Systems Development Method), built for teams shipping on a fixed date with a fixed team who could only vary scope. That constraint is the whole point: most prioritisation frameworks ask "what is most valuable," but MoSCoW asks a narrower, more operational question — "what can this release not go out without" — a question about risk and dependency, not upside. The single sentence Priyanka could say without sounding glib is this: a Must have is anything whose absence means the release has failed, by legal, contractual, or safety measure, not merely disappointed someone.

Figure 1. The four buckets are nested by shrinking cost of omission, not by merit. A Must sits inside a hard constraint; a Won't is simply agreed out of scope for this release, not rejected forever.

How it actually works

The mechanics look deceptively simple, which is exactly why teams misuse them. The first step, which practitioners routinely skip, is to write down the actual constraint the release faces — a date, a regulation, a contractual clause, a safety threshold — before looking at a single ticket. Without that anchor, "must" becomes a synonym for "important," and everything becomes a must. Priyanka's anchor was two sentences: the e-way bill QR generation had to work before 1 January 2027, and the three anchor customers had to be able to complete a live pilot by 15 December to certify it internally.

The second step is to apply a consistent test to every item, not a vote. The test DSDM proposes, and the one Priyanka used, is: if we ship without this, does the release fail its stated purpose, with no acceptable workaround? If yes, Must. If the release survives but a defined class of user is meaningfully worse off and a manual or partial workaround exists, Should. If it is a genuine improvement nobody outside the team will register missing in month one, Could. If the honest answer is "we are not doing this for this release," Won't — said aloud, in the room, so the idea does not quietly reappear in week eleven as a Must.

The step almost everyone leaves implicit is capacity-checking the Must bucket itself. DSDM's rule of thumb is that Musts should consume no more than 60 percent of available effort, leaving room for the Shoulds and Coulds that make the release worth having and for the overrun Musts themselves generate. A team that lets Musts swallow 95 percent of capacity has not prioritised; it has renamed its full backlog and kept the deadline pressure exactly where it was.

A worked example

Rohan's 41 tickets totalled 96 developer-weeks against 54 available. Priyanka ran the test live, item by item, and the table below shows a representative slice of nine tickets out of the full 41.

TicketWeeksBucketWhy
QR code generation on invoice9MLegal requirement from 1 Jan
GSTIN validation at checkout6MNo compliant invoice without it
Offline QR cache for dead zones7M40% of routes lose signal; no workaround for drivers
Bulk QR re-generation tool5SManual re-key is painful but possible
Fleet-owner analytics dashboard v28SOld dashboard still functions
Driver app dark mode3CRequested, zero functional cost of loss
Multi-language SMS receipts4CDesirable, not tied to compliance
Predictive ETA using weather data11WGenuinely good idea, next release
Third-party insurance marketplace14WUnrelated to the December constraint
Table 1. A representative slice of the Dispatch 4.0 backlog, sorted against the two anchor constraints rather than by opinion.

Across the full 41 tickets, the Musts summed to 31 developer-weeks — 57 percent of the 54 available, inside the 60 percent guideline — leaving 23 weeks for Shoulds and Coulds, of which the team fit four Shoulds (19 weeks) and pushed the rest, including every Could, to a fast-follow release in January. The founder's objection, predictably, was the offline QR cache: surely drivers could just retry when signal returned? Priyanka's second pass showed why that assumption mattered more than any single feature debate. Assuming signal loss affected only 8 percent of routes, not 40, the offline cache dropped from Must to Should, freeing 7 weeks that let two more Shoulds — the bulk re-generation tool and a driver-side receipt printer integration — move up. The release's shape pivoted on one field-operations estimate, not on anyone's list of favourite features, which is precisely the discipline MoSCoW exists to expose.

The nuances a learner must sit with

MoSCoW ranks buckets, not items within a bucket

Having sorted three tickets into Must does not tell you which to build first if capacity tightens mid-sprint. MoSCoW is a gate, not a queue; sequencing within a bucket still needs a separate call, often value versus effort, the framework MoSCoW is built on top of.

Must-have creep is the method's most common failure mode

Every stakeholder believes their item is the exception. The discipline is not skill at rejecting people; it is a written test applied identically to every ticket, and a visible ceiling — the 60 percent rule — that makes the trade-off arithmetic rather than a personality contest.

Won't have is a promise, not a rejection

"This time" is doing real work in the phrase. A Won't never revisited quietly erodes trust in the process; the healthiest teams put Won't items at the top of the next release's candidate list rather than letting them vanish.

The Must test changes with the release window

A four-week release and a four-month release do not share a definition of "no workaround." Compressing the window turns previously-Should items into Musts, because manual workarounds tolerable for a month become untenable for a week; MoSCoW must be re-run, not merely referenced, whenever the deadline moves.

MoSCoW answers a narrower question than value

It tells you what the release cannot ship without; it does not tell you what would make the release best. A team that stops at Must-have analysis and never asks the value-versus-effort question behind it will ship compliant, safe, and forgettable releases indefinitely.

It is frequently confused with a scoring framework like RICE

RICE and similar scoring methods rank a continuous list by a computed number; MoSCoW sorts into four discrete, binary-feeling buckets. Using MoSCoW vocabulary while secretly running a popularity vote produces the same inflation problem as any unweighted survey — everything scores high because nobody pays a cost for saying so.

It cannot tell you if the constraint itself is real

MoSCoW takes the anchor constraint as given. If the "legal deadline" is actually a padded internal estimate, or the "must" is a single loud customer rather than a contractual clause, the entire exercise inherits that error with false rigor. The method sorts faithfully around whatever anchor you hand it, including a wrong one.

A thoughtful newcomer should ask what happens if a Must slips anyway

Sorting is not delivery. Priyanka still needed a contingency — in her case, a negotiated grace period with the GST-registered aggregator her platform used — for the scenario where even the Must-only scope missed the date, because a method that only classifies risk does not remove it.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

In a consumer app, Musts are usually thin and externally obvious: app-store policy, payment compliance, a security patch after a breach — consumer users abandon rather than complain, so the cost-of-omission test is blunt and fast. In B2B software like Iravati's, Musts are frequently contractual and customer-specific, discovered by re-reading the master service agreements of the three or four accounts that matter most, which is exactly what Priyanka's compliance officer did before that September meeting. In a marketplace, a Must for supply-side users (fleet owners) can conflict with a Must for demand-side users (shippers), and MoSCoW then needs to be run twice before the lists are reconciled by whichever side is scarcer. Scale changes who defines Must: at an early-stage company the founder often is the anchor constraint, and Must lists stay short because the company cannot afford long ones; at a large company Musts multiply as more contracts, regulators, and legacy integrations each contribute their own non-negotiable, and the harder discipline becomes saying no to a ninth legitimate Must rather than finding a first one.

Common mistakes

Everything lands in Must. Symptom: more than 80 percent of the backlog tagged Must, with the exercise adding no clarity. Underlying error: no written cost-of-omission test, so "important" and "must" collapse into one word. Cheapest diagnostic: for every Must, ask aloud "what specifically breaks, for whom, on day one, if we skip this" — an answer naming no specific breakage is not a Must.

Won't-have items resurface unchanged. Symptom: a feature killed in planning reappears in week nine as an urgent request from the same stakeholder. Underlying error: Won't was never logged as a decision with a reason, so it reads as forgotten rather than deliberate. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether the Won't list has an owner and a next-release date; an unlabelled graveyard will keep reopening.

Should-have items get treated as a strict sequence. Symptom: the team builds Shoulds in ticket order rather than by which one most reduces the pain of the workaround it replaces. Underlying error: conflating a bucket with a priority rank. Cheapest diagnostic: ask which Should, if cut, would generate the most support tickets in month one; build that one first.

MoSCoW is run once and never revisited. Symptom: the release date slips by three weeks and the same buckets stay untouched. Underlying error: treating the classification as a one-time artifact rather than a live decision tied to a moving constraint. Cheapest diagnostic: whenever the deadline or team size changes by more than 10 percent, re-run the test — the buckets are a function of the constraint, and the constraint just moved.

What good looks like

Six weeks later, Rohan's team shipped Dispatch 4.0 on 28 November, three days early, with all 31 Must developer-weeks delivered and two of the four Shoulds included after the capacity buffer came in under estimate. The undelivered Shoulds and every Could were logged, with reasons, as the seed of the January release — not lost, simply sequenced. When the founder asked at the November retro why the insurance marketplace idea had been dropped, Priyanka pulled up the same table from September and pointed to the anchor constraint at the top of it. The conversation took ninety seconds, because the decision had been made visibly, against a written test, three months earlier — not defended from memory in the room.

Closing

Priyanka's decision was to hold the 60 percent ceiling even when the founder pushed for a tenth Must, and to spend her political capital instead on getting the field-operations signal-loss estimate re-measured, because that single number, not any feature debate, was what the entire release shape actually depended on. The next idea worth her team's time is value versus effort, the framework MoSCoW sits on top of, because once the floor of non-negotiables is fixed, the harder and more interesting question — which of the remaining Shoulds and Coulds earns its place — is exactly what value-versus-effort is built to answer. Two questions worth sitting with: when you last called something a Must, could you name the specific failure and the specific party it would hurt, or were you using the word to end an argument? And if your current release's Must bucket exceeds 60 percent of capacity, what does that tell you about the constraint you started from — is it not really more than one deadline pretending to be one?

Delivery & Technology · Prioritisation & Decision-Making

MoSCoW and Must-Have Analysis

What the method actually claims, where its arithmetic comes from, and the seams at which it quietly stops working.

1. Two rooms, two deadlines

On 3 November 2026, Meenal Raghunathan, Chief Product Officer of Darpan Imaging Devices, a Bengaluru firm building trolley-mounted portable ultrasound units for district hospitals, was looking at 74 candidate items totalling 1,180 engineering person-days against a capacity of 640. The date that mattered was 12 February 2027, and it was two dates wearing one costume. Darpan's Class B licence amendment for hardware revision B had to reach the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation with verification evidence attached; a Rajasthan health procurement window worth roughly ₹41 crore over three years closed on 20 February, requiring DICOM-conformant archival, a Hindi operator interface and a signed cybersecurity attestation. Her firmware release, DX-200 3.0, had to satisfy a regulator, a tender committee and a manufacturing line whose enclosure tooling had frozen in September. Her engineering director, Tarun Sabharwal, noted that at least 30 of the 74 tickets carried the word "critical".

Two days later in Gurugram, Sameer Vaidya, Head of Product at Dwarpal Identity Cloud, ran the same exercise on a very different product and got a worse answer. Dwarpal sells a video-KYC and document-verification API used by 26 lenders and four insurers inside their own onboarding funnels, so its release calendar is really twenty-six calendars at once. The Reserve Bank of India's amended master direction on customer due diligence took effect on 1 April 2027, and Dwarpal's largest account, a non-banking financial company contributing ₹9.4 crore of annual recurring revenue, held a clause requiring certified compliance 45 days ahead of any regulatory date. Sameer sized the backlog at 63 items and 940 points against a capacity of 520; when his six squad leads classified it, the Must bucket came back at 880 points, 94 percent of capacity. Every lead had been honest, and every lead had been wrong; the question is not that they inflated but why the method let them.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

MoSCoW sorts scope into four classes — Must, Should, Could, and Won't have this time — on one criterion: what happens to this release if the item is absent. A Must have is one whose omission means the release has failed its stated purpose, with no workaround the affected party can accept inside the release's lifetime. A Should have is painful but survivable, because a degraded workaround exists. A Could have does no measurable harm in the window. A Won't have is a deliberate, recorded, time-bounded exclusion. The acronym was coined in 1994 by Dai Clegg at Oracle UK and absorbed into the Dynamic Systems Development Method, a fixed-date discipline premised on schedule and team being rigid while scope is elastic. That premise is load-bearing: this is a rationing device for a timebox, not a theory of value.

Four schools disagree about how much weight it carries. The DSDM orthodoxy holds that Must means "minimum usable subset" and is meaningful only against a timebox with agreed contingency; it would sign that a release with no Won't-have list has not been prioritised, and would not sign that MoSCoW tells you what to build next quarter.

The economic school, descending from Donald Reinertsen's cost-of-delay arguments and expressed as weighted shortest job first, sees four bins as lossy compression of a continuous quantity. It would sign that priority is cost of delay over duration, and that ordinal bins destroy information exactly at the Must/Should boundary. It would not sign that bucket membership should ever determine build order.

The contractual school, common among regulated and enterprise vendors, reserves Must for obligations enforceable by an outside party — a statute, a regulator's effective date, a signed service commitment. It would sign that a Must needs a named external enforcer, and would not sign that a founder's conviction creates one.

The sceptical school holds that the analytical content is thin and the real function social: a ritual manufacturing consent for exclusion, whose valuable output is the Won't-have conversation held before witnesses. It would sign that the benefit lies in the meeting rather than the artefact, and would not sign that the buckets carry information a cost-of-delay model could not carry better. These positions do not reconcile by synthesis; experts hold two at once depending on the release, and all four reject the reading that Must means important.

Figure 1. The test as experts run it. Two gates do the work: a named victim and a named mechanism, then survivability of the workaround across the release window. Below the second gate everything is a capacity question, not a merit question.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

The competent practitioner runs the two gates in Figure 1 and stops. The expert does four further things, each of which changes the answer.

First, fix the anchor before touching the list. Meenal's team wrote two sentences on the whiteboard before any ticket was read: DX-200 3.0 must permit a complete CDSCO filing on 12 February with verification evidence, and a compliant Rajasthan tender submission on 20 February. Only claims traceable to one of them could produce a Must. This is the highest-leverage step there is: a backlog sorted against an unstated anchor converges on seniority rather than consequence.

Second, take the dependency closure of the Must set. A Must is not an item; it is a subgraph. If a Must cannot be built, tested or shipped without something classified as a Could, that Could is a Must by transitivity, and its label was an artefact of nobody drawing the graph. At Darpan the Hindi interface was a clear tender Must at 38 person-days; nobody had flagged that the string-rendering layer could not handle Devanagari conjuncts at the DX-200's screen density, making a font-rasteriser replacement — parked in Could at 22 person-days as cosmetic — a prerequisite. Closure added 96 person-days nobody had counted.

Figure 2. The analysis operates on a graph, not a list. Three items classified Could or Should were prerequisites of declared Musts, and Darpan's honest total rose from 276 to 372 person-days — 58 percent of the 640 available — the moment the closure was drawn.

Third, estimate the Must set before declaring it closed, and estimate at the eightieth percentile. This is where the folklore that Musts should take no more than about 60 percent of capacity stops being folklore. Suppose actuals run at a median of 1.35 times estimate with a p80 of 1.9 — figures well inside what most organisations observe when they measure. A Must set booked at 60 percent of nominal capacity has expected consumption of 0.60 × 1.35 = 81 percent and p80 consumption of 114 percent, so the Musts alone breach capacity in about one release in five. Book them at 80 percent and expected consumption is 108 percent: late in the median case before a Should is attempted. At 94 percent, as Dwarpal's leads had it, the figure is 127 percent. The rule is the level at which the bucket survives ordinary estimation error, not a moral position about restraint.

Figure 3. Why the 60 percent guideline exists. With 1.35× median and 1.9× p80 estimation error, a Must bucket above roughly 60 percent of capacity is expected to consume the whole release. Teams with tighter estimates can run hotter; few have tighter estimates than they believe.

Fourth, decompose the Musts themselves. The largest reserve of slack is not between buckets but inside Must items, because a Must is rarely binary. Darpan's DICOM requirement, sized at 54 person-days, held a conformant export path worth 21 days, a query-retrieve service worth 19 and a modality worklist integration worth 14. Only the first was in the tender specification. Re-running the test on each fragment returned 33 person-days to the pool; experts routinely free 15 to 25 percent of a Must bucket this way.

4. When the method applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions carry the method, each checkable. Claim one: the date is genuinely fixed and externally imposed. Plainly true at Darpan, where a CDSCO filing window and a tender close are not negotiable by any amount of eloquence. At Dwarpal it holds for the regulatory date and only half-holds for the contractual 45-day lead, which a senior commercial conversation could amend. A Must anchored to a renegotiable date is a Should whose owner has not tried.

Claim two: scope is the elastic variable. True at Dwarpal, where an API can ship narrower; partly false at Darpan, where a device release carries a verification burden that does not shrink proportionally, so cutting a feature after test-protocol authoring saves engineering days but not regulatory ones. Claim three: the items are separable. Both teams failed this in places, which is what the closure exists to catch.

Claim four: the cost of omission is knowable in kind, if not in size. True for compliance and contract items in both companies, sharply false for discovery work — where the method turns actively misleading. An experiment whose purpose is to learn whether a segment exists has no coherent classification, because its cost of omission is the option value of information, which four buckets cannot represent. Teams that force research and platform-health work through MoSCoW bucket it as Could, then wonder in eighteen months why velocity has halved.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies releases nest: a platform team's quarterly release carries the Musts of four application teams, no two sharing an anchor. The honest practice is one platform Must list derived from the earliest binding downstream date, plus a published cut-off after which no new downstream Must enters the current release.

In two-sided marketplaces cost of omission is asymmetric by side, so the exercise runs twice; the reconciliation rule that works resolves in favour of whichever side has the higher switching propensity within the window, not whichever generates more revenue.

In regulated products the Must set includes evidence, not only function: Darpan's cybersecurity attestation was 31 person-days, 19 of them documentation and traceability. Engineers under-classify evidence work because it produces no visible behaviour, and the release ships a compliant feature that cannot be shown to be compliant.

In hardware-plus-software, the Must decision has a date of no return months ahead of the release. Darpan's tooling froze in September, so any February Must needing a physical change was already impossible in November: part of the classification had been made irreversibly by an operations decision nobody framed as prioritisation. Mature hardware firms therefore run the exercise twice — at design freeze for physical dependencies, at code freeze for the rest.

In AI-native products, the Must is usually a quality threshold rather than a capability, and thresholds are probabilistic. Dwarpal's document classifier had to reach a false-acceptance rate below 0.4 percent on 12,000 held-out identity documents to satisfy its risk committee — an item no amount of code marks done, only a measurement that may or may not arrive. The accommodation is to classify the evaluation harness and the fallback path as Must and the threshold as a release gate, so a model that misses the bar degrades to manual review instead of blocking the release. Classify the threshold itself as Must and the ship date becomes a function of a research outcome.

6. The nuances that separate expert from competent

Must is a property of the release, not of the feature

The same item is a Must in a four-week release and a Should in a four-month one, because workaround tolerance scales with duration. The sign is a backlog whose labels persist across quarters unrevised. The obvious reading — that some features simply are more essential — fails because essentiality is a relation between an item, a constraint and a window.

A Must with no named victim is a Should in costume

Ask who, specifically, is harmed, by what mechanism, on which date. "Customers will be unhappy" fails; "the NBFC's compliance officer cannot sign the 45-day attestation on 15 February, triggering clause 7.3" passes. The tell is instant: the advocate answers with an adjective rather than a party. Genuine Musts are boringly specific.

The dependency closure holds the real surprise

The sign is a Must list that is suspiciously tidy while the engineering leads stay quiet. Experts ask each owner what must already exist for the item to be testable in production, and treat any answer naming an unbuilt thing as a classification error. Treating dependencies as downstream scheduling fails because the closure changes the totals, and the totals are the decision itself.

Non-functional work disappears because it has no ticket

Performance, observability, migration and upgrade paths are rarely on the candidate list at all, so they are never bucketed and become Won't by default. The sign is a Must list composed entirely of user-visible features, and the reading that invisible work can wait fails the moment the release ships and cannot be operated.

Won't have is the only bucket that generates trust

Must, Should and Could cost the requester nothing; Won't is the only label that takes something away, and so the only one whose handling is watched. A healthy process has a Won't list with a named owner and a review date; an unhealthy one has Won't items reappearing as urgent Musts late in the timebox, after which stakeholders route around the meeting entirely.

The error cost is asymmetric, and the asymmetry flips

Over-classifying is expensive in a short timebox, crowding out everything and forcing a late, disorderly cut. Under-classifying is expensive in a long one, because the omission surfaces after the release has been committed. Experts test conservatively on short releases and generously on long ones, which looks like inconsistency and is not.

The anchor is usually several deadlines pretending to be one

Meenal's 12 February was two dates with different owners and different consequences. The tell is a Must set that will not decompose cleanly when you ask which anchor each item serves; separating them usually shows that a subset belongs to the later date and can follow the first delivery.

The classification is a revealed preference, not an analysis

A finished Must list encodes who was in the room and what they were willing to defend. The use is diagnostic: if every Must traces to one function, the process has been captured, and the fix is a different attendance list rather than a better rubric.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the Must set is thin and externally defined — app-store policy, payment-rail compliance, a security fix — and because consumers leave rather than complain, cost of omission is estimated from churn rather than negotiated. In B2B and enterprise software Musts are contractual and account-specific, and the honest way to build the list is to read the agreements of the accounts carrying the revenue. In platforms and marketplaces the set is built per side and per consuming team, bound by the earliest downstream commitment. In hardware irreversibility dominates; in AI products Musts attach to evaluation and fallback rather than to model behaviour.

Across stages the difference is real but smaller than claimed. At seed stage the list is short because the company cannot afford a long one and the anchor is usually a funding or pilot event; the risk is that the founder is the anchor. At growth stage it lengthens as contracts accumulate and the 60 percent discipline bites for the first time. At enterprise scale Musts multiply and the hard skill shifts from finding one to refusing a ninth defensible one. What does not differ is the test: the two gates in Figure 1 read the same at every stage.

8. Three worked examples

Darpan Imaging Devices — the disciplined case. After closure and decomposition the Must set settled at 339 person-days against 640 capacity, or 53 percent. Table 1 shows the movements that produced it.

Table 1. Eight of Darpan's 74 candidates. Movement ran both ways: two Coulds became Musts by dependency, one Must became a Won't for want of an anchor, and the largest addition was evidence work never written down as a ticket.

Dwarpal Identity Cloud — the recovery. Sameer's 94 percent Must bucket was resolved not by asking his leads for discipline but by re-reading contracts. Of 63 items, 41 were marked Must because "RBI requires it." Counsel found that 12 of them implemented requirements applying to the lender rather than the verification vendor: Dwarpal's obligation was to make them possible, not to build them. Those 12, worth 214 points, moved to Should. A further eight, 149 points, were parity features requested in sales calls and never committed to; they became Could. The Must set landed at 310 points, 60 percent of capacity, and Dwarpal shipped on 2 February 2027.

Dakshin Freight Exchange — where it failed. A Kochi marketplace matching shippers with regional truck operators ran a competent exercise ahead of a March 2026 release and shipped on time. Its Must list came from shipper interviews, because shippers paid the commission and the growth team owned the release. Two supply-side items — instant settlement for operators, and a Malayalam and Tamil driver app — were classified Should and cut. Within seven weeks operator acceptance on posted loads fell from 71 percent to 48 percent and match times rose from nine minutes to twenty-six. The failure was not the classification but the constituency: cost of omission had been measured only on the side that could complain in English to a product manager. Recovery took eleven weeks and roughly ₹2.6 crore in operator incentives; the fix was structural, two Must lists thereafter reconciled by the scarcer side. No step of the original exercise was performed badly.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Must inflation. Sign: the bucket exceeds roughly 70 percent of capacity at first pass. Diagnostic: for each Must, who is harmed, by what mechanism, on what date? Caught late, the cut happens in the final fortnight, and what goes is whatever was least defended.

Anchor fiction. Sign: the stated deadline has no external document behind it. Diagnostic: ask to see the clause, the notification or the tender paper. Caught late, a release has been shaped around a date that could have moved, with real Shoulds sacrificed to an imaginary constraint.

Closure blindness. Sign: engineering leads are silent during classification and voluble in week six. Diagnostic: what must exist before this Must is testable in production? Caught late, the Must set grows 20 to 35 percent mid-release — the mechanism by which on-plan releases become three weeks late with no single decision being wrong.

Constituency blindness. Sign: every Must traces to one function, one side of a market or one language group. Diagnostic: who is absent who would classify differently? Caught late, it costs what Dakshin paid.

Evidence omission. Sign: a regulated release whose Must list has no documentation items. Diagnostic: what would an auditor ask for that we have not scheduled? Caught late: a feature-complete release that cannot be filed.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether buckets should exist at all. The economic camp argues that four bins discard exactly the information needed at the margin, and that cost-of-delay-over-duration ranking dominates MoSCoW on every dimension except explicability; its evidence is that queueing models show ordinal bucketing yields worse throughput. It would be wrong if cost of delay were not estimable for most items — which, for compliance work, it is not, the cost being a step function at a date rather than a slope.

Whether the 60 percent rule is analysis or superstition. Defenders point to the arithmetic in Figure 3, which falls out of any plausible error distribution. Critics observe that it is applied without anyone measuring their own inflation factor, so the number is carried as doctrine. Both are right; the resolution is to measure, which almost nobody does.

Whether Musts should be estimated at all. One camp holds that estimating a Must is incoherent — if it truly must ship, the estimate changes nothing but morale. The other holds that an unestimated Must set cannot be checked against capacity, the only quantitative claim the method makes. The first would be right if no Must were ever cut under pressure; Musts are cut constantly, which suggests it describes an aspiration rather than a practice.

Whether it belongs outside a timebox. Continuous-delivery practitioners argue that with weekly releases the idea of a release that "fails" dissolves and Must collapses into "the next thing we ship." The counter is that regulators, tenders and contracts ignore deployment cadence: cadence changes when work lands, not the consequence of absence on 12 February.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied MoSCoW produces a tidy four-column artefact and defends it. Someone who has internalised it spends the meeting on two things that are not classification at all: establishing what the anchor actually is, and splitting large items until the question becomes answerable. They arrive with the dependency graph sketched and the inflation factor computed from the last four releases, relaxed about Shoulds and unyielding about the Must ceiling, because they know which decision is reversible. They treat the Won't list as a commitment with a date. And when the sorting is done they can say which Must they would ship first if the timebox halved — a question the framework does not answer and they have answered anyway, because someone will ask it.

12. Closing: what each of them decided

Meenal Raghunathan held the Must set at 53 percent of capacity and spent her authority on two unpopular moves. She pushed the obstetric AI measurement upgrade — the most exciting item on the list, personally championed by her chief executive — into Won't, because it had no anchor and a research dependency. And she separated the CDSCO anchor from the tender anchor, letting 71 person-days of tender-only work follow the filing. She then held the freed capacity as contingency rather than filling it with Shoulds, the decision competent practitioners most often decline to make.

Sameer Vaidya did not run a better workshop. He suspended classification for four days and had counsel read the contracts, on the theory that his team's inflation was an evidence problem, not a discipline problem. The re-test moved 363 of 880 points out of Must without one argument about importance, because the question had changed from "is this required?" to "required of whom, by which clause?" He then wrote the inflation factor — 1.42 over his team's previous six releases — into the planning template, so the next release would not depend on him noticing.

Three questions worth sitting with. First: the last time you called something a Must, could you name the party harmed, the mechanism and the date, or were you using the word to end a conversation? Second: if your Must bucket exceeds 60 percent, is the problem the bucket, or have you bundled two deadlines and treated their union as one release? Third: Dakshin's exercise was correct at every step and still cost nine weeks of liquidity — what does that say about where the real risk in prioritisation sits?

13. Going deeper

Value vs effort is the substrate MoSCoW compresses; it shows what the four buckets throw away and lets you sequence within a bucket. RICE scoring supplies the continuous ranking the economic school prefers. The Kano model explains why some items are must-be qualities whose presence earns nothing and whose absence is fatal — a demand-side account of the asymmetry MoSCoW encodes from the supply side. Weighted scoring and WSJF give you the cost-of-delay arithmetic to argue the Must/Should boundary quantitatively. Buy-a-feature is the cheapest remedy for Must inflation, forcing requesters to spend a finite budget. User story mapping is the technique behind the item-splitting that frees 15 to 25 percent of a Must bucket. Prioritising under constraints generalises the exercise to capacity, dependency and regulatory limits at once.

Fehrist Claims Systems: Three Definitions of Failure

Pune — Sunday, 11 October 2026, 10:50 p.m.

The Baner office was empty but for the guard downstairs. Nandita Bhave, vice-president of product at Fehrist Claims Systems, had drawn three overlapping circles on the glass wall of the seventh-floor meeting room and labelled them: illegal, in breach, inoperable. Into each she had written the items of Release 6.0 that, if left out, would make that word true.

They overlapped less than she had expected. The centre — where an item would be all three at once, and so unarguably a must-have — was empty. Not nearly empty. Empty.

In eleven hours she was due in Mumbai to present the scope of Release 6.0 to the board, including Ashwin Pillai of the Singapore fund that led the Series B, who had asked for one slide: what is in, what is out, and what it costs if we are wrong. She had the costs. She had no defensible line between in and out, because every method she tried produced a different line, each defensible to somebody.

Company background

Fehrist Claims Systems was founded in Pune in 2017 by Sridhar Iyengar and two colleagues from a Hyderabad health-insurance back office. Its product was unglamorous and necessary: a claims-adjudication platform sitting between hospitals, third-party administrators and insurers, which received a claim, checked it against a policy's rules, priced it and routed it for payment. By September 2026 Fehrist processed 2.9 lakh claims a month, served 31 insurers and TPAs and some 640 hospitals, and ran at ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, with engineering in Pune and Hyderabad.

One decision from 2022 shaped everything Nandita could now do. Competing that year against a Bengaluru rival, Wazir Health Technologies, Fehrist was asked by Wasool Benefits Administration DMCC of Dubai for adjudication behaviour the common rules engine could not express: Arabic remittance advice, a different pre-authorisation sequence, a benefit-limit model keyed to UAE plans. Rather than delay eighteen months to generalise the engine, Sridhar approved a fork: a parallel rules engine, the Gulf branch, cut from the trunk and maintained separately.

The fork won the contract. It also meant every later change to adjudication logic had to be written, tested and certified twice; Abhijit Rane, who took over engineering in 2024, put the multiplier at 2.4 times for anything touching the rules layer. Phase 1 of a re-platform to merge the branches shipped in March 2026. Phase 2, which actually retired the fork, sat in Release 6.0 — competing for capacity with the very Dubai requirements that had created the fork.

The industry

Indian health insurance had spent three years being rewired. The National Health Authority's National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX) promised a common protocol between payers and providers, replacing a landscape of portals, spreadsheets and couriered discharge summaries. Insurers had begun pilots, hospital groups such as Apollo and Fortis were building to it, and the IRDAI had been consistent that interoperable claims were the direction of travel. The DPDP Act, 2023, turned consent, notice and erasure into engineering problems for anyone holding health data.

The commercial picture was less tidy. Insurers switched vendors slowly and hospital IT teams slower; Wazir Health Technologies had raised a large round in 2025 and was pricing aggressively; and the integrators, Infosys, TCS and their peers, circled the same accounts.

Abroad, Fehrist had one real overseas market and one imagined. The real one was the Gulf, where Wasool administered employer schemes across Dubai and Sharjah under Dubai Health Authority requirements through eClaimLink and Shafafiya, with the UAE's phased e-invoicing mandate on top. The imagined one was the United States, where Dhruv Saxena had worked a mid-sized New Jersey TPA for seven months, and where SOC 2 Type II was not a differentiator but a gate.

How the situation developed

Release 6.0 took its shape in May 2026, when Sridhar told an all-hands the next release would be "the one that makes Fehrist boring to buy": compliant everywhere, forked nowhere, certified for everyone. Nobody disagreed with the sentence. Everybody heard a different release in it.

In June, Shruti Menon joined from a Mumbai advisory practice as head of compliance and, within three weeks, circulated a memo stating that NHCX conformance and DPDP consent architecture had both to be live by 1 April 2027. It was read as settled fact. It rested, Nandita discovered only in late September, on a draft circular and a working-group note; no gazetted date existed, and two insurer clients had told their own boards they expected slippage.

In July, Faiza Qureshi in Singapore relayed that Wasool's renewal, due 31 March 2027, hinged on eClaimLink conformance and UAE e-invoicing; ninety days' notice put the real decision at 31 December 2026. Her written summary said Wasool was "keen to see progress". The call it summarised had said "we cannot renew against a roadmap slide".

In August, Tanvi Rege in Toronto delivered a model scoring each candidate item by the probability that omitting it caused a critical production failure within sixty days. It was immediately popular, because it appeared to convert an argument into a number. It also ranked NHCX conformance thirteenth of fifteen, which pleased Abhijit and alarmed Shruti.

In September, two things went wrong quietly. Phase 2, tracked green all summer, was re-baselined after a dependency review and found eleven weeks behind; and three engineers on the adjudication squad resigned in a fortnight, two to Wazir. Abhijit rebuilt his capacity model on 2 October and produced a number far below the one the programme office was still circulating.

The people

Nandita Bhave — VP Product, Pune. Owns the scope decision and will present it. Her position is that Release 6.0 needs one must-have list decided on evidence, not seniority. What she has not said aloud is that she no longer believes a single list exists, and that saying so on Monday would read as an absence of leadership.
Sridhar Iyengar — Co-founder and CEO, Mumbai. Wants the release to carry the Wasool renewal, the NHCX story and a first US logo; has twice told the board Fehrist will "clear compliance in FY27". His incentive is a Series C conversation begun informally. What he is not saying is that he told Wasool's CIO in July that eClaimLink was in the March release.
Abhijit Rane — VP Engineering, Hyderabad. Holds that the only item of lasting value is Phase 2, because each year the fork survives costs more than the Dubai contract earns. His incentive is a delivery record. What he is not saying is that Phase 2 slipped partly because he moved two senior engineers onto a Wasool escalation in July.
Shruti Menon — Head of Compliance, Mumbai. Position: NHCX and DPDP are not scope items but conditions of being allowed to operate. Her incentive is institutional — a function four months old proves itself by winning the first argument it picks. What she is not saying is that she knows the April date is not yet binding, and considers it the only lever she has.
Faiza Qureshi — Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Position: Wasool is nineteen per cent of ARR and the only reference Fehrist has outside India. Her incentive is retention, on which her variable pay depends. What she is not saying is how explicit Wasool's CIO was, because she believes an alarmed Pune builds the wrong thing in a panic.
Lena Brandt — Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: patients are the only party to a claim who cannot see what is happening to it. Her incentive is a portfolio of work she believes in. What she is not saying is that she moves to a four-day week in January, and has had an approach from a Munich firm.
Dhruv Saxena — Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Position: without SOC 2 Type II and an X12 exporter the US market does not exist. His incentive is a territory he was hired to open. What he is not saying is that his ₹20 crore pipeline rests on one prospect that has signed nothing.
Tanvi Rege — Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the failure model should decide the list, being the only input that is not an opinion. Her incentive is that the model is her most visible work. What she is not saying, though it sits in an appendix nobody opened, is that regulatory and contractual failures do not generate the incident tickets it learned from.

The options as Nandita sees them

A. The regulatory release

Items 1, 2 and 5 — 308 development-weeks — plus a partial Phase 2. Shruti's definition of failure wins. Wasool enters its notice window with nothing to demo, and Faiza is asked to hold ₹18.4 crore on a promise. The defence is that regulation is the only constraint that cannot be negotiated with; the vulnerability is that the April date may not be a date.

B. The contract release

Items 4, 5 and 9 — 288 development-weeks — with NHCX begun but not conformance-tested and DPDP deferred to June. Revenue is protected on a bet that regulatory timelines slip, as they have before. If they do not, Fehrist is non-conformant in the market that is ninety per cent of its business, and Shruti's memo is on file.

C. Pay for capacity

A Pune services firm can supply twelve engineers from 1 November at ₹2.6 lakh a month each: ₹1.4 crore over four and a half months, inside the ₹2 crore Sridhar can approve alone. Nominal 216 development-weeks; a 25 per cent ramp leaves about 162 against a gap of 196. It nearly closes. It does not, and contractors cannot be put on the rules engine, which is where the work is.

D. Fork again, deliberately

Ship the Dubai items on the Gulf branch alone, behind tenant flags, keeping the trunk for NHCX and DPDP. Both constituencies get a release. The cost is that the 2022 decision is renewed, Phase 2 slips to FY28, and the 2.4 multiplier applies to all regulatory work that follows. Abhijit has said he will not staff it. He has not said he would resign over it, and Nandita has not asked.

All four share an unexamined assumption: that Release 6.0 is one release, on one date, with one scope, decided inside Fehrist. Nobody has asked Wasool what a sufficient December demo contains, nor the National Health Authority what staged conformance looks like, nor Firdaus whether a manual workaround for a quarter is tolerable. The must-have list has been treated as a property of the product. It may be a property of conversations nobody has held.

The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 11:00 on Monday 12 October in Mumbai and expects a locked scope, a cost, and a statement of what breaks. Code freeze is 13 February 2027 and release 27 February; the Wasool notice window closes 31 December 2026; the contract ends 31 March 2027, with SLA penalties capped at ten per cent of the annual fee. Fehrist holds ₹112 crore of cash against ₹4.8 crore a month of burn. A June investor letter imposed a headcount freeze; contract spend under ₹2 crore remains with the chief executive. NHCX sandbox slots cannot be bought forward. Three engineers leave before Diwali; Lena moves to four days a week in January. And the Gulf fork, approved in twenty minutes in 2022 to win ₹18.4 crore a year, still requires every rule written for India to be written again for Dubai.

Questions for discussion

  1. Nine of eleven items arrived labelled "must". What has to be true of an organisation for that to happen, and what does the label mean once nine carry it?
  2. Exhibit 4 ranks NHCX fourth and DPDP sixth; Exhibit 5 implies both may be existential. Which would you show the board, and what must you then say about the other?
  3. Exhibit 6 shows no item inside all three circles. Is that a finding about the backlog, or an artefact of how Nandita drew it? How would you test which?
  4. Item 1 cannot ship at eighty per cent, because conformance testing is pass or fail; item 4 can ship at forty per cent and still demonstrate intent. What does that do to the idea that a must-have is the smallest version that prevents failure?
  5. Whose definition of failure should govern — the regulator's, the contract's, the platform's or the patient's — and by what authority does a VP of Product choose? Would your answer change if Wasool were five per cent of revenue rather than nineteen?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Nandita put on the one slide, what does she deliberately leave off, and what does she say when Ashwin Pillai asks her what happens if she is wrong?

Sunday night

At 11:40 Nandita photographed the glass wall, because housekeeping came at six and the marker was the erasable kind. On her phone the circles looked less like analysis than admission: nine days spent converting a political argument into a geometric one, and arriving at a shape with a hole in the middle.

She thought about writing to Faiza to ask the question she had not asked — what exactly would Wasool accept in December — and decided a midnight message landing at two-thirty in Singapore would read as panic on the eve of a board meeting. She thought about calling Abhijit, and remembered he had taken Monday morning off.

Her phone lit up at 11:52. Faiza, awake. Are you up? Their CIO just forwarded me their Q1 vendor review agenda. We're item three. Nandita looked at the message, then at the photograph of the circles, then back at the message, and did not yet know what she would say at eleven o'clock.
