One-Way and Two-Way Doors: Matching Rigour to Reversibility

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 4 June 2025, in a converted warehouse off the Pune–Solapur road, Ananya Deshmukh, Director of Product at Zameen Agri Devices, had eleven days to release the tooling order for the next run of the company's soil-moisture and canopy-temperature node. Zameen sold the node, plus an agronomy app, to sugarcane and grape farmer-producer organisations across Maharashtra and northern Karnataka; 61,000 units were in the ground and the next run was 40,000. Her hardware lead in Coimbatore, Vignesh Iyer, wanted to move from the incumbent radio module to a cheaper integrated chipset: ₹310 a unit off the bill of materials, ₹1.24 crore across the run, and a cleaner firmware path. The chipset had never been tested through a Konkan monsoon.

Six days later, Sameer Chitnis, Head of Product at Zubaan Support Cloud in Hyderabad, took a decision of comparable weight in a forty-minute call. Zubaan's AI agents handled 11.6 lakh conversations a month for thirty enterprise clients, four of them banks. Sameer proposed retiring the company's fine-tuned model for a vendor frontier model behind a managed endpoint, lifting auto-resolution from 58% to an expected 71%. Rolling out took one configuration change; rolling back, his platform lead insisted, took the same — two hours. Sameer shipped to 40% of traffic that afternoon and to all of it nine days later.

Both were applying the same rule: move fast on what you can undo, deliberate on what you cannot. Ananya bought eleven weeks of monsoon testing on a decision she judged locked; Sameer moved in an afternoon on one he judged free to unwind. By November, one had been right for the wrong reason, and the other had found the door had closed somewhere other than where he was watching.

Zameen Agri DevicesZubaan Support Cloud
DecisionSwitch radio chipset for a 40,000-unit runSwitch resolution engine to a vendor model
Mechanical reversalRetool, retrofit field unitsOne config flag, 2 hours
Where the door actually isTooling and certificationContracts, consent notices, an atrophied team
The two live decisions, June 2025. Neither protagonist had written down the last row.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

The distinction is usually credited to Jeff Bezos's 2016 letter to Amazon shareholders, separating Type 1 decisions — consequential and near-irreversible, “one-way doors” — from Type 2 decisions, cheap to walk back. The argument was organisational, not mathematical: large firms apply Type 1 process to Type 2 decisions, and the resulting slowness is waste, not caution. The lineage is older. Arrow and Fisher showed in 1974 that an irreversible investment under uncertainty carries an extra cost — the option to wait, destroyed by acting — now called quasi-option value; Dixit and Pindyck formalised it in the 1990s, showing the hurdle for committing sits well above a naive net-present-value test. Howard's decision analysis added the value of information, which caps how much deliberation any decision can justify.

Four schools share the vocabulary while disagreeing about what it licenses. The operational school reads reversibility as a routing rule: classify, delegate two-way doors to one owner, reserve committees for the rest. It would sign “most decisions in a large company are over-processed”; not “the classification tells you what to choose.” The real-options school objects to the binary: irreversibility is a continuous term inside a valuation, so the right response is a higher threshold for commitment, not a heavier meeting. The reliability school, descended from Perrow's normal-accident theory, is indifferent to classification: what matters is whether the system can be recovered, so invest in canaries and blast-radius limits rather than typing exercises. Its proposition: “every door can be hinged, more cheaply than deliberated over.” The commitment school — Schelling on credible commitment, Ghemawat's 1991 argument that advantage comes precisely from decisions you cannot undo — holds that optionality is often how firms avoid ever building anything defensible. It would sign “some doors should be welded shut on purpose, and saying so is the point.”

The differences bite. The operational school would call Sameer's afternoon rollout exemplary. The real-options school would price the monsoon data before approving Ananya's delay. The reliability school would tell both to stop classifying and build a shadow-mode harness. The commitment school would note that Zameen's moat is an irreversibility: 61,000 nodes nobody can cheaply replace.

3. Mechanics: what the work actually consists of

Expert practice has five moves, of which the middle three are usually left implicit.

Name the action, with a date. “Modernise the radio stack” cannot be typed as a door; “release tooling for 40,000 units on 15 June” can. Reversibility is a property of a dated commitment, not of a topic.

Decompose the reversal, layer by layer. The number practitioners quote — “two hours” — is almost always the mechanical layer alone. A serious decomposition separates mechanism, data, contract, organisation and expectation. Sameer's platform lead was right about the mechanism; the table is the full picture, assembled in September when finance and legal were finally asked.

Reversal layerAt switch-onAt 6 weeksAt 5 months
Mechanism (config, routing)₹0₹0₹0
Data and consent (DPDP re-notice)₹0₹14 lakh₹0.26 crore
Contract (renegotiated SLAs)₹0₹0₹1.55 crore
Organisation (labelling team redeployed)₹0₹9 lakh₹0.48 crore
Expectation (client workflows rebuilt)₹0₹15 lakh₹0.31 crore
Total reversal cost₹0₹38 lakh₹2.60 crore
Zubaan: reversal cost by layer and horizon. The mechanism stayed free; the decision stopped being reversible anyway.

Treat reversal cost as a function of time. Write it R(t). At t=0 almost every decision is reversible; what differs is the curve. Some doors slam — the tooling order, where R jumps the day the die is cut. Some creak shut, like Zubaan's, as clients build workflows on new behaviour. Some ratchet, stepping up at each signature. The useful question is never “is this reversible?” but “until when, and what closes it?”

Three shapes of R(t). Typing a decision is really a claim about which curve it sits on, and where along it you stand.

Buy down the reversal cost where that is cheap. Reversibility is manufacturable: flags, canaries, shadow mode, pilot geographies, a six-month break clause instead of three years, escrow of the old weights, a second-source component. Each has a price, and an expert quotes it instead of arguing categories. Vignesh's second-source qualification cost ₹22 lakh and three weeks.

Then, and only then, size the rigour. The ceiling comes from the value of information. If p is the probability the decision is wrong and L the loss when it is, perfect foresight is worth at most p·L; any study costing more destroys value however prudent it looks. A pilot moving p from p₀ to p₁ is worth (p₀ − p₁)·L, less the delay it imposes. Ananya's team ran that calculation.

Zameen's June tree. Committing destroys ₹2.52 crore of expected value; the eleven-week pilot leaves −₹0.61 crore. Waiting is worth about ₹1.9 crore.

Vignesh's estimate of L came from the retrofit: 40,000 units at ₹2,650 each to visit, swap and re-commission, or ₹10.6 crore, plus ₹3.2 crore of channel disruption across a sugarcane cycle. At p₀ = 0.25 the expected loss was ₹3.45 crore against a ₹1.24 crore saving. An eleven-week pilot on 900 nodes would cost ₹47 lakh and, on the team's judgement, cut p to 0.06, making the information worth (0.25 − 0.06) × ₹13.8 crore, or ₹2.62 crore. Delay forfeited one season's ₹1.24 crore. Net, waiting was worth about ₹91 lakh. Ananya delayed — and note what did the work: not the label but the arithmetic it pointed her towards.

4. When the framework holds, and when it misleads

The framework rests on four testable claims, each true for one protagonist and false for the other.

Claim the framework needsZameenZubaan
Reversal cost can be priced to an order of magnitudeYes — a known field costNo — only the mechanism
The decision has an identifiable closing eventYes — the die cutNo — it closed continuously
Waiting produces information that changes the answerYes — one monsoonPartly — only live traffic teaches
The firm will actually reverse if the signal arrivesYes — tooling not yet paidNo — nobody unwinds a 71% number

Where all four hold, the framework is close to free money. It misleads in three cases. First, where waiting yields nothing: uncertainty that only committing resolves — whether banks will pay for an agent resolving seven tickets in ten — is not made safer by delay, only later. Second, where reversal is mechanically free but the world does not return to its prior state, the hysteresis problem of section 8. Third, where the framework becomes a vocabulary for evasion: a leader avoiding a hard call declares it one-way and commissions a study; one avoiding scrutiny declares it two-way and ships. Both use classification as cover, which is why experienced operators hear the word as a cue to ask for the number.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulators, silicon and models

The clean version assumes one decision-maker who also bears the reversal cost. Almost no real situation satisfies that.

Across products and platform seams, reversibility depends on the observer's position: a platform team's schema change can be reversible for them and one-way for the four teams that shipped against it. Zameen found this when the agronomy app's irrigation-advisory module, owned in Indore, had hard-coded the incumbent radio's 15-minute telemetry cadence; the new chipset's 5-minute cadence was an improvement the advisory model could not consume without an unbudgeted retraining cycle — a reversal cost externalised to a team with no seat in the June meeting. Mature organisations answer with a standing register of decision types pre-classified as one-way — schema deletions, public API contracts, pricing floors, anything touching payouts — so the classification is not re-litigated by whoever owns the change.

In two-sided markets, the sides have different R(t) curves for one decision. Zanjeer Freight Systems, a load-matching platform, could re-rank shipper results overnight but could not move truck-owner payout timing without those owners re-planning working capital, which they would not un-plan on request. Supply-side memory runs longer than demand-side memory almost everywhere.

Under regulation, some doors are absolute. Deletion of personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is irreversible by design; a consent notice cannot be un-issued. Compliance also works the other way: an approval you will not risk re-opening freezes decisions that are technically reversible.

In hardware plus software, the door sits in the physical layer: tooling, component qualification, BIS and WPC certification, units in the field. Zameen's firmware was fully two-way — over-the-air, staged, revertible in a day — resting on a chipset choice that was one-way for seven years. Experts state the decision at the level of the least reversible layer it touches.

In AI-native products, three irreversibilities are new. Data and mixture choices leave residue that cannot be cleanly subtracted. Customer prompts adapt to a model's behaviour, so behaviour becomes an interface. And the vendor can close the door for you by deprecating a version. Sameer had a rollback plan for his own model and none for the day the vendor retired theirs.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Reversal cost is a curve, not a number

The competent practitioner asks whether a decision is reversible; the expert asks until when, and what closes it. The tell is the follow-up: hearing “we can always roll it back,” an expert asks on what date that stops being true. The obvious reading — reversibility fixed at birth — fails because almost every door is open on day one; the risk is in the slope.

Mechanical reversibility is not practical reversibility

A rollback nobody will authorise is not a rollback. Multiply mechanical reversibility by the probability the firm actually reverts, which is low once a number has been reported upward. The tell is asking when a team last rolled anything back; if the answer is “never,” their flags are theatre. Zubaan's 71% had been shown to three clients' steering committees, and after that no two-hour rollback was going to be exercised.

The irreversibility usually lives outside your system

Code reverts; customers do not. Reference prices, retrained habits, published SLAs, reorganised workflows and reallocated working capital are all one-way, and none appear in a deployment runbook. The tell is a reversal plan written wholly in the language of engineering. If nobody can say what a customer would have to un-learn, the reversal is unpriced.

Reversibility has a price list, and you should quote it

Arguing Type 1 versus Type 2 is less productive than pricing a hinge. Break clauses, dual-running, shadow mode, second sourcing, weight escrow, pilot geographies: each converts a one-way door into a two-way one for a fee. The expert answers a classification question with a quotation — ₹22 lakh and three weeks — and lets the room decide whether reversibility is worth it.

Some doors should be one-way on purpose

Optionality has a cost the framework rarely mentions: a commitment that can be withdrawn is less credible, and credibility is sometimes the product. A platform reserving the right to revoke its API guarantees is worth less than one that cannot. The tell is a team that has kept every option open for eight quarters and built nothing anyone depends on.

The real target is the process tax, not the single decision

The value is aggregate. A firm taking 300 two-way decisions a quarter, each carrying four hours of needless review across six people, spends 7,200 person-hours on ceremony. That total, not the merits of any one call, is what classification exists to reduce. The tell is a leader who applies it to the decision in front of them and never to the calendar.

Reversible decisions compose into irreversible ones

Fifty individually revertible schema tweaks produce a schema nobody can migrate. Path dependence is invisible at the level of a single decision, which is why it escapes classification entirely. The tell is a system where every change is locally reversible and nobody can describe how to reach any earlier state.

Confidence and reversibility are separate axes

The common error is collapsing them. High confidence with high reversal cost is where full commitment belongs; low confidence with low reversal cost is where speed belongs; the dangerous cell — low confidence, high reversal cost — is where the expensive mistakes sit.

The off-diagonal cells decide outcomes. Sameer's error was not the engine but the placement of the dot.

Waiting only works if information is scheduled to arrive

Delay is justified by an arriving signal, and the expert names the observation and its date — one monsoon, ending in September. Where no such observation exists, “let us gather more data” is a decision to be late; the honest move is to commit and instrument. The tell is a study with a stated completion date and no stated decisive measurement.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the one-way doors cluster in trust and reference-setting: a privacy default, an anchor price, an identity merge. In B2B and enterprise they sit in contracts and interfaces, where reversal needs another company's consent — hence enterprise PMs' distrust of the framework's optimism about rollback. In platforms and marketplaces reversibility is asymmetric, and the binding side is the one making capital commitments. In hardware the doors are physical and long-dated. In AI products the model layer is unusually reversible while the data, expectation and vendor-dependency layers are not, inverting the intuition engineers bring from software. Where the difference is smaller than claimed: decomposition, pricing and information value work identically in all of them.

Stage changes the arithmetic, not the logic. At twenty people nearly everything is two-way because absolute reversal costs are small: Zameen in 2020, with 900 nodes deployed, could have swapped chipsets on a whim. The same decision at 61,000 units carries a retrofit bill two orders of magnitude larger. Scale converts structurally irreversible decisions from cheap to ruinous without changing their character — which is why moving fast on everything becomes a liability around Series C. The mirror failure is the scaled firm that carries heavy process into a small new market where reversal is trivial again.

8. Three worked examples

Zameen, the delayed tooling order. The pilot ran in Ratnagiri and Kolhapur from late June. By 12 September, 41 of 900 nodes on the new chipset showed antenna de-tuning above 92% humidity — a 4.6% failure rate against 0.8% for the incumbent. Had the run shipped, some 1,840 of 40,000 units would have failed in the field, a ₹4.9 crore retrofit on that subset alone. The ₹47 lakh pilot returned ten times its cost, and the chipset shipped next run with a firmware fix. The lesson is about slope, not doors: with one sharp step in R(t), delay was unusually cheap for what it bought.

Zubaan, the door that closed elsewhere. Auto-resolution reached 69% by August, close to forecast. Then two things absent from the two-hour estimate happened. Two banking clients re-signed with a 65% auto-resolution floor in the SLA, and the nine-person Kolkata labelling team — the loop keeping the in-house model current — was redeployed. In October the vendor raised inference cost from ₹2.10 to ₹3.40 per conversation, an extra ₹1.81 crore a year. Sameer could absorb it, renegotiate thirty contracts, or return to a model whose training loop was dismantled. The mechanism was still two hours; the decision now cost ₹2.6 crore to reverse.

Zevar Jewellery Retail, where the framework failed outright. Zevar, a 74-store gold and diamond chain in Jaipur competing against national brands, merged its online and in-store customer identity graphs before the 2024 festive season. The product lead, Ritika Bhandari, typed it in writing as a two-way door: full backups of both graphs, restorable in nine hours. She was right about the backup and wrong about the state. Six weeks of transactions were written against merged identifiers; restoring the pre-merge graphs would have orphaned them, and keeping them made channel attribution unrecoverable, because the merge had dropped the channel-of-origin field as redundant. Zevar spent the season unable to say where its ₹19 crore campaign was working, and mis-allocated an estimated ₹6.2 crore. Recovery took nine months and ₹1.1 crore of external re-attribution modelling, plus a rule making channel-of-origin fields append-only. Not carelessness — the standard error of reasoning about a snapshot's restorability while the world keeps writing.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Pricing only the mechanismReversal quoted in hours by one engineerWhat does legal, finance or the customer have to undo?Zubaan's ₹2.6 crore
Snapshot fallacy“We have a backup” as the whole planWhat gets written while we deliberate, and can it be split?Zevar's lost season
Classification as coverThe label appears before any numberWhat figure supports that label?Months of study, or an unreviewed commitment
Rollback theatreFlags exist; nothing has ever been revertedWhen did we last actually roll back?Found out during an incident
Delay without a signalA study with a date but no decisive measurementWhat observation would change our answer, and when?A season of forgone value

Two deserve emphasis because they are cheap to catch and expensive to miss. The snapshot fallacy falls to one question about concurrent writes, which would have saved Zevar nine months. Rollback theatre falls to asking the date of the last actual reversal; a team that cannot name one should treat its reversibility as unproven, exactly as an untested backup is not a backup.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Classification versus valuation. The operational school holds that a crude binary is exactly right, because its purpose is to change behaviour at scale and practitioners cannot estimate p and L well enough for anything finer; its evidence is the observed slowness of large firms. The real-options school replies that a binary is a lossy encoding of a continuous variable that invites the two off-diagonal errors, and cites investment research showing that irreversibility properly valued shifts thresholds materially. The operational position fails if firms using the binary systematically mis-sort decisions near the boundary; the options position fails if the estimates are so noisy that the arithmetic is decoration. Nobody has run the field experiment; both rest on cases.

Optionality versus commitment. Ghemawat argues advantage comes from irreversible commitments and that a firm optimising for reversibility builds nothing durable; Schelling, that the ability to retreat destroys a promise's credibility. Against them, the reliability school holds recoverability near-costless once engineered, and commitment signallable by contract without being technically inescapable. The disagreement is consequential for platform strategy: whether to promise API stability you cannot cheaply withdraw is precisely the question. It settles against the commitment school if credible commitment can always be manufactured contractually, and against the optionality school if firms with the best rollback capability have the weakest moats.

Whether reversibility is the right routing variable at all. A minority view, drawing on Kahneman and Klein, holds the better variable is whether the domain permits reliable judgement: in low-validity domains cheap reversibility is an illusion, because you will not know you were wrong. That is the least discussed and possibly strongest objection — the framework assumes the error is detectable in time to use the door.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether a decision is one-way or two-way and is satisfied by the answer. Someone who has internalised it does four things instead. They restate the decision as a dated action at the level of its least reversible layer. They ask for reversal cost decomposed across mechanism, data, contract, organisation and expectation, and notice when only the first is priced. They ask what event closes the door and when, then check whether the information they await arrives before that date. And they quote a price for a hinge rather than debate a category. The signature: less time on classification, more on execution design — and when they commit to a one-way door, they commit completely, having bought the information they could afford and stopped.

12. What each of them did

Ananya held the tooling order until 19 September, adopted the chipset for the following run once the monsoon data arrived, qualified the incumbent module as a second source, and added a line to Zameen's decision log requiring every hardware proposal to state reversal cost per field unit. Her reasoning was not that the decision was important, but that R(t) had a single step, the step was eleven weeks away, and one monsoon was worth ₹2.6 crore of information.

Sameer could not undo his decision and did not try. He negotiated a two-year price commitment at ₹2.65 per conversation, re-established a four-person evaluation and labelling function in Kolkata, and rewrote Zubaan's launch template so every proposal prices reversal at switch-on, six weeks and six months. His summary in the November review was the sentence this page has circled: the mechanism was never the door.

Discussion questions. (1) Sameer's rollback estimate was technically correct. What should have been asked in the forty-minute call to surface the ₹2.6 crore, and whose job was it to ask? (2) Ananya's pilot returned ten times its cost. Would running it have been defensible had it found nothing? (3) Zevar priced reversibility rightly for the snapshot and wrongly for the world. Is the remedy a framework, a register, or an architectural rule?

13. Going deeper

Mental models for PMs — reversibility is one model in a working set; knowing when a model is the wrong lens is the skill beneath this one. Portfolio of bets and expected value — once a door is typed, bet sizing follows, and that is a portfolio question. Auditing irreversible product decisions — the one-way register and the review of what actually closed; the sequel to section 5. Value vs effort — instructive because it carries no reversibility term. RICE scoring — adds confidence, the grid's second axis, but prices no reversal. Kano model — helps estimate the expectation layer. Weighted scoring and WSJF — quantifies cost of delay, the term opposite information value. Buy-a-feature — a two-way way to buy demand information before committing. User story mapping — shows which slices are entangled, hence where reversible changes compose into irreversible ones.

Decision Frameworks: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors

The Bet

On the morning of 11 March 2024, Radhika Menon, VP of Product at Yugma Mobility Cloud, a Bengaluru-based ride-hailing and last-mile delivery platform running roughly 4.2 lakh trips a day across nine cities, had two decisions sitting on the same page of her notebook, and she was about to treat them identically. The first: whether to retire the phone-based driver-onboarding desk — eleven staff, a vendor contract renewing in seventeen days — and route every new driver through an AI onboarding assistant instead. The second: whether to raise the minimum fare floor in Pune by six rupees, from ₹49 to ₹55, for two weeks, to see whether driver acceptance improved during the evening surge.

Both decisions had a business case, promising roughly the same upside, near ₹1 crore a year. Her engineering lead, Farhan Sheikh, wanted three weeks of sign-off for each, the standard process at Yugma for driver economics; her data lead wanted a two-day test for each. Neither was wrong about process in general; both were treating two decisions that did not resemble each other as the same kind of choice.

Close the onboarding deskRaise the Pune fare floor
If wrong, can it be undone?Slowly, at real costNext Monday, almost free
What reversal actually requiresRehire, retrain, four monthsChange one number in the app
Two decisions of similar size on Radhika's desk, 11 March 2024 — nearly opposite in what a mistake would cost to fix.

If the AI assistant produced a worse driver experience, the desk's staff would already be redeployed and its memory gone; rebuilding it would take roughly four months and ₹85 lakh. If the Pune fare test went badly, Radhika could revert to ₹49 the following Monday. These were not the same decision in different clothes: one was a door that locked behind her, the other a door she could walk back through.

The Idea

The distinction Radhika needed has a name: one-way doors and two-way doors, popularised by Jeff Bezos in Amazon's April 2016 shareholder letter, though the underlying logic — that the process a decision deserves should scale with how expensive it is to reverse, not with how important it looks — is older, and appears in decision theory as the "option value" of keeping choices open. A two-way door is a decision you can walk through, look around, and step back out of at low cost: a pricing experiment, a feature behind a flag, a two-week pilot among three vendors. A one-way door is a decision that, once taken, is expensive or impossible to undo: laying off a team, migrating a database with no rollback, signing a five-year exclusive contract, deleting a customer's data.

Reversibility, not size, is what separates a door you can re-open from one that seals shut.

The single sentence Radhika could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "What would it cost us to reverse this if we're wrong — and does today's process match that cost, or just how nervous the decision makes us?" Bezos's real complaint was that large organisations apply one-way-door process — slow, layered with sign-offs — to nearly every decision, including two-way doors a single senior person could decide that afternoon, and that habit is what makes big companies slow without making them safer.

How It Actually Works

Applying the framework has four steps, and practitioners routinely skip the last one.

StepWhat it meansWhere teams shortcut it
1. Name the decision preciselyA dated, specific action, not a topic"Improve onboarding" instead of "close the Chennai desk on 1 April"
2. Price the reversalReal rupees and real weeks if it turns out wrongSubstituting a feeling for a number
3. Match process to that priceFast and single-owner, or slow and stagedMatching process to visibility instead
4. Separate decision from commitmentExecute cautiously to shrink the reversal costAssuming the door's type is fixed and unchangeable

Step one meant Radhika made Farhan state the decision as "close the Chennai desk on 1 April and route 100% of new drivers to the AI assistant," not a vague ambition. Step two meant putting an actual figure on reversal: severance, the time to rehire and retrain a comparable desk, and driver-churn cost — together, the ₹85 lakh, four-month estimate. A number, not an intuition, is what makes a decision a one-way door in practice. Step three meant matching sign-off weight to that number rather than to how emotionally loaded the room found it. Step four is the one most teams leave implicit: you can decide to migrate a system at 40% confidence and still run it as a canary rollout with an explicit rollback trigger, turning what looked like a one-way door into something closer to two-way — not by gathering more opinions before starting, but by changing how you execute after.

The Arithmetic

Radhika ran both decisions the way the framework asks: not "is this big" but "what does it cost to be wrong, weighted by how likely we are to be wrong."

DecisionP(wrong)Cost if wrongExpected costReversal time
Close onboarding desk30%₹125 lakh₹37.5 lakh~4 months
Raise Pune fare floor45%₹9 lakh₹4.05 lakh~1 week
Cost if wrong for the desk = ₹85 lakh reversal plus ₹40 lakh lost trip volume during the gap, drawn from a smaller Coimbatore pilot's 6-point retention drop.

For the onboarding desk, she estimated a 30% chance the assistant meaningfully hurt driver retention in its first quarter, based on that Coimbatore pilot. The downside if wrong — ₹85 lakh reversal plus ₹40 lakh in lost trip volume — gave an expected cost of ₹37.5 lakh, close enough to the ₹58 lakh annual saving that Radhika treated this as a genuine one-way door: a staged closure, keeping the desk one more quarter where the assistant hadn't yet proven itself.

For the fare test, the "wrong" outcome was that ₹55 cut demand more than it helped driver acceptance, costing perhaps ₹9 lakh over two weeks, at a higher 45% probability since Pune's elasticity was uncertain — an expected cost of only ₹4.05 lakh, reversible within a week. Even though this test was more likely to be wrong, the framework says spend less process on it, because reversal was nearly free. Now change one input: suppose the fare change required a fixed-term contract with a Pune driver-aggregator, unrevisable for a quarter. Reversal cost jumps to ₹22 lakh and ten weeks, and a decision that looked identical on the surface becomes a one-way door. Reversibility is a property of how a decision is executed, not of its subject.

The Nuances

Reversibility is about cost, not feeling

People call a decision "one-way" because it feels consequential — a re-org, a public statement — rather than measuring what reversal would cost. A ₹3 crore campaign can be fully two-way if it's pulled next week; a small configuration change can be one-way if it deletes historical data during a migration. Ask for the number before trusting the feeling.

Expensive-to-reverse is not the same as truly irreversible

Laying off a team is painful and costly to reverse but not literally impossible — Yugma has rehired laid-off staff before, at a premium. True one-way doors, like deleting a customer's data under India's data-protection law, leave no path back at any price. Rigour should scale with both cost and true impossibility, not cost alone.

It is a speed filter, not a stakes filter

The framework doesn't say whether a decision is important; a two-way door can matter enormously, such as which city to enter first. It only says how fast you may move and how much you can lean on a rollback plan instead of consensus.

It is routinely confused with "big vs small"

A decision can be small in budget yet irreversible, like dropping a column from a legacy schema, or large yet fully reversible, like a pilot with a monthly opt-out clause. Size is a poor proxy for reversibility; using it as one over-processes big two-way doors while under-processing small one-way ones.

It cannot tell you which choice to make

Bezos's model is silent on which assistant is better; it only says how much debate the choice deserves before acting. Teams that treat door-typing as an answer, rather than a routing question, end up debating reversibility instead of the underlying decision.

Two-way doors drift into one-way ones

A pilot with three vendors is reversible; the moment a team quietly signs a 24-month contract with the winner "to lock in pricing," the door swings shut, often without anyone re-running the check.

Ownership should follow the door's type

Two-way doors are best delegated to one accountable person who can move fast. One-way doors deserve a named decision-maker too, with a wider information base — consensus surfaces information; it is not a substitute for deciding.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace — and Scale

ContextWhere the one-way doors usually hide
ConsumerData and trust defaults; a price that becomes the customer's reference point
B2BContracts and APIs other companies build production systems against
MarketplaceDepends which side moves — buyer ranking is often reversible, seller payout timing rarely is

In consumer products, the highest-frequency one-way doors are data and trust decisions — a privacy default, or a fare that becomes the reference price in riders' minds, taking years to unwind even after it's technically reverted. In B2B, the classic one-way doors are contractual: a multi-year agreement, or an API other companies build integrations against, where a backward-incompatible change breaks someone else's production system. In marketplaces, reversibility depends on which side you move — buyer-facing ranking is often revertible overnight, while seller payout timing is closer to one-way, since sellers make working-capital decisions against it. Scale matters too: a forty-person company can treat almost everything as two-way, because low volume keeps absolute reversal cost low even for structurally irreversible moves; the same company at Yugma's 4.2 lakh daily trips faces identical decisions with reversal costs multiplied by scale — why a framework that felt like overkill at seed stage becomes load-bearing later.

Common Mistakes

The same four patterns recur among teams that know the framework by name but haven't made it a habit.

SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Every decision goes to the same steering committeeTreating "important-looking" as identical to "hard to reverse"Ask what undoing it in 60 days would cost; if nobody can answer, the process is guessing
A pilot quietly becomes permanentAssuming reversibility is fixed at birth, not checked at each new commitmentFind the calendar date "temporary" terms were meant to expire, and who still owns it
One leader is told to decide a big, genuinely irreversible call in a dayBelieving speed itself is the lesson, not matching speed to reversibilityCheck whether the call is actually two-way before praising the speed
A heavy process wraps a technically two-way decisionConfusing reputational discomfort with real reversal costSeparate the cost of reversing the mechanism from the cost of admitting it was reversed

What Good Looks Like

Six months later, Yugma's product team had a rule pinned above Farhan's decision log: name the decision, price the reversal, then choose the process — never the reverse. When the company later considered replacing its core payments processor, a genuine one-way door given the eight months either side needed to integrate, Radhika didn't reach for a committee by default. She asked the payments and finance leads to price the reversal first — ₹1.4 crore, seven months, a real chance of disrupting driver payouts — before scheduling a single meeting. Because the number was large, the process that followed was deliberately slow: a staged migration on a small share of trip volume, a named rollback trigger, and one accountable decision-maker who could still say "stop" without waiting on a vote.

What Radhika Decided

The Chennai desk was not closed on a single date; it was wound down over one quarter, alongside the AI assistant handling only new cities first, so a failure would show up gradually rather than all at once — acknowledging that the ₹85 lakh reversal cost made this a one-way door, dressed through staged execution as something closer to a two-way one. The Pune fare test ran its original two weeks, decided by the city lead alone, with no committee, because a ₹4 lakh expected cost and a same-week rollback didn't deserve a VP's attention.

What Radhika took from the exercise wasn't a slogan about speed but a habit: before asking how important a decision looks, ask what it would cost to undo, and by when she'd know she needed to. The next idea worth sitting with, since this framework only routes decisions rather than making them, is how to size the bet itself once its door is known — a portfolio of one-way and two-way bets, weighted by expected value, is the natural next lever. Two questions worth keeping: which decision on your desk this week are you over-processing because it feels big rather than because it is expensive to undo — and which one are you rushing because reversing it will, in fact, be nearly free?

Zanjeer Freight Exchange: The Instant Payout Decision

Gurugram, Haryana — 12 October 2026

Ananya Deshpande, VP of Product at Zanjeer Freight Exchange, closed her laptop at 11 p.m. and looked at the calendar pinned above her desk. Twenty-six days to Diwali. In nineteen of them, the board would meet to approve what the founders were calling the festive-season announcement: Instant Payout, a feature that would settle a trucker's earnings within ninety seconds of a delivery instead of the two business days it currently took. The head of sales wanted it announced, company-wide, at the shipper summit in Mumbai the week before Diwali. Her head of engineering wanted six more months. Both had good reasons. Ananya's job was to decide which kind of decision this actually was — one she could reverse if it went wrong, or one she could not.

1. A marketplace built on trust, one truck at a time

Zanjeer Freight Exchange was founded in 2019 to solve a problem every Indian shipper recognised: most road freight capacity sat with single-truck owners who had no digital footprint and were represented, if at all, by a local broker taking a cut at every stage. Zanjeer built a marketplace matching shippers directly with verified truckers, using GPS tracking, GST e-way bill data, and a proprietary risk score. By 2026 the platform carried about 18,000 loads a month across forty corridors, an annualised freight volume of roughly ₹1,850 crore, with Asian Paints, Amul, and two large retail chains among its shippers. It competed directly with BlackBuck and Rivigo, and at the margins with legacy players such as TCI and VRL Logistics.

The company's edge, Ananya liked to say, was not the app but the ledger behind it: truckers trusted Zanjeer because it paid reliably, even if not quickly. Since 2023, Zanjeer had offered fuel-card credit and advance-against-freight financing through its NBFC partner, Ehsaas Payments Cloud, a Mumbai-based embedded-finance provider that ran settlement rails for several logistics and gig-work platforms, held the escrow accounts, and reconciled Zanjeer's ledger nightly against invoices and e-way bill data.

2. The offer on the table

In August, Ehsaas proposed something bigger than a financing tie-up: migrating Zanjeer's payout ledger onto its own real-time infrastructure, using UPI AutoPay to push money within ninety seconds of proof-of-delivery, instead of the current batch NEFT run landing in T+2. Farhan Ansari, the payments engineer in Pune who built the test, called it "the single biggest retention lever we have." Truckers, who often financed the next trip's diesel out of that day's earnings, had been drifting toward cash-settling brokers and BlackBuck's own instant-pay pilot in three states.

But the migration was not a bolt-on. It meant porting the settlement history of all 42,000 active truckers, retiring Zanjeer's own reconciliation system, and routing every future payout, refund, and fuel-card deduction through Ehsaas's rails. Farhan's test had already surfaced a wrinkle: for interstate loads, GST invoice numbers from Zanjeer's system did not always match Ehsaas's expected reference IDs, and reconciling each mismatch manually took nearly four hours. At current volumes, a company-wide cutover meant roughly 600 loads a week needing manual reconciliation in month one — a number that would spike further during the Diwali surge, when volumes typically rose 35 to 40 percent. Once truckers had received even one settlement cycle through the new ledger, Zanjeer's auditors warned, unwinding back to the old system would mean re-matching thousands of already-settled transactions against two different invoice schemes — a job nobody could finish inside a fiscal quarter.

3. The people around the table

Kiran Shetty, Head of Engineering, Bengaluru. Wants the migration phased over two quarters; he has seen ledger cutovers before and does not want the reconciliation backlog to hit during Zanjeer's highest-volume week.

Ritika Bose, Data Scientist, Toronto. Ran the churn model on 1,100 truckers who had used Ehsaas's ninety-second payout in a closed test. Thirty-day churn fell from 11 percent to 6 percent — real, but on a sample too small to generalise to all forty corridors.

Devika Pillai, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Hears less demand from shippers for payout speed than for payout reliability: a missed settlement during a peak week, she warns, damages trucker trust more than a slow one ever would.

Vikram Oberoi, Head of Sales, New Jersey. Is closing two logistics contracts with U.S. 3PL firms that have asked, unprompted, whether Zanjeer offers "instant settlement" the way BlackBuck now advertises. He wants a company-wide announcement at the Mumbai summit, not a pilot in two corridors.

A fifth voice mattered without being in the room. DP World, the Dubai-headquartered ports major, used Zanjeer for the inland leg of export cargo moving to Mundra and Nhava Sheva. Its regional manager, Faisal Al Rashidi, had told Devika plainly: DP World did not care which payment rail Zanjeer used, only that truck availability on its two export corridors did not wobble during the pre-Diwali surge, when port cutoffs were unforgiving.

4. What the numbers showed

Exhibit 1. Current settlement vs. proposed instant payout, company-wide
MetricCurrent (NEFT, T+2)Proposed (Ehsaas instant)
Settlement time~44 hours~90 seconds
Working capital tied up in float₹38 crore₹61 crore
30-day trucker churn (pilot cohort)11%6%*
Loads needing manual GST reconciliation / week<20~600 (month 1 estimate)
Reversal cost once fully live—Not completable within one fiscal quarter, per auditors

*Based on a closed test of 1,100 truckers in three corridors; not yet observed at full scale.

Exhibit 1 was the number Kiran kept returning to: the reconciliation load scaled with volume, and volume was about to rise by up to 40 percent. Ritika's churn improvement was real but thin, drawn from three relatively simple corridors, not proof the gain would hold across forty corridors with more variable invoice patterns.

Exhibit 2. Trucker retention in the closed pilot, by corridor
CorridorTruckers in test30-day retention, before30-day retention, after instant payout
Delhi – Mumbai42087%93%
Delhi – JNPT (Mundra feeder)31084%91%
Chennai – Bengaluru37089%90%

Exhibit 2 mattered for a second reason: Delhi–JNPT was exactly the feeder route DP World depended on. If Zanjeer wanted evidence that mattered to its biggest single client relationship, it already had two months of it.

5. Three options

Option A — Announce and cut over company-wide before Diwali

Zanjeer migrates all 42,000 trucker ledgers to Ehsaas's instant-payout rail in one cutover, live before the Mumbai summit. Upside: it gives Oberoi the announcement his U.S. clients are asking for and removes BlackBuck's main talking point. Cost: it commits the entire settlement infrastructure to an unproven-at-scale system during the highest-volume week, with auditors confirming there is no practical way back once truckers have been paid through it even once.

Option B — Extend the pilot to the two corridors that matter most, keep it reversible

Zanjeer expands instant payout only on Delhi–Mumbai and Delhi–JNPT, the corridor DP World depends on, running old and new ledgers in parallel with a defined rollback procedure. Upside: it produces exactly the evidence Faisal Al Rashidi cares about and keeps Kiran's reconciliation risk bounded. Cost: a smaller story for Oberoi to sell, and BlackBuck may still claim the wider headline first.

Option C — Announce company-wide intent, but build the rollback in first

Zanjeer tells the summit that instant payout is coming network-wide, while engineering spends the twenty-six days building a parallel-ledger architecture and a tested kill switch, so a "company-wide" rollout can still be unwound corridor by corridor if the reconciliation spike proves unmanageable. Upside: it satisfies the announcement pressure without Option A's irreversibility. Cost: real engineering time Kiran has not budgeted, and it only works if the rollback is tested before go-live, not assumed.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of Zanjeer's three options is genuinely reversible, and which only looks reversible until tested under real reconciliation volume?
  2. What in Exhibits 1 through 3 should change how much rigour Ananya applies before a company-wide cutover — and what would she still need to know?
  3. How should Ananya weigh Oberoi's sales pressure and Faisal Al Rashidi's reliability requirement against Kiran's and Farhan's technical caution, given the same deadline binds all three?
  4. What evidence, by what date, would let a reversible pilot responsibly become a company-wide, effectively irreversible commitment?

7. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is reversibility, not speed. Jeff Bezos's distinction between Type 1 decisions (one-way doors, hard or impossible to reverse, deserving slow and deliberate judgement) and Type 2 decisions (two-way doors, cheaply reversed, best made fast) is not about how big a decision feels; it is about what happens if you are wrong. Zanjeer's board felt time pressure because the calendar said Diwali; the framework asks a different question — once even one settlement cycle moves onto the new ledger, can you get back to where you started? The auditors' answer was no. That single fact should govern how the decision is made, regardless of how compelling Oberoi's pipeline or Bose's churn numbers are.

A well-reasoned answer separates two things that got fused in the room: the business need (being seen to have instant payout) and the technical shape of the commitment (a one-time, unreversible ledger migration). They need not be the same decision. Option A borrows Type 2 speed for a Type 1 commitment. Option B keeps them separate but may under-deliver on this quarter's announcement. Option C is the more defensible path: it meets the summit deadline with a public commitment, while using the twenty-six days to turn what auditors called irreversible into something bounded by design — a parallel ledger and a tested kill switch, proven first on the Delhi–JNPT corridor DP World cares about, where two months of pilot evidence already exist. The broader lesson: many decisions labelled "one-way door" are irreversible only because no one has yet built a door back. Rigour here means spending some of the twenty-six days finding out which door Ananya is actually standing in front of, before deciding how fast to walk through it.

Hindola Commerce Network: The Door That Closed Behind Them

Jaipur, Rajasthan — Sunday, 15 March 2026, 11.40 p.m.

The last WhatsApp of the night came from a seller in Sanganer, and Devyani Rajawat read it three times. Madam, the new app is giving me orders directly from Coimbatore. Should I keep uploading on Hindola also, or only there? Rajawat, Senior Vice-President of Product at Hindola Commerce Network, had spent the weekend assembling a board pack that argued three different things on three different pages. On Thursday, 19 March, the board would ask her a question she had been avoiding since June: whether to put all 26,400 sellers onto the open network, keep the 900 already there, or pull them off. What kept her awake was a fourth possibility — that the decision had, quietly, already been made nine months ago by people who believed they were making a small one.

1. A catalogue, and the decision that built it

Hindola Commerce Network was founded in Jaipur in 2017 by Harsh Vardhan Kothari and two classmates from MNIT, to fix an unglamorous problem. India's small manufacturers — block-printers in Sanganer, saree units in Surat, knitwear units in Tiruppur, home-textile mills in Panipat — sold through commission agents who took between eleven and nineteen per cent before goods reached a retailer in Nagpur or Guwahati. Hindola put manufacturer and retailer on the same screen, with credit, logistics and returns handled centrally. In the year to 31 March 2026 it carried gross merchandise value of about ₹2,410 crore across 26,400 sellers and 81,000 active retail buyers, on net revenue of ₹96 crore and an EBITDA loss of ₹38 crore.

The decision that made Hindola work, and that now constrained everything, was taken in 2021. Choosing between letting sellers maintain their own catalogues and building one canonical catalogue owned by Hindola, Kothari chose the second. Every product got a Hindola SKU identifier; photography, attribute tagging and price-band placement were done in-house in Jaipur and Surat. Sellers liked it because it asked nothing of them; buyers liked it because a bedsheet from Panipat and one from Karur could finally be compared. Investors liked it most, because a seller who left took nothing with them: no catalogue, no images, no buyer history. Retention among sellers above ₹50 lakh of annual GMV had run at 94 per cent for four years.

The catalogue was, in other words, a wall, though nobody used that word in public. Internally the 2021 choice was "the SKU decision", and it was why Hindola could charge a blended take rate of 3.98 per cent where competitors could not.

2. The industry: an open network and a crowded middle

By 2026 the Indian B2B commerce middle was crowded and unstable. Udaan had narrowed to categories where it could hold inventory; Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner programme had pushed into kirana and staples but only lightly into textiles; Flipkart Wholesale and Amazon Business competed for the larger retailers; Meesho had trained lakhs of small retailers to expect near-zero commissions. Around all of them sat the Open Network for Digital Commerce, which unbundled commerce into seller-side applications, buyer-side applications and a shared protocol, so that a seller registered through one participant could receive orders from buyers on any other.

The policy logic was explicitly anti-lock-in. For a company whose moat was a proprietary catalogue, participation meant publishing structured product data — titles, attributes, prices, fulfilment promises — into a protocol where other buyer applications could see and address it. Regulatory weather sat on top: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed what retailer data could be shared and on what consent; the Reserve Bank of India capped first-loss cover in digital lending arrangements at five per cent of the portfolio; GST e-invoicing had caught most of Hindola's larger sellers.

Roughly nine per cent of FY26 GMV was export, of which the largest single relationship was Nawras Retail Trading LLC of Dubai, a home-furnishing chain across the UAE, Oman and Bahrain. Hindola also shipped to diaspora buyers in New Jersey and Chicago, and ran a buyer-success operation in Singapore covering the Gulf.

3. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In April 2025 the product leadership argued for two afternoons about network participation and reached what everyone thought was a sensible compromise. Yashodhan Bhave, VP Engineering in Pune, built an adapter translating Hindola SKUs into protocol-compliant catalogue objects, and 900 sellers in two categories — home furnishings, and unstitched ethnic fabric — were enrolled on 12 June 2025. Kothari described it in that month's board note as "a reversible experiment; we can withdraw the catalogue at any point". Nobody disagreed, and the minutes record no discussion of what withdrawal would involve.

Three things were believed in June 2025 that were no longer believed in March 2026.

The first was that network orders would be incremental. Rohan Chakravarti, Principal Data Scientist in Toronto, reported in September that 71 per cent of network GMV was genuinely new. By January his refreshed model put that at 44 per cent, the rest cannibalised from Hindola's own buyer app at a fifth of the take rate. He flagged, in a footnote nobody read aloud, that neither figure could be trusted much: the cohorts were not randomised, because Seller Operations had picked pilot sellers by "readiness".

The second was that the adapter was temporary scaffolding. It was not. Two contract engineers in Pune maintained a mapping table by hand each week for attributes the protocol schema had no slot for — thread count, weave, bandhani tie type. Bhave had estimated five months to build the real thing; Rajawat learned in February that roughly seventy per cent of it already existed, built without a budget line.

The third, and the one that changed the nature of the decision, was that sellers could simply be withdrawn. Technically they could: Hindola could stop publishing. But by March, 213 pilot sellers had been onboarded independently by other seller-side participants, using catalogue structure they had first seen through Hindola's own adapter, and fourteen had registered their own GSTIN-linked storefronts. The wall of 2021 had not been breached; a copy of its blueprint had been handed over the top of it, one weekly publish at a time.

4. The people

Devyani Rajawat, SVP Product, Jaipur. Owns the recommendation. Believes the June 2025 classification was the error and that the current options inherit it. Her incentive is a product organisation of 46 people whose roadmap is frozen until this is settled. What she is not saying: she approved the pilot note without asking what withdrawal would cost.

Harsh Vardhan Kothari, co-founder and CEO, Jaipur. Wants full participation, arguing the network is where the next five crore retailers will transact. His incentive is the second Series C tranche of ₹140 crore from Nauka Growth Partners, conditional on ₹500 crore of annualised network-originated GMV by 31 March 2027. What he is not saying: he negotiated that milestone definition himself, in September 2025, when the pilot was three months old.

Sujata Menon, Head of Seller Operations, Surat. Wants retreat; says pilot sellers are confused by two price lists and her field team absorbs the confusion. Her variable pay depends on cost-to-serve per seller. What she is not saying: her agents' retention bonus makes them poor instruments for measuring whether sellers are drifting.

Yashodhan Bhave, VP Engineering, Pune. Officially neutral, privately in favour of building the real adapter; estimates five months and 14 engineers. What he is not saying: much of it exists already, and if he admits that, five months becomes eight weeks and the decision leaves his hands.

Rohan Chakravarti, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Will not commit to a number; says any cannibalisation estimate from a non-randomised pilot is directional at best. His incentive is a reputation for not being wrong in board decks. What he is not saying: his attribution window is thirty days, and the pilot spanned both Diwali and the wedding restock.

Aarti Bhandari, CFO, Bengaluru. Focused on the credit book: ₹214 crore outstanding to 19,000 retailers, co-lent with Nishchay Credit Services against a five per cent default loss guarantee of ₹10.7 crore. Wants no decision that changes order flow, because underwriting is calibrated on Hindola's own buyer-app behaviour. What she is not saying: the ninety-day exit notice is one Nishchay can serve too.

Lena Fischbach, Design Director, Berlin. Argues that sellers cannot hold two mental models of price, and wants one surface. Her incentive is a design-system consolidation she has proposed twice. What she is not saying: her recommendation is identical under all three options.

Grace Tan Wei Ling, Director of Buyer Success, Singapore. Protects the Nawras Retail Trading relationship — ₹58 crore in FY26 under a three-year category exclusivity signed in February 2025 — and warns that network participation may breach it. What she is not saying: Nawras's sourcing head asked her in January whether the Panipat sellers could be reached directly.

Pradeep Kurup, Head of International Accounts, New Jersey. Wants the exclusivity untouched and the network deferred; his book is 4 per cent of GMV at a 9 per cent take rate. What he is not saying: two of his accounts have asked for network-native integration.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 is the pilot's performance; Exhibit 3 is Chakravarti's leakage model; Exhibit 4 is Seller Operations' field survey, run by agents whose bonuses depend on seller retention.

Exhibit 2. Pilot cohort performance, 900 sellers, June 2025 to February 2026
QuarterNetwork GMV (₹ cr)Marketplace GMV, same sellers (₹ cr)Blended net take rateContribution per order (₹)
Jul–Sep 2025311483.61%214
Oct–Dec 2025861393.02%161
Jan–Feb 202679962.48%118

Source: Hindola finance data warehouse, extracted 11 March 2026. Oct–Dec includes Diwali and the wedding restock; Jan–Feb is a two-month quarter and has not been annualised. Contribution per order excludes the cost of the two contract engineers maintaining the adapter.

Exhibit 3. Chakravarti leakage model, pilot sellers, February 2026
SignalPilot sellers (900)Matched control (900)
Receiving >30% of orders via non-Hindola buyer apps23%n/a
Onboarded by another seller-side participant21331
Own GSTIN-linked storefront registered146
Share of network GMV judged incremental44%—

Model run 27 February 2026 on a thirty-day attribution window. The control group was matched on category, GMV band and city, but not randomised: pilot sellers were selected by Seller Operations on "readiness". The September 2025 version of this model reported incrementality at 71 per cent.

Exhibit 4. Seller Operations field survey, 312 respondents, February 2026
QuestionYes
Have you received a direct enquiry from another platform since June?9%
Do you understand why you have two price lists?38%
Would you stay with Hindola if network orders stopped tomorrow?91%

Administered by 26 field agents across Jaipur, Surat and Panipat, in person, between 2 and 19 February 2026. Field agents are compensated in part on seller retention in their territory. 312 of 900 pilot sellers responded; non-response was not analysed.

Read naively, Exhibit 4 refutes Exhibit 3: nine per cent report an approach, against a model claiming twenty-three per cent already receive volume elsewhere. Read carefully, they measure different things by different instruments, and the ninety-one per cent loyalty figure is the least reliable number on the page — it asks a seller, face to face, whether he would leave the company whose agent is asking.

Exhibit 6. What it would cost to go back, three estimates
DoorEngineering (Bhave)Finance (Bhandari)External auditors
Withdraw 900 pilot sellers from the network3 weeks, ₹40 lakh₹4–11 crore of lost GMV, one quarterNot estimable; seller relationships already formed
Un-publish catalogue structure already distributedNot possibleNot quantifiedNot possible
Exit the Nishchay co-lending arrangement6 weeks integration₹10.7 crore guarantee crystallises; 90-day notice₹18–26 crore all-in, two quarters
Terminate Nawras category exclusivity early—₹58 crore revenue at riskContractual damages untested; legal opinion split
Onboard all 26,400 sellers, then reverseNot estimatedNot estimatedNot estimated

Compiled by the office of the CFO, 13 March 2026, from three separate submissions that were not reconciled. The final row was requested on 9 March and returned blank by all three parties.

Exhibit 6 is the one Rajawat kept returning to, less for what it contains than for what it does not. Three of the five doors carry no number at all, and the one that matters most — the cost of reversing a full rollout — is blank because nobody could construct the counterfactual. It also quietly reframes the question: two of its five rows have nothing to do with the network.

6. Voices

"We are not deciding whether to join a network. We joined nine months ago. We are deciding whether to keep pretending we can leave."

— Devyani Rajawat, product leadership review, Jaipur, 6 March 2026

"Devyani, with respect, this is a reversible experiment. The whole point of the June structure was that we could stop. If we now say we cannot stop, then what were we telling the board in June?"

— Harsh Vardhan Kothari, same meeting

"Directionally, network orders look dilutive. I will not sign a number. The cohorts were not randomised and I have said this since September. If the deck says 44 per cent, please put my footnote next to it in the same font size."

— Rohan Chakravarti, Slack thread #ondc-decision, 9 March, 02.14 IST (21.14 Toronto, 8 March)

"Two price lists. Every single visit, forty minutes explaining two price lists. My agents in Surat are now telling sellers to ignore the network price. I did not authorise that and I am not going to stop it."

— Sujata Menon, seller-ops weekly, 10 March

"The design question is the same whichever way you go: one price, one surface, one promise. What I cannot design is a company that has not decided what it is."

— Lena Fischbach, email to Rajawat, 11 March, 19.02 CET

"Their sourcing head asked, casually, whether he could deal with the Panipat units directly. I said that was not how we worked. He said the network made it how everyone worked now. I would not put this in the board pack as a risk. I would put it as the position."

— Grace Tan Wei Ling, call notes, 14 January

"Whatever you decide, decide before the 31st. I can absorb a change in order mix. I cannot absorb a change in order mix during a quarter in which Nishchay is entitled to give us ninety days' notice."

— Aarti Bhandari, note to the CEO and SVP Product, 12 March

7. The options as Rajawat sees them

Option A — Full participation

Onboard all 26,400 sellers by 30 June, fund the real adapter, and accept a structural fall in take rate in exchange for reach and the Series C milestone. Kothari's position. The bet is that Hindola's advantage shifts from catalogue ownership to credit, logistics and quality. It also makes every later question — pricing, underwriting, Nawras — one asked inside a world Hindola no longer controls.

Option B — Hold at 900

Seek a renewal of the pilot exemption, keep the cohort where it is, revisit in FY27 with better data. This feels cautious and may not be: the adapter is two contractors and a spreadsheet, the exemption is not in Hindola's gift to renew, and another year lets other participants finish onboarding the 900.

Option C — Withdraw

Stop publishing, re-close the catalogue, defend the 3.98 per cent take rate, forfeit the tranche and re-plan around ₹126 crore of cash. Menon's position. Exhibit 6 prices the mechanics at three weeks and ₹40 lakh, but does not price the 213 sellers already onboarded elsewhere, and cannot price the structure already distributed.

Rajawat had written all three on a whiteboard on Friday and then stood looking at them with the feeling that she had drawn the wrong diagram. All three were about the network; two of the five rows in Exhibit 6 were not. The ₹10.7 crore guarantee and the Nawras exclusivity were commitments Hindola had walked into without ever calling them decisions, and both were harder to undo than anything on the whiteboard. It was possible, she thought, that the network question was the loudest rather than the biggest, and that the discipline the board needed was not about this door at all.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board met on Thursday, 19 March. Hindola's pilot exemption from full network-participation obligations lapsed on 31 March 2026; after that the company would either commit to the participation agreement in its standard form or stop publishing. Cash stood at ₹126 crore against a burn of ₹9.4 crore a month, thirteen months without the second tranche. That tranche of ₹140 crore required ₹500 crore of annualised network-originated GMV by 31 March 2027 — achievable under Option A, arithmetically impossible under Option C, and, on the Jan–Feb run rate in Exhibit 2, uncertain under Option B.

There was a hiring freeze: Bhave had 34 engineers and no approved additions. The Nawras agreement ran to February 2028, its category exclusivity drafted before the pilot and silent on network channels; two law firms had given opposite readings. The Nishchay co-lending agreement allowed either party ninety days' notice, and the default loss guarantee sat at the regulatory ceiling of five per cent. Under the DPDP Act, sharing retailer-level behavioural data with buyer-side participants required consent Hindola had not collected, which meant Bhandari's underwriting models would degrade for every order arriving through the network rather than through Hindola's own app — a fact in no exhibit, because nobody had been asked to quantify it.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the five doors in Exhibit 6 are genuinely reversible, and on what evidence? Where does Hindola's own data run out?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 disagree. What would you need to know about how each was produced before you allowed either into a board pack, and which would you trust more on Monday morning?
  3. In June 2025 the pilot was minuted as "a reversible experiment". What specific test, applied at that meeting, would have shown otherwise — and would it have been reasonable to expect anyone to apply it then?
  4. Option B appears to preserve optionality. Under what conditions is standing still in a doorway more irreversible than walking through it?
  5. Kothari negotiated the tranche milestone that now makes Option C unaffordable. How should Rajawat treat a constraint created by a stakeholder who is also advocating one of the options? Does the answer change if the milestone is commercially sensible on its own merits?
  6. It is Monday, 16 March. Rajawat has three days. What does she do first, what does she refuse to decide this week, and what exactly does she say to the board on Thursday — including about the decision the board itself approved in June?

10. Sunday night

At a quarter past midnight Rajawat opened the June 2025 board note again. Two pages. The phrase sat in the second paragraph, unhedged: a reversible experiment. Beside it in the margin was her own comment from that week, forgotten, now reading like something addressed to her from a distance. Reversible how? Ask Yash for the unwind plan. There was no reply thread. She had never asked.

Outside, the last Holi hoardings were still up on Tonk Road, and a truck was loading behind the block-printing units. She typed a reply to the seller in Sanganer, deleted it, typed it again. Thursday was in four days; the exemption lapsed in sixteen. She did not know which of the three boxes she would circle, or whether she would tell the board that all three were the wrong shape.
