Case study · Prioritisation & Decision-Making

Ikhtiyaar Wealth Systems: What the Register Says

ISB Product Management Programme · Delivery & Technology module

1. Sunday night, Powai

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 6 September 2026, Shreya Nambiar could still hear the drums. A visarjan procession was working down the lake road in Powai, Mumbai, and the sound came through the window of the flat where three printouts lay across the dining table. In nine hours she would walk into Ikhtiyaar Wealth Systems' leadership review and say what the company would build between October and March.

The printouts disagreed. The first was the top of the Register, Ikhtiyaar's open record of customer requests: 1,730 live items, scored, ranked and visible to every employee and most clients. The second was a deduplication audit Rhea Fernandes had run from Toronto on Friday, unasked, collapsing those items into 402 asks from 168 firms and reordering the list almost completely. The third was Arvind Kelkar's capacity ledger from Pune: 110 squad-weeks available, 186 spoken for.

Shreya had joined eighteen months earlier to make the roadmap defensible. The Register was the instrument she had inherited and improved, and tonight she was no longer sure what it measured. At 9:30 on Monday she had a call with the chief operating officer of Uthaan Capital Advisors, the largest client, who wanted to know which of his three asks had made the cut. Two, under a contract signed before she arrived, he was arguably entitled to.

2. The company, and one decision made in 2021

Ikhtiyaar Wealth Systems was founded in 2016 in Mumbai by Kabir Anand, formerly operations head at a mutual-fund transfer agency, and two engineers. Its customers were not investors but the firms that served them: mutual-fund distributors, registered investment advisers, wealth boutiques, the advisory arms of regional brokers. It gave them a white-labelled investor app, order routing to BSE StAR MF and NSE NMF II, reconciliation against CAMS and KFintech feeds, commission computation and consolidated reporting.

By September 2026 the platform carried ₹1.94 lakh crore for 2.1 million investor accounts across 310 client firms, on an ARR of ₹64 crore. Of 470 employees, 96 were engineers, in five product squads and one platform squad across Pune and Bengaluru. Upavan Growth Partners had led a ₹310 crore Series C in 2024 and held two board seats.

The decision that shaped everything Shreya could do in 2026 was made in late 2021, when Ikhtiyaar was losing mid-sized deals to faster rivals. Rather than keep refusing client-specific behaviour, engineering built the Rachna layer: a sandboxed scripting tier in which a solutions engineer could change a tenant's commission logic, statement template or approval chain without touching the core product. Sales closed the deals, and the phrase "we can script that" entered the company's vocabulary and never left.

Five years on there were 612 live scripts across 190 tenants, nothing deprecated since 2023, and every release regression-tested against a thicket of tenant-specific behaviour. More subtly, the layer had changed what a "no" meant: a product manager who declined a request was not declining the work, only declining it on the roadmap, after which the account team would ask whether it could simply be scripted. It usually could.

3. The industry

India's retail investing base had grown faster than anyone at Ikhtiyaar modelled in 2016. Direct-to-investor platforms — Groww, Zerodha's Coin, Paytm Money, Kuvera, INDmoney — had taken the self-directed customer and raised what every advised investor expected an app to look like. Ikhtiyaar's clients competed against interfaces they could not build themselves — the company's opportunity, and the source of a stream of requests whose real content was "make us look like Groww".

Regulation set the tempo. SEBI's tightening of nomination and re-KYC norms, AMFI's data standards, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the demands of MF Central meant a material share of the engineering year was neither negotiable nor requested by anybody. No client had ever filed a Register item asking for a compliant consent artefact.

Competition came from two directions: larger vendors selling scale at the top of the market, and, from Hyderabad, Ibtida Platform Technologies selling to the mid-market at forty per cent of Ikhtiyaar's price, with client-specific development as a headline feature rather than an exception. Sales lost four deals to Ibtida in the June quarter, each debrief citing responsiveness to requests.

The exposure was not only domestic. About nine per cent of ARR came from firms serving non-resident Indians in Dubai, Singapore and New Jersey, shaped by the DIFC and by the tax reporting their clients faced abroad. Inayat Family Advisors DMCC, a Dubai practice with ₹1.1 crore of ARR, had anchored that segment since March, and Vikram Sahni had promised in July that multi-currency reporting would be live in November.

4. How the half came to be over-committed

The Register had been built in January 2024 in answer to a complaint Kabir heard repeatedly: that Ikhtiyaar listened well and remembered badly. Any employee could file against an account; clients with a customer-success manager could file through a portal; every item carried a requester, an age, an ARR tag and a score from reach, impact, confidence and effort. Shreya's first all-hands slide had said it: an honest backlog is a competitive advantage.

Through 2025 it did what it promised. Then three things happened, each reasonable alone.

In April 2026, at Vikram's request, the deal desk began filing items during live sales cycles, tagged with the opportunity's pipeline value; prospects' needs are evidence too. The effect was that ARR attached to a theme began to include revenue that did not exist — by September, ₹41 crore of it — and nothing in the interface said so.

In June, customer success required a CSM to log an item for every substantive ask in a quarterly business review, which stopped asks dying in meeting notes. It also meant one conversation in which an adviser mentioned five irritations produced five items, and a need raised by thirty accounts appeared as thirty, each in the CSM's own words.

In July the Customer Advisory Council — twelve clients, convened twice a year — was given a fast lane: its asks entered pre-scored at a confidence nobody else could earn, because members had been vetted as representative. Nobody revisited whether they were. The twelve were the twelve largest accounts by ARR.

By late August the top ten themes came to 186 squad-weeks against discretionary capacity of 36. Shreya began cutting from the bottom, which is when Rhea's audit made the exercise incoherent: three of the top five themes were one problem filed in five vocabularies, and the largest by unique firms — failed mandates — ranked seventh because each firm had filed once and moved on.

There was one more discovery she had told nobody. Ushakaal Investment Services in Nashik, paying ₹2.4 lakh a year, had not renewed in July; nor had ten other firms in the same band. None had ever filed a Register item, and none had a CSM — the portal was licensed per seat and their plan excluded it. Their exit surveys said the app felt slow on older Android phones.

5. The people

Shreya Nambiar — Director of Product, Mumbai
Owns the Register and the roadmap. Position: the backlog must be re-derived from problems, not requests. Not saying: she suspects her own dashboard has misled the board for two quarters, and she approved the Council fast lane without argument.
Kabir Anand — Founder and CEO, Mumbai
Position: publish on time, whatever it contains; slipping twice is worse than being wrong once. Incentive: a Series D conversation begins in January. Not saying: he has promised Upavan a margin improvement, hard while the Rachna layer eats platform engineering.
Vikram Sahni — Chief Revenue Officer, New Jersey
Position: the company loses deals on responsiveness, so the roadmap should follow revenue, realised and pipeline alike. Not saying: the Dubai date was given without an engineering estimate, and two of the four deals lost to Ibtida went on price.
Prerna Bhatt — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Position: requests logged for clients are the only systematic listening channel. Not saying: her service standard produced much of the duplication, and her team covers nothing below ₹5 lakh ARR.
Arvind Kelkar — Vice-President of Engineering, Pune
Position: capacity binds, and something must be cut publicly rather than quietly. Incentive: attrition in a squad that has done maintenance for three quarters. Not saying: his estimates carry no confidence intervals, and the regulatory number predates the annexure.
Rhea Fernandes — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: the scores are not comparable across items and should not rank anything. Incentive: she built the model and dislikes seeing it quoted as truth. Not saying: her threshold was chosen by eye, and others yield 340 or 480 asks.
Jonas Brandt — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: the top themes describe solutions, not problems, and nobody has spoken to an end investor in fourteen months. Incentive: a discovery budget. Not saying: his own sample was eleven advisers, all introduced by customer success, all from large firms.
Suhail Rehman — Product Manager, Regulatory, Mumbai
Position: compliance work is immovable and should leave the table before prioritisation begins. Not saying: about a third of his 31 squad-weeks is undisclosed contingency, and part could be phased past January.

Exhibits 1 and 2 cannot both rank the half, and Shreya had not worked out which she believed. Exhibit 2 is more careful about double counting and less careful about everything else: two evenings, one person, a threshold chosen by eye, pipeline discarded.

7. Voices

"I am not asking product to take orders from sales. I am asking that when a chart says ₹34 crore is waiting on rebalancing, somebody treats it as information. If we publish a half without it, I explain that to Dubai."

— Vikram Sahni, revenue review, 1 September

"Read the annexure before Monday. Clause 7.2 gives them two roadmap slots a year and a forty-five-day right of review. It does not define a slot. Legal has never tested it; we have simply always given them two features."

— Kabir Anand, message, 4 September, 22:41

"Rebalancing is the word my clients use because it is the word in a competitor's brochure. What they actually say is that they cannot show a family what changed since last Diwali without exporting to Excel. Whether that is rebalancing or reporting, I cannot tell you."

— Customer-success call notes, Tier A client, 28 August

"Please stop quoting the score. It was built to sort forty items filed by one team in one format. It now ranks a thousand filed by four teams with different meanings of impact, half carrying a confidence I did not choose. The ordering is arithmetic, not evidence."

— Rhea Fernandes, comment on the Register dashboard, 5 September

"Eighty-eight firms is my whole renewal book for Q3. I have been telling those accounts it is on the list. It is on the list. It is on the list at number seven."

— Prerna Bhatt, Singapore, weekly product-CS sync

"We are not renewing. The app takes eleven seconds to open a client portfolio on the handsets my team carries. I told your support desk in November. I do not know who else to tell."

— Non-renewal email, Ushakaal Investment Services, 14 July

8. The options as Shreya sees them

By Sunday night she had four options on the back of the capacity ledger.

A. Publish from the Register as it stands

Take the top themes by score, fund what fits in 36 squad-weeks, ship. Fast, defensible as process, faithful to a system clients were told would be used. It also sets the half by the twelve largest accounts and by pipeline that may not close, and leaves mandate failures another six months.

B. Freeze and reset

Close intake for six weeks, re-file every item as a problem with a named user and an observed consequence, re-score on realised ARR, publish in late October. Shreya believes this yields the only honest ranking available. Kabir says a second slip looks like drift; Vikram says six weeks of silence falls inside the Q3 deal cycle.

C. Ring-fence the lanes

Split capacity by rule rather than score: 25 per cent contractual, 50 per cent platform, 25 per cent discovery, published as policy. It survives contact with Uthaan and gives Arvind something to plan against, but decides nothing about any individual request, and the platform half must still be filled from a backlog nobody trusts.

D. Price the door

Charge for customisation: a rate card for Rachna scripts and bespoke builds, the revenue funding a services squad. Finance likes it. It filters requests by willingness to pay, a real signal; it also guarantees that the firms who can pay set the product, and Exhibit 3 suggests those are not the firms driving growth.

Each option treats the Register as the thing to be fixed. None addresses that nobody has spoken to a Tier C or D adviser this year, that the eleven lapsed contracts were never entered as evidence anywhere, or that one need has been described in five vocabularies by four teams without anyone writing down what the need is. Shreya had noticed this around ten o'clock, and had not worked out what a fifth option would be.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The leadership review is at nine on Monday, after the Uthaan call; the roadmap goes to the board on 18 September and to clients on 1 October. The regulatory work must be live before 1 January 2027, though Suhail's 31 squad-weeks hides a contingency. Uthaan's annexure runs to 31 March 2027 with two slots and a forty-five-day review right whose meaning has never been tested; the account is ₹6.2 crore, 9.7 per cent of ARR. The November commitment to Inayat is verbal. Headcount is frozen until the Series D. The Rachna layer cannot be switched off without renegotiating 190 tenant configurations. And the festival calendar takes two weeks out of October and November whatever anybody decides.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Taking Exhibit 1 at face value, what would Ikhtiyaar build? What does that exhibit measure, and what does it not?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 rank the same evidence in nearly opposite orders. What would you need to know to choose between them, and could you get it before Monday?
  3. For any theme in Exhibit 1, write the problem it might be evidence of. How many distinct problems could produce that request, and how would you tell them apart?
  4. Exhibit 3 shows that the firms who file most are not the firms who grow most. Is that a finding about customers or about Ikhtiyaar's intake channels — and what would change if it were the latter?
  5. The Rachna layer made saying yes cheap. Trace its consequences through Exhibits 4 and 5. What does it now cost Ikhtiyaar to say no, and who pays that cost?
  6. What should Shreya do on Monday — in the Uthaan call and in the leadership review — and what would she tell the board on 18 September about how Ikhtiyaar decides what to build, knowing the Register she championed is the instrument in question?

11. After midnight

The drums stopped somewhere past one. Shreya laid Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 side by side and looked at the two orderings the way one looks at two witnesses who cannot both be telling the truth and who both seem sincere. Rhea was awake in Toronto, offering to re-run the clustering at a second threshold: four hours, possibly a third ordering. Prerna had sent, at 00:50 Singapore time, the list of eighty-eight firms behind the mandate failures, noting that she had promised nineteen of them a date.

Somewhere in the Register was a line filed in November by a distributor in Nashik who no longer paid Ikhtiyaar anything, about an app that took eleven seconds to open. It had a score of nine.

She opened a blank document, typed H2 FY27 — what we will build and why, and sat looking at it. At 9:30 the phone would ring from Uthaan.
exp40v2-prio.customer.requests:
Delivery & Technology · Prioritisation & Decision-Making · Exp40

Pricing the commitment: feature requests from customers and sales

A request arrives mispriced twice — once in the population it is assumed to represent, once in what saying yes actually costs. Translating a request into a problem repairs only the first error.

1. Two decisions, one October

On 14 October 2025, Meera Rajagopalan, vice-president of product at Hastakala Craft Exchange in Bengaluru, had 214 open buyer-side requests and one demand with a date on it. Hastakala was a two-sided marketplace: 9,400 artisan workshops across Jaipur, Moradabad and Channapatna on one side, 1,180 retail buyers on the other, the largest of them Hasti Lifestyle Stores, a 74-store home-decor chain. Devansh Chitale, who ran key accounts from Mumbai, put it plainly: Hasti wanted three-level purchase-order approval — buyer, category manager, finance — committed in the renewal order form before December. The renewal was worth ₹18 lakh of take-rate revenue in year one, ₹54 lakh over three. Her engineers could build Hasti's exact chain in three weeks, which was precisely what worried her.

Eleven days later, Aniruddh Barve, director of product at Hriday Cardiac Systems in Pune, faced a smaller-looking request. Hriday made a 72-hour ambulatory ECG patch, sold with a portal in which cardiologists reviewed traces and issued signed reports. Hitakari Hospitals Group, eleven hospitals headquartered in Nagpur, was its second-largest account at ₹1.9 crore, renewing in March; its clinical director wanted the physician's signature applied to reports automatically rather than uploaded by hand. Jaspreet Sahni, the field sales head in Delhi, called it a two-day job. It was not. The reporting module was regulated software inside the device's CDSCO licence, and any change entered a fourteen-week verification cycle, of which Hriday ran four a year carrying nine changes each. The currency was not engineer-days but one-ninth of a release slot — thirty-six places a year against 340 open requests.

Both requests were reasonable, both carried revenue, and in both the standard advice — translate the request into a problem first — was necessary and nowhere near sufficient.

2. The idea, and who disagrees

Define it precisely. A feature request is a proposition of the form: a named party believes a named change to the product would relieve a pain they are experiencing, and wants something from you in response. Three objects are fused there: the ask, the pain as the requester diagnosed it, and the commitment sought — acknowledgement, a date, a contractual clause, or merely the feeling of having been heard. Handling requests well means separating the three, estimating the population that shares the pain, pricing the commitment, and returning a decision with its reasoning.

The intellectual history runs on two rails that met in the 2010s. The first studies why customers describe wants badly: Christensen and Moesta's jobs-to-be-done research established that customers hire products to make progress and borrow their vocabulary for it from solutions they already know, while Kano's 1984 classification showed that satisfaction is not linear in features. The second rail is industrial: as subscription revenue turned the roadmap into a commercial instrument, Des Traynor and Marty Cagan named the pathology of the team that builds exactly what was asked and watches adoption sit at four percent. Donald Reinertsen supplied the rest of the vocabulary: cost of delay, batch size, and the observation that an expedite lane without reserved capacity destroys the throughput behind it.

Four schools disagree about what follows, sharply enough to state as propositions each would and would not sign.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Translation
jobs-to-be-done		"The literal ask is evidence, not a specification.""A customer's ask should be built as stated because they are paying."
Revenue integration
sales-led enterprise		"A request attached to a renewal is priced evidence of willingness to pay.""The largest deal of the quarter should set the order of the roadmap."
Queueing
Reinertsen, WSJF		"Reserve bounded capacity for expedites; never reorder the queue to absorb them.""Every inbound request deserves to be scored."
Empirical aggregation
telemetry, Kano		"Who files is a biased sample; prevalence must be measured, not counted.""Requester interviews reveal the job reliably enough to build on."

The argument here cuts across all four. A request's population is misestimated by an unknown factor, because articulating a request is a behaviour correlated with account size rather than with pain. Its cost is almost always understated, because the visible price is the build while the real price is the commitment: opportunity cost, fork maintenance, precedent for the next three requesters, and contractual exposure once a date reaches an order form. Translation repairs the first error; only pricing the commitment repairs the second, and that is the move most teaching omits.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Take the population problem first. Of Meera's 214 buyer-side requests, 46 touched approvals or purchase orders: 46 of 1,180 accounts, under four percent, which is what her last roadmap review had concluded. Farhan Qureshi, Hastakala's analyst in Hyderabad, looked instead for a telemetry signature of the pain rather than a report of it. In a sample of 80 buyer accounts he counted orders created, cancelled within 48 hours and re-raised at similar value — the fingerprint of an order taken off-platform through an approval chain by email. Thirty-seven showed the pattern twice or more; only 12 of them had ever filed a ticket.

That ratio — 12 of 37, or 32 percent — is the articulation rate for this problem in this book of business, and it converts complaints into prevalence. Forward: 46 percent of sampled buyers show the pattern, implying roughly 546 affected accounts against 46 who spoke. Backward: 46 tickets divided by 0.32 imply about 144. The gap between 144 and 546 is itself the finding; an expert reports the range, not the flattering end. The measurement also changes who files: once Meera published cluster prevalence, sellers' managers in Jaipur began naming populations rather than accounts.

Figure 1. Payout reconciliation drew 112 tickets and affects roughly 196 accounts; the GST credit-note flow drew 19 and affects roughly 316. Ranked by tickets the four go 112, 87, 46, 19; by prevalence the order nearly inverts.

The second half of the mechanics prices the commitment. Meera built a cost-of-delay table — value lost per month of not having the thing, combining recoverable leakage, probability-weighted deal movement and support cost — divided by job size.

CandidateCost of delay (₹ lakh/month)Size (eng-weeks)WSJF
A. Hasti's three-level chain, as configuration for one account4.031.33
B. Generalised approval framework: roles, thresholds, delegation9.8110.89
C. Seller payout reconciliation ledger6.041.50
D. ONDC catalogue synchronisation3.280.40

Read literally the table says C, then A, then B, then D: the generalised framework, which the translation school would call the real problem, ranks third. Experts notice two facts it cannot express. First, A is a prefix of B: those three weeks build the approval state machine B needs, so A-then-B costs 3 + 9 = 12 weeks rather than 3 + 11 = 14, while A alone leaves a hard-coded chain to unwind later. No common scoring model represents shared substrate. Second, A's ₹4.0 lakh per month is not a property of the problem but of a commitment Devansh has not yet made.

So Meera priced the commitment instead of the feature. Devansh's estimate was that a written date raised the renewal's close probability from 0.55 to 0.85; on ₹54 lakh of three-year take that increment is worth 0.30 × ₹54 lakh = ₹16.2 lakh. Against it: three weeks pulled forward displace C by three-quarters of a month, costing ₹4.5 lakh; a single-account chain carries maintenance Hastakala's history put at half an engineer-week per quarter for twelve quarters, ₹9 lakh fully loaded; and the clause creates a liability that cannot be renegotiated if the framework slips. Net: ₹2.7 lakh before any allowance for precedent — noise on a ₹30 crore base, which is what let her stop arguing about legitimacy and design a third option.

4. The conditions, stated as claims

Claim one: the requester's diagnosis is less reliable than yours. True at Hastakala, where Hasti's procurement head knew their own approval matrix but could not see 546 other buyers routing orders off-platform. False at Hriday: Hitakari's clinical director knew the accreditation requirement for attributable authorship far better than Aniruddh did. Where the customer holds domain authority you lack, reframing is a tax on their expertise.

Claim two: the marginal cost of yes is dominated by the build. True at Hastakala, shipping weekly with engineer-weeks as the constraint; emphatically false at Hriday, where a two-day change consumed the same validated slot as a two-month one. Where the constraint is a batch rather than a rate, small requests are not cheap.

Claim three: the population sharing the pain exceeds the population reporting it. Usually true, occasionally inverted. Hastakala's catalogue tools had no silent majority left to find, and at Hriday the direction reversed: 340 requests came from 27 accounts, and one cardiologist filing eleven tickets can make a single workflow look like a market.

Claim four: the decision is reversible. Broadly true of a configuration flag, false of a contractual date, false of a regulated change that once notified becomes part of a device's documented intended use. This claim's failure is why the fourth column of an honest request register is not priority but reversibility.

Where the idea actively misleads deserves naming. Below about forty customers, prevalence estimation is theatre: the sample is the market. In a commoditised category where the buyer compares feature lists in a tender, the problem is the checklist. And when a request restates a mandate from the Reserve Bank of India or GSTN, there is nothing to translate — only a date.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided businesses break the arithmetic because the population that benefits and the one that pays differ. Hastakala's approval framework, holding orders pending for a median 2.3 days, would push sellers' days-to-payment from 21 to 29 — workshops of four to twelve people for whom that was material. The reframed statement could not be "buyers cannot approve orders"; it had to be "orders needing internal approval leave the platform, and no fix may lengthen seller cash cycles". Releasing payment terms on submission rather than approval added two engineer-weeks and won over the seller-side product manager, who held a veto.

Multi-product companies fail at the seam. When a request spans two lines with separate profit-and-loss statements the honest owner is neither, and the symptom is a ticket bouncing between backlogs for months while both teams behave rationally. Mature companies name one owner for cross-line problems and give that person a budget: an organisational answer to a process-looking question.

Hardware changes the unit of the answer. Several Hriday accounts wanted seven-day recording, which is not a software request at all: it implies a battery change, a bill-of-materials revision, the next hardware generation eleven months out. The competent answer is "not on the roadmap"; the expert answer is a date in hardware cycles.

AI-native products invert the grammar. Hastakala's automated product-description generator drew 340 tickets in six weeks, nearly all of the form "it got this wrong". Those are defect reports about a probabilistic system; the correct translation is into evaluation cases, not backlog items. Farhan clustered them into twelve failure classes, nine of which a retrieval change and a threshold addressed without any feature. Two of the rest asked for determinism, which the system could supply only by caching away the freshness the feature existed to provide.

The deepest seam lies between what companies say about sales commitments and what they do. The stated position is that sales does not commit to dates; the practice in most mature enterprise companies is a commitment budget — a declared ten to twenty percent of capacity the commercial organisation may spend, with a ledger of where it went. Hriday's version was starker: one of nine change slots per validated release was permanently sales-allocated, and Jaspreet had to choose. Making the scarcity explicit improved his requests more than three years of asking him to stop making them.

6. What separates an expert

The expert counts the silent, not the loud. Their first question is never "how many asked for this" but "how many have this and did not ask". Ticket volume looks like demand but is not, because filing is a behaviour correlated with account size and with the requester's confidence that complaining works. A count of requests older than eighteen months with no decision tells you how long ago the channel stopped working.

The expert prices the commitment, not the feature. Watch for "what does the customer need to hear, from whom, by when?" asked before any estimate. Often they need not a date but a named owner, written acknowledgement that the problem is real, and a workaround for the quarter — the cheapest option on the menu, and the one a build-or-not framing discards.

The expert treats cheap requests as the dangerous ones. The sign is suspicion of a two-day ask and calm about a ten-week one. Small asks bypass the decision process because they are small, accumulate as per-account configuration nobody owns, and become the reason a migration is impossible four years later.

The expert knows a reframe is a claim that can be false. They state it back to the requester and abandon it when the customer's version survives contact. The obvious reading — the customer proposed a solution, so the solution is wrong — assumes your model of their world beats theirs. In regulated, accounting and procurement domains it usually does not.

The expert keeps provenance and prevalence in separate columns. Folding deal value into a reach score destroys information: one account worth ₹2 crore tells you about willingness to pay, a pattern across 300 accounts about market need. Price the first; build the second.

The expert asks who consumes the output, not who filed. The tell is a required intake field naming whoever receives what the feature produces. Requesters often file for a manager, an auditor or a regulator, and a reframe built on interviewing the requester alone solves the wrong person's job while sounding rigorous.

The expert prices precedent before the first yes. The question is "if I do this for Hasti, what do I say to the next three?", asked before the decision rather than after. The second identical request costs more to decline than the first, because the answer is no longer "no" but "no, unlike them", which reads as favouritism.

The expert looks for prefixes before scoring. The sign is a shared-substrate line drawn before any arithmetic: which candidate is a strict subset of which. Scoring models rank items as if independent, and sequencing swamps the score differences teams argue over for weeks.

7. How it varies by product type and stage

The variation that matters most is not consumer versus enterprise but whether requests arrive with an owner attached. In consumer they do not: volume is high, provenance thin, and the discipline collapses into aggregation and Kano-style classification, where articulation rates are low but stable enough to reuse. In B2B and enterprise every request has a person whose quarter depends on it, and the problem shifts from estimation to governance. Platforms and marketplaces add the externality above: a problem statement lacking a named side is not yet a problem statement. AI products change the type of the object, and a team that routes evaluation material into a feature backlog builds features to paper over model behaviour.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. Below roughly forty customers a single design partner may legitimately set the roadmap, and the failure mode is mistaking one customer for a market. From forty to a few hundred, articulation rates become estimable and the first fork decisions arrive. Above that the constraint is governance, not judgement: the arithmetic is not hard, but making three hundred people apply it consistently is.

8. Three worked examples

Aggregation done well. Haritima Agri Networks, an input-distribution platform in Indore, logged 61 dealer requests over two seasons for a higher credit limit; granted literally that meant ₹7.4 crore of exposure. The reframe came from asking what dealers did when a limit was exhausted: they stopped ordering for a median nine days until collections cleared, and 38 percent of those pauses ended with an order through a competing distributor. The problem was the float, not the limit. Haritima built an insurer-backed 72-hour bridge limit capped at ₹40,000 per dealer: five engineer-weeks, ₹94 lakh of exposure, ₹2.9 crore of recovered order value in a kharif season.

Declining well. Hiranya Metals Exchange had accumulated 34 bespoke extract scripts over four years, and three of its four largest customers now wanted custom export formats. Rather than add a fourth, the team declined all three in the same week with the same written reason and shipped a field-mapping layer in three weeks that let customers define formats themselves. All three migrated, and 34 scripts retired, freeing 11 engineer-weeks a year. The instructive detail is that declining three requests at once was easier than declining one, because no account could read the decision as being about them.

Where it failed. Hetu Analytics Cloud in Gurugram held 38 requests for scheduled email reports. Rajeev Bhandarkar, head of product, ran a textbook reframe: nine interviews converged on "I don't want to log in just to check three numbers", and the team built an in-app digest and a chat integration in nine engineer-weeks. Adoption reached four percent. The reframe had interviewed the wrong population. The requesters were analysts; the consumers were their vice-presidents, who needed a PDF in an inbox on Monday because that was what got forwarded into a business review, and no digest can be forwarded into a review deck. Two accounts worth ₹66 lakh churned citing reporting. Recovery took two moves: the literal feature shipped in three weeks and reached 41 percent of accounts in a quarter, and intake gained a required field — "who receives the output of this?" — plus a rule that every reframe is read back to the requester.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Reframing theatreProblem statements written in triage, never read back to a customerFor the last five shipped items, who validated the reframe?Nine wasted weeks plus ₹66 lakh of churn
Roadmap as deal collateralDates in signed order forms product never reviewedHow many of the last eight contracts contain a deliverable commitment?A queue that cannot be reordered
Fork accumulationRelease notes that mention account namesHow many configuration flags serve exactly one customer?Migrations that become undoable; support cost that never falls
Silent backlogRising median age of undecided requestsHow many open requests are older than eighteen months with no decision?Sales stops filing and promises directly
Expedite as the only modeEvery sprint contains an unplanned interruptWhat share of last quarter's shipped work entered the quarter unplanned?Above 40 percent there is no queue at all
Articulation blindnessThe roadmap tracks the top ten accounts' ticket listDoes telemetry prevalence rank known problems as tickets do?A roadmap fitted to your loudest decile

Each diagnostic can be answered in an afternoon from data the company already holds, which is why the mature move is a standing quarterly review. Four of the six are governance failures, not judgement failures.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is deal attachment information or noise? Revenue integration, steelmanned: willingness to pay is the scarcest signal an enterprise company can obtain, and a request backed by a renewal is the only one tested against a budget holder's alternatives. Translation, steelmanned: deal attachment measures which customer has a procurement cycle this quarter, and honouring it yields a product shaped like the last four large deals, which is the shape that loses the next forty. For the first position to be wrong, requests from deal-attached accounts would have to predict adoption no better than requests from silent ones — a comparison straightforward to run that almost nobody runs.

Should a commitment budget exist? Against: naming a fraction of capacity that sales may spend converts an exception into an entitlement and guarantees it is spent every quarter regardless of merit. For: the promises are being made anyway, and an undeclared flow is larger and less visible than a budgeted one. Neither camp has evidence beyond case histories, and those point both ways.

Should declines be published? For: a public "not doing this, and why" register is the only mechanism that makes a no final, and finality is what stops a request cycling for three years. Against: a published decline is competitive intelligence, is quoted back during renewals, and commits you against a reversal new evidence might justify.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives at triage with a scoring spreadsheet and defends its output. Someone who has internalised it arrives with two numbers they had to go and measure — an articulation rate and a cost of delay — and with a third option nobody asked for, because the choice as presented lay between two answers both slightly wrong. They answer requests within the week whether or not they build them; they price precedent before the first yes; they know which configuration flags serve one customer; and they are more nervous about small requests than large ones. Most distinctively, they treat intake as a product whose users they are shaping.

12. What they decided

Meera declined the contractual clause and built the prefix. Hasti got a three-week approval chain delivered as the first increment of the generalised framework, its state machine built to carry roles and thresholds from the start; Devansh got a signed letter naming the capability and the increment, with no date in the order form. Her reasoning was not that Hasti's request was wrong but that the clause was worth ₹2.7 lakh against an unpriced precedent liability, and a decision that marginal should be made the way that keeps most options open. She also proposed a ledgered commitment budget of fifteen percent of buyer-side capacity, which the committee approved and the seller-side manager opposed.

Aniruddh declined the automatic signature and moved the boundary instead. Shalini Mahanta, Hriday's regulatory lead in Guwahati, read automated attestation as touching the device's documented intended use, and a signature on a report no physician had opened as unacceptable exposure. But the reframed problem — turnaround from upload to signed report of 31 hours against a 12-hour service level, 26 of them waiting for attestation — could be attacked outside the device boundary. A separate web application queuing studies to a cardiologist's phone for two-tap attestation needed no re-validation, shipped in five weeks, consumed no release slot, and cut median turnaround to nine hours across 148 cardiologists. Hitakari renewed. The risk Aniruddh circulated was explicit: if guidance shifts to treat attestation workflow as part of the device, the shelter disappears and the tool inherits the fourteen-week cycle.

Three questions for discussion. Meera's calculation made the clause nearly value-neutral; at a close probability of 0.95 it would have been worth ₹8 lakh — when does a sales estimate of close probability stop being evidence and start being negotiation? Aniruddh moved work outside a regulatory boundary: when is that legitimate design, and when arbitrage that will be corrected? And articulation rates read telemetry customers never offered as a request — where is the line between listening and inference?

13. Going deeper

  1. Saying no — where declining is practised; the reason's specificity decides whether a no holds.
  2. Roadmap commitments in deals — who may put a date in a contract, and what is owed when it slips.
  3. Enterprise feature requests and custom work — when the problem truly belongs to one account, someone pays for the fork forever.
  4. Value vs effort — the right instrument before cost-of-delay data exists.
  5. RICE scoring — articulation rates make its reach column honest rather than a ticket count.
  6. Kano model — why a basic attribute draws requests when absent and no satisfaction when present.
  7. Weighted scoring and WSJF — the arithmetic used above, and its blind spot around prefixes.
  8. Buy-a-feature — the cheapest willingness-to-pay proxy: relative value under a budget constraint.
  9. User story mapping — exposes which candidate is a prefix of which before anything is scored.

From request to problem: handling feature requests from customers and sales

On the second Monday of September, Ananya Deshpande, head of product for the store-operations line at Vitaran Retail Cloud in Bengaluru, opened her backlog to fifty-one open tickets tagged "customer request" and one message from the head of enterprise sales, Rohit Kapadia, that read: "Vasant Fashion Retail won't sign unless we commit the custom GST invoice fix in writing by 30 September. ₹38 lakh ARR. Please just say yes." Vitaran sold inventory and order-management software to mid-size Indian retail chains; Vasant Fashion Retail ran forty apparel stores across four states and wanted every store to print GST invoices with its own numbering series, a demand that sounded narrow and specific. Ananya's engineering team had six weeks of free capacity before the next release froze. If she said yes to the literal request, she would spend it on one customer's invoice template. If she said no, she risked losing a deal Rohit had spent four months building. Both answers felt wrong, which was the first sign that the request itself, not the decision, was the thing she had not yet finished examining.

1. The idea

The discipline Ananya needed has a plain name: turning a request into a problem before it is prioritised. A feature request is not a specification; it is a customer's or salesperson's best guess at a solution to a pain they may not have fully diagnosed themselves. The practice asks the product manager to hold every inbound request at arm's length long enough to answer one question — what job is this person actually trying to get done, and what happens to them if we do nothing — before it is scored, scheduled, or promised. Only after that translation is complete does it make sense to compare the request against everything else competing for engineering time.

The lineage runs through two traditions that met in software product management. Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta's "jobs to be done" research in the 1990s showed that people hire products to make progress on a job, and that the words they use to describe what they want are an imperfect translation of that job. Separately, as SaaS companies scaled sales-led revenue in the 2010s, writers such as Des Traynor at Intercom and Marty Cagan at the Silicon Valley Product Group named the failure mode of teams that skipped this translation: the "feature factory," which builds exactly what was asked and wonders why usage stays flat. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a feature request is a hypothesis about a problem, not a spec, and my job is to find the problem before I price the hypothesis.

2. How it actually works

Figure 1. The translation step (boxes 2–4) sits before any scoring model, not inside it.

Mechanically, the practice has six moves, and the two that practitioners most often skip are the second and the last. First, every request is logged in one visible backlog regardless of whether it arrived by CRM note, support ticket, or a Slack message from a salesperson, because a request that lives only in someone's inbox cannot be compared to anything. Second — the step Ananya's team had been skipping — each new ticket is checked against existing ones for the same underlying job before it is treated as new; without this, a single problem fragments into a dozen differently worded tickets that each look individually small. Third, the requester is asked what they will do differently once the feature exists, and what they do today without it; the answer usually reveals the job. Fourth, the job is written as a problem statement in plain language, detached from the requester's proposed solution. Fifth, the population affected and the value at stake are sized, not just the one loud account. Sixth, the problem re-enters the team's ordinary prioritisation model, and whatever the decision, the requester is told the decision and the reasoning, on a schedule, so that silence never has to substitute for "no."

3. A worked example

Ananya pulled the backlog and found that "custom GST invoice template," "store-wise invoice numbering," and "printable invoice layout fix" were three separate tickets, filed over eight weeks by three different accounts, worth a combined ₹1.02 crore of annual recurring revenue. Read individually they looked like cosmetic requests. Read together, with the question "what happens if we don't fix this," they were the same problem: Vitaran's invoicing engine issued one numbering series per company, but GSTN's e-invoicing rules expect a coherent series per registered GSTIN, and chains with multiple state registrations were reconciling numbering by hand at month end. She wrote the problem statement as: "Multi-store retailers with more than one GSTIN cannot produce a numbering scheme their auditors accept without manual correction."

CandidateReach (₹ ARR affected)Impact (1–3)ConfidenceEffort (weeks)Score
GST invoice numbering (literal fix, Vasant only)₹38 lakh270%20.27
GST invoice numbering (reframed as GSTIN hierarchy)₹1.02 crore380%64.08
Dark mode (unrelated backlog item, for contrast)₹18 lakh150%20.45

Score here is (reach in ₹ crore × impact × confidence) ÷ effort in weeks. The literal, single-customer fix scores 0.27; folding in the two other accounts and treating it as one architectural problem lifts the score to 4.08, comfortably above dark mode's 0.45 — a ranking that a naive ticket count would never have produced, since dark mode had more individual requesters. Ananya then ran a second pass: she asked her solutions architect what franchise-model deals in the pipeline, worth roughly ₹4.2 crore over two quarters, needed the same GSTIN hierarchy capability to close. Reach rose to ₹5.2 crore, effort held at six weeks because the two builds shared the same schema change, and the score rose past 40 — at which point the question stopped being whether to build it and became only how soon.

4. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Loud is not the same as wide

One account with a deal deadline generates urgency that has nothing to do with how many other accounts share the pain. Urgency is a scheduling input, not a validity input; treating a single vocal request as proof of demand is the single most common error in this practice.

Reframing is not overriding

Translating a request into a problem statement means detaching the customer's proposed solution from their diagnosis of the pain, not second-guessing that they have a real pain. Vasant Fashion Retail was right that invoicing broke their audit process; they were only incidentally right about the fix being a template change.

"No" without a reason is read as "later" forever

A backlog that goes quiet on rejected requests trains sales to route around product and promise features directly to customers, because silence is indistinguishable from neglect. A visible status — declined, merged, or scheduled — with a one-line reason is what keeps trust intact.

Scoring models cannot tell you about strategic fit

RICE-style arithmetic ranks problems that are already inside the roadmap's boundaries; it says nothing about whether Vitaran should be building GSTIN hierarchy at all versus buying a compliance module, or whether the six weeks would be better spent exiting technical debt that slows every future release.

Saying yes to the problem is not saying yes to the timeline

The topic this builds on — saying no — is practised most often right here: Ananya could accept that the problem was real and still decline Rohit's 30 September date, offering a manual workaround for Vasant Fashion Retail while the durable fix shipped in October.

Merging tickets can hide the true size if done carelessly

Collapsing three tickets into one problem is correct only when the underlying job is actually shared; merging dissimilar requests to make a backlog look tidier produces a badly informed impact estimate in the other direction.

Custom work for one account is a different decision than a platform feature

A fix built only for Vasant Fashion Retail's contract terms is enterprise custom work, governed by different economics — who pays for maintenance, does it fork the codebase — than a capability every customer with multiple GSTINs will use, which is what "enterprise feature requests and custom work," the topic this unlocks, exists to separate.

5. Consumer, B2B, and marketplace — and early versus large companies

In consumer products, requests arrive in volume without an attached deal, so the discipline leans on aggregation and statistical patterns across app-store reviews and support tickets rather than negotiation with any one voice. In B2B software like Vitaran's, each request usually has an owner — an account executive or customer success manager who has already made an implicit promise — and the danger is a roadmap quietly negotiated by whichever salesperson is loudest that quarter. In marketplaces, the same feature can serve one side of the transaction at the other side's expense, so the problem statement has to specify which side's job is being solved before value can even be sized. Stage matters as much as business model: an early-stage company with thirty customers risks treating any single request as a market signal when the sample is simply too small, while a large enterprise sales organisation needs a formal intake process with service-level commitments, because informal habits that work for thirty accounts collapse under three thousand tickets.

6. Common mistakes

Symptom: the backlog has a dozen tickets that read as different features but describe the same pain in different words. Misunderstanding: treating the requester's phrasing as the specification rather than searching for the shared job underneath. Cheap diagnostic: cluster open tickets by the answer to "what happens if we don't," not by their titles, and count distinct jobs against raw ticket count.

Symptom: sales has started promising ship dates directly to customers without checking the backlog. Misunderstanding: prioritisation was treated as a private ranking exercise instead of a decision that gets communicated. Cheap diagnostic: count how many features shipped last quarter originated as an unlogged verbal promise rather than a backlog entry.

Symptom: a feature ships on schedule and the account that requested it barely uses it. Misunderstanding: the team built the literal solution the loudest voice asked for without checking whether quieter, affected accounts described the same underlying job the same way. Cheap diagnostic: before building, interview two or three silent accounts tagged with the same problem and compare their account of it to the vocal requester's.

Symptom: the roadmap keeps getting reordered every quarter by whichever deal is largest that month. Misunderstanding: conflating one deal's size with the underlying problem's true reach across the customer book. Cheap diagnostic: before approving an expedite, compute the ARR-weighted reach of the problem across all accounts, not the single deal that triggered the request.

7. What good looks like

Six months later, Vitaran's intake ran on a simple rhythm: every request landed in one tagged backlog within a day, a weekly thirty-minute triage merged duplicates and wrote problem statements before anyone touched RICE arithmetic, and every decision — yes, no, or merged — got a one-line reason back to the requester within a week. Rohit's team could see, in the same tool they filed requests in, exactly where each one stood and why, which meant he stopped promising features unilaterally because there was no longer any need to. Nothing about the process was exotic; the difference was that a request never reached a scoring model until someone had written down, in one sentence, the job behind it.

Closing

Ananya told Rohit she would not commit the literal invoice-template fix by 30 September, but she would commit a GSTIN-hierarchy capability, covering Vasant Fashion Retail and two other accounts plus the franchise pipeline, for a 20 October release, with her customer success team providing a manual reconciliation workaround in the meantime. Vasant signed. The reasoning she gave the leadership team was not that the request was wrong, but that pricing the literal request would have spent six weeks solving eight percent of a ₹5.2 crore problem. From here the useful next step is the topic this unlocks — enterprise feature requests and custom work — because the harder version of this decision is what to do when the problem genuinely is unique to one account. Two questions worth sitting with: when a request and a deal deadline arrive together, whose clock should set the pace of the investigation, and not just the build? And how would you design a backlog so that a "no" costs the requester nothing to hear?

Qissa Kitchen Cloud: The Osara Renewal

ISB Product Management Programme · Delivery & Technology module

On Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Ananya Kulkarni, VP of Product at Qissa Kitchen Cloud, opened the company's request tracker — the Ask Board — and counted 214 open items. She had until Friday's leadership review to tell the founders what Qissa would do about one: a bespoke wastage dashboard the sales head had already, verbally, promised to its largest customer.

1. The scene

Ananya's cabin in Qissa's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru looked out over a lane of cloud kitchens the company had helped digitise. Qissa sold restaurant-operations software — point of sale, kitchen display, inventory, and loyalty — to multi-outlet restaurant chains across India. In three weeks, Osara Dining Group, a 68-outlet casual-dining chain and Qissa's largest account at ₹1.35 crore ARR, would decide whether to renew. Rohit Malhotra, VP of Sales, had told Osara's operations head three days earlier that Qissa would deliver an SAP-integrated wastage dashboard "by the end of Q4." Product and engineering had not been in that conversation. Diwali was three weeks away, half of engineering had already booked leave, and the reconciliation feature that 58 customers had waited on, some for over a year, was due to start that same week. Ananya had four days to decide what Qissa would actually do, and what Rohit should say back.

2. Company background

Qissa Kitchen Cloud was founded by Karthik Rao and two co-founders who had run operations for a Bengaluru cloud-kitchen chain and had felt, first-hand, the pain of reconciling a day's sales across point-of-sale terminals, delivery aggregators, and a paper wastage register. Qissa's product stitched these together: a dashboard for owners, a kitchen display system that cut order errors, and a loyalty layer spanning dine-in and delivery. By late 2026 it served roughly 450 restaurant brands and 3,200 outlets, from single-city QSR chains to national casual-dining groups, on an ARR of about ₹38 crore after a Series B round earlier in the year. Competitors were familiar names — Petpooja and UrbanPiper sold overlapping tools, and Zomato and Swiggy each pushed lightweight tools into the same back offices to keep partners inside their own ecosystems. Qissa's pitch was that it alone unified operations across channels; that pitch depended on trust that its roadmap reflected what restaurants generally needed, not what the loudest customer that quarter had asked for.

3. The situation

The Ask Board was Qissa's shared, honest record of what customers wanted: any employee could see every open request, who had asked, how long it had sat, and what happened to it. That visibility was now working against Ananya. Devika Menon, Head of Customer Success in Chennai, had flagged that the reconciliation theme — matching a restaurant's sales records against what Zomato and Swiggy actually paid out — represented 58 open requests and roughly ₹9.4 crore of ARR, some open fourteen months, and engineering had only just cleared capacity to start it. Rohit's promise to Osara landed on top of it, unscoped and specific to Osara's SAP Business One system in a way no other customer used.

From Gurugram, Rohit saw a plain fact: Osara was the account his forecast turned on, and its ops head had said a rival vendor had already demonstrated a wastage dashboard. From Chennai, Devika saw forty smaller customers whose own wastage requests had sat for months, and worried what it told them if Osara jumped the queue by threatening to leave. From Pune, Farhan saw a pattern he disliked: the fourth time in a year a client-specific integration had displaced a promised platform feature, always pulling his best engineers off it. Ananya's task was not to referee whether Osara mattered — it did — but to work out what problem the request actually described, and whether the literal ask was the best way to solve it.

4. The people

Ananya Kulkarni — VP of Product, Bengaluru
Owns the Ask Board. Wants a decision defensible to engineering and the board, keeping the backlog honest rather than reshuffled by whoever shouts loudest.
Rohit Malhotra — VP of Sales, Gurugram
Carries the renewal number. Wants a firm commitment he can repeat to Osara this week.
Devika Menon — Head of Customer Success, Chennai
Manages Osara and forty other accounts on the same underlying request. Wants any Osara commitment explainable to everyone else waiting.
Farhan Sheikh — Senior Engineering Manager, Pune
Would staff whichever option is chosen. Wants fewer one-off client builds and a roadmap the team can plan a quarter around.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Ask Board, open requests by theme (13 October 2026)
ThemeOpen requestsOldest (months)ARR represented
Aggregator payout reconciliation5814₹9.4 cr
Ingredient wastage & inventory4211₹6.8 cr
Multi-outlet menu sync317₹4.2 cr
Loyalty & coupon stacking245₹2.1 cr
Custom ERP integrations (incl. Osara)123₹3.6 cr
Other / miscellaneous479₹5.1 cr

Source: Qissa Ask Board export. Osara's request sits inside the wastage theme but is logged again under ERP integrations for its SAP dependency — one need, filed twice.

Exhibit 1 is what made Ananya pause before answering Rohit. Osara's request was not a new problem; it was one instance of a wastage-and-inventory theme that 42 customers, representing ₹6.8 crore of ARR, had already raised. Build only what Osara needed — a direct SAP feed — and it satisfies one account, leaving the other 41 where they were. Build the general version, and Osara's particular integration still would not exist unless someone separately wired it up.

Exhibit 2 — the three-week window between Rohit's promise and Osara's renewal decision, set against the Diwali dip in engineering capacity.

Exhibit 3 — Comparing the three options Ananya is weighing
OptionEngineering effortTimelineCustomers servedRoadmap effect
A. Build Osara's exact SAP dashboard7 person-weeks6 weeks1 (Osara)Reconciliation feature slips ~6 weeks
B. General wastage module + CSV bridge for Osara9 person-weeks4 weeks (bridge); 10 (full)42 today; SAP laterReconciliation proceeds in parallel
C. Manual interim report; no new build now<1 person-weekImmediateOsara only, temporarilyNo roadmap disruption

Estimates from Farhan Sheikh, 12 October 2026. Option A uses the same two senior engineers already assigned to reconciliation.

6. The options

Option A — Build exactly what was promised

Ananya could honour Rohit's word and direct Farhan's two senior engineers to build the SAP dashboard to Osara's spec. The upside is immediate: Osara renews, and sales learns commitments get protected. The cost: reconciliation, already overdue fourteen months for 58 customers and ₹9.4 crore of ARR, slips six weeks into the Diwali dip, and the roadmap becomes, again, whatever the quarter's largest deal requires.

Option B — Solve the underlying problem, bridge Osara

Ananya could decline the literal SAP build and fast-track a general wastage module, usable via CSV export rather than a live SAP feed, in four weeks — offered to Osara as a bridge alongside a written 90-day commitment to deeper integration once proven. Reconciliation continues on schedule. Forty-two customers get value quickly and the backlog stays honest; the risk is Osara, having seen a rival's live demo, sees a CSV export as lesser and pushes back on terms.

Option C — Buy time without a build

Ananya could ask Devika's team to compile Osara's wastage figures manually each month, as a service rather than a feature, while engineering proceeds untouched. This protects the roadmap and costs almost no engineering time, but treats a renewal-threatening gap as an account-management problem and gives Rohit nothing new to tell a client already promised a dashboard.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the underlying problem behind Osara's request, and how does it differ from the literal feature Rohit promised?
  2. How should Ananya weigh Osara's ₹1.35 crore renewal against the ₹9.4 crore of ARR behind the reconciliation theme, and does Exhibit 1 change that comparison?
  3. What does Rohit's verbal promise reveal about how requests enter Qissa's roadmap, and what should change?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what exactly would Ananya say to Rohit, Devika, and Osara by Friday?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks a narrower question than "should we say yes or no": what problem is the request evidence of, before any decision is made? A feature request, taken literally, is a customer's proposed solution to a problem they have not fully described. Osara's ops head did not want an SAP integration for its own sake; he wanted to stop losing money to unrecorded spoilage and show that to his own management. Rohit's promise skipped the translation step, converting a business problem into a technical commitment before anyone checked whether that was the best way to solve it, or whether the problem already existed, at scale, elsewhere on the Ask Board.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it decomposes the request into the underlying job — tracking and explaining wastage — and checks it against the visible backlog, exactly what Exhibit 1 lets a reader do: the same problem already sits behind 42 requests and ₹6.8 crore of ARR, a more defensible question than "keep our biggest account happy." Second, it protects the honesty of the backlog: whichever option Ananya chooses should be equally explainable to the 41 other waiting customers. Third, it treats saying no as something practised on the literal ask, not the underlying problem — Ananya is not refusing Osara, she is refusing to let one client's phrasing set Qissa's priorities alone.

On that reasoning, Option B is the most defensible path. It resolves the shared problem for the most customers on the fastest timeline, keeps reconciliation intact for 58 waiting accounts, and still gives Rohit something true to tell Osara: a working interim solution now, and a dated commitment to deeper integration. Option A rewards the loudest voice over a larger commitment already made to everyone else; Option C avoids the roadmap cost by asking Osara to accept less than promised. The lesson going forward is procedural: no one outside product should promise a build date before checking the Ask Board.
exp20v2-prio.hw.tradeoffs:
Prioritising for Hardware: Cost, Weight, Power, Schedule

Why a milliamp is never just a milliamp once it is multiplied by every unit you ship.

1. Four numbers, one meeting

On Monday 9 March 2026, Sumeet Chaggar, head of product at Jalori Devices of Mohali, entered a steering review carrying what looked like a feature list. The company's first product was a Bluetooth fall-detection pendant for elderly users, worn on a lanyard and paired with a relative's phone. Housing tooling would freeze on Friday 3 April. Retailers had ordered 39,000 units for a thirteen-week festive window opening 1 October, and would not move the date.

Two requests were pending. Sales wanted two-way voice so a fallen wearer could speak to family; another executive wanted optical heart-rate sensing. Sargam Chandna, the mechanical lead, guarded a mass ceiling of 38.0 g taken from the 2025 wear trial; her estimate stood at 37.04 g. Suhani Chhina, who ran sourcing and finance, held a landed-cost target of ₹1,000 per unit against an estimate of ₹968.60. Sarthak Channa, the firmware lead, owned a promise of fourteen days between charges.

Chaggar's difficulty was that the four limits could not be traded one at a time. A request that added a milliamp also added grams and rupees, and a request that added a week lost sales that his colleagues believed would mostly never return. Approve the wrong pair and Jalori would miss its date or ship a pendant too heavy to wear.

2. The idea

Constraint compounding is the practice of restating every hardware request in the same units, per unit shipped, after its knock-on effects are included, and then testing the result against the limits that bind. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation of 1903 showed that each extra kilogram of payload needs propellant that must itself be lifted. Leonid Kantorovich, from the late 1930s, formalised the shadow price: the worth of one more unit of a limit that is binding. Design-to-cost, adopted in United States defence procurement from the early 1970s, made unit cost a requirement rather than an outcome.

Chaggar's version fits one sentence he could say without sounding glib: "Every request is paid for in grams, milliamps, rupees and weeks, so we price it in all four before we rank it." Table 1 shows the three exchange rates that sentence needs; later sections derive each one.

Table 1. Exchange rates at the 9 March design point. Both power rates assume the housing can still change.
CurrencyRate per unit shippedSource
Schedule₹54.24 per week of slip₹21,15,360 ÷ 39,000 units
Power₹13.65 and 1.26 g per 0.1 mABattery chain, Figure 2
MassNo price; cap of 38.0 gHeadroom 0.96 g

3. How it works

Step one fixes the gates: ₹1,000 landed cost, 38.0 g, fourteen days, 1 October. Step two builds a baseline ledger for each, because a request can only be judged against what remains. Figure 3 gives the mass ledger.

Step three, which practitioners usually leave implicit, derives the exchange rates. Fourteen days is 336 hours. A draw of 0.60 mA over 336 hours is 201.6 mAh; Jalori adds a 25 per cent reserve for cold, ageing and tolerance, giving 252 mAh. Milliamp-hours measure charge, not energy; at the cell's 3.7 V that charge is 0.9324 Wh. Each extra 0.1 mA therefore needs 42 mAh more cell. At 50 mAh per gram and ₹0.30 per mAh that is 0.84 g and ₹12.60, and Chandna's rule from the previous product adds 0.5 g of housing, at ₹2.50 per gram, for each gram of cell. The total is 1.26 g and ₹13.65 per unit, or ₹5,32,350 across 39,000 units.

Step four prices time. Demand runs at 3,000 units a week. Sales judged that 80 per cent of a missed week never returns, and each unit realises ₹1,850.00 after GST and channel margin against ₹968.60 of cost, a contribution of ₹881.40. One week's slip loses 2,400 × ₹881.40 = ₹21,15,360, which is ₹54.24 per unit over the whole 39,000. Step five restates each request as totals. Step six, usually skipped, checks feasibility before ranking by value: a request that breaks a binding cap is out however attractive.

4. A worked example

Chhina's team priced four candidates. Option D is not a feature but a motion sensor with an on-chip fall-detection engine: ₹18.00 dearer, yet it lets the processor sleep through ordinary movement and cuts average draw by 0.14 mA to 0.46 mA. The cell can shrink by 1.4 × 42 = 58.8 mAh to 193.2 mAh, shedding 1.764 g and ₹19.11 of cell and housing. After paying the ₹18.00, D saves ₹1.11 per unit and frees mass.

Table 2. Options priced per unit. Total cost = direct ₹ + power ₹ + weeks × ₹54.24. Net = uplift − total cost. Pass 2 re-prices a week at ₹27.12 and changes nothing else. Total grams = direct g + 12.6 g per mA.
OptionDirect ₹Direct gΔ mAWeeksUplift ₹Total cost ₹Total gNet ₹, pass 1Net ₹, pass 2
