The recovery was a re-scoping, not a reversal of judgement. Gakhar's team split the candidate at the isolation barrier and took the components downstream, where a change needs a ₹6 lakh file update rather than a retest: ₹410 a unit, ₹50.84 lakh a year, repaying its K in 1,464 units, about six weeks of earning. The ₹2.35 crore was never spent; had it been, the supply would still have netted ₹136.6 lakh, 1.58 times K against 24.37 for the re-scope. What failed was not the candidate but the method: a ranking on ₹ per unit with no K column put the worst-returning option first.

8c. The cut nobody took

Mandhata never costed the UV deletion — the right outcome by the wrong route. Gaind was correct that ₹28.16 crore a year deserved a number; Galgotra, that it was not available. The disciplined version puts it through the gate, records why it failed, and keeps it on a register, so that if the carton is redesigned the arithmetic is already done.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

  • Pricing a saving without its K. Sign: a savings column and no spend column. Diagnostic: what does the first unit of this saving cost? Caught at Medini only when the quotation landed: ₹2.35 crore of K nobody had priced.
  • Crediting a saving on something that cannot go. Sign: the biggest line is the one nobody will discuss. Diagnostic: is this part named in a claim, a certificate or a warranty specification? Caught after launch it is a relabelling and a recall, not a reversal.
  • Double-counting across exhibits. Sign: two sheets imply the same annual figure and differ. Diagnostic: multiply per-unit by volume — ₹199 × 11.4 lakh must equal ₹22.69 crore, and does. Late, it means a board-level number that cannot be rebuilt.
  • Letting gross realisation stand in for net. Sign: realisation near a hundred per cent for two quarters. Diagnostic: what has warranty accrual per unit done since the cut shipped? Unasked, the harness would have cost Mandhata ₹1.48 crore a year.
  • Serial approval of interacting cuts. Sign: approvals weeks apart with no combined build. Diagnostic: has anyone built a unit with all of these in it? Found in the field, both cuts reverse together.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Can noticeability be measured before shipping? The measurement camp holds that blind panels and conjoint designs predict perceived-quality effects well enough to price them, and that firms running them reverse fewer cuts. The field camp holds that perceived quality is holistic and emerges over months, so the only honest instrument is a limited-market ship with a reversal plan. The first is wrong if those effects are mainly interactions between cuts, which panels testing one change cannot see; the second, if reversal costs rise faster with time than information does.

Is a cost-down roadmap a capability or a confession? The target-costing position is that a standing roadmap is evidence of a design-freeze failure; the opposing position, that component markets move, so a roadmap is how a firm harvests deflation it could not have designed in. The first is wrong if cost curves move more than any freeze could anticipate; the second, if roadmap savings are mostly recovery of avoidable design decisions — and nobody has published a clean decomposition.

Gate or multiplier? The multiplier position is not naive: gates get captured, "claim-bearing" expands until nothing is cuttable, and a weighted score at least forces an estimate onto the table. It is right wherever the gate is drawn by whoever benefits from drawing it widely, and wrong wherever the loss distribution has a step in it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this produces a ranked list. Someone who has internalised it produces three and says which constraint selects between them. They ask for the addressable base before the target, the gate before the ranking, the warranty accrual before the realisation report. They quote paybacks in units, price calendar time in rupees, and know which cuts they could undo and by when. And when the biggest number on the sheet is the one nobody wants to discuss, they write down why it is excluded with its arithmetic intact — because the gate may move.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Galgotra funded all five cuts in the week of 20 July 2026, declared the ₹199 against her ₹200 mandate as a shortfall rather than rounding up, and changed two things. She added an addressable-base line to the target, restating the ask as 6.59 per cent of ₹3,037 rather than 6.09 per cent of ₹3,284; and she required one combined build of all five cuts before any shipped, which is how the harness-to-pump clearance problem was found — late, but not in the field.

Gurwara cancelled the February approval in September 2026, took the ₹410 downstream re-scope, and put the ₹2.35 crore candidate on a register against the next platform, where the requalification happens anyway. His standing rule afterwards: no candidate reaches a review without a quotation for its own requalification attached.

Questions for discussion.

  1. Mandhata's ₹199 comes within ₹1 of its mandate without touching the largest candidate on the sheet. Had the mandate been ₹400, where would the next ₹201 come from, and what evidence would justify reopening the UV exclusion?
  2. The risk term was 1.2 per cent of Mandhata's gross and was set aside at Medini. At what combination of volume, contribution and remaining life does a risk multiplier earn its place beside a hard gate?
  3. Mandhata's reversibility on the harness expires in March 2028. What is that option worth, and who should own the decision to let it lapse?

13. Going deeper

  • Prioritising for hardware: cost, weight, power, schedule. Cost is one of four coupled currencies; this page held three fixed.
  • BOM, COGS and cost-down. The costing discipline behind Exhibit 1: landed cost, overhead absorption, what belongs in COGS.
  • Cost-down roadmaps. Sequences the ranked list, with tooling calendars rather than value setting the order.
  • Value vs effort. The two-axis ancestor of V; shows what is lost when K and Teff collapse into one axis.
  • RICE scoring. Reach × impact × confidence over effort is s · Q with a confidence term, and shows why multipliers misbehave where gates belong.
  • Kano model. The vocabulary for noticeability: cut in the indifferent category, never the must-be, and treat delighters as claim-bearing.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF. Its cost-of-delay numerator prices the calendar cost of Medini's blackout.
  • Buy-a-feature. Elicits what customers pay to keep — section 10's missing instrument.
  • User story mapping. Maps the interactions that make a part noticeable, operationalising nuance five.
exp20v2-prio.tech.debt.alloc:
Allocating capacity: features, debt, bugs, bets

Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making

1. A quarter that nobody had planned

On Monday 6 July 2026, Parvati Adiyodi, head of product at Hemavan Software Private Limited in Kochi, opened the planning document for the quarter running to 30 September. Hemavan sells shift-rostering software to 140 hospitals across Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, with annual recurring revenue of ₹48 crore. Two hospital groups, together worth ₹3.6 crore a year (7.5 per cent of that revenue), had told the sales team that their renewals depended on two things: a shift-swap approval flow, and an end to the rostering errors that had put nurses on duty twice on the same night.

The engineering organisation had 50 engineers and twelve planning weeks, which is 600 engineer-weeks, the unit this page uses throughout: one engineer working one week. Prasoon Azhikode, the engineering lead, had subtracted 100 engineer-weeks for leave, on-call rota and meetings, a sixth of the total, leaving 500 of net capacity. The ledger for the previous quarter showed where those 500 had gone.

Features had taken 310 engineer-weeks (62 per cent), bug fixing 125 (25 per cent), bets 40 (8 per cent) and technical debt 25 (5 per cent). Sales had requested 340 engineer-weeks of features. Pavithran Alungal, who ran customer support, wanted bug capacity protected. Prasoon wanted a fifth of the quarter for debt: a full test run took 41 minutes and releases had slipped to every third week.

Each described a real cost, but a backlog compares one item with another, and this argument was about how many engineer-weeks each kind of work could claim before any item was compared. If the habit continued, debt would stay at 5 per cent, releases would slow further, and the renewals would rest on a team too slow to deliver what had been promised.

2. The idea

Capacity allocation means deciding, before looking at individual requests, what share of the team's net capacity each category of work may use in a period. Four categories cover most software teams. Features are new customer-visible capability. Bugs are defects in what already ships. Technical debt is the accumulated cost of earlier shortcuts, which makes every later change slower or riskier. Bets are speculative work whose payoff is uncertain and whose purpose is to find out whether an opportunity exists.

The idea combines two older ones. Ward Cunningham used the debt metaphor in a 1992 experience report on a financial portfolio system: a shortcut is like a loan, useful now and charged interest later. Portfolio thinking supplies the rest. Google's much-quoted "70-20-10" rule of thumb for core, adjacent and transformational projects, popularised in the mid-2000s, is an allocation rule of this kind. Both address one problem: in an unmanaged backlog, urgent and visible work crowds out important and quiet work without anyone choosing it.

The sentence Adiyodi could repeat without sounding glib was this: “Before we compare any two requests, we agree how many of our 500 engineer-weeks each kind of work may take, and what we expect back from each share.”

3. How it works

Figure 1. Hemavan's allocation, last quarter against the proposal. Features fall by 110 engineer-weeks.

The mechanics take five steps, and the first two are usually left implicit.

Step one is to fix the denominator: net capacity, after leave, on-call and meetings. Step two is to write down what counts in each category, because the boundaries decide the numbers. Hemavan's rule: a fix to a customer-visible defect was a bug, a change that removed a recurring cost without altering behaviour was debt, and anything new was a feature or a bet.

Step three sets bugs first, since they behave like a demand rather than a choice: the previous quarter's 125 engineer-weeks was the best estimate of what defects would claim. Step four prices debt as interest rather than as a wish. Step five sizes bets as a small, capped slice of time-boxed experiments, each with a kill criterion agreed in advance. Features then receive what remains, and the sales list is trimmed to fit. The result: 200 features, 100 debt, 125 bugs, 75 bets, summing to 500. The 200 funds 59 per cent of the 340 requested.

4. A worked example: pricing the debt envelope

Technical debt has two components. Principal is the one-off engineer-weeks needed to remove it. Interest is the engineer-weeks it keeps costing each quarter until removed. The payback of a debt item is principal divided by quarterly interest, measured in quarters. Prasoon listed four items. Interest for A, C and D is a stated input from postmortems and tagged tickets, booked outside the bug bucket, so recovering it does not shrink the 125 bug weeks. Item A changes no rostering behaviour; the double-duty defect is fixed separately inside those 125.

Debt itemPrincipal (eng-weeks)Interest per quarter (eng-weeks)Payback (quarters)
B. Parallelise the test suite15121.25
A. Rebuild the rostering rules module60302.00
C. Retire the legacy SMS gateway2054.00
D. Clean up the shift database schema4595.00
All four, pooled140562.50

Table 1. First-pass debt inventory, Monday 6 July. Payback in the pooled row is 140 divided by 56.

The interest on item B shows how such a figure is built. Fifty engineers ran the suite about three times a week for twelve weeks: 1,800 runs. A sample found 16 minutes of each 41-minute run was dead waiting, assuming the engineer does nothing else meanwhile and that parallelising removes all of it. That is 28,800 minutes, or 480 hours, or 12 engineer-weeks at 40 hours.

The rule Adiyodi adopted was to fund items in ascending payback until the 100 engineer-week envelope is spent, and to refuse any item whose payback exceeds four quarters, however much money remains. B costs 15, A brings the total to 75, and C brings it to 95. D would take 140 against an envelope of 100, and its payback of five quarters fails the rule anyway. The funded items recover 12 + 30 + 5 = 47 engineer-weeks a quarter for 95 spent, an aggregate payback of 2.02 quarters.

Figure 2. Payback by item. The purple bar is item A after the second-pass re-estimate of its principal from 60 to 80 engineer-weeks.

In Figure 2 only D crosses the four-quarter line. On Thursday 9 July, Prasoon reported that item A was larger than first thought: its principal was 80 engineer-weeks, not 60, while its interest stayed at 30. Payback rose from 2.00 to 2.67 quarters (80 ÷ 30). The order stayed B, A, C, D, but the money no longer reached. B and A cost 95; adding C would take the total to 115 against 100. The funded set became B and A, recovering 12 + 30 = 42 engineer-weeks a quarter, an aggregate payback of 2.26 quarters (95 ÷ 42).

The alternatives confirm it: A and C cost exactly 100 and recover 35; B, C and D cost 80 and recover 26. One changed estimate removed an entire item from the plan, which is why estimates deserve more argument than percentages.

5. What a learner must become aware of

The percentages are a hypothesis about returns

Twenty per cent for debt is not a virtue. It is a bet that the interest on the debt exceeds the return on the features those 100 engineer-weeks would otherwise buy.

Categories are definitions, and the boundaries leak

A defect fix that requires restructuring a module is part bug, part debt. Fix the rule before the quarter, and classify when work starts, or the debt share will shrink.

Bugs are demand, not discretion

Arrivals are not chosen, so set a floor from recent history and treat a persistent overrun as evidence about quality, not as a reason to raid another bucket.

Principal and interest answer different questions

Principal tells you what removal costs; interest tells you what waiting costs. An expensive item with large interest may be the best purchase on the list.

A bet is funded like an expense and judged like an option

Hemavan's 75 engineer-weeks were split into three bets of 25 each. Most bets are expected to fail, so review asks whether learning per engineer-week was good and failures stopped early.

Allocation is not prioritisation, and it does not replace it

Inside each bucket, items still need ranking, for example by RICE, which scores each item as Reach times Impact times Confidence, divided by Effort. The allocation only decides which items compete with which. A debt item should not have to out-score a feature, because the two are measured in different currencies.

It cannot tell you the right percentages

The method makes the choice explicit, not correct. Two sensible leaders could defend 15 and 25 per cent for debt.

Ask before relying on it

What is the denominator? Who classifies, and when? Is the interest measured or guessed? What happens at week six if a bucket is running 20 per cent over? A plan with no answer to the last has no re-planning rule.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In a consumer product, bets are most natural: many small experiments on live traffic. In B2B, as at Hemavan, contractual commitments make part of the feature share non-negotiable, and a severity-one defect at one customer can outweigh a hundred small ones elsewhere. A marketplace must protect two sides, and trust-and-safety work often needs its own line.

Stage matters as much. In a five-person startup one person's illness moves the numbers more than any policy, so the useful form is a single rule, such as “one week in five is for debt”. A large company can set percentages per team, but must not apply one uniform split to teams whose demand differs entirely.

7. Common mistakes

Percentages that follow the request queue

Symptom: the plan says 20 per cent debt; the ledger says 6. The misunderstanding is treating the allocation as a forecast, not a constraint. The diagnostic: compare planned and actual engineer-weeks per bucket, and demand a cause for any gap above five percentage points (25 engineer-weeks).

Debt as an unexamined lump

Symptom: the same large refactor appears on the plan for the third quarter running. The misunderstanding: debt is always worth paying. The diagnostic: ask for each item's interest in engineer-weeks per quarter; with no figure, even a rough one, the item is unjustified.

A bug bucket that is quietly raided

Symptom: the age of the oldest severity-two defect keeps rising while the bug share looks on plan. The misunderstanding is that the bucket was a ceiling rather than a floor against arrivals. The diagnostic is to track the age of the oldest open defect of each severity.

Bets with no kill criterion

Symptom: a bet is in its fourth quarter and has been renamed twice. The misunderstanding: a bet is a small feature. The diagnostic: ask what week-six result would end it.

8. What good looks like

Here is the ledger Adiyodi would hope to read on 30 September, as a target rather than a prediction: features 205, debt 100, bugs 120, bets 75, which sum to 500, or 41, 20, 24 and 15 per cent. Every bucket lies within five engineer-weeks (one percentage point) of plan. Debt items carry a recorded before-and-after interest, so the claimed 42 engineer-weeks a quarter can be checked. Each bet ended at week six with a written continue-or-stop decision. Sales received a dated statement of what was funded and what was not. Each percentage was defended by a number, not by roundness.

9. The decision, and what to read next

On Friday 10 July, Adiyodi adopted 200 engineer-weeks for features, 100 for debt, 125 for bugs and 75 for bets. Debt funded the test suite and the rules module, with C and D deferred and 5 engineer-weeks held as slack. She told Alungal the bug floor would be reviewed at week six, not quietly eroded. Her reasoning: the plan might be wrong, but visibly.

Next comes prioritising platform work against features: comparing work repaid in different currencies.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the interest on item A were halved to 15, would the funded set change, and what would then decide the choice? Second, what evidence, available by week six, would tell Adiyodi that 20 per cent for debt was too high rather than too low?
exp40v2-prio.tech.debt.alloc:
Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making

Allocating capacity: features, debt, bugs and bets

How much capacity goes to each kind of work — and can you defend the numbers when the quarter turns against you?

1. Two quarters that would not add up

On Monday 13 July 2026, twelve days into a quarter that had begun on 1 July, Raveena Bellare opened the capacity plan for its thirteen weeks to Wednesday 30 September at Ishira Money, a Bengaluru consumer savings-and-investing app with 41 lakh monthly active users and ₹96 crore of annual commission revenue. Her 60 engineers gave 780 engineer-weeks gross across those thirteen weeks, one engineer for one week. Rijul Banavasi, her engineering director, had taken out leave, on-call and meetings, leaving 600 of net capacity (Table 1).

The previous quarter's ledger showed where 600 had gone: 372 engineer-weeks to features (62.0 per cent), 126 to bugs (21.0), 42 to technical debt (7.0) and 60 to bets (10.0). Nobody had chosen them. Release cadence had slipped from weekly to one release in three weeks, a full test run took 71 minutes, and the KYC re-verification service, written in six weeks in 2023 to meet an RBI circular, had to be touched for every new product.

Three days later, on Thursday 16 July, Ritwik Bolar faced the same question in a shape that looked nothing like hers. Inthiram Retail Systems, in Pune, sells billing software and the point-of-sale terminals it runs on to 1,180 pharmacy-distributor branches across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. Rukshana Bejai, its chief financial officer, had asked the board for a single governing number and got it: 60 per cent of engineering on features. But Inthiram's 38 engineers were not interchangeable: twelve wrote firmware, 26 the application.

Both are the same decision: how much capacity each kind of work may claim before any two items are compared. Allocation sizes the pots before ranking begins, and it is almost always settled by default. What separates competence from expertise is the denominator, the measurement behind each category's claim, and the symmetry of the weighting on both sides.

2. The idea, and the four positions people actually hold

Capacity allocation is the practice of fixing in advance the share of a team's net capacity each category of work may consume in a period. Features are new customer-visible capability; bugs are defects in what already ships; technical debt is the cost of earlier shortcuts, which makes every later change slower or riskier; bets are time-boxed work meant to discover whether an opportunity exists.

The idea grafts two older ones. Ward Cunningham's 1992 experience report gave the debt metaphor its precision — a shortcut is a loan, charged interest until repaid — and Martin Fowler's later quadrant added that only prudent, deliberate debt is worth having. Portfolio thinking supplies the other half, in Google's 70/20/10 heuristic and in Bansi Nagji and Geoff Tuff's innovation ambition matrix. Both address one pathology: urgent, visible work crowds out important, quiet work. Four positions are worth stating.

The standing-envelope school

From the portfolio literature, by way of the frameworks that reserve capacity for "enabler" work. It would sign: a percentage published in advance and held for two periods is the only thing that survives an urgent quarter. It would not sign: the percentages encode value. They commit; they do not price.

The single-queue school

Donald Reinertsen's flow economics and the rules built on it. It would sign: every item competes on cost of delay divided by duration. It would not sign: debt needs a protected share. Real cost of delay wins on the merits; unquantifiable cost of delay is being subsidised.

The continuous-hygiene school

Kent Beck's refactoring discipline, and Tom DeMarco on slack. It would sign: repayment belongs inside every feature's estimate. It would not sign: a debt envelope, which it reads as permission to ship dirty the rest of the time.

The empirical-share school

The DORA tradition, which measures capacity consumed by rework. It would sign: measure what the categories took, publish it, drive rework down. It would not sign: a forward-looking target at all. The percentages are an output of how well the system is built, not a planning input.

3. Mechanics: six steps, and the two usually left implicit

Step one: fix the denominator. A fifth of gross is 156 engineer-weeks, a fifth of net 120; a share quoted over gross overstates delivery by 30 per cent.

Step two: define each category before any number is attached. Ishira's definitions: a fix to a customer-visible defect is a bug; a change that removes a recurring cost without altering behaviour is debt; a bet is time-boxed work with a kill criterion agreed in advance and no external commitment to ship; anything else customer-visible is a feature.

Step three: set the bug envelope from arrival, not appetite. Ishira's defect inflow had run at 42 a week for five quarters: 546 over thirteen weeks, of which 284 of 546 were fixed (52 per cent), the rest closed as duplicates or won't-fix. Fixes averaged 1.8 engineer-days, so 284 cost 102.2 engineer-weeks at five days to the week; triage on the 262 unfixed averaged 0.45 engineer-days, another 23.6. That is 125.8, so the envelope was set at 126.

Step four: price debt as interest and fund by payback. Principal is the one-off cost of removal; interest is what the item costs each quarter until removed; payback is principal divided by interest. Item B's measurement: 1,950 suite runs in the quarter (60 engineers, about 2.5 a week for 13 weeks), a sample finding 30 of each 71 minutes dead waiting — 58,500 minutes, 975 hours, 24 engineer-weeks at a 40-hour week.

The envelope itself was a judgement. Bellare capped debt at 21 per cent of net capacity — 126 engineer-weeks, the same share as bugs — because Table 2's 74 engineer-weeks of quarterly interest ruled out anything smaller, and a larger envelope would have cut features below half. The rule — ascending payback until the envelope is spent, refusing anything above four quarters — funds B and A, 108 engineer-weeks of the 126 available. The remaining 18 buy none of C's relief, because debt principal is lumpy: half a migration yields nothing. They went to features, recorded as an envelope deliberately underspent.

Step five: weight for probability on both sides. Ishira's feature estimates assume adoption, at a historical rate of 0.55. The debt case assumes the measured interest is actually reclaimed: 0.70 on Banavasi's record. Bets assume a hypothesis survives: three hits in Ishira's last fifteen, or 0.20.

The last column says something uncomfortable, though not about all three categories. Features at 2.20 and debt at 2.22 are the same number, about one per cent apart and well inside the error on any input, so nothing in Table 3 discriminates between them. Bets are not in that position: 2.40 sits about nine per cent above features and eight above debt. But their 0.20 is three hits in fifteen, a one-standard-error band of plus or minus 0.10, which puts the bet column anywhere between 1.20 and 3.60 — so that margin is not evidence either. What discriminates is each return's shape — a near-certain recurring saving, a one-in-five chance of something large, a dated commitment — and the fact that bugs are not in the choice set. The arithmetic disqualifies rather than ranks: Table 2's four-quarter cap rules out item D, and Table 3 rules out last quarter's 7.0 per cent share, which left 74 engineer-weeks of interest standing.

Step six: audit class membership before publishing. Every number above counts a class's members, so each class must be tested against its own definition; the bets are the one worked here. Ishira's four bets, 15 engineer-weeks each: goal-linked recurring deposits (kill criterion: under 8 per cent of a 20,000-user cohort create a second goal in six weeks) passes; a credit-line marketplace (under 3 per cent of 50,000 users reach a lender hand-off) passes; vernacular voice onboarding in Kannada and Marathi (under 25 per cent complete onboarding) passes; the UPI autopay reminder redesign fails, being already in a published quarterly objective with a dated ship commitment and no kill criterion. It is a feature, so bets fall from 60 engineer-weeks to 45 and features rise from 306 to 321.

4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

The practice rests on four testable claims; for Inthiram two are false.

C1: the categories can be measured after the fact to within about a tenth. True at Ishira, where time is logged against tagged work items. Partly true at Inthiram, where firmware time is logged against work orders, but the application figures were right about features and bugs and wrong about bets.

C2: capacity is fungible inside the envelope. True at Ishira, one stack and one rota. False at Inthiram, and this failure is what makes a blended percentage actively misleading rather than merely imprecise: 12 firmware engineers and 26 application engineers cannot substitute for each other.

C3: the period is long enough for the work to land and short enough to be re-decided. Thirteen weeks suits Ishira. False for Inthiram's firmware, where a BIS re-certification cycle runs about twenty weeks.

C4: at least one category's demand is exogenous. True for both, and what keeps the exercise honest: bugs arrive whether or not they are planned for.

Three situations make it misleading rather than merely rough. When the binding constraint is one scarce specialism, an organisation-wide percentage is an average no team experiences. When the period holds a dated external obligation, that claim is unbounded and the rest are percentages of a smaller base. In a team of six, one envelope is one person.

5. Hard edges

Inthiram shows this hard edge in its clearest form. Firmware's 120 net engineer-weeks must first fund the e-invoice conformance release and the BIS re-certification, 72 engineer-weeks carrying external dates, then 24 of debt, the over-the-air update reliability without which a bad release cannot be rolled back. That leaves 24 for features, against a costed firmware roadmap of 54. The application group, with 260 net, funds its whole feature demand of 182 after 52 for bugs and 26 for debt. Its bet column does not survive the membership test either: the 8 engineer-weeks held for a reorder-prediction model were already committed to a named distributor group, with no kill criterion, so those 8 sit inside the 182 as a feature and Inthiram's bet capacity is zero.

The other hard edges rhyme with it. In a multi-product company, per-product envelopes make cross-subsidy visible and one company envelope hides it. In a marketplace supply-side debt stays invisible in demand-side metrics for a year: allocate by side first, category second. In a regulated product — Inthiram under GST e-invoicing and drug-licensing rules, Ishira under RBI and SEBI requirements and the account aggregator framework — compliance is a fifth category with a date and an unbounded claim, and calling it a feature corrupts the feature number. In hardware plus software the scarce resource is certification and production windows, not engineer-weeks. In AI-native products debt is denominated in cash: an uncached inference path lands on an invoice, the easiest kind of debt to price and the easiest to under-fund.

At seams the envelope gets gamed rather than broken. A platform team's features are an application team's debt relief, so the same work lands in different categories either side of the seam and consolidated percentages mean nothing. What mature companies run, as against what they publish, is a standing exception process — so the real allocation is in that log.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

The denominator is most of the argument. Tell: percentages quoted over headcount. A fifth does not mean a fifth until leave, on-call and meetings are out: Ishira's gross-to-net haircut is 23.1 per cent.

Debt principal is lumpy, so an envelope is a ceiling and not a plan. Tell: the envelope is spent to the last engineer-week every quarter, which is back-filling, not discipline. Ishira's answer is 108 of 126, with 18 unspendable.

Interest must be measured, not inferred from a trend. Tell: the debt case rests on a feeling of slowness. Item B's 24 engineer-weeks rest on 1,950 counted runs; a cross-quarter comparison would have been confounded by hiring.

Probability weighting has to be symmetric. Tell: the bets are discounted and the features are not. Such a comparison has compared nothing, and the asymmetry tends to run one way, because only some categories have advocates who will state odds.

Debt's value is denominated in feature value, which makes it circular if you are careless. Tell: a debt case in rupees with no feature rate behind it. Table 3's 3.18 exists only because a feature engineer-week is worth 2.20, so an identical item is worth more in a growing product.

Bugs are a demand, so cutting their envelope buys a queue. Tell: open-defect count flat while median age rises. A flat count reads as keeping up; it is a team closing today's arrivals and never reaching June's.

Every category is a class, and classes are gameable. Tell: a bet with a launch date, an "enabler" with a customer name on it. A quarter of Ishira's stated bet capacity was not a bet, and Inthiram's was not 8 engineer-weeks but zero. A percentage over a mislabelled population is worse than none, because it looks defensible.

Published percentages work by being boring. Tell: the allocation changes more often than the strategy. A number re-decided each quarter commits to nothing; re-decided mid-quarter, it teaches the team to escalate in week seven.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Four differences are real. In consumer products a single defect is cheap and the aggregate is not, because ratings and uninstalls aggregate it; debt shows up as release cadence, which is why Ishira's slip to three-weekly moved the plan. In B2B and enterprise, bug demand concentrates in a few accounts and allocation is negotiated inside renewals, so the feature share is partly commercial. On platforms there is no feature category in the ordinary sense, so the split is capability, reliability and migration support. In hardware the envelope is denominated in certification windows; in AI products in cash, because inference spend per unit of work makes debt directly priceable.

Stage changes the mechanism's purpose rather than its arithmetic. Below fifteen engineers, publishing percentages is theatre and a work-in-progress limit does the job. Through the growth stage the published number is the practice's whole value, being the only thing that survives an angry customer. At scale the problem inverts: percentages are easy, the exception process hard. What does not differ by type or stage: the gross-to-net build-down, the lumpiness of principal, and bug capacity being a forecast.

8. Three worked quarters

Ishira Money, July 2026. Net 600 engineer-weeks; the plan in Figure 1 is features 321 (53.5 per cent), bugs 126 (21.0 per cent), debt 108 (18.0 per cent), bets 45 (7.5 per cent). The debt share more than doubled because 74 engineer-weeks of measured quarterly interest sat against a 42-engineer-week share.

Inthiram Retail Systems, July 2026. Net 380 engineer-weeks across two non-fungible groups. The blended 60 per cent target is missed by 22 engineer-weeks, and the 30 engineer-weeks of feature work that cannot be funded at all sit inside a group of twelve.

Ingita Labs, where it failed. Rajaram Bantakal's 18-engineer document-extraction company set a 25 per cent debt envelope in October 2025 and hit it for three consecutive quarters: 45 engineer-weeks a quarter out of 180 net, 135 in all. Median change lead time nonetheless rose from 6 days to 11, and inference cost per processed document from ₹1.90 to ₹2.60. The envelope had been met and the outcome had got worse, because the percentage was all anybody measured, so capacity went to the most legible debt — naming, module boundaries, lint — and the dearest items were never costed. The recovery, from July 2026, spent the same 45 engineer-weeks against measured interest: a regression-eval harness (principal 28, interest 19 a quarter, payback 1.47 quarters) and prompt caching with batching (principal 17), which took unit cost to ₹1.75 on 42 lakh documents a quarter — ₹109.2 lakh falling to ₹73.5 lakh, a recurring saving of ₹35.7 lakh. Landing at the end of the quarter it is built in, year one captures three quarters, ₹107.1 lakh, or an expected ₹74.97 lakh at Ishira's 0.70 weighting. The envelope was never the problem; the absent measurement was.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

The envelope is published and then funded out of the bug queue. Early sign: open defect count flat, median age rising. Diagnostic: what is the median age of an open priority-two defect, and what was it twelve weeks ago? Figure 3 prices catching it late: cutting the bug envelope from 126 to 84 engineer-weeks leaves 60.4 for fixes after triage, or 168 against a demand of 284 — 116 defects hidden in one quarter.

Debt chosen by legibility. Early sign: the funded items are the easiest to describe in a planning meeting. Diagnostic: what is each one's measured interest, and who measured it? Ingita Labs lost three quarters this way.

One blended envelope over a non-fungible organisation. Early sign: the company number is met while one group's queue grows. Diagnostic: which skill is binding, and what is its envelope? Late, it costs a dated regulatory commitment.

Re-deciding mid-period, or quietly relabelling. Early sign: more than one exception in a quarter, or a category mix that shifts while the work does not. Diagnostic: what did we publish, what did we spend, and does a membership test on ten random items hold? The cost is the mechanism itself, which no amount of republishing rebuilds.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether debt deserves a protected share at all. The single-queue position, at its strongest: a protected share admits you cannot price the work, and protecting unpriceable work guarantees the capacity goes to whatever is easiest to justify inside the protection — what happened at Ingita Labs. It rests on items like B, at a payback of 1.00, which would win any open contest. The envelope position, at its strongest: Ishira's figures put debt and features within about one per cent of each other, so an open contest is decided by advocacy, and features have the better advocates. It rests on last quarter's 7.0 per cent share, against interest now measured at 74 engineer-weeks. For the first to be wrong, debt's cost of delay would have to be no harder to measure than a feature's benefit; for the second, teams would have to spend a protected share well with no ledger.

Whether to publish the percentages company-wide. Publication buys durability and invites negotiation: once sales knows the feature share is 53.5 per cent, that is what gets lobbied against. The counter-case is that an unpublished envelope cannot be defended in the week it matters.

Whether the denominator is capacity or cash. Ingita's ₹35.7 lakh a quarter is the argument for cash; Table 3 is the argument against, since every rupee figure there rests on a feature rate that is itself an estimate.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this arrives with percentages. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a denominator, an interest ledger and a list of category definitions, and derives the percentages last rather than arguing them first. They report the envelope they underspent, because a ceiling honestly reported is worth more than a ceiling hit. They weight both sides of a comparison or neither. And they call their percentages a commitment device rather than a valuation, which lets them defend the number without claiming it is optimal.

12. What each of them decided

Bellare published 53.5 / 21.0 / 18.0 / 7.5 for the quarter to 30 September, committed to holding it for two quarters, named the 18 unspent engineer-weeks in the plan, and put the exception log beside the percentages. Her reason: 74 engineer-weeks of measured interest had been serviced with 42.

Bolar refused the single number. He published two envelopes, told the board the roadmap's firmware content was 54 engineer-weeks against a supply of 24, and asked it to choose between a contracted firmware team and a dropped commitment — while reclassifying the reorder-prediction model from a bet to a feature, which was, he argued, the more important of the two findings.

Discussion questions

  1. What would you have to believe about Ishira's interest measurement for the 18-engineer-week underspend to be the wrong answer, and what would you do with those 18 instead?
  2. Table 3 puts features and debt within about one per cent of each other and bets about nine per cent above features. Does that argue for a published envelope or against one, and which school does your answer commit you to?
  3. Inthiram's bet capacity is zero once the membership test is applied. Is that a finding about its allocation, its contracts or its definition of a bet — and which would you change?

13. Going deeper

  • Prioritising under constraints — the envelope is the constraint every ranking runs inside.
  • Prioritising platform work against features — the seam where consolidated percentages stop meaning anything.
  • Value vs effort — what Table 2's ledger disciplines.
  • RICE scoring — its confidence term is where the symmetry problem returns.
  • Kano model — why debt and bug work can be invisible in satisfaction research while dominating churn.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — the single-queue school's machinery.
  • Buy-a-feature — a budget game that makes a stakeholder feel an envelope.
  • User story mapping — how a feature envelope becomes a releasable slice.
exp20v2-prio.multi.stakeholder:
Prioritising across conflicting stakeholders

A case-style explainer: how one product head turned four rival rankings into one order that the losers could defend.

1. Four spreadsheets, one budget

On Monday 5 October 2026, Evneet Lalotra, head of product at Tolpa Systems, opened four spreadsheets in one sitting. Tolpa sells approval-workflow software to mid-sized manufacturers, with 210 customers and ₹38 crore of annual recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly subscription value of live contracts). Eight engineers were nominally free for the quarter, but maintenance, leave, on-call duty and the Diwali fortnight left 40 engineer-weeks for new features. Each spreadsheet ranked the same six items, and no two agreed.

Ekpreet Lakhtakia, vice-president of sales, put single sign-on (SSO, which lets a customer's staff log in with their company identity) first, citing five stalled deals worth ₹150 lakh. Eshnoor Lakhra, head of support, put bulk edit with undo first, citing 14 accounts and ₹90 lakh of ARR that had complained about it. Ekdev Lail, the engineering director, put replacement of the ageing job queue first. Evanjot Laroya, the chief executive, put a usage-billing dashboard first, as the precondition for a pricing change.

The six items together needed 45 engineer-weeks against 40 available, and the board would see the plan on Friday 16 October. If Evneet simply chose, three of four senior colleagues would conclude he had fixed the vote. If he averaged the lists, he would produce an order nobody had argued for. He needed a ranking that the people it disappointed could repeat.

2. The idea

Prioritising across conflicting stakeholders means producing one ordered list of work from several parties who each hold a different, legitimate view of what matters, and doing so in a way that the parties accept as fair even when they lose. The problem is that the inputs are incommensurable: sales speaks in deals, support in tickets, engineering in risk, leadership in strategy. Ranks cannot be added, because a rank says nothing about how much more one item matters than the next.

The ingredients are old. R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book on stakeholder management established that the parties with a claim on a firm are plural. Kenneth Arrow's 1951 impossibility theorem showed that no rule for merging several rank orders satisfies a short list of reasonable fairness conditions at once. Donald Reinertsen's cost-of-delay work, popularised from about 2009, supplied the remedy product teams now use: convert every claim to a common value, divide by cost, then rank.

The sentence Evneet could repeat without sounding glib was this: “We are not ranking functions, we are ranking claims, and every claim must carry a price, a probability and a name.”

3. How it actually works

The first step is the one practitioners skip: fix the capacity before anyone argues. Evneet announced 40 engineer-weeks, so every later debate was about how to spend a known sum rather than about whose request was legitimate. The second is to separate constraints from claims. A regulatory deadline or a contractual commitment is a constraint and enters the plan without a vote; everything else is a claim.

The third step translates each claim into one currency, here expected twelve-month value in ₹ lakh. A claim is a gross amount multiplied by a confidence, and confidence is a probability that the gross amount materialises. The fourth assigns each number an owner and a source: who supplied it, and from what evidence. The fifth divides expected value by engineer-weeks. The sixth ranks by that ratio and fills capacity from the top. The seventh changes the most doubtful input and records whether the order moves. The eighth writes down the dissent and a review date.

Before any numbers existed, Evneet printed the four rankings side by side, shown below, so each executive could see the disagreement was symmetrical.

Item (engineer-weeks)SalesSupportEngineeringLeadershipRank sum
A. Single sign-on (10)145212
B. Bulk edit with undo (6)512614
C. New job queue (12)651315
D. Usage-billing dashboard (8)464115

F. Mobile approvals (4)326516
Total / sum2121212184

Rank 1 is first choice. Each column is a permutation of 1 to 6, so it sums to 21; four columns give 84.

Summing ranks, the oldest voting device, ties A with E at 12 and C with D at 15, and puts mobile approvals last although sales and support both rank it in their top three. It also hides one fact: audit-log export sits in three of the four top-three lists, and no item sits in all four.

4. A worked example, with a second pass

Each owner now converted their claim into the common currency. The table sets out gross value, confidence and its source, expected value, cost and the ratio. Evneet insisted that confidence come from a track record where one existed.

Expected = gross x confidence; value per week = expected / weeks. Total row sums columns only.

Ranking by value per week gives B (7.50), E (6.40), A (6.00), F (4.50), D (3.75), C (3.50). Filling 40 weeks from the top: B takes 6, E brings the total to 11, A to 21, F to 25, D to 33. C needs 12 and would reach 45, so it does not fit. The plan uses 33 weeks and captures 60 + 45 + 32 + 18 + 30 = 185 lakh of the 227 on offer, or 81.5 per cent. Seven weeks stay unspent.

Now change one input. On Wednesday 7 October the queue stalled again, the second incident in four months. Ekdev raised his twelve-month probability of a serious outage from 0.60 to 0.90, a judgement, not a measurement. Expected value for C becomes 70 x 0.90 = 63 lakh and its ratio 63 / 12 = 5.25, which lifts it above F, D. The fill now runs B 6, E 11, A 21, C 33, F 37; D would reach 45, so it drops out. The plan uses 37 weeks and captures 60 + 45 + 32 + 63 + 18 = 218 of 248 lakh, or 87.9 per cent. One number moved and the chief executive’s item left the quarter. That is why the table, not the ranking, is the deliverable.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Ranks cannot be averaged, only valued

Arrow’s result is the formal version of what the rank-sum table showed: two ties and a last place for mobile approvals that only engineering gave it.

Magnitude and confidence are different questions

Sales asked for credit on ₹150 lakh; history supported 0.40 of it. Ask each owner for both, and take confidence from a base rate, here 2 deals in 5, before conviction.

Ratios are a heuristic, not an optimum

Ranking by value per week approximates the best use of a fixed budget but ignores indivisibility and dependencies. In the first pass seven weeks were left unspent because the next item needed twelve, and an exact fill would have taken C instead of D: 197 lakh, not 185. If B depended on A, the sequence would change though the ratios did not.

Expected value flatters or punishes tail risks

Item C is insurance. An expected loss avoided of 42 lakh (63 after the revision) conceals a distribution in which most years are quiet and one is ruinous. If the firm cannot survive that year, the item is a constraint, not a claim, and enters the plan before the arithmetic.

The method cannot say the numbers are right

A transparent ledger exposes weak inputs; it does not repair them. The chief executive’s 0.25 has no history behind it. Nor can it say whether strategy is sound: if Evanjot is right that pricing is the bottleneck, D is a bet whose value a ratio understates.

It is not RICE, WSJF or MoSCoW

RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort), weighted shortest job first and must-should-could sorting are containers. The discipline here is upstream: who owns each number, where it came from, what moves it. Taught as vocabulary, without forcing a choice, they become decoration.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In B2B products, as at Tolpa, the stakeholders include customers’ staff reached through sales and support, and a loud single account can dominate; the guard is to require named accounts and a track-record confidence. In consumer products the users are not in the room and rarely have a spokesperson, so the conflicts are among internal goals such as growth, monetisation and trust, and the common currency is usually a behavioural metric measured in experiments rather than rupees promised in deals.

In a marketplace the conflict is structural. A change that helps suppliers, such as lower fees, costs buyers or the platform, and the ledger needs a column for each side because one side’s gain is the other’s loss. Stage matters as much. In a six-person seed-stage company the founder decides and the ritual compresses into an hour. In a large firm, capacity itself is negotiated across teams, and the dissent log matters because the people who disagree will be in the room again.

7. Common mistakes

Scoring to a preordained answer

Symptom: the output always matches what the most senior person wanted, and weights get adjusted after the first run. Misunderstanding: the model is a persuasion tool, not a test. Cheapest diagnostic: write down the expected top three before computing, and count how often the result surprises you. A model that never surprises is decoration.

Negotiating positions rather than claims

Symptom: the order tracks who spoke last or who is more senior, and the debate is about rank, not numbers. Misunderstanding: stakeholders are treated as voters instead of sources of evidence. Diagnostic: look at the top three items and ask whether each has a gross figure, a confidence source and a named owner. Any blank is the next argument.

Treating the order as final

Symptom: the same fight reopens within a month and the losing function stops attending. Misunderstanding: the ranking is read as a verdict instead of a decision under stated assumptions. Diagnostic: find the flip condition. If the document does not say which input, if changed, would reorder the list, nobody knows when to reopen it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision looks quiet. Evneet circulates the ledger two working days before the meeting, with every claim written in its owner’s own words and signed off by that owner. The meeting argues only three or four cells, the ones where the confidence source is judgement and the ratio sits within a rank of its neighbour. The order is adopted with each function’s dissent recorded in one sentence, the flip condition named (the outage probability: above 0.643 C displaces D) and a review date set. Losing executives can explain why their item missed using a number they supplied.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Friday 9 October, Evneet took the second-pass plan: bulk edit, audit-log export, SSO, the job queue and mobile approvals, 37 weeks, with 3 held in reserve. He told Evanjot plainly that the billing dashboard fell out because it had the lowest value per week once the job queue’s ratio rose, and its 0.25 rested on no history, unlike the 0.40, 0.50 and 0.80 that carried base rates, and offered a two-week spike to test pricing demand. Evanjot objected, was recorded, and took the spike.

To go further, study negotiation for product managers, since the ledger ends in a conversation, and prioritising under constraints, which covers dependencies and tail risk more fully than this page could.

Two questions to sit with. First, which number in your own backlog is held with most conviction and least evidence, and who owns it? Second, if the person who lost the last prioritisation round were asked to explain the result, could they do it without mentioning anyone’s seniority?
exp40v2-prio.multi.stakeholder:
Prioritising across conflicting stakeholders

One ranking from five functions that want five different ones — and what makes it defensible rather than merely final.

1Two rooms, four weeks apart

On Thursday 14 May 2026, Gurjot Mankotia had ninety minutes and six candidate items. Mankotia ran product for the claims platform at Veraya Systems, an enterprise software firm with ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue across 148 paying insurer accounts, a mean of ₹64.9 lakh each. Veraya's three delivery squads had together completed 418, 425 and 431 story points in the preceding three quarters; for the quarter beginning 1 July, Gurnaam Mattu, the VP of engineering, committed 420 — 1.1 per cent below that three-quarter mean of 424.7. The six items cost 720 points.

Govindraj Malhi, the chief revenue officer, wanted a bulk claims import API, priced at ₹7.2 crore of blocked pipeline across four deals. Gayana Mander, who owned support and customer success, wanted an audit-trail export demanded by six accounts whose renewals fell inside the quarter, together worth ₹11.4 crore of the ₹96 crore book, or 11.9 per cent — and a permissions editor her two teams had asked for thirty-one times. Mattu wanted a queue re-architecture scoped at 110 points in January and now 180, a factor of 1.64. Gulnaz Madahar, the chief executive, wanted an adjudication copilot.

Twenty-eight days later, on Thursday 11 June, Geetha Mehrok faced the same problem with a harder edge. Mehrok was head of product at Vireo Instruments, maker of connected benchtop analysers: 2,400 units across 760 diagnostic laboratories, a mean of 3.2 each. Vireo's firmware train had one factory cut-in before the fiscal year closed, on Friday 4 September; the next fell 182 days later, on 5 March 2027. Code freeze was Friday 17 July — five clear weeks away, with three firmware engineers and one engineer-week already committed to a certification re-test. Fourteen engineer-weeks, then, against three items wanting twenty-four. Mehrok's conflict was about which two of three things fitted.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the problem precisely. Prioritising across conflicting stakeholders is the production of a single ordering over scarce delivery capacity from parties holding different objective functions, different beliefs about the same facts, or different views about who may decide — such that the ordering survives challenge by any one of them. The last clause is the whole difficulty: any ordering can be produced, but one that survives challenge is a different artefact.

The intellectual history runs down two tracks that practitioners conflate. The first is decision-analytic: Keeney and Raiffa's Decisions with Multiple Objectives (1976) and Saaty's Analytic Hierarchy Process (1980) made a choice over several attributes explicit by eliciting weights and scoring options against them. Every modern scheme — RICE, weighted shortest job first, the value-versus-effort grid — is a descendant, usually impoverished. The second track, social choice, bites harder. Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951) proves no rule for aggregating individual rankings into a group ranking satisfies a short list of innocuous conditions at once; Gibbard and Satterthwaite showed any non-trivial rule can be manipulated by a participant who misreports. Weighted scoring does not escape Arrow: it chooses, and conceals, a dictator.

Four positions follow, all genuinely held. The scoring school will sign that a published weight vector beats a manager's unexamined judgement; not that the weights measure value. The social-choice sceptics will sign that every scoring model smuggles in a dictator and that a disclosed rule invites gaming; not that the product manager should therefore decide alone. The negotiation school, descended from Fisher and Ury and Hohmann's buy-a-feature games, will sign that a stakeholder who spends a scarce token has conceded the items they did not buy; not that the bargain maximises value. The constraint school, after Reinertsen, will sign that most stakeholder conflict is an artefact of undeclared capacity; not that cost of delay is measurable for platform work.

3Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has five steps. The first and fourth are left implicit, and are where the work is.

Figure 1. Five intake lanes converge on one translation step; translation feeds the score, the score the frontier, the frontier the negotiation, and only the negotiation the published order. The single return arrow runs from that order back to the weights, never to one item's score.

Step one is translation. In the six weeks from 20 March to 1 May 2026, Veraya logged 212 requests from 63 named people; 141 mapped onto one of six shortlisted options and 71 duplicated one another or described something already shipped. The import API drew 38 of the 141 mapped requests, 27.0 per cent, and was on that measure the most-requested item on the board — filed by eleven people, nine in sales. The permissions editor drew 31 requests from twenty-seven people. A share of requests is not a share of requesters, and neither is a share of revenue.

Second, the shape of the change: the transfer moved 0.10 from one criterion to exactly one other, so each score shifts by 0.10 times the gap between its strategy and ARR scores and by nothing else.
