Step three converts score into a plan, and most arguments never reach it. The six options cost 720 points against 420 available. Filling in score order — A, E, F, stop — consumes 370 points for 9.05 of weighted value, 50 idle. Filling by score per point — B, F, E, C — consumes 390 for 11.15, 23.2 per cent more value from the same quarter. Full enumeration of all sixty-three subsets confirms 11.15 is the maximum at 420 points under weighting 1, and that two sets reach it: {B, C, E, F} at 390 points and {A, B, C, F} at 410. The optimum is not unique, and the two sets differ precisely on A versus E, the pair that tied at 3.05. The arithmetic has narrowed the decision to the one choice it cannot make — and only under this weighting, since under weighting 2 the optimum is the single set {B, C, E, F} at 11.45.

That is step four, and why the negotiation school is not wrong: the frontier hands back a slack region, and the bargain belongs inside it rather than over the whole board. Step five is publication of the order, the weights and what did not fit.

4When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each testable. One: capacity is genuinely scarce and roughly known. Veraya passes — 720 points of demand against 420 committed, 1.71 to 1. Vireo passes equally, not harder: twenty-four engineer-weeks against fourteen is the same 1.71 to 1. Only when the mandatory labelling change leaves the contest, as condition Two requires, does Vireo's ratio widen, to twenty against ten. Two: the options are substitutes competing for the same capacity. Veraya passes. Vireo partly fails: the labelling change is a legal precondition for shipping anything, not a candidate, and takes four of the fourteen weeks before scoring begins. Three: the disagreement is about preference rather than fact. Veraya fails on two items, as below. Four: the decision repeats, so a disclosed rule accumulates credibility. Veraya passes quarterly; Vireo nearly fails, since cut-ins 182 days apart give it two shots a year, so each decision carries more weight and gaming has longer to pay off.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where one stakeholder holds a veto — a regulator, a safety function, a platform owner who can decline — a weighted score dressed up as a decision invites that veto to be exercised late and at maximum cost. Where capacity is not actually fixed, scoring suppresses the better question, whether to buy more. And where the conflict is about authority, scoring is a category error: it answers "what is worth most" when the room asks "who gets to say".

5Hard edges, and what mature firms really do

Classify the disputes, not the people. A preference conflict is agreement on facts with different objective functions; a belief conflict is agreement on the objective with different forecasts; an authority conflict is disagreement about who decides. Applied to Veraya's six: B and C are preference conflicts, since nobody disputes that six renewals are at risk or that twenty-seven people filed thirty-one requests for the editor; the dispute is ranking renewal protection against new revenue. A and E are belief conflicts: the ₹7.2 crore of pipeline is four deals at a mean of ₹1.80 crore, and at Veraya's historical 31 per cent close rate from that stage the expectation is ₹2.23 crore, a factor of 3.2 apart; the copilot's 5 on strategy is assertion without measurement. D is an authority conflict, Mattu holding that platform sequencing is engineering's to set. F is no conflict: it is the only option no criterion scored 1 or 5. Two preference, two belief, one authority, one uncontested — not every item on a contested board is contested.

The seams are worse than the items. In multi-product firms conflict relocates to shared platform teams, where an item's weighted score is undefined because its criteria belong to other products' P&Ls. In two-sided marketplaces the decisive parties are absent: supply and demand have no vice-president, so whoever owns the supply metric argues for them and wins. In regulated and hardware contexts the binding constraint is a date nobody controls, which is a mercy: a cut-in converts a preference fight into a feasibility fact. In AI-native products the points column is itself a disputed forecast. What mature firms do, as against what their documents say, is pre-allocate, keeping the central model for the remainder.

6Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

The weight vector is a position, not a measurement. The tell is timing: weights get revised after a ranking is revealed, as Madahar's were. The obvious reading is that the first weights were wrong. The expert reading is that they were never beliefs about value, so arguing their accuracy concedes the frame.

A weight transfer is one-dimensional. The tell is an option that does not move when the weights do — F, at 2.95 under both vectors. Novices read robustness; it is arithmetic. Moving 0.10 from ARR to strategy shifts each option by 0.10 times its strategy-minus-ARR gap. F's gap is zero.

Requests, requesters and revenue are three bases. The tell is an option with many requests from few filers — A's 38 from eleven people. Reading that as highest demand confuses intensity with breadth: C had fewer requests and nearly two and a half times as many requesters.

The decision lives in the score-per-point column. The tell is a room arguing the score column while the plan is set by the ratio. A's density of 0.0203 is second lowest of the six; only D's 0.0128 is worse. The item fought over hardest was close to the worst buy.

Capacity is the stakeholder nobody invited. The tell is behavioural: give a stakeholder the real number and they stop arguing rank and start arguing the number. That is progress — it is among the few claims in the room auditable against last quarter.

Ties are information. The tell is a tiebreak criterion invented during the meeting. A and E tying at 3.05 under weighting 1, with the frontier's two optimal sets differing on exactly that pair, says the model has done all it can there. An expert hands the tie to the negotiation; a competent practitioner buries it under a new criterion.

Belief conflicts resist preference instruments. The tell is a stakeholder who absorbs more evidence and does not move. Re-weighting cannot settle whether ₹7.2 crore of pipeline is real; only a cheap test or a written trigger can. A scoring workshop here yields consensus about procedure and none about fact.

Platform work is structurally under-represented. The tell is in the intake: engineering filed 28 requests from seven people — fewer than sales, support or customer success — while its item carried the highest platform score, a 5 no other option reaches, and the worst density. Scoring rewards items with external claimants; nobody files a ticket for a queue.

7Where the practice genuinely differs

Exhibit 3. Where the mechanism genuinely changes.
ContextWhat actually changes
ConsumerConflict is between metrics, not functions. Weighting is real work, negotiation light.
B2B and enterpriseNamed accounts arm stakeholders with evidence, so belief conflicts dominate and need triggers, not weights.
Platform and marketplaceThe decisive parties are absent; pre-allocating capacity by side beats scoring.
Hardware and physical goodsCut-in dates bind absolutely. Feasibility replaces preference.
AI productsThe points column is a live forecast; scores look firm while costs move.

Stage changes less than is claimed. At seed scale the mechanism is a founder and a weighted model is theatre; what matters is that the rejected list exists. From thirty to three hundred people the model does real work, because functions exist and capacity is newly scarce. Above that the honest pattern is pre-allocation plus a contested remainder. One asserted difference is not real: large firms are no more rigorous about weights than small ones, only about the capacity number — where rigour pays.

8Three worked examples

One: the frontier beats the ranking. The score-ordered plan {A, E, F} spends 370 of Veraya's 420 points for 9.05 of weighted value; the density-ordered plan {B, C, E, F} spends 390 for 11.15, both under weighting 1 — same weights, same scores, 23.2 per cent more value, the difference lying entirely in the order of filling.

Two: the constraint settles it at Vireo. Mehrok's three items were a mandatory labelling change at four engineer-weeks, a self-diagnostic at nine and reagent tracking at eleven, against fourteen available. Labelling plus self-diagnostic is thirteen and fits; labelling plus reagent tracking is fifteen and does not. The commercial case looked one-sided. For reagent tracking, Gopeshwar Multani's channel forecast 180 placements a year at ₹2.6 lakh of gross margin each, ₹4.68 crore. For the self-diagnostic, Gurditta Mahey's saving of 22 per cent of 3,120 annual field visits — about 686 visits at ₹14,200 each, or ₹97.4 lakh a year, 4.8 times smaller. But Vireo's last three launches delivered 41 per cent of the channel's pre-launch forecast, at which the module is worth 74 placements and ₹1.92 crore a year, still 2.0 times the saving. Arithmetic favoured reagent tracking; capacity forbade it.

Exhibit 4. Veraya's January 2026 buy-a-feature round: five functions, 100 tokens each, an item clearing only if pledges reach its price. Prices are in tokens, set against a 500-token pool, and are not story points.
OptionPriceTokens pledgedCleared?
A bulk import API180185yes
B audit-trail export12060no
C permissions editor140145yes
D queue re-architecture16095no
E adjudication copilot9015no
F mobile adjuster app500no
Total7405002 of 6

Three: the failure, and the recovery. In January, Veraya ran the round above. Sales put all 100 tokens on A; Madahar added 85, taking it to 185 and clearing it. Support put 100 on C, customer success 40, Mattu 5 — 145, cleared. Clearing bought Q1 capacity, not completion: C's first phase shipped in March and A delivered only its single-file path, so both returned to the May board as remainders, C at 110 points and A at 150. Engineering's remaining 95 went to the queue work, 65 short of its 160 price, and no function would coalition with it. The mechanism worked as designed and produced a bad outcome: buy-a-feature prices options and does not price risk. Across February and March the queue failed three times: 41 hours of degraded service across 23 accounts, ₹38 lakh in SLA credits at a mean of ₹1.65 lakh per account, and the queue work re-scoped from 110 points to 180. The recovery was not a better auction. In April Mankotia ring-fenced 20 per cent of capacity — 84 of 420 points — as a platform floor decided before any scoring, splitting the queue work into an 84-point write-path isolation and a 96-point remainder. One tempting lesson was discarded: monthly support tickets fell from 2,940 to 2,810 after C shipped, 130 against a monthly SD of 190 over the preceding eight months — 0.68 of an SD, not a finding.

Figure 3. Scale: 1 story point = 1 px, rule 0 to 420, ticks every 60; dashed blocks are idle capacity. Both optimum packings reach 11.15 under weighting 1 and differ only on A versus E. The chosen plan spends 84 points on the platform floor first, so its scored items reach 8.75.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Weight-shopping. Sign: a request to revisit criteria a day after the ranking circulates. Diagnostic: would you have proposed this weight before you saw the order? Caught late, the model loses authority and seniority decides.

Scoring a belief conflict. Sign: a raw score the owner cannot source. Diagnostic: what measurement produced this 5, and when? Caught late, Veraya spends 150 points on a ₹7.2 crore claim worth ₹2.23 crore in expectation.

Ranking without capacity. Sign: a prioritised list with no cumulative cost column. Diagnostic: at what line does the quarter run out? Caught late, the top five all start and none finishes.

Silent platform starvation. Sign: platform items in every intake and in no plan for two quarters. Diagnostic: what did we defer, and what has it cost? Veraya's late catch cost ₹38 lakh of credits and 70 extra points.

Consensus theatre. Sign: everyone agrees and nothing is cut. Diagnostic: name the item each function gave up. If nobody can, the meeting ratified a list instead of choosing.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Disclose the weights, or do not. The disclosure case: stakeholders who can see the rule argue the rule rather than the outcome, and the rule is the better thing to argue about. Its evidence is the collapse of one-off escalations once weights are published; it is wrong if submissions degrade, and Gibbard–Satterthwaite says they should. The concealment case: scores stay honest when nobody knows the exchange rate, and the manager keeps slack to do the right thing. Its evidence is score drift in disclosed schemes; it is wrong if concealment reads as favouritism, which it reliably does after the second surprise.

One global ranking, or capacity shares. The global case: only a single frontier reveals that score-ordering leaves 18.8 per cent of attainable value unspent, and shares guarantee a locally rational, globally poor plan. The shares case: most inter-functional conflict is not resolvable and consumes senior attention out of proportion to the stake, so partition capacity, let each owner rank within it, and argue only over the remainder. It fails where items are complements rather than substitutes.

Cost of delay, or weighted score. The cost-of-delay camp holds that weights are preferences while delay cost is money, and that pricing delay dissolves the argument. Its weakness is Vireo's: the channel's ₹4.68 crore and the realised ₹1.92 crore are both delay costs, and choosing between them is a belief, not a measurement. Nobody has shown how to price a platform item's delay, which is why Veraya's floor was administrative rather than computed.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a scoring template and runs the meeting. Someone who has internalised it arrives with the capacity number verified against the last three quarters, and spends the meeting on two questions: which disputes are about facts, and where the frontier leaves slack. They publish ties rather than break them, state the base of a count before using it, read a request to re-weight as information about the requester, and keep the rejected list, because next quarter's credibility is built from this quarter's rejections. And they can say without defensiveness which parts of the order the model decided and which parts they did — a distinction the competent practitioner blurs by accident.

12What they decided

Mankotia funded the 84-point platform floor first, then B, E and F — 364 of 420 points, 8.75 of weighted value, with 56 points held as a declared buffer. That 8.75 is the most the 336 points outside the floor can buy, reached here and by {A, B, F}; the floor itself carries no weighted value, because D's 2.30 prices all 180 points of the queue work rather than the 84 funded. The reasoning: the floor was a standing April commitment, not re-litigable in May; B protected ₹11.4 crore of renewals falling inside the quarter; and A, rather than being rejected, became a conditional, taking the first 150 points of the following quarter if two of its four deals reach a stage Veraya closes at better than 31 per cent. Of the 63 filers, 48 attended a review session and 41 signed the published order; inclusion and exclusion put the floor at 26 who did both, and the figure was 37, four signatories having attended neither.

Mehrok took labelling and the self-diagnostic, thirteen of fourteen engineer-weeks, and moved reagent tracking to the 5 March 2027 cut-in. Multani received the 41 per cent realisation figure in writing with an offer: fund a six-month pilot in three laboratories, and the forecast becomes a measurement before the next train leaves.

  1. The chosen plan delivers 8.75, against 11.15 with no floor. Was the floor worth that 2.40 of weighted value, and what evidence would settle it?
  2. A and E tie at 3.05 under one weighting and part by 0.20 under the other. Which weighting should Veraya publish, and who may propose the next change to it?
  3. Vireo's constraint decided its question. What would Mehrok have done differently had the next cut-in fallen six weeks later rather than 182 days later?

13Going deeper

  • Prioritising under constraints — the capacity number, without which scoring has nothing to pack against.
  • Negotiation for PMs — the instrument for step four; unlocks trades no weighting can express.
  • Value vs effort — ancestor of the score-per-point column; shows why ratios beat ranks.
  • RICE scoring — a weight vector hidden inside a formula; shows what disclosure costs.
  • Kano model — must-haves against delighters, which is how Vireo's labelling change stops being a candidate.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — section 3's machinery, plus cost of delay as an alternative numerator.
  • Buy-a-feature — the mechanism that failed in example three; study what it cannot price.
  • User story mapping — exposes the complements that item-level scoring breaks apart, where capacity shares fail.
exp20v2-prio.kill.decisions:
Killing features and projects

When do we stop something we have already spent a quarter on?

1. A Monday review at Rivaaz

On Monday 12 October 2026, Charanya Jandu, head of product at Rivaaz Home Services, a marketplace that sends plumbers, electricians and cleaners to homes in four Indian cities, sat down with Cavita Johar, her finance partner, and Charandeep Jaswal, who led engineering for a project called Smart Scheduling. It matched each booking to the technician predicted to arrive on time. Eleven people had worked on it since 6 July. The quarter had cost ₹120 lakh.

The kickoff document, dated 6 July, carried a kill criterion: a defined result that, if missed, forces a review of whether to stop. Smart Scheduling had to cut the failed-visit rate by at least 1.5 percentage points in a pilot. A failed visit is one where the job is not completed in the promised slot because someone is absent or more than thirty minutes late. The pilot ran from 14 September to 4 October. Control bookings failed at 9.0 per cent; Smart Scheduling bookings at 8.1 per cent. The criterion was missed.

Charandeep wanted another six weeks. Finishing needed ₹60 lakh more, and 1,800 technicians in the pilot cities had already been told the feature was coming. Stopping meant writing off ₹120 lakh. What she decided would show the company whether a kill criterion was a rule or a decoration. Her own view at the start of the meeting was that the pilot looked encouraging, and she distrusted that feeling for exactly that reason: she had sponsored the project in June.

Exhibit 1 draws the problem. The long grey bar is the past. The short bar is the future, and its orange slice is a data pipeline that Rivaaz must harden whether or not Smart Scheduling lives. The rest of this page is about why the grey bar must not influence the review, and why the orange slice must not be counted as a saving.

2. The idea

Killing a feature or project means stopping work already approved and under way, because a forward-looking comparison now favours something else. The discipline was invented to counter escalation of commitment, the tendency to pour more into a failing course because so much has gone in already. Barry Staw documented it in 1976; Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer showed in 1985 that theatre-season subscribers who paid full price attended more performances early in the season than those given a discount, having been randomly assigned to price. Robert Cooper's Stage-Gate process, developed through the 1980s, built the remedy into product development: scheduled Go/Kill gates with criteria agreed beforehand.

Charanya could say it in one sentence: “We are not deciding whether the last quarter was wasted; we are deciding what the next ₹46 lakh of avoidable spend should buy.” Three kinds of money need separating, and most arguments about killing are really arguments about which kind a given figure is. Mixing them is what makes stopping feel like a loss.

Kind of moneyExample at RivaazIn the forward ledger?
Sunk: spent, unrecoverable under any choiceThe ₹120 lakhNever
Unavoidable: still to be spent under any choicePipeline hardening, ₹14 lakhCancels between options
Avoidable: spent only if the option is chosenBuild ₹30 lakh, rollout ₹16 lakhYes

3. How it works

The mechanics have five steps, and practitioners usually leave the second and fourth implicit. The table follows Charanya through them.

StepQuestionAt Rivaaz
1Did a pre-agreed trigger fire?0.9-point gain against 1.5 required
2How noisy is the evidence?Interval from −0.1 to +1.9 points
3What is avoidable cost from today?₹46 lakh, not ₹60 lakh
4What is the best use of that money and team?Repeat-booking nudges
5Who is told what, and when?Technicians, customers, team

Step 2 matters because 486 failures in 6,000 treated bookings against 540 in 6,000 control bookings is 54 fewer failures, and a gap that size could appear by chance. The standard error of the difference is about 0.51 points, so a 95 per cent confidence interval, the range of true effects consistent with the data, runs from −0.1 to +1.9 points. It contains zero and it contains the 1.5 target. The pilot neither proved nor disproved the feature. It converted an argument into a probability. A common habit is to read a missed target as proof of failure or a near miss as proof of promise; the interval says neither.

Step 3 is where money is usually mis-stated. Killing Smart Scheduling saves the build and the rollout, ₹46 lakh. The ₹14 lakh pipeline work is still done, because the alternative needs it too. Step 4 supplies the comparison, since stopping is rarely compared with nothing: it is compared with what the freed team does next.

4. A worked example

Cavita priced twelve months after launch. Smart Scheduling would run in the four cities, which together take 40,000 bookings a month, 4,80,000 a year. A 1.5-point cut in failed visits saves 7,200 visits, and at ₹1,100 contribution each (revenue less direct costs of a completed visit) that is ₹79.2 lakh. The alternative, repeat-booking nudges that remind customers to rebook, would add about 6,000 bookings at ₹1,500 contribution: ₹90.0 lakh. Both benefits are weighted by the chance of delivery, which is expected value. The probabilities are judgements: 50 per cent for scheduling given the pilot, 70 per cent for nudges, which a manual WhatsApp test had supported.

Exhibit 2. Forward ledger, ₹ lakh. The ₹120 lakh already spent appears nowhere.
LineA: ContinueB: Stop, build nudges
Finish scheduling build300
Technician rollout160
Pipeline hardening1414
Nudges build040
Total forward cost6054
Benefit if delivered79.290.0
Chance of delivery50%70%
Expected benefit39.663.0
Net: expected benefit less cost−20.4+9.0

Option B wins by ₹29.4 lakh. Notice what a careless reader would do: put the ₹120 lakh against option B as a “write-off”. It is in both futures, so it differs by nothing. Now change one input: the chance of delivery for scheduling, from 50 to 90 per cent.

Exhibit 3. Second pass: only A's chance of delivery changes, ₹ lakh.
LineA at 50%A at 90%B
Expected benefit39.671.2863.0
Net−20.4+11.28+9.0
A minus B−29.4+2.28–

The answer flips. Exhibit 4 plots it: A's net value rises with its probability, B's is flat, and the lines cross at 87.1 per cent (₹69.0 lakh of needed benefit, divided by ₹79.2 lakh). Continuing is right only if one believes scheduling is better than 87 times in a hundred. A pilot whose 1.5-point target lies 1.2 standard errors above the observed gap does not support that belief.

5. Nuances a learner must hold

Sunk, committed and avoidable are different

A signed, non-cancellable vendor contract is not yet spent but is unavoidable, so it behaves like sunk money. A cancellable one is avoidable. The test is whether the choice changes the spend, not whether the money has left the bank.

Spent money can still be informative

The ₹120 lakh bought a pilot, a pipeline and a prediction model. Those assets enter the forward ledger as value they can still produce, never as a debt owed.

Kill, pause and pivot are not the same

A pause keeps a team half-assigned and a feature half-remembered, so it carries holding costs. A pivot keeps the problem and changes the solution. Name which one you mean, because each has a different owner and a different date on which the team gets its time back.

A trigger starts a review; it does not end one

Kill criteria exist because people judge their own work badly. But a missed number with an interval this wide justifies a decision meeting, and the meeting must still price alternatives.

The probability is a judgement

Fifty per cent was not measured. Exhibit 4 therefore matters more than Exhibit 2: it shows how far the judgement would have to move. At the observed 0.9 points, benefit would be 4,80,000 × 0.009 × ₹1,100 = ₹47.52 lakh. On the ledger's basis A would then net 47.52 − 60 = −₹12.48 lakh against B's +₹9.0 lakh, so even certainty at the observed gap loses by ₹21.48 lakh.

Killing needs a named alternative

Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone use of the same resources. Without a named alternative, killing is merely pessimism.

The builders should not be the sole judges

Charandeep was candid, and still the person least able to see the pilot as a loss. Put the gate decision with someone whose bonus does not depend on the answer.

Not saying no, and not sunsetting

Saying no happens at intake, when little is lost. Sunsetting retires something customers already use. Killing sits between: work in flight, not yet in anyone's hands.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

SettingWhat makes killing different
ConsumerFew promises are made, so killing is cheap; the danger is cheap experiments that never end
B2BRoadmap promises sit in contracts, so goodwill and penalties are real avoidable costs of killing
MarketplaceBoth sides were told; at Rivaaz 1,800 technicians expected the feature, so supply trust belongs in the ledger

Size matters as well. A start-up with eight engineers kills quickly because the founder holds every fact; its risk is killing too late, from attachment. A large company has a portfolio, so a kill is a reallocation with an obvious destination; its risk is zombie projects that no committee owns. Rivaaz, with eleven people on one project, is in the middle. Both extremes share one remedy: the review date and the kill criterion are fixed when the work is approved, while everyone is still neutral about the outcome.

7. Common mistakes

Counting the past

Symptom: reviews open with cumulative spend. Misunderstanding: that stopping “wastes” it. Diagnostic: ask whether the team would approve the remaining ₹46 lakh of avoidable spend today, starting from zero.

Counting a saving that cannot happen

Symptom: a kill case claims the full remaining budget. Misunderstanding: that every line is optional. Diagnostic: list which lines continue under the other option; here ₹14 lakh does.

Moving the threshold

Symptom: the criterion at the review differs from the kickoff document. Misunderstanding: that a criterion is an opening bid in a negotiation. Diagnostic: compare the dated file with the slide shown at review.

Starving instead of deciding

Symptom: the project is never cancelled, but staffing drifts away. Misunderstanding: that avoiding the conversation is kinder than having it. Diagnostic: compare planned and actual headcount for the last six weeks.

8. What good looks like

Good handling had the criterion written on 6 July, with the pilot design and an independent reviewer named. At review, the interval and the break-even probability are shown beside the point estimate; the forward ledger omits ₹120 lakh. The decision is made in the meeting and announced to the team within a day, with a reopening condition, so the team hears reasons rather than rumours. Technicians who were promised a feature hear first, from a person, with the reason and what replaces it. The engineers hear that the pilot was well run, which is true, and that the work on the pipeline continues, which is also true. Nobody is told the quarter was wasted, because the pilot bought information.

9. What Charanya decided

She stopped the build and rollout, kept the pipeline work, and moved the team to nudges. The reasoning was Exhibit 4: continuing required believing in an 87.1 per cent chance of success that a pilot whose target sits 1.2 standard errors above its result could not support. She wrote one reopening condition: if a further pilot's 95 per cent interval lay wholly above 1.5 points, scheduling returns. Technicians were told first, in person, in group sessions in the pilot cities. Charandeep asked for the interval to be kept in the written decision so that nobody could later claim the pilot had shown the feature did not work; it had shown only that Rivaaz could not yet tell.

Next, read about sunsetting a product or feature, which applies the same forward discipline to something customers already use, and about saying no, because killing is saying no to yourself.

Questions to sit with. First: which line of the last project you stopped was truly avoidable, and which only looked it? Second: who, in your organisation, could declare a project dead without losing something personally?
exp40v2-prio.kill.decisions:
Killing features and projects

Sunk-cost discipline, kill criteria, and the arithmetic of stopping something already in flight.

1. Two rooms, October 2026

On Wednesday 14 October 2026, at Sutlej Systems in Pune, Dhwanit Kalra opened the quarterly portfolio review with a number he then refused to mention again. Sutlej sells production-management software to mid-market discrete manufacturers: 412 customers, ₹78 crore of annual recurring revenue. Since 6 January its Maintenance Advisor project — eleven people, predictive maintenance on vibration and temperature data — had consumed ₹340.00 lakh. Kalra's slide said so once, in grey, beside the words already spent, unavailable either way. Two quarters and ₹226.00 lakh stood between the project and general availability. Nine pilot plants had run the model since June; their unplanned downtime had fallen 6.8 hours a month. The business case, written in December 2025, required fifteen.

In Bengaluru, Darshita Khaira of Sruti Labs held a different line. Sruti is an AI-native voice product — dictation, transcription and summarisation, 2.6 million monthly actives, fourteen months old. Its Companion project, begun 20 April with fourteen people and ₹336.00 lakh spent by 30 September, puts an always-listening agent behind the notes app to draft follow-ups unprompted. On 8 September Companion went live to a randomised cell of 41,000 users; by early October seven-day retention there was running 5.3 points below control. On 6 October a memo proposed stopping Companion outright, and its strongest sentence was the honest one: we have spent two quarters making the product worse. Khaira's reading was that the memo had measured the wrong thing. Both decisions were due on 3 November.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A kill decision is the choice to stop funding work already under way and to reassign the capacity it holds. Three phrases do the work. Already under way: starting is a forecast, while stopping is a withdrawal from people, customers and commitments that now exist. Funding: the decision is about a forward flow of money and attention, never about what has been consumed. Capacity: a kill that frees nothing reassignable is an announcement, not a decision.

The problem it was invented to solve is escalation. Barry Staw's 1976 experiments showed people allocating more to a course of action because their earlier allocation had gone badly; Arkes and Blumer formalised the sunk-cost effect in 1985. Four traditions answered. Robert Cooper's stage-gate systems of the 1980s put evidence-bearing decision points between phases. Finance priced the option to abandon, after Stewart Myers coined “real options” in 1977. McGrath and MacMillan's discovery-driven planning (1995) asks teams to write down, before spending, the assumption whose failure would end the plan. Reinertsen's 2009 account of development flow blames most damage attributed to bad projects on throughput lost to running too many at once.

Three of those traditions hardened into schools and a fourth grew up beside them in practice, without a founding text; Cooper's gates are machinery all four can use. The real-options school repurchases continuation every period at its forward price. It signs: a project in flight has no claim on next quarter's budget that a new project lacks. It refuses: the kick-off threshold binds the gate — later information changes the strike. The pre-commitment school holds the reverse: ownership corrupts judgement at the moment of decision, so the criterion is written in advance and the decision delegated to it. It signs: a criterion written after the evidence is a rationalisation. It refuses: the team closest to the work should weigh the evidence at the gate. The flow school holds kills to be a symptom. It signs: a portfolio needing frequent kills has a work-in-progress problem, not a decisiveness problem. It refuses: kills deserve their own ceremony. The commitment school, closest to customers, holds most apparent escalation to be an obligation honoured. It signs: a feature with contractual or regulatory dependents is a migration programme with a budget, not a kill candidate. It refuses: kill fast and apologise.

3. Mechanics: the forward comparison, worked

Experts do four things competent practitioners skip: wall off the sunk figure, compute what the kill frees, price the alternative first, and ask whether the next spend buys a decision or buys hope. Take Sutlej. The forward cost is eleven people at a fully loaded ₹9.50 lakh per person-quarter, ₹104.50 lakh, plus ₹8.50 lakh of cloud and gateway licences: ₹113.00 lakh a quarter, or ₹226.00 lakh to launch. The revenue case assumes an 18 per cent attach rate on 412 customers — 74 of them — at ₹2.40 lakh each: ₹177.60 lakh of recurring revenue, ₹145.63 lakh of contribution at 82 per cent margin, ₹436.90 lakh over three years. Gross, that needs a success probability of 226.00 ÷ 436.90 = 51.7 per cent — and the second move shows why it is the wrong base. Kalra's own figure after the pilot was 25 per cent: his written odds that a second architecture clears fifteen hours. The meeting is no longer about whether predictive maintenance is a good idea, but whether anyone will defend a number above the break-even.

Exhibit 1. Both options are compared marginally: the ₹63.40 lakh gateway is spent either way, so CONTINUE's cost is ₹162.60 lakh, not the gross ₹226.00 lakh. The sunk band shows its size only. Contribution bars are three-year expected values at the stated probabilities; cost bars are two quarters of spend.

The second move is where Sutlej's first memo was wrong. It claimed the kill would free eleven engineers and the whole ₹226.00 lakh. But the project had built the sensor-ingestion gateway, now also the data path for Compliance Logbook — a module 63 customers pay ₹1.50 lakh a year for and present at factory-licence inspections. The gateway cannot be switched off. Three engineers and ₹3.20 lakh a quarter of licences stay: ₹31.70 lakh a quarter, ₹63.40 lakh over two quarters. The kill frees ₹162.60 lakh and eight people: the memo was 39.0 per cent high on money and three high on capacity, and proposed a redeployment sized for eleven. More important, that ₹63.40 lakh is spent whichever option wins, so it belongs in neither comparison. Marginally, then, Maintenance Advisor's forward cost is ₹162.60 lakh, its break-even 162.60 ÷ 436.90 = 37.2 per cent, its expected return 109.22 ÷ 162.60 = 0.67. Every figure below is marginal; the gross 51.7 per cent is dropped.

The third move prices that redeployment. Quoting has 37 customers asking for it today; the plan assumes a 22 per cent attach rate, 90 of 412, at ₹1.80 lakh — ₹162.00 lakh of recurring revenue, ₹132.84 lakh of contribution, ₹398.52 lakh over three years. At 55 per cent — Kalra's figure, on 37 unprompted requests and a working prototype — that is ₹219.19 lakh expected against a forward cost of eight people for two quarters, ₹152.00 lakh, plus ₹4.00 lakh of infrastructure: ₹156.00 lakh, a ratio of 1.41 against Maintenance Advisor's 0.67 on the same marginal basis. Note what the kill does not do: ₹162.60 lakh freed against ₹156.00 lakh needed leaves ₹6.60 lakh. Stopping creates no slack; at best it pays for its replacement.

Exhibit 2. Sutlej's pilot: nine plants, June to September 2026, unplanned hours per plant per month, same instrumentation throughout. The 90 per cent interval is the pair of one-sided five per cent bounds. Two caveats the page owes the reader: this is pre/post with no concurrent control, so any seasonal difference between the baseline and a June-to-September pilot is not separated out; and the rejection of fifteen is thin, reversing at an SD of 13.2 rather than 12.6.
