The fourth move turns on Exhibit 2. A reduction of 6.8 hours carries a standard error of 4.20, and the interval that matters runs from −1.01 to +14.61: the two one-sided five per cent bounds at eight degrees of freedom (1.860), read at one level so both conclusions are comparable. It contains zero, so the pilot cannot show the product does anything; it excludes fifteen — the 8.2-hour shortfall is 1.95 standard errors, one-sided p = 0.04 — so it can show the product does not do enough. Those are different nulls, and the second governs funding: a kill needs no proof of failure, only rejection of the threshold the plan was underwritten against. A two-sided 95 per cent interval reaches +16.49 and rejects neither, which is why the level must be stated before a gap is called a lesson.

The second-order effects are where kills get expensive. One is informational: how this decision is taken sets the price of candour next quarter. The other is structural. Charged to Compliance Logbook rather than a growth project, the gateway costs Logbook ₹31.70 lakh a quarter — ₹126.80 lakh a year against ₹94.50 lakh of revenue. The kill does not create that loss; it reveals who was subsidising whom. Engineering's steady-state estimate is lower — 1.2 engineers plus ₹3.20 lakh a quarter, so ₹14.60 lakh a quarter or ₹58.40 lakh a year, under which Logbook clears by ₹36.10 lakh. The answer flips on an allocation nobody had written down.

Exhibit 3. A dependency map; every figure in it is repeated from the text. Shift Handover appears because it depends on the gateway, not as part of the decision.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each testable, each applied to both protagonists.

One: the capacity freed must be reassignable inside one planning period. Sutlej passes for 8 of 11, fails for 3. Sruti fails harder: of fourteen on Companion, five sit on the shared inference pipeline the paid product runs on, so stopping it frees nine. Two: a kill criterion is useful only where the measurement that tests it already exists. Sutlej passes — downtime hours were instrumented at all nine plants before the pilot. Sruti fails, and this is its real problem: Companion trades retention for conversion, and with no agreed exchange rate between a retained free user and a conversion, no threshold on net user value was ever testable. Three: sunk-cost discipline binds only where the sunk asset carries no forward option value. Both fail, usefully: Sutlej's gateway and Sruti's pipeline outlive their projects, so “walk away from all of it” is wrong twice. Four: the idea misleads when the thing in flight is a commitment rather than a bet. Compliance Logbook has 63 inspection dependencies; treating it as a portfolio line is a category error, and the right frame is migration with a funded end date.

5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies the kill unit and the cost unit diverge, as at Sutlej, where a sibling absorbed the deliverable. In two-sided markets usage share lies about value share. Skandha Freight, a load-matching marketplace, retired Instant Bid because only 6.1 per cent of its 4,180 active shippers used it; those 255 had posted 11,904 of June's 38,400 loads — 31.0 per cent, or 46.7 each against 6.75 for the other 3,925. Usage understated volume 5.1-fold. In regulated settings the retirement date is not yours; the kill becomes a negotiation with an inspection calendar. In hardware plus software the kill has a cash date, because tooling deposits and distributor commitments crystallise the day you stop — which is why hardware kills cluster before a tooling milestone, not at the review. In AI-native products the substrate moves under the decision: the bet is on a model generation, and a kill against this quarter's capability can be obsolete in two. Variable inference cost compounds it — Companion's economics at 2.6 million actives were invisible in a pilot paying for 41,000.

At the organisational seams the pattern is consistent: the kill memo is written by whoever owns the cost line and read by whoever owns the revenue line, so it overstates what is freed and understates what is owed. What mature companies do, as against what their stage-gate documents say, is starve rather than announce: starvation needs no sign-off, no customer communication, and sets no precedent sales can cite. It also produces the zombie.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert

Stopping is not one state. Four tests separate four: is the thesis alive, is it funded to improve, does it clear its carrying cost, has it its own paying demand? Failing — thesis contested, funded, does not clear, no paying demand yet: Maintenance Advisor at ₹113.00 lakh a quarter. Zombie — thesis dead, unfunded, does not clear, no demand: Shift Handover, 11 users of 412, earning nothing and blocking a gateway schema change, no paying demand. Finished — thesis alive, not funded to improve, own paying demand: Compliance Logbook, ₹94.50 lakh a year. Whether it clears is undetermined: the ₹58.40 lakh is a gateway charge at the steady-state allocation, not Logbook's own run cost, which nobody has measured, and the allocation Kalra booked is the build-era ₹126.80 lakh, under which it does not clear. Logbook is the member whose class the page cannot settle — hence the booked review. Retained dependency — thesis alive but borrowed from a dependent, unfunded, no demand of its own: the gateway, which clears only when charged to Logbook. The fourth test is the tell: file the gateway as a zombie and be overruled by an inspection schedule.

The sunk figure belongs in the record once, and nowhere in the arithmetic. The tell is not a manager arguing for continuation because of spend — rare, and easily refuted — but a memo where the sunk number appears in the denominator of a return, or after “to recover”. The obvious reading is a bias to suppress; the better one is an accounting error smuggled in as a ratio.

A kill is only as good as the priced alternative. Most memos compare a project against unpriced “higher-value work”. Sutlej's comparison became decisive only when Quoting carried its own cost and probability. The tell: the freed engineers' destination is named, never costed.

Reject the threshold, not the effect. Exhibit 2's two tests look like pedantry and are not. Teams demanding proof of zero effect never kill anything, because proof of zero is unobtainable at pilot sizes. The tell: “not significant, so we need another quarter” — the wrong null.

Distinguish the bet from the bug. Sruti's 5.3-point fall is the canonical case: one release changed Companion and the transcription latency together. Kill a failing bet; fix a bug and re-measure the bet. The tell is that the thing being killed shipped in a build containing anything else at all.

Ask whether the next spend buys a decision. The expert computes the plausible range of the next experiment's result and asks whether any value in it changes the choice. If not, the spend is hope with a budget line. The obvious reading — more data is better — ignores that information has a price.

Announce nothing you have not funded. A kill announced before the migration is paid for turns an internal decision into a promise the company cannot keep. The tell is a communication plan with a date and no owner for the customers on the retired path.

Kill rate is not a virtue. Organisations celebrating kill counts select for killable projects — small, legible, low-variance — the opposite of upside. The tell is a kill rate quoted without the distribution of what survived.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the kill is cheap outside and expensive inside: users leave quietly, but the team learns what the company tolerates. In B2B and enterprise it reverses — engineering is cheap and the contractual cost is the whole problem; Sutlej's constraint is 63 inspection dependencies, not code. On platforms and marketplaces the binding question is whose behaviour the feature held up: Skandha's 31.0 per cent against 6.1 per cent. In hardware the kill date is set by cash, not evidence. In AI products two things genuinely differ: forward cost scales with usage rather than headcount, and the capability floor moves, so a kill is better framed as a dated option to re-enter.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. A seed-stage company kills by reallocating its only team and needs no process; at Sutlej's scale the kill is a cross-functional transaction and needs one; at enterprise scale it is mostly migration planning. What does not change is the forward comparison, and claims that early-stage companies should reason differently about sunk cost are simply wrong: the walled-off figure is walled off at every size.

8. Three worked examples

Sruti Labs: the decomposition that saved a project. Dilreet Kanwal, Sruti's analyst, had kept a third cell, all three closed to new entrants on 8 September so that every user carries the full six weeks. Cell A, control, 41,000 users, 41.6 per cent seven-day retention. Cell B, Companion plus the new pipeline, 41,000 users, 36.3 per cent. Cell C, the new pipeline alone, Companion disabled, 12,000 users, 37.9 per cent. The 5.3-point fall decomposes exactly: 3.7 points from latency (A against C, 7.3 standard errors), 1.6 from Companion itself (C against B, 3.2 standard errors), and the interim read in early October gave the same 5.3. Companion's own retention cost is real and 30 per cent of what was charged to it. The other 3.7 points are a latency regression in the new pipeline itself, which cell C carries with Companion disabled: median latency 1.1 to 2.8 seconds. Conversion runs the other way, and on the same clean contrast. Six-week paid conversion was 2.1 per cent in A (861), 2.2 per cent in C (264 of 12,000) and 2.9 per cent in B (1,189), so Companion's own lift is B against C: 0.7 points, standard error 0.16, 4.4 standard errors. Latency cost conversion nothing measurable.

Exhibit 4. Bars invert on the stated scale: 41.6 per cent sits 7.6 points above the 34 per cent origin, 7.6 × 20 = 152 units. Standard errors of the differences, from the cell sizes shown, are 0.34, 0.51 and 0.50 points.

Skandha Freight: the kill that cost volume. Instant Bid went in July 2026. Within sixty days 61 of the 255 affected shippers had stopped posting, 23.9 per cent, against 9.4 per cent of the other 3,925 in the same window. The excess is 14.5 points, or 37 shippers, which at the group's mean of 46.7 loads a month is about 1,730 loads, 4.5 per cent of marketplace volume, against an engineering saving of two people. Whether that was a bad trade Skandha cannot say, having no value per load — the same missing exchange rate that stalled Sruti. Its error was a denominator: it measured who touched the feature, not what flowed through it.

Sindhura Instruments: where the approach failed. Sindhura makes bench-top water-testing instruments with a cloud dashboard. In January 2026 Damanveer Khinda wrote pre-committed criteria for a reagent-free turbidity sensor: kill at the 30 June gate unless unit cost reached ₹4,200 or below and ninety-day field drift stayed within 2.0 NTU. At the gate, drift was 1.4 NTU and quoted unit cost ₹5,150. The criterion failed; nine engineers moved that week. But the quote stood on January's assumption of 2,000 units a year, and by June a distributor had committed to 6,400 — 3.2 times as many, at which the same bill of materials quoted ₹3,870, inside the criterion and 24.9 per cent lower. Nobody re-based the parameter the criterion was conditional on. The project restarted on Monday 12 October, 104 days later; of the nine, four returned, two had left, three were load-bearing elsewhere. A ₹28 lakh tooling deposit forfeited in July was re-quoted at ₹34 lakh, 21.4 per cent more. Pre-commitment had not removed judgement; it relocated it to January, when it was least informed.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The criterion written after the data. Early sign: the threshold first appears in the deck with the result. Diagnostic: where was this number on the day we started? Cost: criteria become decoration and the next gate is unwinnable. The saving booked on a shared dependency. Early sign: freed headcount equals project headcount exactly. Diagnostic: which of these eleven can be assigned on Monday? Cost: Sutlej's 39.0 per cent. The confounded release read as a verdict. Early sign: one build, two changes. Diagnostic: what else shipped in that build? Cost: the wrong half dies, and Sruti's 0.7-point conversion gain with it. Noise read as a lesson. Early sign: a gap quoted without a standard error. Diagnostic: what is the standard error, and at what level? Cost: a decision nobody can defend. The partial kill that leaves a zombie. Early sign: nobody is on call. Diagnostic: who owns it, and what is their next commit? Cost: schema drag taxing every neighbour, as Shift Handover does.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Pre-commitment against periodic re-underwriting. The pre-commitment position rests on evidence that ownership corrupts judgement at the moment of decision, and on the observation that organisations which re-underwrite almost never stop anything. For it to be wrong, stale conditioning parameters would have to be commoner than escalation — which is what Sindhura's ₹5,150 is evidence for. The re-underwriting position holds that a criterion is a model, and models must be re-estimated; for it to be wrong, managers would have to re-estimate without re-estimating their way to continuation. Neither side has data clean enough to settle it, so the choice turns on which error your organisation makes more often — which most firms never measure.

Whether sunk-cost escalation is a real managerial problem. The sceptical position, steelmanned, is that laboratory escalation does not transfer: a manager who continues often holds private information a reviewer lacks, so apparent escalation is rational updating invisible in the data. For this to be wrong, continuing managers would need no information advantage — testable against outcomes, and almost never tested.

Where the decision should sit. The portfolio view holds that no team can kill itself. The team view holds that the people with the evidence hold the detail, and that removing their authority guarantees they stop volunteering bad news. The second has the stronger mechanism, the weaker record.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this differs in five observable ways. They write the kill criterion with its conditioning parameters attached and a date to re-base them. They state the sunk figure once, then police every sentence that reintroduces it as a ratio. Before claiming a saving they ask what cannot be retired, and they ask the architecture rather than the project plan. They separate the bet from the bug before reading any result, which usually means refusing to interpret a release that changed two things. And they fund the migration in the decision that authorises the kill, the expensive part of stopping never being the stopping.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Kalra stopped Maintenance Advisor on 3 November, on the marginal break-even: continuing required better than a 37.2 per cent chance of clearing a threshold the pilot rejects at a one-sided p of 0.04, and the alternative returned 1.41 on its forward cost against 0.67. He retained the gateway with three engineers, charged it to Compliance Logbook, moved eight people to Quoting, and booked a review of Logbook's economics for the quarter to 31 March 2027 — because on the allocation he has just booked, Logbook does not clear. Devanshu Kullar's objection went in unedited.

Khaira did not kill Companion. She killed the always-listening trigger, kept the drafting surface, and sent the pipeline back to the 1.1-second path, since cell C puts 3.7 of the 5.3 points there with Companion disabled and the trigger alone recovers only 1.6. She declined to spend ₹98.10 lakh on a clean retention re-run — fourteen people for six weeks at ₹4.10 lakh a person-month, ₹86.10 lakh, plus ₹12.00 lakh of inference — because the plausible interval for Companion's own retention effect runs from about −2.6 to −0.6 points, every value negative and small, and none of them changes the decision without an exchange rate the company does not have. She bought the exchange rate instead.

Q1. Sutlej's marginal break-even probability is 37.2 per cent. What evidence, obtainable within two quarters for under ₹50 lakh, would move a reasonable person above it — and if none exists, is that a fact about the product or about the measurement?

Q2. Sruti has no exchange rate between a retained free user and a conversion. Who should own that number, and what would you accept as evidence that it is right rather than convenient?

Q3. Sindhura's criterion failed on a stale parameter. Would you re-base criteria at each gate, restoring the judgement pre-commitment was meant to remove, or hold them and accept that some good projects die on January's arithmetic?

13. Going deeper

  • Saying no — the same decision before commitment exists; the habits transfer.
  • Sunsetting a product or feature — what the kill must fund: migration, dates, communication.
  • Value vs effort — the simplest forward comparison, once effort means what remains.
  • RICE scoring — makes the reach denominator explicit, where Skandha went wrong.
  • Kano model — separates features whose removal is unnoticed from those whose removal is a defect.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — prices delay, so freed capacity gets a value.
  • Buy-a-feature — tests willingness to pay before the project flies.
  • User story mapping — shows which slices carry the dependents, so what a partial kill retires.
exp20v2-prio.opportunity.scoring:
Opportunity Scoring: Importance versus Satisfaction

Which outcomes matter a lot to customers and are badly served today?

1. A roadmap with ₹1.8 crore attached

On Monday 6 July 2026, Inchara Pallath, group product manager at Aranmula Labs in Kochi, had eleven days to turn a list of 31 requests into a roadmap the board would fund. Aranmula sells payroll and statutory-compliance software to about 1,900 small manufacturers in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, each with 50 to 400 workers, at an average of ₹62,000 per customer per year. Annual churn ran at 14 per cent: 266 customers, or roughly ₹1.65 crore of recurring revenue, walking out each year. The board had released ₹1.8 crore for two quarters of work by two engineering squads, and the roadmap was due on Friday 17 July.

The requests pulled in different directions. Ihsan Peruvemba, head of engineering, wanted to rewrite the engine that computes provident fund (PF) and employees' state insurance (ESI) contributions, the statutory deductions every Indian employer files monthly. Sales wanted customisable payslip layouts, which appeared in 17 of the last 40 lost-deal notes. Iravathi Pazhayidam, who ran customer success, said her team's calls were about something else entirely: attendance data that did not match the factory floor.

Each claim came with an anecdote. Picking the most persuasive advocate would spend a year of engineering on whatever the loudest voice had noticed. Between 22 June and 3 July Inchara had therefore surveyed 120 customers.

2. The idea

Opportunity scoring is a method for ranking customer outcomes by how underserved they are. An outcome is a measurable result a customer is trying to achieve, written as a direction, a metric and a context: “minimise the time to reconcile attendance before payroll closes.” Customers rate each outcome twice: how important it is, and how satisfied they are with how well it is achieved today. Important and poorly served is an opportunity; well served but unimportant is a candidate for simplification.

Anthony Ulwick developed the approach in the 1990s through his consultancy, Strategyn, as part of what he called outcome-driven innovation, and set it out for general readers in a 2002 Harvard Business Review article and his 2005 book What Customers Want. It addressed a specific problem: customers describe what they struggle to get done well and specify solutions poorly, so a feature-request list is a noisy proxy for need. It also builds on pains and gains: importance is how strongly customers rate a gain, and satisfaction is how much of it they now receive.

The sentence Inchara could repeat in the room was this: “We are not asking which feature people want; we are asking which results they need most that they are getting least.”

3. How it actually works

The mechanics take seven steps. Inchara began by collapsing the 31 requests into eight outcomes, each phrased without naming a solution. Practitioners often skip this step, yet the rest depends on it: “customisable payslip templates” is a feature, whereas “minimise effort to restyle the payslip layout” is an outcome that several features might serve. Next, she asked each respondent two questions per outcome on a five-point scale. The third step was to count the share who rated importance 4 or 5 (the top-two-box share), then the same for satisfaction, and convert each share to a ten-point score, so that 104 of 120 becomes 8.7.

Step four is the gap, importance minus satisfaction. Step five is the formula that gives the method its name: opportunity = importance + max(importance − satisfaction, 0). Importance is counted twice when an outcome is underserved, once as itself and once through the gap, so that important things outrank trivial ones with the same gap. The max sets the gap to zero when satisfaction exceeds importance, so an overserved outcome never earns a negative penalty that would cancel its importance. Steps six and seven are to rank, then to look at the plot, because clusters and outliers carry information a single column hides.

In Exhibit 1 the upper left is where customers need something badly and are not getting it; the lower right is where Aranmula has built more than was asked. Outcome 8, restyling the payslip, sits there.

4. A worked example, line by line

Exhibit 2 shows the arithmetic. Each score is the count divided by 120 and multiplied by ten, rounded to one decimal place; the gap and opportunity columns are computed from those rounded scores. Take outcome 1. Of 120 respondents, 104 rated its importance 4 or 5, which is 8.7; only 49 rated satisfaction 4 or 5, which is 4.1. The gap is 8.7 − 4.1 = 4.6, and the opportunity is 8.7 + 4.6 = 13.3. Outcome 3 is the contrast: importance 7.4, satisfaction 8.8, a gap of −1.4, which the formula treats as zero, so its opportunity is just 7.4.

The order is outcome 1 (13.3), outcome 2 (11.0), outcome 4 (10.8), outcome 6 (10.0), outcome 5 (8.5), outcome 3 (7.4), outcome 7 (6.1) and outcome 8 (4.2). The payslip layout that sales had championed is last, and the PF and ESI outcome, the one Ihsan's rewrite would serve, is second. The table does not say the rewrite is needed, only that wrong filings matter and are reasonably well handled.

Now change one input. Iravathi pointed out that the respondents were mostly owners, who hear about wrong PF filings only when a notice arrives. She re-asked the satisfaction question on outcome 2 alone, this time of the person who actually files the return at each of the same 120 firms. Only 55 of 120 rated it 4 or 5, a satisfaction of 4.6 rather than 7.2. The gap becomes 9.1 − 4.6 = 4.5, and the opportunity becomes 9.1 + 4.5 = 13.6, narrowly ahead of outcome 1.

One re-asked item moves outcome 2 to the top, but the other seven were not re-asked, so the comparison is not like-for-like. Each opportunity score counts importance twice, so its sampling error is roughly 0.7 points, and about 1.0 for a difference between two. The 0.3-point lead is far inside that, so the honest reading is a tie at the top, not a new winner.

5. Seven nuances

Importance is not frequency, revenue or willingness to pay

Respondents rate how much an outcome matters to them. An outcome used once a year can be vital. The score says nothing about what customers will pay.

Satisfaction is about today's alternatives, not about your product

Customers who run payroll in spreadsheets are rating the spreadsheet. Ask about the whole way they get the outcome done.

Overserved is information

Outcome 8 scored 8.1 on satisfaction against 4.2 on importance. The formula floors it, but the finding is that effort spent there has little return.

Who answers decides what you learn

The second pass showed it: owners and filers rated the same outcome 2.6 points apart (7.2 against 4.6). In B2B, buyer, user and payer are often three people, and the sample should say which of them was asked.

Precision is an illusion at small samples

Scores to one decimal invite arguments about noise. Treat differences under about half a point as ties and look at the leading group.

It is not RICE, and it is not Kano

RICE scores a proposed initiative on reach, impact, confidence and effort. Kano classifies features by how satisfaction responds to them. Opportunity scoring ranks customer need, before any solution exists, and it contains no cost term at all.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot say why an outcome is underserved, what to build, whether it can be built cheaply, or how many customers lie outside your sample. Before relying on it, ask who was surveyed and whether the outcomes were written without solutions in them.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; early and late

In a consumer product the respondent is the user and samples can run to thousands, but people overstate importance, so satisfaction usually carries the signal. In B2B, as Aranmula found, the buyer, the user and the person who bears the failure are different; samples are small, and scoring by role is essential. In a marketplace one side's satisfaction often depends on the other, so a driver's “find fares quickly” is partly rider supply; score each side separately.

An early-stage company has no installed base to be dissatisfied with, so the satisfaction question must be asked about the alternatives customers use now, and 15 to 20 interviews may stand in for a survey. A large company faces the opposite temptation: averaging across segments, which hides the underserved niche.

7. Common mistakes

Surveying solutions. The symptom is a table in which nearly every item scores high on importance and the ranking is flat. The misunderstanding is that a feature name is an outcome. The cheapest diagnostic is to strike any statement containing a noun a developer could build.

Treating the ranking as a roadmap. The symptom is a top item needing a year of engineering; the misunderstanding is that opportunity equals priority. The diagnostic is to add a cost column beside the score before anyone discusses order.

Averaging across segments. The symptom is a top outcome that nobody in any single segment names as their own. The diagnostic is to rescore each segment separately and see whether its top three match the pooled top three.

Defending the decimals. The symptom is a meeting spent on 0.3 points. The diagnostic is to compute the standard error, or to redraw the sample twice, and see whether the order survives.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the decision rests on one page: the plot, the table with a cost estimate beside every outcome, and a statement of who answered. It would name the top four outcomes (1, 2, 4 and 6), note that 1 and 2 are effectively tied once outcome 2 is re-scored, and say plainly which question was left open. Each advocate would be told where their request landed and why.

9. What Inchara decided

On Friday 17 July she took one squad to outcome 1, attendance reconciliation, and gave the other a six-week mandate for outcome 2: add validation checks before filing, and test whether they closed the filers' gap before touching the engine. Ihsan's rewrite stayed listed, justified only if the checks proved insufficient. Payslip customisation was declined, though the survey cannot see the lost prospects behind sales' 17 notes. With a two-way tie at the top she funded both and delayed the expensive commitment.

To go further, study the jobs-to-be-done framing from which outcomes are drawn, and then a cost-aware method such as RICE, so that need and effort meet on one page. Two questions to sit with: if you rescored your own team's backlog with the filer rather than the buyer, what would move? And which of your best-scoring outcomes would a competitor's cheap fix make irrelevant?
exp40v2-prio.opportunity.scoring:
Opportunity Scoring: Importance, Satisfaction and the Outcomes Nobody Serves

Which outcomes matter a lot to customers and are badly served today — and when the question itself is the wrong one.

1. Two decisions, both due in September 2026

On Tuesday 8 September 2026 Jayanthi Ramanunni, vice-president of product at Bhramara Workshop Systems, had forty-one requests and a board resolution for ₹2.4 crore. Bhramara sells job-card, parts and billing software to commercial-vehicle service workshops — 1,140 of them, at an average of ₹2.6 lakh a year, or ₹29.64 crore of recurring revenue. In the year to 31 March 2026, 126 workshops had left — 11.1 per cent of the base, ₹327.6 lakh of revenue. The ₹2.4 crore bought four squad-quarters at ₹60 lakh each.

The requests had advocates: Jagdish Ramachandran, who ran engineering, wanted the parts-availability service rewritten, and sales wanted warranty-claim automation, which had appeared in four of the last six dealer-group tenders. Jyoti Ravunni, who ran research, had something else: between Monday 15 and Friday 26 June she had surveyed 296 workshops on nine outcomes, two questions each.

The same week in Bengaluru, Jinoy Raghavan, head of product at Bevu Home Water, faced a harder version. Bevu makes connected reverse-osmosis purifiers and competes with Eureka Forbes, HUL's Pureit and Kent. It had 2,30,000 units in homes, of which 94,300 — 41.0 per cent — had an active app account. The next revision's bill of materials froze on Friday 25 September, and he had ₹310 a unit of headroom in it. He had surveyed 1,480 app users between 14 and 22 August — and had run this method once before, in November 2025, shipped against its top-ranked outcome, and watched the number refuse to move.

2. The idea, and the four schools

Opportunity scoring ranks customer outcomes by how underserved they are. An outcome is a result a customer is trying to achieve, written as a direction, a metric and a context with no solution inside it: “minimise the time to tell a waiting customer when the vehicle is ready.” Respondents rate each twice: how important the result is, and how satisfied they are with the way it is achieved today, by whatever means. The two ratings become ten-point scores and combine:

Opportunity = Importance + max(Importance − Satisfaction, 0)

Martilla and James published importance-performance analysis in the Journal of Marketing in 1977: plot attributes on importance against performance, act on the top-left quadrant. Kano's 1984 work, building on Herzberg, held that satisfaction responds asymmetrically to performance. Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry's SERVQUAL (1988) made service quality a gap between expectation and perception, and Cronin and Taylor attacked gap scores in 1992, showing performance alone predicted better. Anthony Ulwick's contribution, developed at Strategyn from the early 1990s and set out in a 2002 Harvard Business Review article and in What Customers Want (2005), was not the arithmetic but the unit of analysis: outcomes from a job map, not features.

Four positions remain live, told apart most easily by what each will and will not sign. The outcome-driven school will sign that a solution-free outcome statement is stable across time and technologies and so can be re-measured, but not that feature requests can be scored this way. The asymmetry school around Kano will sign that importance and satisfaction are both real, but not that one importance axis fits a must-be outcome and a delighter alike. The choice-modelling school, descended from Green and Srinivasan's 1978 conjoint survey and now practised as MaxDiff, will sign that weights come only from trade-offs, but not that a stated five-point rating carries usable information. The gap-score sceptics will sign that performance should be measured carefully, but not that a difference of two ratings is more reliable than either alone.

3. Mechanics, worked through

The visible steps are: write outcomes, survey, count top-box shares, take the gap, apply the formula, rank. Three are left implicit and decide everything: collapsing requests into outcomes without a solution surviving the translation — Jyoti's forty-one requests included “WhatsApp alert to the customer”, a mechanism that became part of the promise-time outcome; framing satisfaction, since a workshop running a paper job-card book rates the book, not Bhramara; and deciding who counts as a respondent.

Take outcome 1. Of 296 respondents, 254 rated its importance 4 or 5 on a five-point scale, 85.8 per cent, or 8.6 on the ten-point scale; 103 of 296 rated satisfaction 4 or 5, 34.8 per cent, giving 3.5. The gap is 8.6 − 3.5 = 5.1 and the opportunity 8.6 + 5.1 = 13.7. Outcome 8 runs the other way: importance 5.9 against satisfaction 8.2, a gap of −2.3 which the max term floors at zero, leaving 5.9; the floor stops an overserved outcome ranking below an unimportant one.

Two properties are rarely stated. First, the score equals 2 × Importance − Satisfaction whenever the gap is positive, so it moves twice as far for a point of importance as for a point of satisfaction. Second, the score has a standard error. Outcome 1's top-box shares, 0.858 and 0.348 over 296 respondents, carry standard errors of 0.203 and 0.277 on the ten-point scale; with the within-respondent correlation between the items at 0.31, the opportunity score's standard error is 0.41 and outcome 3's 0.45. The standard error of the difference is 0.61 against an observed 13.7 − 13.0 = 0.7, or 1.1 standard errors — treating the two scores as independent, which if anything overstates the error, since both rest on the same 296 respondents. At a correlation of 0.3 between them the standard error is 0.51 and the gap 1.4 standard errors. Either way, outcomes 1 and 3 tie.

4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

The method rests on four testable claims.

Every respondent can attempt the outcome. This fails most often, and silently: a respondent who cannot attempt an outcome does not abstain, they answer. It holds for Bevu's outcomes, which every owner attempts weekly, and fails for Bhramara's outcome 4, since an independent workshop cannot file a manufacturer warranty claim at all — and 174 of 296 respondents were independents.

Satisfaction is measured against the customer's whole current method. It holds for Bhramara, whose respondents were asked how the job gets done today without the product being named, and half-fails for Bevu, whose survey ran inside the app, so respondents rated what they had already chosen.

Something the company controls could move the satisfaction number. This is a claim about supply, which the survey cannot see. It holds for Bhramara's top two, both software, and failed for Bevu in 2025.

The sample is one population for this outcome. Not one market, not one commercial segment, but one population for this particular result. Bhramara's sample is one population for eight of its nine outcomes and two for outcome 4.

When is the idea actively misleading rather than merely weak? In a new category, where nobody is dissatisfied with a result they have never attempted and the gap is zero everywhere; in compliance-driven demand, where importance is imposed rather than felt and satisfaction is binary; and where the dissatisfaction is with price, which no engineering closes.

5. Hard edges

In a multi-product company one customer rates outcomes served by two products, and a gap scored at company level is owned by neither; it must be attached to whichever product would close it. In a two-sided business one side's satisfaction is the other side's supply: a workshop's satisfaction with “find a qualified technician for this job” is largely the local labour market, and funding software against it is a category error unless the platform means to change that supply.

In a regulated product the gap may be one the company is not permitted to close. Bevu's owners rate “know the water leaving the tap is safe” as important and poorly served, but what would satisfy them is a potability claim, and Bevu's regulatory counsel will not let it make one on a sensor reading, with BIS and FSSAI labelling to answer to.

In hardware plus software the closure has a bill of materials and a tooling lead time, so the ranking must be read against a calendar: Bevu's filter-state gap needed a sensor, and a sensor meant fourteen months.

In AI-native products the baseline moves without anyone shipping: satisfaction with “get a usable answer first time” drifts with model releases, including competitors', so a six-month-old score is not evidence about today.

At the organisational seams the highest-scoring outcome is usually the one crossing two teams: Bhramara's outcome 1 needs both the job-card and the notifications team. The institutional response is to re-run the survey per owning team, re-pooling respondents and reintroducing the dilution section 8 describes. What mature companies do, as against what they publish, is use the ranking as a veto on the obviously overserved rather than a selector of the best bet.

6. Eight things an expert sees

The score is importance-dominant, and importance is the weaker measurement

A point of importance moves the score twice as far as a point of satisfaction, and importance is the rating that compresses: six of nine outcomes scored above 6.0. The tell is a ranking that reproduces the importance column; where that rank correlation approaches one, the satisfaction question has contributed nothing.

Satisfaction is a rating of the incumbent workaround

The respondent rates whatever they use now, which is usually not your product. The tell is a satisfaction score that moves after a competitor ships. An expert records the competitive frame beside the number, since a year-on-year comparison without it compares two different worlds.

A non-attempt reads as satisfaction

Someone who has never attempted an outcome has nothing to be dissatisfied about and will usually rate it 4. In outcome 4, 121 of 174 independents — 69.5 per cent — rated satisfaction 4 or 5 on a claim process they never touch. The tell is high satisfaction beside empty free-text comments; the diagnostic is a “have you attempted this in ninety days?” screen.

Stated and derived importance disagree, and the disagreement is the finding

Regress overall satisfaction on the per-outcome satisfaction items and the implied weights rarely match the stated ones. Outcome 2 ranks third on opportunity but first on derived weight, at 22.6 per cent of explained variance in Exhibit 2's last column. The tell is an outcome that ranks lower on what customers say than on what predicts whether they stay.

Overserved is a budget line, not a compliment

Outcomes 8 and 9 sit well below the diagonal in Exhibit 1. The obvious reading is that these are strengths to protect; the expert reading is that the next rupee there returns nothing and what is built there is a candidate for reduction. The tell is a team proudly reporting a score nobody asked it to raise.

The top of the list is a cluster, and the decimals are theatre

One decimal invites argument at a resolution the sample cannot support: the top two differ by 0.7 against a standard error of 0.61. The tell is a meeting about the order of the first two items; an expert names the cluster and funds inside it on grounds the survey does not contain.

A gap you cannot close is not an opportunity

The method measures demand and is silent on supply. The tell is a top-ranked outcome for which nobody can name a mechanism, only an aspiration; the diagnostic is “what is the cheapest change that would move this number, and do we control it?” An expert puts a closure cost beside every score before anyone discusses sequence.

Re-measurement is the only validation the method has

An opportunity score makes one falsifiable prediction: serve this outcome and its satisfaction rises. Almost nobody checks. The tell is three years of surveys with no paired before-and-after on one funded outcome; an expert schedules the re-measure in the document that funds the work, sample size included.

7. By product type and company stage

The arithmetic is identical everywhere; most claimed differences are not in the method but in who can answer and what a fix costs.

In consumer products the respondent is the user, samples run to thousands, and the binding constraint is that importance ratings are generous: even the Bevu outcome Jinoy chose not to fund scored 7.2 on importance. In B2B and enterprise the buyer, the user and the person who absorbs the failure differ, samples are in the hundreds, and the frame matters more than its size: Bhramara's segment split moved one outcome by 9.3 points, which no larger sample would have done. In platforms and marketplaces each side must be scored separately and the cross-side dependency named; in hardware the score is read against a tooling calendar; in AI the satisfaction measurement has a short half-life.

By stage, an early company has no installed base to be dissatisfied with, so satisfaction must be asked about incumbent alternatives, and fifteen to twenty interviews beat a thin survey. A late-stage company has the opposite problem: enough respondents to pool, and enough segments that pooling destroys the signal.

8. Three worked examples

One: the outcome that pooling inverted. Among the 122 dealer-captive workshops — those under a manufacturer's authorised-service agreement, and so the only ones that can file a claim — 115 rated importance 4 or 5 (94.3 per cent, or 9.4) and 52 rated satisfaction 4 or 5 (4.3): a gap of 5.1 and an opportunity of 14.5, the highest score in either company's data. Among the 174 independents, 38 rated importance highly (2.2) and 121 satisfaction (7.0), a gap of −4.8 and an opportunity of 2.2. Pooled, the counts are 153 and 173, giving 5.2 against 5.8 — a negative gap, so outcome 4 ranks eighth of nine and reads as overserved. Base-weighting makes it worse: the sample was 41.2 per cent captive against a base share of 35.4 per cent, and weighting both sides gives importance 0.354 × 9.4 + 0.646 × 2.2 = 4.7 against satisfaction 0.354 × 4.3 + 0.646 × 7.0 = 6.0, an opportunity of 4.7. The weights were not wrong; pooling was the wrong operation on a class whose members do not share the job.

Two: weighting both sides. Bevu's service-visit outcome scored 7.2 importance and 5.8 satisfaction among app users, an opportunity of 8.6. Since app users are 41.0 per cent of the base, Jinoy telephoned 240 owners without accounts between 2 and 9 September: 182 rated importance highly (7.6), 96 satisfaction (4.0). Weighting both scores to the base gives importance 0.410 × 7.2 + 0.590 × 7.6 = 7.4 and satisfaction 0.410 × 5.8 + 0.590 × 4.0 = 4.7, a gap of 2.7 and an opportunity of 10.1. The shortcut — correct the app-biased satisfaction, leave importance as surveyed — gives 7.2 + (7.2 − 4.7) = 9.7, understating by 0.4, because it sets a base-weighted satisfaction against an app-only importance. A correction applied to one side of a difference is an error.

Three: the one that failed. Bevu's November 2025 survey of 960 app users put “minimise the effort to know the filter is actually working” top of its list; 280 of 960 rated satisfaction 4 or 5, a score of 2.9. Bevu built a filter-health screen into the firmware of 17 March 2026. The August 2026 survey re-measured it at 432 of 1,480, which is also 2.9 — a difference of 0.0 against a standard error of 0.19, so not a small effect but no effect. The reason sat in the hardware, where the survey could not look: the unit had no sensor able to observe filter state, so the screen showed litres elapsed against a nominal cartridge life, the inference the owner was already making and already distrusting. The recovery was ₹310 a unit of conductivity and dissolved-solids sensing in the next revision, whose bill of materials freezes on 25 September 2026 for shelves in January 2027, fourteen months after the survey.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Surveying solutions. The early sign is an importance column with nothing below 7 and a flat ranking, because respondents rate every proposed feature as desirable; the diagnostic is whether a developer could build the noun in each statement. Caught late, it costs a quarter of engineering on the loudest request, with a survey's authority attached.

Pooling populations that do not share the job. The early sign is a segment owner calling the top-ranked outcome irrelevant; the diagnostic is what share of respondents has attempted it in ninety days. Bhramara caught this before the roadmap; later would have cost a year.

Ranking without a closure cost. The early sign is a scored table with no column beside the score; the diagnostic is the cheapest-change question of section 6. Bevu's cost was six months between shipping the wrong fix and freezing the right one.

Reading the decimals as an order. The early sign is a meeting arguing about 0.3 of a point; the diagnostic is the standard error of that difference. Miss it and sampling noise, not judgement, selects the quarter's work.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

That stated importance carries real information. The outcome-driven position is that a concrete, solution-free outcome statement can be rated honestly, unlike an abstract attribute, and that opportunity rankings have proved stable under re-measurement. For it to be wrong, top-box importance would have to compress until the doubled term is mostly noise — testable by comparing stated against choice-based ranks on one sample.

That only trade-offs reveal weights. The choice-modelling position is that people cannot introspect on relative importance but can choose, and that derived weights predict behaviour better; Bhramara's regression is evidence: outcome 2 stands third on stated opportunity and first on derived weight. For it to be wrong, the dependent variable would have to be contaminated: if overall satisfaction is a halo, derived weights measure what customers say about you, not what they need.

That gap scores are unsound in principle. The performance-only position, which Cronin and Taylor argued against SERVQUAL in 1992, is that a difference of two ratings imports two error terms and is less reliable than either, and that performance alone predicted better in their data. For it to be wrong, the decision must need a counterfactual: performance alone cannot tell a low score that matters from one nobody minds, and prioritisation is that distinction.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a ranked table and defends its order. Someone who has internalised it produces four things: the ranking, a screen for what share of respondents could attempt each outcome, a closure cost beside each score, and a date for the re-measure. They talk in clusters rather than ranks, treat a negative gap as a budget question, and care more about who was not asked than who was. Asked why the top item won, they give a reason the survey does not contain — which is where the judgement lives.

12. What each of them decided

Jayanthi's first question was whether to divert a squad to the captive segment on the strength of that 14.5, and she priced both sides the same way. Outcome 1, served for all 1,140 workshops, was expected to cut annual churn by 2.0 percentage points if it worked — 22.8 workshops, or ₹59.28 lakh of recurring revenue — at a probability of 0.55, an expected ₹32.60 lakh a year. Outcome 4, served for the 404 captive workshops, was expected to cut their churn by 6.0 points — 24.24 workshops, ₹63.02 lakh — at a probability of 0.40, an expected ₹25.21 lakh a year. Both figures are retention only, so both understate in the same direction, and both bets cost one squad-quarter. The unweighted comparison favours outcome 4 by 6 per cent, 63.02 against 59.28; had only outcome 1 been discounted, the factor would have been 1.93; the symmetric comparison favours outcome 1 by 29 per cent.

She funded outcomes 1 and 3 with one squad-quarter each, declining to let 0.7 of a point choose between them, and held the remaining ₹1.2 crore for a November re-survey of the 404 captive workshops alone. Jinoy spent his ₹310 of headroom on the sensor pair, since the filter-state score had not moved in nine months and no software could move it, and gave his app squad the outcome of restoring flow after the unit stops, where 1,310 of 1,480 rated importance 4 or 5 (8.9) and 714 rated satisfaction highly (4.8), an opportunity of 13.0 that needs no new sensing.

Three questions for discussion. First: outcome 4 scored 5.2 pooled and 14.5 in the segment that can use it, so by what rule should a manager decide in advance which outcomes get split and which get pooled? Second: outcome 2 is first on derived importance and third on stated opportunity, so which column should fund a squad, and what evidence would settle it? Third: what must be added to an opportunity exercise for a supply constraint like Bevu's to surface before the money is spent, and who would answer for it?

13. Going deeper

Pains and gains is where the outcome statements come from; without a job map the survey measures the customer's vocabulary. Value versus effort supplies the supply-side axis that turns a ranking into a sequence. RICE scoring adds reach and confidence, the next step once a closure cost exists. The Kano model explains why a high-importance, low-satisfaction outcome and a delighter should not share one axis. Weighted scoring and WSJF show how the arithmetic behaves once cost of delay enters. Buy-a-feature forces the trade-off the choice-modelling school says ratings cannot elicit, and user story mapping turns a chosen outcome into work that ships in a quarter.
exp40v2-prio.bets:
Portfolio of bets and expected value

Prioritising by expected value and learning rather than by certainty: what the arithmetic says, where it stops saying anything useful, and why the practitioners who command it spend their effort restructuring bets rather than scoring them.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Monday 7 September 2026, Nivedh Yanwal, vice-president of product at Guthli, a Bengaluru savings application with 18.4 lakh monthly active users, sat down with a planning sheet holding nine team-quarters of credible work and five pods to do it with. A team-quarter is one squad for one quarter; Guthli's five squads give five between 1 October and 31 December. Six candidate bets had survived intake, each with a sponsor who could defend it, and the chief executive wanted one number per bet by Friday.

Eleven days later, on Friday 18 September, Neharika Yalotra, chief product officer of Gahvara Instruments in Pune, faced a narrower decision with more money attached. Gahvara builds neonatal monitoring hardware and the ward software that reads it, and sells to private hospital networks. Its next cot sensor needed ₹3.2 crore of injection-mould tooling committed in November, and clearance from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, which Gahvara's regulatory lead, Nuzhat Yandhu, put at 0.70 on first submission. Neharika could commit the tooling now and find out later, or spend ₹0.45 crore and eleven weeks on a pre-submission review first.

Both decisions turn on one question: am I prioritising by expected value and learning, or just by certainty? Nivedh's instinct was to rank by how confident he felt; Neharika's was to protect the launch date. Both are expensive, and the correction is arithmetic rather than attitude.

2. The idea, and the four camps

The expected value of a bet is the sum, over mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive outcomes, of each payoff weighted by its probability. Exhaustiveness is not a technicality: if your listed outcomes do not sum to exactly 1, you have described part of a bet. A portfolio of bets is the whole set of commitments an organisation holds at once, treated as one object with one distribution of returns.

The mathematics is old; the application is young. Pascal and Fermat established the expectation calculus in 1654, and Daniel Bernoulli showed in 1738 that people maximise something concave in money — which is why a sensible firm declines some EV-positive bets. Von Neumann and Morgenstern axiomatised utility in 1944; Savage in 1954 licensed subjective probability, which makes the method usable where frequencies do not exist. Markowitz's 1952 paper supplied the other half: risk is a property of a holding's relation to everything else you own. Product management inherited it late, through discovery-driven planning and the reversibility framing of Amazon's shareholder letters.

Four camps disagree substantively. The decision-analytic camp signs a well-elicited subjective probability is a legitimate input even with no frequency data and refuses if you cannot measure it, do not score it. The portfolio-theoretic camp signs the unit of management is the portfolio's distribution, refusing the best portfolio is the highest-EV items. The options camp signs most of a bet's value is the option it creates, so restructure rather than re-estimate, refusing a point estimate is a decision. The sceptical camp signs ranking by a number nobody can calibrate launders politics, refusing therefore prioritise by conviction; it wants ordinal classes and a survival constraint.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Nivedh's six bets appear below, each with a three-outcome partition — fails, half-lands, fully lands — whose probabilities sum to 1 in every row. Payoffs are annual contribution margin in ₹ lakh, and two are derived. Bet B works on 1,20,000 know-your-customer starts a quarter at ₹500 of annual contribution per funded account, so a 2.0-point lift is 2,400 accounts a quarter, 9,600 a year, ₹48 lakh, and 5.0 points gives ₹120 lakh. Bet A carries ₹2,000 per swept user a year: 3,000 users is ₹60 lakh, 12,000 is ₹240 lakh.

The exhibit breaks the ranked list Nivedh was asked for. By raw expected value the order is D, A, B, F, E, C, and taking bets greedily down it until five team-quarters are gone buys D at three and A at two — ₹141.0 lakh. By expected value per team-quarter the order is B, A, F, E, C, D, and the same rule buys B, A, F and E for exactly five team-quarters and ₹195.9 lakh: ₹54.9 lakh, or 38.9 per cent, more from identical candidates and capacity. Exhaustive search confirms {A, B, E, F} is the unique maximum, though {A, B, C, F} at ₹194.4 lakh sits only ₹1.5 lakh behind.

Next the mean stops being comforting. Treat the four selected bets as independent — an assumption that must be stated, because it is doing work — and their payoffs give eighty-one combinations collapsing to forty-eight distinct totals, with probabilities summing to exactly 1. Expected value adds with no independence assumption at all: ₹69.0 + ₹62.4 + ₹31.5 + ₹33.0 = ₹195.9 lakh whatever the bets do to one another. Variance does not: under independence the portfolio's standard deviation is ₹103.34 lakh, against ₹174.33 lakh for the four added up.

Three second-order effects follow. Mean and bound must be computed on the same object: the fifth-percentile total is ₹60 lakh — 2.50 per cent of the mass sits at or below ₹48 lakh, 5.29 per cent at or below ₹60 lakh — a percentile of that same distribution, not a re-scoring of bets. Second, the chance at least one bet lands fully is 1 − 0.80 × 0.70 × 0.80 × 0.70, or 68.6 per cent, while the chance all four fail is 0.45 × 0.15 × 0.30 × 0.10, or 0.20 per cent; those figures, not the mean, are what funding four bets buys. Third, all of it depends on the partition: split bet D's failure state in two and its expected value moves with no new fact.

4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

Four testable conditions carry the method. One: the bet repeats often enough for the mean to be realised. Guthli funded four bets on its five team-quarters this quarter, sixteen a year at that rate, so its mean forecasts something; Gahvara's tooling decision arises once per device generation, so its mean ranks rather than predicts. Two: the worst outcome is survivable. Guthli's is a lost quarter of capacity, Gahvara's ₹3.2 crore of scrapped tooling against a balance sheet that absorbs it — holding for both, failing for the firm in section 8. Three: payoffs share a scale and a horizon. Guthli's six are all annual contribution margin; Gahvara's three-year, with one-off tooling netted inside each branch. Four: the probabilities carry information. Bet F's 0.10 is one failure in ten prior performance releases; bet D's 0.75 is shared pessimism about a new surface.

The idea actively misleads in three cases. Where one outcome is ruinous, expectation averages over futures in which the firm no longer exists, and averaging is the wrong operation. Where the payoff is strategic position — a standards foothold, a data asset, a regulatory precedent — the units are not additive and the sum looks like money without being money. And where a probability is a negotiating position, the arithmetic launders it: a sponsor who wants bet C funded need only move its full-landing probability from 0.15 to 0.17, taken from its failure probability, and C's expected value rises from ₹30.0 lakh to ₹33.0 lakh — level with bet F, which anything above 0.17 displaces.

5. Hard edges, and what mature firms do

Multi-product firms hit the seam first. Guthli's bet A depends on a partner bank's deposit API, while the partnership team's roadmap holds a bet on switching partners. Each portfolio is coherent and the pair is not, because the two expectations run over incompatible states of the world. Mature firms do not answer this with a bigger spreadsheet; they name a few shared assumptions and tag every bet that depends on one, so correlated exposure becomes visible without being quantified.

Two-sided and marketplace products break independence more deeply, because a supply-side bet changes the payoff of every demand-side bet rather than merely co-varying with it; bet-by-bet expected values then overstate the total, and the fix is to model the sequence, not the set. Regulated hardware inverts the usual advice: the gate is a genuine probability with a frequency base, so the arithmetic is more trustworthy than in software, while the cost of error is lumpier. AI-native products invert it again — the capability can improve underneath you, so a bet's probability is non-stationary inside its own quarter.

At the organisational seam, what mature companies say is that they allocate by expected value. What they do is allocate shares — a fixed fraction of capacity to maintenance, a fixed fraction to large uncertain bets — and use expected value to choose within each share. That is robust to the defect that matters most, that one team's elicited probabilities are not comparable with another's.

6. Eight expert distinctions

Expectation adds; risk does not. The tell is a sheet that sums expected values and sums a "risk" column beside them. Guthli's four selected bets have standard deviations of ₹89.55, ₹41.15, ₹24.50 and ₹19.13 lakh; the portfolio's is ₹103.34 lakh, not their ₹174.33 lakh sum. Expectations add with no assumption; deviations do not.

The mean is not the modal experience. An expert reads Exhibit 3 as saying ₹195.9 lakh is an outcome Guthli misses in 59.0 per cent of worlds, and reports a median and a low percentile beside it. The obvious reading makes a well-executed plan look like a miss.

Defining the payoff is harder than estimating the probability. The tell is a payoff with no denominator or horizon. Bet B's ₹48 lakh is a number only because 1,20,000 quarterly starts, ₹500 of annual contribution and a twelve-month window are named. Teams argue for hours about 0.55 versus 0.60 and minutes about annual versus lifetime.

Correlation hides in the shared assumption, not the shared team. Practitioners look for bets staffed by one squad and call that the dependency; the expensive correlation is the premise two bets share, which ties together bets that never touch the same code.

Expected value rises by restructuring, not by arguing. The tell is a review spending forty minutes relitigating a probability. The expert asks instead what sequence would let the firm learn it cheaply before committing the cost — what section 8 prices at ₹0.51 crore.

Learning is a payoff, not a tiebreak. Information value not entered as a payoff is entered as zero, and portfolios built that way underfund the cheap bet that would resolve the expensive one. Ask which decision the result changes; if none, the claim is decoration.

"Big bet" is a class defined by cost, not ambition. Guthli's stated definition is a bet consuming more than one team-quarter and having a best case of at least ₹200 lakh. Tested row by row against Exhibit 1: A qualifies on both limbs, D on both, and B, C, E and F each fail both. Guthli holds two big bets, accounting for 5 of the 9 requested team-quarters, which is 55.6 per cent, and ₹141.0 lakh of the ₹297.9 lakh of candidate expected value, which is 47.3 per cent. The selected portfolio holds exactly one, using 2 of its 5 team-quarters and ₹69.0 lakh of its ₹195.9 lakh. The competent practitioner's tell is a deck calling the loudest bet the big one.

Ruin truncates the series. Expected value assumes you play again. A bet with a branch that ends the game needs a survival constraint before the arithmetic, never a risk weight inside it: an average over a world in which you continue and one in which you do not is not a quantity anyone can spend.

7. Product type and company stage

Less changes than the literature implies, and in a specific direction: the arithmetic is identical everywhere, while the trustworthiness of its inputs and the cost of error are not. In consumer products probabilities are most defensible, because experiments are cheap and base rates accumulate — bet F's 0.10 is a measured frequency — while payoffs are least defensible, because retention effects decay over longer horizons than a planning cycle. B2B and enterprise reverse this: the payoff is a contract of known value, the probability a judgement about a few named accounts. In platform and marketplace products neither input is the problem; additivity is.

Hardware makes irreversibility visible, which helps: tooling is a date and a number, so sequencing gets designed instead of hoped for. AI products are the one genuine novelty. On stage, the honest statement is blunt: a seed-stage company has a portfolio of one, and expected value says little about one beyond ruling out gambles it cannot survive. The method pays where a firm runs enough simultaneous bets for averages to mean something, and the late-stage pathology is the reverse, with allocation shares calcified and the arithmetic a ritual after the decision.

8. Three worked examples

Guthli's quarter, resolved

Nivedh funded B, A, F and E. The quarter closed with B half-landing at ₹48 lakh, A fully landing at ₹240 lakh, F half-landing at ₹25 lakh and E failing: ₹313 lakh against ₹195.9 lakh expected, on a combination of prior probability 0.55 × 0.20 × 0.60 × 0.30 = 1.98 per cent.

The instructive residue was bet F. Neerav Yaneja, Guthli's head of analytics, had tested the change on 4,000 users an arm: 440 conversions in control at 11.0 per cent, 488 in treatment at 12.2 per cent. The 1.2-point gap has a standard error of √(0.110 × 0.890 ⁄ 4,000 + 0.122 × 0.878 ⁄ 4,000) = 0.716 points, so z = 1.68 and the 95 per cent interval on the difference runs from −0.20 to +2.60 points — estimate and interval both differences in proportions over the same arms. At 4,000 an arm the test detects about 2.0 points at 80 per cent power, two-sided with α = 0.05 and variance pooled at 11.6 per cent; 1.2 points would need roughly 11,200 per arm. The review called it a win; at z = 1.68 the two-sided p is 0.094, so the data cannot distinguish 1.2 points from zero.

Gahvara's gate

Neharika's decision is a two-stage tree. Committing tooling now gives three exhaustive outcomes: no clearance at 0.30, paying −₹3.2 crore; clearance then high adoption at 0.70 × 0.40 = 0.28, paying +₹14.0 crore; clearance then low adoption at 0.70 × 0.60 = 0.42, paying +₹2.0 crore. The three sum to 1.00 and the expected value is 0.30 × (−3.2) + 0.28 × 14.0 + 0.42 × 2.0 = −0.96 + 3.92 + 0.84 = ₹3.80 crore. Both clearance payoffs are net of the tooling, which is why only the failure branch carries it. Eleven weeks from 18 September returns the review on 4 December, after the November tooling date, so Option 2 is also a decision to slip.

Where it failed: Gilehri Learning

Gilehri Learning, a school-market ed-tech, entered the year to 31 March 2025 with ₹14.0 crore of cash and fixed burn of ₹0.45 crore a month, ₹5.4 crore for the year. It approved six independent bets at ₹1.2 crore each — ₹7.2 crore committed — each with a 0.25 chance of a ₹5.4 crore payoff and nothing otherwise. Every bet was EV-positive: 0.25 × 5.4 = ₹1.35 crore gross against ₹1.2 crore of cost, so ₹0.15 crore net each, ₹0.90 crore for six. Outflow of ₹5.4 + ₹7.2 = ₹12.6 crore left ₹1.4 crore at year end, 3.1 months of runway. Payoffs arrived the following year, so the Series B needed proof and investors wanted two bets to land. At p = 0.25 the chance of zero successes is 0.75⁶ = 17.80 per cent and of exactly one 6 × 0.25 × 0.75⁵ = 35.60 per cent, so failing that test had probability 53.39 per cent — 17.80 and 35.60 are each rounded, so they sum to 53.40 on the page.

The recovery, forced in the third quarter, was not cleverer estimation. Gilehri cut to three bets, ₹3.6 crore committed, leaving ₹14.0 − ₹5.4 − ₹3.6 = ₹5.0 crore, or 11.1 months of runway at the same burn, while expected value fell from ₹0.90 crore to ₹0.45 crore. It bought eight months of survival for ₹0.45 crore of expected value — not a departure from the discipline, since a survival constraint belongs to the problem's specification.

9. Failure modes and early warnings

Probability inflation by sponsor. The sign is a probability that moves upward between two meetings with no new evidence between them. Ask: what observation changed this? Caught late, the portfolio's expected value is a sum of advocacy.

Certainty bias. The sign is a funded list on which every bet's failure probability sits below 0.20; Guthli's four selected bets run from 0.10 to 0.45. Ask: what was the expected value of the bet we dropped? Caught late, the firm compounds reliably at a rate it cannot raise.

Dividing by the wrong resource. The sign is a per-unit column headed by whatever the template named rather than by what ran out last quarter — design review, one staff engineer, how many experiments users absorb. Ask: what did we run out of? The cost is section 3's ₹54.9 lakh, every quarter, invisibly.

Averaging over ruin. The sign is a positive expected value for a plan whose downside includes a financing event. Ask: in how many of these worlds do we still exist? Caught late, recovery costs a quarter of execution and the board's confidence.

Judging ex-ante decisions ex post. The sign is a retrospective that praises bet A and buries bet E. Ask: would we take this bet again at these odds? Caught late, teams learn to propose only bets that look good in hindsight, and the elicitation everything rests on dies.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Elicit and compute. At its strongest this is not a claim that product managers are calibrated, but that they already make implicit probability judgements, that written numbers are auditable while intuitions are not, and that calibration improves with feedback. Its evidence is the forecasting literature and the improvement of teams that score and review. It would be wrong if ten quarters of scoring narrowed no gap between stated and realised rates.

Allocate shares, never score items. At its strongest: cross-team probability estimates are not comparable, so item-level ranking across teams is measurement error dressed as a decision, and a fixed allocation to risk classes delivers most of the diversification with none of the spurious precision. It would be wrong if item rankings beat share allocation on realised returns, which nobody has measured.

Restructure, do not estimate. At its strongest: the elasticity of a bet's expected value to its structure dwarfs its elasticity to better estimation, as Gahvara's ₹0.51 crore against an argument about 0.70 shows, and effort on probabilities is effort not spent finding the cheap experiment. It would be wrong wherever bets cannot be decomposed and sequencing buys nothing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a spreadsheet with a probability column. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They argue about the partition and the payoff definition before anyone says a probability aloud. They never report a mean without a median and a low percentile on the same object. They treat disagreement about a probability as a signal to buy information, and can price it before buying. And they hold the survival constraint outside the arithmetic, so whether the firm lives through the bad branch is settled first. The tell: more meeting time on what would have to be true than on what the number is.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Nivedh funded B, A, F and E — ₹195.9 lakh against the ₹141.0 lakh his raw-EV ranking would have bought — and declined D, asking its sponsor to return with a one-team-quarter probe rather than a three-team-quarter build. He reported the ₹168 lakh median and ₹60 lakh fifth percentile beside the mean, which was the harder decision. Neharika bought the review, deferred the tooling commitment to its December outcome, and told her board the launch date was contingent rather than promised.

Question 1. At what capacity would the raw-EV ranking and the EV-per-team-quarter ranking select the same portfolio, and what does that tell you about when the distinction is worth fighting over?

Question 2. Gahvara's review is treated as a perfect predictor. Suppose it is right four times in five. Below what accuracy does ₹0.45 crore stop being worth paying, and who should be allowed to estimate that accuracy?

Question 3. Exhibit 3 assumes independence. Identify the single assumption most likely to be shared across all four bets; if it fails, which figure in the exhibit moves first, and how far can the portfolio's standard deviation rise before the fifth-percentile outcome becomes unacceptable?

13. Going deeper

  • Decision frameworks: one-way vs two-way doors — the move behind Gahvara's ₹0.51 crore; unlocks pricing reversibility before payoff.
  • Strategic bets and reversibility — the same logic where payoff is position, section 4's misleading case.
  • Managing a portfolio of problems — shifts allocation to problems, protecting the partition from sponsors.
  • Balancing a portfolio across horizons and risk — section 5's shares as a design, not a default.
  • Value vs effort — Exhibit 2 with certainty assumed.
  • RICE scoring — the framework with an explicit confidence term; compare it with partitions.
  • Kano model — supplies the payoff shapes, and why some are not additive.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — per-unit ranking with another numerator; the knapsack argument holds.
  • Buy-a-feature — elicits payoff weights from customers, not sponsors.
  • User story mapping — how a large bet decomposes into a sequence that makes restructuring possible.
exp20v2-prio.bets:
Portfolio of Bets and Expected Value

Delivery & Technology, Prioritisation & Decision-Making

1. Four proposals, thirty-two weeks

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Manjot Virmani, head of product at Emberlane Payments, opened a spreadsheet. Emberlane, a Chandigarh company, collects card and UPI payments for about 8,000 small merchants. The quarter beginning Monday 4 January 2027 would give her team 32 engineer-weeks for new work, after leave, on-call duty and maintenance. An engineer-week is one engineer working one week. Four proposals asked for 42.

Each proposal carried an estimated payoff: extra gross profit (revenue less direct costs) over the twelve months after launch, in lakh rupees (one lakh is 100,000). Smart payment reminders for merchants' invoices would take 6 weeks. A rebuilt merchant onboarding flow, 10. Same-day settlement of merchants' takings, 12. A working-capital credit line, offered through a lending partner, 14.

Mahtab Vaid, the finance lead, wanted the list ordered by confidence: fund what is most likely to work until the weeks run out. Virmani suspected that ordering would leave money on the table, but she needed a number, and an argument she could say aloud.

2. The idea

The expected value of a bet is the average result you would get if you could place it many times: list every outcome, multiply each outcome's payoff by its probability, and add. Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat worked this out in 1654, in letters about how to divide the stake of a gambling game interrupted halfway. In 1738 Daniel Bernoulli observed that a rupee matters less to a rich person than a poor one, so averages of money differ from averages of benefit. In 1952 Harry Markowitz, studying investments, argued that a portfolio (a set of holdings judged together) should be assessed as a whole, not holding by holding.

Product work borrowed both ideas. Each initiative is a bet: a spend of scarce effort with an uncertain return. The roadmap is a portfolio of such bets. Ranking by confidence asks only one question, how likely is this to work. Expected value asks a second as well, how much is it worth if it does, and divides by the scarce resource, here engineer-weeks.

The sentence Virmani could repeat: “We are not choosing the bets most likely to work; we are choosing the set that pays most on average for the weeks we have, and buying cheap evidence about the ones we are unsure of.”

3. How it works

Practitioners leave several steps unspoken. First, fix the unit and horizon of payoff: here, annual gross profit in lakh, twelve months after launch. Second, list the outcomes, including the failure branch. Virmani gave each bet two outcomes, works or does not, and let failure pay zero; the probabilities of a bet's outcomes must sum to exactly 1. Third, compute expected value. Fourth, divide by the constrained resource, because the question is value per week, not value alone. Fifth, choose the best combination that fits the budget. Sixth, inspect the spread of the combined result, not just its average. Seventh, schedule a revision when evidence arrives.

Table 1. Emberlane's four bets (payoffs in ₹ lakh a year)
BetWeeksChance it worksPayoff if it worksExpected valueEV per week
A. Payment reminders60.904036.06.00
D. Onboarding rebuild100.709063.06.30
B. Same-day settlement120.5012060.05.00
C. Credit line140.2040080.05.71

Expected value is chance times payoff; EV per week is expected value over weeks, to two decimals. Failure pays zero, and each bet's two outcome probabilities sum to 1.

Figure 1 shows why the two rankings differ. Ordered by chance of working, the sequence is A, D, B, C. Ordered by expected value, C leads at 80, ahead of D at 63, B at 60 and A at 36. The credit line is least likely to succeed yet most valuable on average: its payoff is ten times the reminders', its chance under a quarter of theirs.

4. A worked example, and what moves it

Virmani's constraint was 32 engineer-weeks. Three combinations are maximal, meaning no further bet fits beside them; every other feasible set is a subset of one of these. Table 2 prices them by adding the bets' expected values from Table 1, first at the credit line's 0.20 chance of working and then at 0.10.

Table 2. Maximal portfolios and their expected value (₹ lakh a year)

At 0.10 the credit line's expected value is 0.10 × 400 = 40, so the last two columns differ only by 40 in any portfolio containing C.

Filling the budget by confidence gives A, D and B: 28 weeks, expected value 36 + 63 + 60 = 159. Filling it by expected value gives A, D and C: 30 weeks, 36 + 63 + 80 = 179. At the assumed 0.20, the difference of 20 lakh a year is the cost of preferring certainty.

Now change one input. Suppose Virmani's lending partner is more cautious than she assumed, and she lowers the credit line's chance to 0.10. Its expected value halves to 40, A + D + C falls to 139, and the certainty portfolio becomes best. The break-even is 0.15: A + D + C exceeds 159 only when 36 + 63 + 400p > 159, that is when p > 0.15. Equivalently, at p = 0.20 a payoff below 300 flips the decision. A ranking that flips at 0.15 rests on an assumption that deserves effort.

That effort is a pilot: two engineer-weeks building a throwaway version for 40 merchants. Suppose it comes back strong with chance 0.20, after which the credit line's chance of working is 0.50; or weak with chance 0.80, after which it is 0.125. These are consistent with the original: 0.20 × 0.50 + 0.80 × 0.125 = 0.20.

The tree's value is 0.20 × 299 + 0.80 × 159 = 59.8 + 127.2 = 187.0, against 179 for committing blind. The pilot is worth 8 lakh a year, and costs nothing in forgone bets because no proposal fits into two spare weeks. Its value comes from the weak branch, where it prevents a 14-week commitment worth 149 rather than 159.
