Table 3 shows what the extra 20 lakh costs. The higher-EV portfolio is more likely to disappoint (a 24.0 per cent chance of 40 or less, against 15.0) and less likely to reach 130 (70.4 per cent against 80.0). Its average is higher because of a thin, large upside. Whether to take that trade depends on how much disappointment Emberlane can absorb.

5. What a learner must become aware of

A probability is a judgement, not a measurement

Nobody measured 0.20 for the credit line. It was someone's belief, shaped by the lender's past behaviour and by optimism. Multiplying precisely cannot make a guess more accurate than the guesser. Ask where each probability came from.

An average is not an outcome

Expected value describes many repetitions; a quarter gives one draw. A portfolio of many small bets approaches the average. Three bets, as in Table 3, do not: the credit line either pays 400 or nothing. Bernoulli's point also applies: a firm that cannot survive a bad year should value downside more heavily than the arithmetic does.

Independence is an assumption

Table 3 multiplies probabilities as if the bets were unrelated. If reminders and the onboarding rebuild both depend on one clean-up of merchant records, their failures arrive together, and the true chance of a poor quarter is higher than either row of the table says.

Expected value is not RICE

RICE scores initiatives as reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort. It resembles expected value, since confidence plays the part of probability, but it takes one impact figure, with no failure branch, no spread and no comparison of combinations.

Learning has a price and a value

The pilot in Section 4 was cheap because spare weeks existed. Information is worth buying when it can change the decision and costs less than the error it prevents. A pilot that cannot alter the plan has no value.

What the method cannot tell you

It cannot say whether the payoff estimates are honest, whether the list omits a better idea, or what an irreversible commitment is worth. A bet that cannot be undone, a one-way door, deserves more caution than its average suggests. Before relying on a result, ask what the break-even probability is, who set the inputs, and what evidence would change them.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products, experiments are cheap and numerous, so probabilities can come from base rates (the historic share of tests that win) and the portfolio really does average out. In B2B products, bets are few and large, each tied to a handful of customers, so Emberlane's lumpiness is typical and probabilities rest on judgement of named accounts. In marketplaces, a bet's payoff often depends on both sides reaching a threshold, so payoff is not proportional to effort and bets share a hidden dependence on liquidity.

Size matters too. An early-stage company with one runway and two possible bets cannot diversify; ruin is possible, and expected value alone is dangerous. A large company funds dozens of bets, can treat failures as a cost of doing business, and can come closer to simple expected-value maximisation.

7. Common mistakes

Sorting by confidence

Symptom: every project ships on time, yet growth is flat. Misunderstanding: that certainty is a form of value. Diagnostic: add a payoff column and see whether the highest-expected-value item sits at the bottom.

Treating a guess as precise

Symptom: probabilities such as 0.35 with no source. Misunderstanding: that arithmetic confers accuracy. Diagnostic: compute the break-even probability, as the 0.15 above, and ask if anyone doubts the estimate by that much.

Funding the long shot whole

Symptom: one 14-week commitment with no checkpoint. Misunderstanding: that a bet is all or nothing. Diagnostic: ask what the first two weeks could prove, and whether a different answer would change the plan.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Virmani's decision fits on one page. It shows Table 1, the portfolios of Table 2 and the break-even probability. It names who set each probability. It reserves weeks for a pilot, states in advance what result would change the plan, and shows the spread as well as the average. Vaid can object to any number, and each objection concerns an input, not taste.

9. The decision

Virmani took the page to the board. She committed 16 weeks to the reminders and onboarding rebuild, starting 4 January, and two weeks to the credit-line pilot, run by one engineer from the same day. After the readout on Friday 22 January she would build the credit line if the pilot were strong, and same-day settlement if it were weak. Vaid accepted, on one condition: that the weak branch be written down before the pilot ran, so that nobody could reinterpret it afterwards. Her reasoning: 179 already beat 159 by 20, but 187 beat it by 28, because the uncertain bet became a question to answer before it became a commitment.

To go further, read about strategic bets and reversibility, which handles the one-way doors this page only named; managing a portfolio of problems, which applies the same logic upstream of solutions; and balancing a portfolio across horizons and risk, which treats the spread in Table 3 deliberately.

Two questions to sit with. Which bet on your own roadmap would you drop if its probability were halved, and do you know the probability at which you would? And what is the cheapest two-week experiment that could change what you build next quarter?
exp40v2-prio.cost.delay:
Cost of Delay

Price the wait, not just the work — and why teams that compute it get the arithmetic of uncertainty backwards.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Thursday 15 January 2026, in a converted mill building in Pune, Ratandeep Bandral watched a slide go up that he already distrusted. Itbaar Technologies sells regulatory-reporting software to forty-one non-bank lenders, all of which must meet a tightened monthly credit-bureau reporting requirement from Tuesday 31 March 2026. Itbaar can patch its pipeline, certain to make the date and leaving a reconciliation mess behind, or rebuild the reporting layer, which removes the mess and might miss the date. Ratnesh Bhagotra, the finance analyst, had priced the choice: the rebuild, his slide said, destroyed roughly ₹140 lakh. Ratandeep's objection was to one arithmetical move inside it, and it took him three weeks to name it.

On Monday 9 February 2026, in Rajkot, Rasleen Baweja took a call from Rohtash Bhalotra at Ibtekaar Devices' contract manufacturer. Ibtekaar builds retrofit cold-chain monitoring units for milk-chilling vans and has 1,240 under contract with dairy unions in western Maharashtra. Fitment can begin in the week of Monday 2 March 2026, van by van — or Ibtekaar can wait for a factory tooling slot in the week of Monday 23 March 2026 and fit the fleet at once, far more cheaply. Her engineering lead put the cost of waiting at ₹59.52 lakh, her commercial lead at ₹19.84 lakh, from the same spreadsheet.

Both firms were pricing the wait rather than the work, and both had a defective calculation of a kind that survives review because it resembles prudence.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Cost of delay is the rate at which economic value is destroyed per unit of time that a decision or a delivery waits. It is a flow, not a stock: a figure quoted without a time unit is not a cost of delay. It is the difference in net present value between two otherwise identical schedules — the same work, done later.

It was invented to solve an accounting problem: firms measured cost and headcount because those appear in a ledger, but nothing converted time-to-market into either. Preston Smith and Donald Reinertsen's Developing Products in Half the Time (1991) made the conversion its centrepiece, popularising a figure attributed to McKinsey — a product six months late earns about a third less profit over five years, while a fifty per cent cost overrun costs a few per cent. That figure is unsourced, and a slogan rather than evidence. Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supplied the machinery; Joshua Arnold and Özlem Yüce's work at Maersk Line turned it into the practice called cost of delay divided by duration, or CD3.

Four schools sign different propositions. The quantified-economics school signs: a team that cannot state its top item's cost of delay in money per week is not prioritising, it is negotiating. It will not sign that Fibonacci scoring substitutes. The relative-scoring school — most of agile practice, and weighted shortest job first as taught — signs that prioritisation needs only ordinal accuracy, and will not sign that each item needs a defended rupee figure. The real-options school, from Dixit and Pindyck's Investment under Uncertainty (1994) and the Poppendiecks' last responsible moment, signs that under irreversibility and self-resolving uncertainty the cost of delaying a decision can be negative, and will not sign that delay always destroys value. The flow school signs that most delay cost comes from utilisation, batch size and queue length, not queue order.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice begins with shape, not magnitude: a per-week figure is meaningful only inside one of four shapes.

A standing loss is a run-rate that never arrives. A fixed-date item costs almost nothing until its date, then steeply — Itbaar's shape, and why compliance work should be scheduled to just finish, not started first. A degrading window loses most of its value in the middle and little at the end, by which point little is left to lose. Pure deferral is the shape mistaken for a standing loss: the cash flow is pushed right, so the loss is only the discount on the shift.

That distinction is worth arithmetic. Take a feature adding ₹9.00 lakh a month of gross margin for thirty months, at 1.0 per cent a month, delayed one month. If the window shifts right, the firm loses month one and gains month thirty-one: 9.00 ÷ 1.01 = ₹8.911 lakh out, 9.00 ÷ 1.0131 = ₹6.611 lakh back, net ₹2.300 lakh. If the window ends at month thirty regardless, month one is lost and nothing comes back: ₹8.911 lakh, 3.87 times as much. Only the window's end differs, and no template asks about it.

Sequencing: why the rule is a ratio

For one team and independent items, the order minimising total delay cost is descending cost of delay divided by duration — Smith's rule (1956), which minimises the weighted sum of completion times.

Exhibit 2. Itbaar's queue, one team, items worked to completion in turn; delay cost accrues from week zero to the ship week.
Item, CD3 orderCoD, ₹ lakh/weekDuration, weeksCD3 ratioShips weekDelay cost, ₹ lakh

Rank the same four by cost of delay alone — "biggest value first" — and the order becomes A, C, B, D, shipping in weeks 4, 10, 11 and 13: 48 + 90 + 66 + 65 = ₹269.0 lakh against ₹218.0 lakh. Nothing but sequence produces that ₹51.0 lakh. Shortest duration alone gives ₹222.0 lakh: ₹4.0 lakh worse.

The second-order effect that dwarfs the first

Sequencing is the visible lever and the smaller one. Delay cost is paid for the whole time an item sits in the system, which utilisation governs. Model the team as one server under M/M/1 — Poisson arrivals, exponentially distributed service times — so that mean time in system is S ÷ (1 − ρ) for a mean service time S. Exhibit 2's four durations average 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25 weeks, so S = 3.25 and the service rate is 1 ÷ 3.25 = 0.3077 items a week.

At ρ = 0.80 arrivals are 0.2462 items a week — 0.2462 × 52 = 12.8 a year — each waiting 16.25 weeks, so at ₹8.00 lakh a week the annual bill is 12.8 × ₹130.0 lakh = ₹16.64 crore. At ρ = 0.95 the team takes 0.2923 a week, 15.2 a year, each waiting 65 weeks: 15.2 × ₹520.0 lakh = ₹79.04 crore. Loading to 0.95 buys 19 per cent more items at 4.75 times the bill. Two caveats the exhibit cannot carry. The ₹8.00 lakh is the simple mean of Exhibit 2's four rates, which is the right base for a per-item cost; the duration-weighted pooled rate would be 118 ÷ 13 = ₹9.08 lakh. And service variability does most of the work: a team with near-deterministic service times, M/D/1 with mean S + ρS ÷ 2(1 − ρ), would wait 9.75 and 34.125 weeks instead, 40 and 48 per cent less. The direction survives both: arguing about order at that utilisation optimises the wrong term.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions make the figure load-bearing, each testable. First, value must be schedule-dependent: shipping later must produce a different lifetime cash flow, not merely a later one. Itbaar passes decisively — forty-one clients incur service credits from 31 March — and Ibtekaar passes, since spoiled milk is not recoverable. A loyalty-points redesign with no competitor racing it and no fixed window usually fails, and its honest cost of delay is a deferral discount.

Second, the figure must trace to a line somebody owns. Itbaar's ₹14.00 lakh a week is 41 clients × ₹0.24 lakh of weekly contractual service credit = ₹9.84 lakh, plus ₹4.16 lakh for a manual-filing desk, both signed by a budget holder. Ibtekaar's ₹19.84 lakh a week is 1,240 vans × ₹1,600 of avoided weekly spoilage. Third, the queue must bind: where capacity is elastic, delay cost prices staffing, not ordering.

The idea actively misleads in one situation above all. When uncertainty resolves without work — a consultation closing, a competitor's launch — the cost of delaying the decision is negative, and a team pricing only the build commits early and expensively.

5. Hard edge cases

Platforms. A platform item's cost of delay is the sum of the delays it causes downstream, so it is not knowable from the platform team's own backlog. Mature firms use a chargeback fiction: consuming teams state what it is worth per week to them and the platform ranks on the sum. What they say they do is compute it; what they do is cap each claim at a budget the claimant forgoes elsewhere — the only thing that disciplines a claim.

Two-sided markets. Delay on one side changes the other side's cost of delay, so the figures are not additive: a supply-side tool launched late suppresses liquidity, and the demand-side item behind it depends on the first's ship date. Smith's rule assumes independence; sequence the pair as one bundle.

Regulated and hardware. A compliance date is a step function, near zero before and enormous after, and the expert behaviour — schedule it to just finish — is almost never observed, because the penalty is asymmetric for whoever sequences it. Hardware adds tooling slots, and these fit none of the four shapes cleanly: Ibtekaar's loss is a standing rate scaled by a fitment ramp, gated by a binary event — the slot holds or it does not — rather than a step at a date.

AI-native products. Here the window degrades for a reason unique to the category: a capability that differentiates this quarter may be absorbed into a foundation model's next release, collapsing the rest of its value on a date nobody controls. The honest treatment is a hazard rate, not a standing loss. At the seam, the product team holds the numerator and the platform team the denominator, so whoever is in the room computes the ratio.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

Deferral is not destruction. The tell-tale sign is a cost of delay equal to a feature's full monthly contribution. The obvious reading treats every delayed rupee as lost; the question is whether the window's end moves. The ₹9.00 lakh case differed 3.87-fold on that alone.

The clock starts at information, not the ticket. Experts date the cost of delay from the moment the firm could have acted. The sign is a backlog of short-duration items whose outcomes are late: the delay sat in discovery, invisible to a ratio built from an engineering estimate.

The denominator is the blocking resource's time, not the calendar. An item with a six-week calendar duration that occupies the constrained team for one week has a duration of one. The sign is a ranking that buries vendor-dependent work, cheap to start and expensive to wait for.

Costs of delay are not additive across items sharing a trigger. Two items that both unblock the same renewal cannot each claim its weekly value. The sign is a summed cost of delay exceeding revenue run-rate, read as an unusually valuable portfolio.

Fibonacci bucketing is not order-preserving. Two items from a later Itbaar quarter, outside Exhibit 2's queue: E at ₹10 lakh a week over seven weeks (ratio 1.43) and F at ₹11 lakh over eight (1.38), so E goes first. Round each onto 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and E becomes 8 ÷ 8 = 1.00, F 13 ÷ 8 = 1.63: the order inverts. A ratio survives a common scale factor, not a re-bucketing, and relative scoring assumes otherwise.

A fixed-date item should not be done first. Its cost of delay is near zero until the date. The sign is a team finishing compliance work in January for a March date while a standing loss accrues behind it: prudent for the sequencer, expensive for the firm.

Cost of delay can be negative. When a commitment is irreversible and information is arriving anyway, waiting has option value. The sign is a decision whose dominant uncertainty resolves without work; the obvious reading — delay always costs — produces expensive early lock-in.

Weight both sides, or neither. The frequent serious error is an expected value on one side of a comparison and a worst case on the other; a churn rate built from an annual number is a cousin, assuming every cohort is exposed every week. The sign is a slide where one figure carries a probability and the figure it is subtracted from does not. It is Ratnesh Bhagotra's error.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products costs of delay are degrading windows driven by attention and seasonality, estimable in aggregate and hopeless per feature; price the window, not the item. In B2B and enterprise the figure is frequently exact, because contracts carry service credits, renewal dates and penalties — Itbaar's ₹14.00 lakh a week is a contractual fact, which is why enterprise teams can run CD3 honestly and consumer teams mostly cannot. Platforms and marketplaces suffer the additivity problems above: their sequencing is a bundling problem in ranking clothes. In hardware the dates are physical, so shape matters more than rate; for AI products the hazard that a model release absorbs the window is distinctive.

By stage the difference is smaller than claimed. A seed-stage firm's dominant cost of delay is runway, one standing loss applying identically to everything it might build, so ranking by cost of delay adds nothing and ranking by learning rate adds much. From roughly Series B, contracts and seasonality create real per-item variation and the ratio earns its keep. At scale the binding term reverts to queueing. That cost of delay matters more as firms grow holds only in that the spread grows; the arithmetic is the same at every stage.

8. Three worked examples

Example 1 — sequencing, and what it is worth

Exhibits 2 and 3 are the example: ₹51.0 lakh from re-ordering four items on one thirteen-week queue, or, assuming four such batches a year, 4 × ₹51.0 = ₹204.0 lakh, which is ₹2.04 crore. Set that against Exhibit 4 on the same annual footing. At ρ = 0.90 arrivals are 0.2769 a week, 14.4 a year, each waiting 32.5 weeks at ₹260.0 lakh — ₹37.44 crore — so moving from 0.95 to 0.90 saves ₹79.04 less ₹37.44 = ₹41.60 crore and costs 0.8 items of annual throughput. On those assumptions load is worth about twenty times what order is: ₹41.60 crore against ₹2.04 crore. Sequencing is real but not where the money is.

Example 2 — Itbaar, and the asymmetric weight

The rebuild avoids a ₹64.00 lakh re-platforming bill due at month fifteen — but only if the product line survives a board review, which Ratnesh Bhagotra put at 0.80: 0.80 × (64.00 ÷ 1.0115) = 0.80 × ₹55.13 lakh = ₹44.10 lakh. It also removes ₹0.42 lakh a month of reconciliation, worth ₹0.42 × 13.865 = ₹5.82 lakh — unweighted, because the drag accrues over the fifteen months up to the review, so the review's outcome cannot reach back and cancel it — and costs ₹22.00 lakh more in engineering. Then he priced the schedule risk at the worst case his own table held — a twelve-week slip — as though certain: 12 × ₹14.00 lakh = ₹168.00 lakh, netting −₹140.08 lakh.

That table put the twelve-week slip at probability 0.10 and a five-week slip at 0.20, with 0.70 on hitting 31 March. Expected slip is 0.20 × 5 + 0.10 × 12 = 2.20 weeks, so expected delay cost is ₹30.80 lakh. The patch's is zero, since it makes the date with certainty: both sides are expected values, one of them zero.

Example 3 — Imtihaan Learning, where CD3 failed

Imtihaan Learning, a Bengaluru consumer-education marketplace with ₹96 crore of revenue in the year to March 2025, adopted CD3 in July 2024, each product manager estimating cost of delay for their own items. By March 2025 its thirty-four live items carried claims of ₹412 lakh a week, or ₹214.24 crore a year — 2.23 times revenue. Reetinder Basran, the chief product officer, used that aggregate as the diagnostic: a portfolio cannot destroy more by waiting than the firm earns by operating. The recovery was to make each figure name a cash-flow line and a budget holder who would accept a cut if the claim proved wrong. Nine items lost more than four-fifths of their claim, the surviving total was ₹71 lakh a week or ₹36.92 crore a year, and four of the original top five fell out of it. The method had not been wrong, only unbudgeted.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Inflation. Sign: summed cost of delay exceeds revenue. Diagnostic: who loses budget if this figure is wrong? Caught late, the whole ranking must be rebuilt and the method loses credibility.

Asymmetric weighting. Sign: one side of a comparison carries a probability and the other a worst case. Diagnostic: which quantities in this subtraction are expected values? Caught late, as Itbaar nearly found, it removes the decision rather than informing it, turning a near-tie into an apparent rout.

Ramp priced as fully ramped. Sign: a cost of delay multiplied by a staged rollout's end state. Diagnostic: what is the exposure in each week of the ramp? Caught late, the figure can be wrong by the ratio of ramp to slip — three times over, for Ibtekaar, giving the same ₹59.52 lakh that is correct only for its slot-failure branch.

Optimising order at high utilisation. Sign: an elaborate prioritisation ritual and a lead time nobody can predict. Diagnostic: what is ρ, and what is S ÷ (1 − ρ)? Caught late, a year of sequencing recovers a fraction of one point of utilisation.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Quantify or stop pretending. At its strongest this rests on the claim that ordinal rankings are not auditable and so not contestable: a figure with a named owner can be challenged, a story cannot. Its evidence is the Maersk work, where per-week figures reordered a portfolio defensibly. It fails if estimation error exceeds the spread between items.

The ratio is a ritual. Steelmanned, this holds that CD3's inputs are unknowable to better than a factor of two in most contexts, that the ranking is therefore unstable, and that the ritual's function is to force a conversation a plain forced ordering forces more cheaply. Its evidence is Imtihaan's inflation, which appears wherever estimators are also claimants. It would be wrong wherever the figures are contractual, which is most of enterprise software.

The figure prices capacity, not order. This accepts the arithmetic and rejects its application: the dominant term is queueing, so the proper use of the figure is to justify slack or an extra team. Its evidence is Exhibit 4's shape. It would be wrong in a firm that genuinely cannot add capacity, where ordering is the only lever left.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks about shape before magnitude, and about the window's end before its start. They notice which quantities in a comparison are probability-weighted and refuse it until all are. They treat the figure as a claim on someone's budget, and ask who pays if it is wrong. They will argue for scheduling a compliance item last, and distrust their own backlog's summed cost of delay by reflex. And they spend more effort on utilisation and dependency than on ranking, having done Exhibit 4's arithmetic. Someone who has merely studied the topic produces a tidy CD3 table and defends its ordering.

12. The two decisions

On Thursday 5 February 2026 Ratandeep Bandral replaced the certain twelve weeks with the expected 2.20 and presented a −₹2.88 lakh near-tie hinging on a 0.852 break-even against an 0.80 estimate. He chose the patch, because the deciding figure was a board judgement nobody in the room owned, and committed to the rebuild next quarter with the slip risk gone. The arithmetic did not make his decision; it told him which judgement was making it.

On Friday 27 February 2026 Rasleen Baweja settled the dispute by integrating the ramp instead of multiplying by its end state. Retrofit fitment reaches 10 per cent of the fleet in week one, then 30, 60 and 100 — so fitting from 2 March and waiting to 23 March differ, on any horizon of three weeks or more, by exactly 0.10 + 0.30 + 0.60 = 1.00 full-exposure week: ₹19.84 lakh, not three times it. But the slot was only 0.75 certain, and if it fell through the retrofit would start three weeks late, costing 3.00 full-exposure weeks — ₹59.52 lakh — on any horizon of six weeks or more.

Exhibit 7. Waiting for the tooling slot, against fitting from 2 March; ₹ lakh, brackets a cost. Labour: retrofit 1,240 × ₹2,350 = ₹29.14 lakh, factory 1,240 × ₹900 = ₹11.16 lakh. The weighted column is the difference of its two rounded lines; unrounded the total is 16.275.

Rasleen asked the break-even question anyway: waiting pays when 17.98q exceeds 19.84q + 59.52(1 − q), needing q = 59.52 ÷ 57.66 = 1.032 — above one, so no probability of the slot holding makes waiting pay. She began fitment on 2 March and took the slot for the second contract.

Discussion questions

1. Itbaar's break-even survival probability is 0.852 against the team's 0.80. Whose estimate is that, and is the response to re-estimate or to change the option?

2. On Example 1's assumptions, load is worth about twenty times what order is at Itbaar. Which of those assumptions would you attack first, and why would you still expect the firm to spend its effort on order?

3. Imtihaan's claims fell from ₹412 lakh a week to ₹71 lakh once each named a budget holder. Was the original an estimate, a forecast or a bid — and which of the three can a prioritisation method legitimately consume?

13. Going deeper

  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — cost of delay is its numerator made explicit; unlocks what bucketing does to order.
  • Value vs effort — the two-by-two CD3 replaces; shows why a ratio beats a quadrant when durations differ.
  • RICE scoring — a sibling ratio with confidence as a multiplier; unlocks where probability weighting belongs.
  • Kano model — supplies the window shape cost of delay assumes rather than derives.
  • Buy-a-feature — makes claimants spend a budget, the discipline that fixed Imtihaan.
  • User story mapping — finds the smallest slice whose delay costs, shortening the denominator.
  • Prioritising under constraints — where queueing re-enters and Exhibit 4 becomes the main event.
exp20v2-prio.cost.delay:
Cost of Delay

Pricing the wait, not just the work

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 5 October 2026, at ten in the morning, Pritpal Aurora, head of product at Halcyon Ledger, a Mohali company whose software handles GST invoicing for small traders, faced three requests for one engineering squad and thirteen weeks. Sales wanted festive bulk upload, so that a shopkeeper could load a season of invoices from a spreadsheet. Customer success wanted automated payment reminders. Prabhleen Ahlawat, head of engineering, wanted to rewrite the sync engine that kept every customer's books consistent across devices, which had failed twice in the spring. Each sponsor called the work urgent.

The squad could build only one thing at a time: four weeks for upload, three for reminders, six for the rewrite, thirteen in all. Aurora asked Parneet Ahooja, the finance lead, to price the wait rather than argue it. Ahooja's first answer was unwelcome. On her base-case figures, the best and worst orderings differed by more than ₹50 lakh of first-year plan value, a sum nobody in the room had been debating. And the festive trading peak would end on a date no one controlled. A costly outcome was not a missed build but a finished feature that went live after the people who needed it had stopped needing it.

2. The idea

Cost of delay is the economic value lost for each unit of time that a capability is not yet in use, stated as money per week. It was invented to correct a lopsided habit. Teams measured what was easy to see, the cost of building, and neglected the larger, invisible cost of work that could be finished standing in a queue. Don Reinertsen, a product-development consultant, developed the argument through the 1980s and 1990s and set it out in The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009). Joshua Arnold and colleagues later popularised standard shapes for the figure.

Dividing cost of delay by build duration gives a ranking number, often called CD3. Weighted shortest job first (WSJF), a scoring method in the Scaled Agile framework, uses the same division but fills the numerator with relative points. This page fills it with rupees, which is what makes the argument checkable. Aurora's sentence for the meeting: “Everything on this list is worth building; tell me what each week of waiting costs, in rupees, and when that number stops being true.”

3. How it actually works

The method has five steps, and practitioners usually leave the third implicit. First, name the event whose date moves: here, the day each feature becomes live for customers. Second, price one week with the feature and one without, counting only the difference and only in expectation. Ahooja priced upload at 40 extra shops a week signing a ₹30,000 plan, which is ₹12 lakh of first-year plan value. Reminders retained 25 shops a week at ₹20,000, which is ₹5 lakh. The rewrite had a 4 per cent chance each week of a failure costing ₹25 lakh in refunds and churn, an expected ₹1.0 lakh, plus ₹0.5 lakh of weekly support effort: ₹1.5 lakh.

Third, find the shape: whether the weekly figure holds still or changes with the calendar. Upload's ₹12 lakh exists only during the festive peak, which Ahooja's daily invoice counts suggested ended on Sunday 15 November; afterwards the feature earns about a sixth as much, ₹2 lakh. Fourth, estimate the duration. Fifth, rank by the weekly figure divided by duration, then confirm by totalling the value forgone under each full ordering, because the ratio rule quietly assumes things that a total does not.

Figure 1 shows why the bend matters. Reminders and the rewrite lose value at a constant rate, so launching either a week later always costs the same. Upload does not: every week before 16 November costs ₹12 lakh, every week after costs ₹2 lakh. A bent line is cheap to start late only once you are already past the bend.

4. A worked example

Table 1 collects Ahooja's inputs. Dividing each weekly figure by its duration gives upload 12 ÷ 4 = 3.00, reminders 5 ÷ 3 = 1.67 and the rewrite 1.5 ÷ 6 = 0.25. The ratio says: upload, reminders, rewrite.

Table 1. Inputs, in first-year plan value. Build cost is omitted because all three are built in every ordering.

The check is a total. Each item forgoes its weekly figure for every week before it goes live. In order A, B, C, upload is live at week 4 and forgoes 12 × 4 = 48; reminders at week 7 forgo 5 × 7 = 35; the rewrite at week 13 forgoes 1.5 × 13 = 19.5; the sum is 102.5. In order B, A, C, reminders forgo 5 × 3 = 15, but upload goes live at the end of week 7, a week after the peak, and forgoes 12 × 6 + 2 × 1 = 74, so the sum is 15 + 74 + 19.5 = 108.5. Table 2 gives all six. The ratio rule picked the cheapest base-case sequence, ahead of B, A, C by ₹6.0 lakh.

Now change one input. Re-cutting the daily counts, Ahooja found that the peak could instead have ended on Sunday 1 November, four weeks in. Upload first would then go live on 2 November, with nothing left to catch: it still forgoes 48, while delaying it to week 7 forgoes only 12 × 4 + 2 × 3 = 54. The ratio rule gets this right only if upload's numerator is repriced to what it will earn on arrival, ₹2 lakh, giving 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50, which falls below reminders' 1.67.

Ahooja could not say which window was true. She put 60 per cent on six weeks and 40 per cent on four. Weighting both windows the same way, B, A, C costs 15 + (0.6 × 74 + 0.4 × 54) + 19.5 = 100.5, beating A, B, C at 102.5 by ₹2.0 lakh, about 2 per cent. 5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

A rate is not a total

Cost of delay is value lost per week of waiting, not the value of the feature. A feature worth ₹3 crore over its life can carry a small cost of delay if that value accrues slowly, while a modest one carries a large cost if it earns ₹12 lakh every week it is live. The quantity that moves the sequence is the slope, not the height.

The shape decides the answer

Figure 1's bend is the whole story of upload. A steady item can be postponed at a predictable price. A deadline item is either urgent or nearly worthless, and the question is which side of the bend you land on.

Price on arrival, not today

The relevant weekly figure is the one in force when the feature goes live. Upload's ₹12 lakh is true today and false on 23 November. This is why the second pass reversed the ranking.

Weight uncertainty on every side

The rewrite's expected loss is 4 per cent × ₹25 lakh = ₹1.0 lakh a week, which over 13 weeks is ₹13 lakh, though the chance of at least one failure is 1 − 0.9613, about 41 per cent if weeks are independent. Treating a failure as certain within the quarter would price it at ₹25 lakh, nearly double the ₹13 lakh expectation. Weight risks and windows on the same footing, as the 60/40 column does, rather than weighting one side of a comparison and not the other. The order flips when confidence in the six-week window reaches 70 per cent, since 88.5 + 20q = 102.5 at q = 0.70.

The ratio rule has conditions

Ranking by weekly figure over duration is optimal for one team doing indivisible jobs with no dependencies and constant weekly costs. Split the work, add a second squad, or make one item unlock another, and totals must be recomputed.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether the inputs are right, whether the feature should be built at all, or what an option such as learning something first is worth. Ask of any figure: who estimated it, against what baseline, what range, and who in the room would be embarrassed if it were wrong.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

In consumer products cost of delay usually decays fast: seasonal peaks, a rival's launch, attention that moves on. The shapes are cliffs, and the hard part is monetising engagement. In B2B it is lumpy and often attached to named contracts and renewal dates, so a single signature can dominate and probability-weighting matters most. In marketplaces delay compounds: a late supply-side feature slows listings, which slows demand, which slows listings, so the weekly cost can rise with time rather than hold still.

Early-stage companies mostly pay for delayed learning, with runway as the clock and very wide ranges on every input; the discipline is to use rough numbers rather than none. Large companies have better data but many teams sharing dependencies, so the ratio rule fails more often and a portfolio-level total matters more.

7. Common mistakes

Scores without a currency. Symptom: every item is rated high and the ranking matches whoever spoke last. Misunderstanding: relative points feel like pricing but hide the unit. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for rupees per week and a name beside each number.

Certain lumps against weekly flows. Symptom: the rewrite jumps to the top after a scary outage. Misunderstanding: a possible one-off loss was set against a certain weekly gain. Diagnostic: write the probability beside every lump and recompute.

Pricing at today's rate. Symptom: deadline features shipped a week after the deadline. Misunderstanding: the weekly figure was assumed constant. Diagnostic: ask what the weekly figure will be on the day it ships.

8. What good looks like

A good version of Aurora's meeting has one page: three rows, each with a weekly figure, a shape, a probability, a duration and a named estimator; two or three plausible worlds; and a total for each ordering. It shows the regret of each choice, meaning how much worse it is than the best choice if the other world turns out true, and commits only to the first slot, with a date to reprice the rest.

9. What Aurora decided

She chose reminders first. Under the six-week world that choice costs 6.0 lakh more than upload first; under the four-week world upload first costs 14.0 lakh more than reminders first. At 60 per cent confidence in the longer window the expected regrets are 0.6 × 6.0 = 3.6 against 0.4 × 14.0 = 5.6. Reminders also finish by Sunday 25 October, so on Monday 26 October she has three more weeks of invoice counts, which may sharpen the 60/40 split, and can reprice upload and the rewrite.

To learn next, study WSJF's relative scoring, which this page makes explicit, and then decisions under uncertainty: expected value, regret, and the value of information. Reinertsen's work on queues and batch size explains why the ratio rule holds at all.

Two questions to sit with. At what confidence in the six-week window would you start with upload, and who in your organisation could move that number? Which item at the top of your own list has a weekly cost of delay you could state in rupees before this meeting ends?
exp40v2-prio.ice:
ICE and confidence calibration

Score fast, then interrogate the confidence number — the one term in the formula that is a forecast about yourself.

1. Two desks, one suspect number

On Monday 5 October 2026, in Bengaluru, Bhavleen Ichhpujani opened the fourth-quarter planning sheet for Paramiti, the consumer money app she had run product for since 2023. Paramiti had 11.4 million installs and six candidates for the quarter, each scored a fortnight earlier on the company's ICE sheet: Impact, Confidence and Ease, one to ten, averaged. It took eleven minutes to fill.

What changed was a memo. On Thursday 1 October, Bhuvanika Ikhanwal, the growth pod's data scientist, audited every experiment launched between 1 January and 30 September 2026. Ninety-six were launched; eighty reached a resolvable read; sixteen did not, having been stopped early or left running. For each of the eighty the pod had recorded at launch a stated probability that the pre-registered primary metric would move in the predicted direction by at least the predicted magnitude. Forty-six did, at an average stated probability of 74.25 per cent.

Three days after that Monday, on Thursday 8 October, Balbir Ismotra faced the same column with none of the same options. Ismotra ran product at Pulsegrid Energy Systems in Pune, which sold feeder-monitoring hardware to state electricity distribution companies with the analytics service that read it. Pulsegrid shipped firmware twice a year. Across eleven quarters, from the first quarter of 2024 to the third of 2026, he could find nineteen bets precise enough to have resolved; eleven came good.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

ICE is a prioritisation heuristic popularised by Sean Ellis for ranking growth experiments: rate each candidate on Impact, Confidence and Ease, one to ten, and order by the composite. It is RICE — Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort, from Intercom's 2016 formulation — with reach dropped and effort inverted into ease. It solved throughput, not accuracy.

Confidence entered as a discount for epistemic risk. In Ellis's usage it is an honest subjective rating. In the decision-analytic tradition — Brier's 1950 forecast-verification score, Murphy's 1973 decomposition of it, Lichtenstein and Fischhoff's surveys of probability assessors, Tetlock's forecasting tournaments — it is a probability on a falsifiable claim that can be scored. Calibration is the property that of all the claims you called 80 per cent likely, about 80 per cent happened. Resolution is the separate property that high-confidence claims happen more often than low-confidence ones.

Four positions divide. The speed school signs “a score's job is to break ties quickly, not to be right” and refuses “confidence should be a calibrated probability.” The decision-analytic school signs “if you will not mark the claim later, put no number on it” and refuses “an uncalibrated rating improves a ranking.” The flow school signs “halve the batch size and the problem dissolves” and refuses “forecast accuracy is a skill worth measuring.” The discovery school signs “a score avoids an argument” and refuses “a scoreboard of past accuracy should decide whose estimate counts.”

3. Mechanics, worked through

Two instruments get confused. The ICE sheet scores backlog candidates one to ten at planning time. The forecast log records, at launch, a probability on a written claim, and later whether it came true. Paramiti had both; most teams have only the first, and so cannot audit their own confidence.

The page's one formula, used for every row below. ICE score = (I + C + E) ÷ 3, each term an integer from 1 to 10 unless a rescore replaces it with a rate, to two decimals. The variant I × C × E is shown alongside for every row, never for some only. The one mapping from rating to probability is C ÷ 10: a C of 8 asserts an 80 per cent chance the impact claim holds.
Exhibit 1 — Paramiti's Q4 candidates, scored 21 September 2026. Score = (I+C+E)/3; Product = I×C×E.

Read the rank columns against each other. Leader and laggard are identical under both forms, and three of the six rows move: the credit-score tile rises from fourth to second, the streak falls from joint second to fourth, the UPI Lite default from joint second to third. The averaging form rewards the sum, so a balanced 7/7/7 loses to a lopsided 10/9/3; the product form punishes any low term severely. But the product form has one reading the averaging form lacks: if C is genuinely a probability, a score proportional to C is an expected value, and an averaging form that lets a confidence of 3 be rescued by an ease of 10 estimates nothing.

The second-order effect that matters more is what a scored confidence does to its author. A C that never gets marked is a free parameter that drifts toward whatever its author wants the ranking to say. The only defence is a criterion written before launch: metric, horizon, direction and minimum magnitude. Without the magnitude clause a one-basis-point move counts as a hit.

4. What the log says, and what it cannot say

Exhibit 2 is Ikhanwal's audit in five bands. Nothing in the log sat below 50 per cent, itself a finding: a bet the sheet puts at 3 or 4, like the SIP rebuild, had been dropped before it was ever launched, so the lower half of the scale never reached the log.

Exhibit 2 — Paramiti forecast log, 1 January to 30 September 2026; eighty resolved forecasts. SE is √(p(1−p)/n) at the band midpoint, the stated probability used for every forecast in the band.

The total row's midpoint is the forecast-weighted mean stated probability, (12×.55 + 18×.65 + 22×.75 + 20×.85 + 8×.95) ÷ 80 = 59.4 ÷ 80. Its hit rate is pooled, 46 ÷ 80, not the mean of the band rates. Its SE uses Σnbpb(1−pb) = 14.12, so SD = 3.758 hits and 3.758 ÷ 80 = 4.698 points.

Now the discipline that separates a finding from a story. Four bands sit below their stated confidence and the instinct is to read the column as overconfidence. Three of the five gaps will not support it. The 50–59 band is 3.3 points above its midpoint against a standard error of 14.36 points: twelve forecasts near a coin flip carry about fourteen points of noise. The 60–69 band's 9.4-point shortfall is 0.84 of its standard error. The 70–79 band at 1.72 would not survive a correction for looking at five bands at once. Only the top two clear two standard errors, at 3.76 and 4.22; on eight forecasts the normal approximation is crude, and the top band's exact binomial tail is 0.006.

The claim the log supports is the pooled one. Expected hits across the eighty were 59.4; observed were 46; the shortfall of 13.4 hits is 3.57 times the 3.758-hit standard deviation. That is the finding: in aggregate, Paramiti's stated confidence runs about seventeen points hot. It is not the claim that each band is overconfident by its own gap. Exhibit 3 plots the five bands against the diagonal.

Flatness has a name. Murphy's decomposition splits a Brier score — mean squared error of probabilistic forecasts, (p − outcome)² averaged — into reliability (each band's hit rate against its stated probability; lower is better), resolution (each band's hit rate against the base rate; higher is better) and uncertainty. From Exhibit 2 the bands' squared-error contributions are 2.93, 4.605, 5.875, 6.75 and 2.72, summing to 22.88, so Brier = 22.88 ÷ 80 = 0.2860. Reliability is 0.0422, resolution 0.0006, uncertainty 0.575 × 0.425 = 0.2444, and 0.0422 − 0.0006 + 0.2444 = 0.2860.

That is the sting. A forecaster who said “57.5 per cent” to everything would have scored 0.2444 against Paramiti's 0.2860: resolution of 0.0006 means the pod's high-confidence bets came good barely more often than its low-confidence ones.

Then the denominator. The rate is 46 of the 80 resolved forecasts, 57.5 per cent — not of the 96 launched. Had every unresolved forecast hit, the rate over all ninety-six would be 62 of 96, 64.6 per cent; had every one missed, 46 of 96, 47.9 per cent. For the stated confidences to be calibrated across the ninety-six, their mean would have to sit at or below that optimistic bound of 64.58 per cent, requiring 0.6458 × 96 = 62.0 expected hits. The resolved eighty already account for 59.4, leaving 2.6 across sixteen forecasts: a mean stated confidence of at most 16.25 per cent, below the log's 50 per cent floor.

5. The conditions, applied to both protagonists

“Calibrate your confidence term” rests on four testable conditions. One: enough resolved forecasts. Detecting a ten-point overconfidence at a stated 80 per cent, one-sided at five per cent with 80 per cent power, needs (1.645√0.16 + 0.8416√0.21)² ÷ 0.10² = 109 resolved forecasts. Paramiti's eighty fall short of 109, though its pooled gap of 16.75 points — larger than ten — cleared 3.57 standard errors anyway; its three lower bands cannot be read at all. Pulsegrid produced 19 in 11 quarters, 1.73 per quarter; 109 is 63 quarters, just under sixteen years. Two: a criterion written before launch. Pulsegrid's bets resolve against procurement decisions it does not control. Three: a stable question set. Calibration on growth tweaks does not transfer to pricing. Four: the forecaster survives the window.

Where the idea actively misleads: when conditions one and two fail, the exercise yields a number with the authority of statistics and the content of a vibe. Ismotra's nineteen forecasts included twelve stated at 80 per cent or above, all scored here at exactly 80, so the gap is a floor; seven hit, 58.3 per cent. The gap to 80 is 21.7 points, between Paramiti's 70–79 and 80–89 band gaps of 15.9 and 30.0; the standard error on twelve forecasts at a stated 80 per cent is 11.5 points, so the gap is 1.88 standard errors, short of the two that section 4 asks for; the exact binomial tail is 0.07.

6. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies the term is scored by the team that owns the surface and consumed by a committee that owns the portfolio, so aggregation must be per-scorer. In two-sided marketplaces a hit on one side can be a miss on the other, so the criterion must name which side's metric settles the bet. Regulated products break condition two: the bet is often “the regulator will permit this”, resolving once, without replication. Hardware plus software is Pulsegrid's bind — firmware bets resolve in weeks and board revisions in eighteen months, so pooling yields a curve dominated by the cheap forecasts. AI-native products add a different problem: the base rate shifts as the model changes.

At the seams, what mature companies do rather than say: they take confidence out of the score and put it in a gate, routing any claim below the team's own base rate to the cheapest test that could resolve it.

7. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

Calibration and resolution are different diseases. The tell is Exhibit 4: reliability 0.0422 is a calibration problem, resolution 0.0006 an information problem, and training fixes the first while only better evidence fixes the second. Subtracting two points from every C leaves the averaging form's ranking as useless, because a constant preserves order.

A flat curve means the scores rank nothing. The tell is the ordering of band hit rates: 58.3, 55.6, 59.1, 55.0, 62.5 against bands that rise monotonically. The obvious reading blames the top bands; the real one is that the bands cannot be told apart.

The lower half of the scale is dead. Nothing in the log sat below 50 per cent, so a C of 1 to 4 is a rhetorical marker, not a probability. The tell is a sheet whose low-C items never ship and never resolve: C is a veto dressed as a weight.

The formula's shape decides whether confidence can veto. Under the averaging form a C of 3 rather than 10 costs 2.33 points of score and can be bought back by ease and impact; under the product form the same swap divides the score by 3.33. The tell is low-confidence, high-ease items reaching the top: arithmetic, not a taste for quick wins.

Noise is not a gap. Ten forecasts at 50 per cent carry about sixteen points of standard error — √(0.25/10) = 0.158 — so a band landing twelve points from its midpoint is silent. A 32-point gap on eight forecasts looks severe; in Paramiti's top band it clears the bar, and often it will not.

The log is a survivorship sample. Only shipped bets resolve, and bets ship partly because confidence was high, so the population producing the curve is selected on the variable under study. The tell is a resolved count short of the launched count; the remedy is a bound.

Calibration belongs to a person on a question class, not to a company. The tell is a single company-wide curve in a quarterly review. Pooling a calibrated forecaster with an optimistic one describes neither, and the pooled gap sits between their true gaps.

Training collapses variance before it improves accuracy. Told it is overconfident, a team writes the middle of the scale. The tell is a C column whose range narrows as its mean falls; that looks like improvement, and the column has stopped discriminating.

8. What differs by product type and stage

The mechanics do not change by product type; only the achievable sample size and the resolution criterion do. Consumer products at Paramiti's scale resolve a forecast in eleven days on 11.4 million installs, so the hundred or so forecasts a curve needs arrive within a year. B2B and enterprise cannot: the bet is about a buying committee, n is in the tens, and the instrument is the reference class. Platform teams face a resolution problem, not a sample problem: their metric is somebody else's adoption. Marketplaces must name the settling side in advance. Hardware cannot calibrate the bets that matter. AI products forecast fast but their question set drifts.

By stage: a seed-stage team has no sample and should not pretend, but should still write the claim down, which is the log's whole value at that stage. Growth stage is where a curve first becomes affordable and is almost never built. At scale the problem inverts: plenty of data, wrong pooling.

9. Three worked examples

One: the base-rate rescore

Ikhanwal's proposal was blunt. Resolution is 0.0006, so the stated confidences carry no discriminating information; replace every C with the pooled base rate, 57.5 per cent, which under the page's mapping is C = 5.75, and re-rank. Scores become 7.25 for the autopay nudge, 6.58 for KYC re-verify, 6.25 for the streak, 6.58 for the credit-score tile, 6.58 for the UPI Lite default and 5.92 for the SIP rebuild. The autopay nudge, fifth of six on the original sheet, is now first. The three middle items tie exactly at 6.58 because their I + E totals are identically 14. Using each band's own observed rate instead — 6.25 for the 90–99 band, 5.50 for the 80–89, 5.91 for the 70–79 — moves no score by more than 0.17 of a point, and cannot be done at all for the autopay nudge or the SIP rebuild, whose C values of 4 and 3 map to bands the log does not contain.

Two: Pulsegrid borrows a reference class

Ismotra could not build a curve, so he built a denominator. Pulsegrid had run eleven utility pilots since 2024, of which five converted into fleet orders: 5 of 11, or 45.5 per cent. His sheet scored the next pilot-to-fleet bet at I = 9, C = 9, E = 4, a score of 22 ÷ 3 = 7.33. Replacing the stated 90 per cent with the class's rate, rounded to 45 per cent, gives C = 4.5 and 17.5 ÷ 3 = 5.83, a fall of 1.50 points. A reference class is weaker than a personal curve: it assumes the next pilot resembles the eleven. It is also the only instrument he had.

Three: the calibration programme that backfired

Paramiti had tried this before. In April 2026 the pod ran a calibration workshop and the C column on the next two sheets collapsed. The eight items scored in the first quarter carried C values of 9, 8, 9, 7, 8, 6, 9 and 8 — a sum of 64, a mean of 8.00, spanning 6 to 9. The eight scored after the workshop carried 6, 6, 5, 6, 6, 7, 6 and 6: a sum of 48, a mean of 6.00, spanning 5 to 7. Mean stated confidence had fallen exactly two points, which looked like success. But under the averaging form a C range of 2 points can move a score by 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67, against 9 ÷ 3 = 3.00 for a full-range impact term. Confidence had stopped breaking ties in those two quarters, and the second shipped the three easiest items. By September the range had drifted back out, Exhibit 1 spanning 3 to 9.

The recovery had two parts. C came out of the score and became a gate: a claim whose stated probability sits below the team's base rate goes to a cheap test rather than onto the roadmap. And the pod kept measuring. Of the 22 forecasts in the 70–79 band, 14 were logged in the third quarter of 2026 and 9 of those hit, a rate of 64.3 per cent; the 8 earlier forecasts in that band produced 4 hits, 50.0 per cent. That 14.3-point improvement sits against a standard error of the difference of 21.8 points — √(0.5909×0.4091×(1/14 + 1/8)) — so it is 0.66 standard errors and means nothing yet. Separating the Q3 band's remaining 10.7-point gap from 75 per cent at twice its standard error needs 0.1875 ÷ 0.0535² = 66 forecasts in that band.

10. Failure modes and their early warnings

Confidence as an eraser. Sign: C moves after the ranking is seen. Diagnostic: were all three terms written before anyone sorted the sheet? Late cost: a quarter justified by a reverse-engineered number.

No resolution criterion. Sign: a hit rate above 85 per cent. Diagnostic: name the metric, horizon and magnitude for the last bet you called a win. Late cost: an unfalsifiable log.

Reading noise as a lesson. Sign: a band of fewer than fifteen forecasts quoted in a review. Diagnostic: what is the standard error? Late cost: a correction applied in the wrong direction.

Pooling scorers. Sign: one company curve. Diagnostic: do the halves bracket the pooled gap? Late cost: the calibrated forecaster penalised.

Variance collapse after training. Sign: a C column with a range of two. Diagnostic: how much score can C now move? Late cost: the sheet reverts to ranking by ease.

Mixing formula forms. Sign: two decks with different ICE numbers for one item. Diagnostic: a mean or a product, and the same one on both sides?

11. Where experts genuinely disagree

The speed school, steelmanned: scores are tie-breakers under time pressure, their value lies in forcing three explicit judgements where there were none. Wrong if a flat curve like Paramiti's is typical, because then the score ranks noise. The decision-analytic school: probability judgements improve when scored, and a confidence term nobody marks is the one number free to lie. Wrong if the samples product teams can reach — nineteen, for Ismotra — make the measurement itself noise. The flow school: confidence is a function of batch size, and a team shipping in three-day increments can observe rather than forecast. Wrong where batch size is set by physics, which is Pulsegrid entirely. The discovery school: the score's function is political cover and a curve adds a second layer. Wrong where curves route work to cheap tests rather than settle arguments.

Unsettled: whether calibration transfers across question classes, and so whether a growth pod's curve says anything about its pricing bets; and whether the unit of calibration is the individual or the forum.

12. Mastery

Someone who has internalised this writes the claim before the number and the horizon before the claim. They quote a standard error unprompted, and will say “that band has twelve forecasts, so I cannot tell you” where that is unwelcome. They can state their own pooled hit rate and its denominator from memory. They distinguish being hot from being uninformative, and keep one formula on both sides of every comparison.

13. The decisions

Ichhpujani did not adopt the base-rate rescore as a ranking, because a constant C ranks no claim above another: the same three items tie at 6.58 under the rescore and again at 14 on I + E. On Thursday 15 October she installed the gate the recovery had specified but never enforced, and took C out of the score. Three of the six went to cheap tests: the autopay nudge at C = 4 and the SIP rebuild at C = 3, both below the 57.5 per cent base rate, and the rewards streak, whose C = 9 had no written claim behind it and so no stated probability at all — the first entries the log will carry below its 50 per cent floor. The three that stayed — KYC re-verify, the credit-score tile and the UPI Lite default — tie at 14 on I + E, so she broke the tie on ease and shipped the UPI Lite default first, at E = 10.

Ismotra, on Tuesday 20 October, did the opposite of what he had been advised. He abandoned calibrating himself, kept the reference-class denominator, and required a named prior case for any C above 7 — and wrote down the sixteen-year figure.

  1. Paramiti's 90–99 band misses its midpoint by 32.5 points on eight forecasts. Ikhanwal reports it as a finding; Ichhpujani does not act on it. Which is right, and what would change your answer?
  2. Resolution of 0.0006 implies the confidence column carries no information. Does that argue for removing the column, or for fixing the evidence behind it? What does each cost next quarter?
  3. Ismotra's reference class rests on eleven pilots. At what number would you prefer his personal curve — and what would you need to know about the eleven to answer?

14. Going deeper

RICE scoring
Adds reach and makes confidence an explicit multiplier; where the formula's shape stops being arbitrary.
Value vs effort
The two-axis parent; shows what is lost when confidence collapses into value.
Kano model
Supplies a theory of impact, the term ICE leaves least defined.
Weighted scoring and WSJF
Makes the weights explicit and shows how sensitive a ranking is to them.
Buy-a-feature
Replaces stated confidence with revealed preference under a budget.
User story mapping
Changes the unit scored from feature to journey slice, which makes small batches possible.
Prioritising under constraints
What to do when the ranking is feasible and the plan is not.
exp20v2-prio.ice:
ICE and Confidence Calibration

Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making

1. Six ideas, one squad

On Monday 5 October 2026, Amrit Hira, head of product at Nayab Kitchens, a Ludhiana company that sells ready-to-cook meal kits to about 41,000 monthly active households, had an eight-week problem. Starting 12 October, one squad of six engineers, costing roughly ₹30 lakh for the period, could build exactly one of six candidate features. The quarter's target was to lift the thirty-day repeat-order rate from 31 per cent to 36 per cent. A wrong choice would burn the squad's only window this quarter, and the next planning cycle was twelve weeks away.

The team had already scored the six candidates with ICE, a method this page will define shortly. The ranking looked decisive. Then Arvinder Hans, the engineering lead, asked a question that stopped the meeting: "The top item has a confidence of nine. How many of our nines have actually come true?" Nobody knew. Amrit had a planning spreadsheet that recorded every past forecast, and he had until Thursday to answer.

The stakes were not abstract. The three engineers who had built the previous quarter's favourite, a referral prompt that had forecast a gain of two points and delivered closer to half of one, were in the room. Amrit knew that if the ranking was merely repeated with more conviction, the team would learn nothing, and the same overconfidence would be priced into the next quarter's list.

2. The idea

ICE is a scoring method for ranking a backlog, the list of candidate work waiting for a team's attention. Each candidate gets three ratings from 1 to 10. Impact is how much the item should move the metric the team is trying to move. Confidence is how sure the scorer is that the impact estimate is right. Ease is how cheap and quick the item is to build. In this page the score is the product: ICE = Impact × Confidence × Ease, a number from 1 to 1,000. Some teams average the three instead; any version works if used identically for every row.

The method grew out of growth teams in the early 2010s, popularised by practitioners such as Sean Ellis, who needed to pick among dozens of cheap experiments without a month of debate. Its sibling RICE, associated with the software company Intercom, adds a fourth factor, Reach, the number of users affected. ICE is RICE without Reach, with the same confidence problem: the factor that matters most is the one people fill in most casually.

Amrit's repeatable sentence for the meeting: "A confidence score is a forecast about our own forecasts, so we should check its track record before we trust it."

3. How it actually works

Five steps appear in most textbooks; two more usually stay implicit. First, fix the metric. Impact is meaningless until the team names it; Nayab's was the thirty-day repeat-order rate. Second, define the scale anchors: a 10 on Impact might mean "plausibly adds two points of repeat rate", a 1 "under a tenth of a point". Third, each scorer rates every item alone, before anyone speaks. Fourth, the numbers are revealed and large disagreements discussed. Fifth, scores are multiplied and sorted.

The anchors deserve a sentence more. Ease at Nayab was anchored in engineer-weeks: 9 meant under one week for the squad, 5 meant about four, 3 meant seven or more. Without such anchors, two scorers share a number and not a meaning, and the product of three loose numbers inherits the looseness of all three.

Step six is the implicit one: ask what each confidence number was based on, and what confidence numbers like it have delivered before. Step seven re-scores with that evidence and only then decides. Everything below walks through steps five to seven with Nayab's data.

4. A worked example

Table 1 shows the team's first pass. Each ICE value is the product of the three ratings printed on its row.

Table 1. First pass, ICE = I × C × E.

Regional recipe pages win, 486 against 448. Now the audit. Forty past items, released between October 2025 and mid-August 2026, each carried a recorded confidence, so that every one had six weeks of data by 5 October. A "hit" meant the item moved its target metric by at least half the forecast amount within six weeks of release. Table 2 groups them by stated confidence.

Table 2. Forty past forecasts by stated confidence. Hit rate = hits / forecasts.

In aggregate the team is overconfident: its forecasts averaged a stated 73.75 per cent ((10×55 + 20×75 + 10×90) / 40) and hit 52.5 per cent, a gap of 21.25 points against a standard error of about 8, roughly 2.7 of them. Only the 9 bucket is clearly off on its own: 40 points against a standard error near 9.5. The two lower gaps, 15 points each, are about one to one and a half standard errors, so they are suggestive, not proven. The 50 against 60 between the top two buckets is noise: the standard error of that difference is about 19 points.

The second pass changes one input only. Each stated Confidence is replaced by ten times the observed hit rate of its bucket: 4 for the 5 to 6 bucket, 6 for the 7 to 8 bucket, 5 for the 9 bucket. Impact and Ease stay untouched.

The winner flips. One-tap reorder (A) takes first place with 336, ahead of regional recipe pages (D) on 270, and wallet cashback (B), once fourth, falls to last. Nothing about the product changed, only how much the team believed its own optimism. But the flip rests on the 50 against 60 gap just called noise. Pool the two top buckets (17 hits in 30, 56.7 per cent, so C is about 5.7) and A still leads D, but only 317 to 306. A stays ahead under both calibrations, narrowly.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Confidence is about the estimate, not the idea

A scorer who loves an idea tends to give it a high Confidence. But Confidence should measure the evidence behind the Impact figure: a survey, a prototype test, a past launch. Figure 5 shows why it matters. A single point of confidence, from 9 down to 8, drops D from 486 to 432, below A.

The scales are ordinal

An Ease of 8 is not twice an Ease of 4. Multiplying ordinal ratings produces a number that looks like a ratio but is not one, so small differences between scores, such as 336 against 270, are weaker evidence than they appear.

ICE is not RICE

Without Reach, ICE cannot tell a feature touching 400 households from one touching 40,000 unless the scorer hides that difference inside Impact. State which one you did.

Calibration needs a record

Table 2 was possible only because someone wrote down each forecast beforehand. Without a log, the only calibration available is memory, which favours the hits. And with ten forecasts in a bucket, treat a ten-point gap as noise.

Easy items feel certain

Ease and Confidence often move together, because familiar work seems predictable. The pattern double counts: an item scores high twice for being familiar. Score Confidence only about Impact, and keep estimating time under Ease.

Scores rank; they do not decide

ICE cannot see dependencies, strategy or what an item teaches the team. It ranks candidates a person has already judged worthy. It says nothing about the seventh idea nobody listed.

Anchoring and shared rooms

If the most senior person speaks first, others drift toward that number. Hence step three: score alone, then reveal. Where one scorer sets all three ratings for an item, a good impression of it leaks into each, which a second independent scorer on Confidence alone partly cures.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Which metric? Who scored, and in what order? What evidence sits behind each Confidence? What does this team's record say about numbers like it?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products like Nayab's, experiments are cheap and outcomes arrive within weeks, so a calibration table can be built fast, as here. In B2B software, a feature may be requested by five buyers and used by three hundred, outcomes take quarters, and the history for Table 2 accumulates slowly; Confidence there should lean on named customer evidence. In a marketplace, a change that helps one side can hurt the other, so Impact needs two scores or a stated side. At an early-stage company with a short log, calibrate against industry habit or admit the numbers are guesses. A large company has the record, but often has several teams scoring on different scales, which breaks comparison across teams.

7. Common mistakes

Scores that never change. If Confidence is 8 or 9 on almost every top item, the symptom is a backlog where everything looks safe. The misunderstanding is treating Confidence as enthusiasm. The cheapest diagnostic is to tabulate past stated confidence against outcomes, as Table 2 did.

False precision. A team argues over 336 against 270. The misunderstanding is reading an ordinal product as a measurement. Diagnostic: change one input by one point and see whether the order survives.

Scoring as a ritual. The ranking is announced and then overridden. The misunderstanding is using ICE to justify a choice already made. Diagnostic: ask who scored before the preferred item was named.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Amrit's Monday has a named metric, anchor definitions, independent scoring, and a one-page calibration table already in the planning sheet before anyone asks. The team shows both the stated and the calibrated ranking and says plainly where they differ. The squad also schedules a cheap test, a two-week prototype of the one item whose rank depends on Confidence, rather than betting all eight weeks.

9. What Amrit decided

On Thursday 8 October, Amrit presented Tables 1 to 3. He argued that the stated ranking rested on confidence numbers whose track record, 50 per cent for the nines, did not support them, and that the calibrated order was therefore the better estimate, though not a certain one. He chose One-tap reorder for the squad. He also kept a one-week spike on regional recipe pages, because the margin was thin: in the stated ranking one point of confidence (9 to 8) dropped D below A, and in the calibrated ranking D trailed by 66 points and needed a confidence of 7 to overtake, and he recorded all six new confidence numbers in the log for next quarter's table. His reasoning was that the calibrated numbers were still rough, built on forty cases, but they were evidence, whereas the original nines were habit.

What to learn next: RICE scoring, which restores Reach, and then structured experiments, which are the cheapest way to earn a higher Confidence honestly.

Two questions to sit with. If your team's nines were hit half the time, what would you do with your next nine? And which of your current rankings would survive a one-point change in Confidence?
exp40v2-prio.portfolio.balance:
Balancing a portfolio across horizons and risk

A roadmap is a portfolio whether or not anyone manages it as one. The question is whether the mix of sure things, growth bets and options was chosen — and whether the firm can say what is missing.

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, on the fourth floor of Goshree Systems in Bengaluru, Namitha Yadiyal put one slide up and asked the room to argue with it. Goshree sells lending-operations software to Indian non-banking financial companies; calendar 2026 revenue is running at ₹168 crore — ₹121 crore (72.0 per cent) from 31 enterprise accounts, ₹47 crore (28.0 per cent) from 140 mid-market ones, an average of ₹3.90 crore per enterprise account against ₹33.6 lakh per mid-market one. The slide was the draft 2027 plan: fourteen squads, four quarters each, 56 squad-quarters across five bets. Nithyashree Yennamadathil, the chief financial officer, had one objection, and it was not about any bet. "Every line here is defensible," she said. "I cannot tell from it what we have decided."

Ten days later, on Friday 23 October, Nivrutti Yerlapady was having the opposite argument in Pune. Gharonda Living rents water and air purifiers on monthly subscription and services them with its own technicians. At 30 September 2026 it had 2,14,000 subscribers paying an average of ₹610 a month — ₹13.05 crore of monthly recurring revenue, ₹156.6 crore annualised. In March the board approved a 60/30/10 split of engineering capacity across three horizons. A reconciliation of tickets and timesheets, finished the previous evening, said the organisation had executed 75.5/19.5/5.0. Nobody overrode the plan; nobody was told it was abandoned. Neelakanta Yedapadithaya, who runs hardware engineering, put it flatly: "We did not choose that. It happened to us."

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the object. A product portfolio is the full set of commitments of scarce capacity over a planning period, each with an uncertain payoff. Balancing it means choosing, ex ante, how that capacity spreads across two axes: the horizon at which a bet pays — how far its revenue sits from today's product and buyer — and the dispersion of its payoff, the width of the outcome range rather than the size of the mean. It answers a pathology of large 1990s firms: companies that met every quarterly plan for five years and then found they had nothing new to sell. Baghai, Coley and White named the three horizons in The Alchemy of Growth (1999) to make that deficit visible; the plumbing is Markowitz's 1952 portfolio selection, which made the decision object a set of holdings' covariance structure, not any one holding's merit.

Nothing can be counted into a horizon before the horizon is defined. Goshree's, from the slide. H1: defends or extends what is already sold to buyers already paying, against demand already observed, inside twelve months. H2: an adjacent module for the existing buyer, or the existing module for a new one, where the capability exists but demand is inferred. H3: a capability the firm lacks, a demand nobody has priced.

Five positions contend, and disagree about the control variable.

  • Horizon-ratio (Nagji and Tuff, 2012). Signs: set and defend a target split across horizons before the year begins. Will not sign that any ratio is prescriptive — their 70/20/10 was an observed correlation.
  • Real options (McGrath and MacMillan, 1995). Signs: the control variable is the kill point, not the slice. Will not sign that a capacity ratio controls anything.
  • Mean-variance. Signs: dispersion is the decision object, and correlation between bets matters more than the odds on any one. Will not sign that product bets are independent.
  • Resource dependence (Christensen and Bower, 1996). Signs: any declared mix is overridden by the resource-allocation process unless distant work has separate decision rights. Will not sign that a number in a deck changes behaviour.
  • Focus (Pisano, 2015). Signs: portfolios are diversified because nobody would choose, and balance funds everything too weakly to win. Will not sign that balance is an objective.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start where Namitha started: every bet carrying capacity, probability, and value if it arrives.

Exhibit 1 — Goshree Systems, draft calendar-2027 plan as presented on 13 October 2026
