Value is management's own three-year estimate of gross profit: rows 1 and 5 hold value protected, rows 2-4 value incremental, so the column and its total are a mixed base (section 6). Expected value is probability × value, rows rounded to one decimal; the total is the sum of the rounded rows (218.5 against 218.45 unrounded). Shares are rounded and sum to 100.0. The last column divides printed EV by printed capacity; the total-row 3.90 is the pooled ratio (218.5 ÷ 56), not the mean of the five row ratios, 5.14.

The first thing an expert does with Exhibit 1 is refuse its ranking. Per unit of capacity the copilot is best at ₹7.50 crore and the core work worst at ₹2.04 crore, so the efficient plan is to cancel the core work. Why nobody believes that is not in the exhibit: the five rows have wildly different dispersions. Treat each bet as one Bernoulli draw — value V with probability p, nothing otherwise — so its variance is p(1−p)V². Row by row that gives standard deviations of ₹13.1, ₹47.3, ₹58.8, ₹107.1 and ₹5.4 crore. Summed as independent draws the variance is 17,364.8, so the standard deviation is ₹131.8 crore against an expected value of ₹218.5 crore — a coefficient of variation of 0.60. That figure, not the mean, is what the plan is. It also disciplines the post-mortem: a three-year outcome of ₹120 crore sits 0.75 standard deviations below expectation, and is not evidence of a bad mix.

Now the move an expert makes, a trade rather than a ranking. Suppose Goshree shifts three squad-quarters from the copilot into collections. Its own planning assumption: halving the copilot's capacity halves its probability, 0.15 to 0.075, since a discovery bet's only output is learning; collections rises from 0.55 to 0.65, because the extra capacity buys the second ledger integration the module needs to be usable. Weight both sides. Collections rises from ₹52.3 crore to ₹61.8 crore, the copilot falls from ₹45.0 crore to ₹22.5 crore: the portfolio loses ₹13.0 crore of expected value — 5.9 per cent — and its standard deviation falls from ₹131.8 crore to ₹109.3 crore, a cut of 17.0 per cent, taking the coefficient of variation from 0.60 to 0.53. The ₹13.0 crore is 5.9 per cent of the mixed total and 8.9 per cent of the ₹145.3 crore in the three growth rows: quote the base with the rate.

The step left implicit is independence. All three non-core bets need one thing to be true — that Indian NBFC credit books keep growing. Correlation is not free to assume, though: two Bernoulli draws cannot correlate beyond √(p(1−q) ÷ q(1−p)), which for the copilot's 0.15 against collections' 0.55 is 0.38. So take 0.5 for the pairs that admit it — collections with the ledger, ceiling 0.74, and the ledger with the copilot, 0.51 — and the capped 0.38 for collections with the copilot. The covariance terms 2 × (0.5 × 47.3 × 58.8 + 0.38 × 47.3 × 107.1 + 0.5 × 58.8 × 107.1) raise the variance to 30,294 and the standard deviation to ₹174.1 crore, 32.1 per cent higher, coefficient of variation 0.80. Three bets on one macro assumption are one bet in three hats.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions. First, capacity is rivalrous: an hour given to one bet is taken from another. True at Goshree, where all fourteen squads are full-stack. Only partly true at Gharonda, whose firmware and mould engineers cannot move onto the subscriber app — so Gharonda has two portfolios, and one 60/30/10 target across both is arithmetic without meaning.

Second, the horizons have different clocks: if every bet pays inside one quarter, dispersion is the only axis. Both firms pass — the copilot and the sensor both pay years after the work defending today's revenue. Third, the firm can survive the bad tail. Goshree can: 50 per cent of its capacity sits on a bet with p = 0.95 and its revenue is contracted. Gharonda cannot as easily, because its H1 work defends a service operation whose failure shows up as churn within a month.

It misleads in two situations. One is a firm with a single unprofitable product, where "balance" licenses diverting capacity from the only thing that could make it viable: the question presupposes a portfolio worth having. The other is a regulatory obligation, which is not a bet. Goshree's compliance work has no real probability of being skipped, and putting p = 0.95 on it is what makes row one the worst line on the page.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product firms face composition: three lines each at 70/20/10 give a firm at 70/20/10 and no bet large enough to matter. Balance belongs where the cash is owned. Two-sided marketplaces break the horizon definition, because supply pays through demand: an H2 bet on seller tooling is an H1 bet on buyer conversion, so the work is classified twice. In regulated settings the mandatory slice should leave the denominator before any ratio is computed, or a compliance-heavy year reads as collapsing ambition. Hardware-plus-software firms face asymmetric reversibility — software can be abandoned on a Tuesday, tooling cannot — so the halves need different instruments. AI-native bets invert the cost curve: the expensive part is evaluation, and a six-week prototype carries a two-year measurement obligation.

At the seams, mature firms do not do what they describe. They describe a ratio; they operate a separate gate — distant bets reviewed against learning milestones by different people on a different calendar, the ratio a reporting artefact produced afterwards. The ratio follows the governance, not the reverse.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The declared mix is not the revealed mix, and only the revealed one is real. The tell is a firm that can quote its ratio but has never reconciled it against delivered work. Gharonda's gap was 15.5 points, moved by nobody in particular. The obvious reading — that the team disobeyed — is wrong: interrupt-driven H1 work wins a tie, and a tie is an unprotected plan's default.

Every bet must be tested against the horizon definition, one at a time. The tell is a portfolio in which no bet has ever been reclassified downward. Goshree's co-lending ledger was presented as H2 — adjacent demand, inferred not observed — yet Goshree already sells a co-lending ledger to two of its thirty-one enterprise accounts as a bespoke build, and the planned bet productises those same installations for the same enterprise book, not the 140 mid-market accounts — so observed demand covers its whole scope. Demand observed and capability present is H1 by Goshree's own definition. Reclassification moves the horizon, not the probability: the 0.40 is build risk, not demand risk. It moves 8 squad-quarters and shifts the mix 14.3 points, 31/19/6 to 39/11/6 — 55/34/11 is really 70/20/11.

A protected slice with unprotected decision rights is not protection. The tell is distant bets dying at a revenue gate. Capacity is the easy half; the hard half is agreeing in advance what evidence lets one survive review.

Probability weighting has to be symmetric. The tell is a benefit quoted with no probability on it, usually the near-term one, because it feels certain. Had Goshree valued collections at its full ₹95 crore while still halving the copilot's probability, the shift would have appeared to add ₹20.3 crore rather than cost ₹13.0 crore — a ₹33.3 crore swing and a reversed decision, from one unweighted cell.

Options are defined by their kill point, not their size. The tell is "we are keeping our options open" with no date and no price. Goshree's copilot at six squad-quarters, one annual line reviewed in month eleven, is a small bet wearing the word. Gharonda's ₹34 lakh cavity is an option: it buys a decision on a named date.

Only differential uncertainty changes a ranking. The tell is a sensitivity analysis that haircuts the frightening number and leaves the comfortable ones alone. Cut the copilot's ₹300 crore by 20.0 per cent to ₹240 crore and it ties the ledger at ₹6.00 crore per squad-quarter; at ₹180 crore it falls from first to fourth. Haircut all five rows equally and the ranking is untouched: a uniform haircut is scale-invariant.

A value column mixing protected and incremental profit flatters the distant bets. The tell is an exhibit where defending a ₹121 crore revenue base scores below a speculative new line. Rows one and five of Exhibit 1 are protection, rows two to four growth; they are not commensurable, and the per-squad-quarter column treats them as if they were.

Thin staffing is how a distant bet gets cancelled without anyone cancelling it. The tell is a headcount adequate in aggregate. Gharonda's H3 work absorbed 78 engineer-weeks in six months — three engineers' worth of continuous effort — but logged by eleven engineers, an average of 7.1 weeks each across a 26-week window. Eleven people averaging seven weeks each are not an option. They are a rumour.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products horizons are short and feedback fast, so the constraint is attention rather than capital and the failure is a portfolio of look-alike H1 features. In B2B and enterprise the buyer's planning cycle sets the clock: Goshree cannot ship an H2 module faster than customers can procure it, which is why its one surviving H2 bet sits at 0.55, not near 1. Platforms and marketplaces should classify by which side pays. For hardware the tooling calendar is the gate. For AI products outcomes are bimodal rather than merely wide, which is why staging beats ratios.

Where the difference is not real, say so: the horizon definitions do not change by product type, and nor does the arithmetic. What changes is clock speed and irreversibility. By stage: before product-market fit a company has one horizon; a growth-stage firm's question is whether anything survives the pull of the core; only at scale is the deficit the dominant risk.

8. Three worked examples

The trade Goshree can price

Section 3's reallocation: ₹13.0 crore of expected value — 5.9 per cent of the mixed total — for a 17.0 per cent cut in dispersion, both sides weighted. Namitha's contribution was to insist that rate be stated first.

Gharonda prices an option, and the prize cancels out

Gharonda must commit purifier tooling on Friday 15 January 2027 to reach a 1 November 2027 launch — forty-one weeks. The moulder will instead sell a sensor-ready cavity plus an expedite clause for ₹34 lakh and no exercise fee, deferring the decision to Wednesday 30 June 2027, eighteen weeks out. Tooling is ₹1.85 crore, and Gharonda judges the FY28 business case lands with probability 0.35. The prize is a run-rate, on three assumptions the case states and has not tested. The fleet logged 1,29,200 service visits in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 against a trailing-twelve-month average installed base of 1,90,000 — below the 2,14,000 closing count, because the base grew through the year — a rate of 0.68 visits per unit per year. Hold that rate, take the plan's FY28 average fleet of 3,10,000 (45 per cent above September 2026), and assume a fully sensored fleet: 2,10,800 visits at ₹385 each, ₹8.12 crore a year, of which the case assumes the sensor removes 55 per cent — ₹4.46 crore a year. FY28 carries neither of the last two, since the sensor ships with the new tooling on 1 November 2027 and only units built after it have one.

Committing now is worth −₹1.85 crore + 0.35 × ₹4.46 crore = −₹0.29 crore. Staging is worth −₹0.34 crore + 0.35 × (₹4.46 − ₹1.85) crore = +₹0.57 crore. The gap is ₹0.86 crore, which equals tooling × (1 − p) − premium = ₹1.85 crore × 0.65 − ₹0.34 crore. The prize has cancelled out — for any prize above the ₹1.85 crore of tooling it pays for. Staging is worth the irreversible commitment avoided times the probability of not needing it, so the breakeven premium is ₹1.20 crore and ₹34 lakh is 28.3 per cent of it. Neelakanta objected to the 55 per cent, a target: the sensor predicted 39 of the 112 filter failures recorded in the pilot, or 34.8 per cent. Substitute it and the prize falls to ₹2.83 crore, staging is worth almost nothing, committing −₹0.86 crore — and the gap is still ₹0.86 crore. Staging landing on zero is luck: it breaks even at ₹2.82 crore and the pilot implies ₹2.83 crore. The two being equal and opposite is not luck — when staging is worth nothing the committed branch is worth exactly minus the gap. The prize decides whether to make the bet, not whether to stage it.

Where the approach failed: Gharonda's FY25 ten per cent

In FY25 Gharonda ran an explicit 70/20/10 rule. The team was 28 engineers, so a nominal 10 per cent was 146 engineer-weeks; 148 were logged, across four H3 bets. All four were killed within a quarter, each having to clear the same quarterly contribution gate as the core business. Output: zero shipped features, three memos, ₹91.8 lakh of fully loaded cost at ₹62,000 per engineer-week. The allocation had been honoured to the week; the ratio was defended and the gate was not. The FY26 recovery cut the slice: 104 engineer-weeks — two engineers for four quarters — on one bet, judged against a learning milestone. That is 29.7 per cent less capacity, and it produced the sensor pilot, live in 1,100 homes since Monday 2 March 2026 — the first distant bet to survive a year since the FY25 rule.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

  1. Horizon inflation. Near-term work relabelled to balance the deck. Sign: no bet has been reclassified nearer. Diagnostic: which bet moved down last year, and who moved it? Cost late: the firm learns its distant slice was zero when a competitor ships.
  2. The unprotected gate. Capacity defended, decision rights not. Sign: distant bets die at their first contribution review. Diagnostic: what evidence, named now, lets one survive a quarter? Cost: Gharonda's ₹91.8 lakh and a year.
  3. Correlated bets read as diversification. Sign: every bet needs the same macro sentence. Diagnostic: name the assumption whose failure zeroes three rows. Cost: dispersion understated by about a quarter, found in the year it matters.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Ratios versus staging. The ratio camp rests on evidence that firms without a declared split under-invest in the distant horizon, the deficit being invisible until it is fatal, and on ratios surviving personnel changes while judgement does not. The staging camp rests on equally strong evidence that protected slices get spent without producing anything — Gharonda's FY25 — and that the live variable is the next gate. For the ratio camp to be wrong, firms would have to under-invest no more than they over-invest; for the staging camp, gates would have to fund the distant horizon unaided, which the growth-gap literature exists because they did not.

Does dispersion belong here at all? The mean-variance position is that ignoring variance is how firms end up with portfolios they cannot survive. The objection is serious: product bets are indivisible, untraded and correlated through one demand environment, so diversification is largely illusory and the arithmetic lends invented probabilities a spurious authority. For that position to be wrong the probabilities would have to carry no information — and the correlation ceilings above concede they carry less than they seem to.

Inside or outside. Christensen's successors hold that distant bets inside the product organisation are starved and belong in a separate vehicle. The counter is that separation removes what made the bet worth making — the core's distribution, customers and data. The evidence is stage-dependent.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes a ratio. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions: what did we execute last period, by what definition is each bet classified, and what does each distant bet's next stage cost? They state exchange rates rather than preferences — "we give up 5.9 per cent of a mixed expected value for 17 per cent less dispersion" — and weight both sides unasked. They can say what is missing, which a ranked backlog never does. And they conclude, when true, that balance is wrong for this firm this year.

12. What they decided

Namitha reclassified the co-lending ledger to H1, exposing a plan 70 per cent weighted to the near horizon rather than the 55 per cent the slide claimed. She did not raise the distant slice. She split the copilot's six squad-quarters into two stages of three with a kill decision on 31 January 2027, and re-stated row one as revenue protected rather than a bet won, so the next comparison would not score an obligation against an option. Nivrutti bought the ₹34 lakh cavity, re-declared the H2 target at 22 per cent to sit nearer what the firm had proved it would execute, and gave the H3 bet two named engineers for twelve months.

Questions for discussion:

  1. Goshree's compliance work carries p = 0.95. If that row is an obligation rather than a bet, how should it enter the arithmetic — and what happens to the ranking once it is removed?
  2. Nivrutti re-declared a target to match executed behaviour. When is that discipline, and when surrender?
  3. Gharonda's staging gain is independent of the prize. Where else here does a decision not depend on the number the argument is about?

13. Going deeper

  • Portfolio of bets and expected value — the arithmetic Exhibit 1 rests on.
  • Three horizons and bet sizing — the classification axis, and where its sizing conventions come from.
  • Value vs effort — the ranking this replaces; study what it cannot see.
  • RICE scoring — a confidence term is a probability in disguise, and where the symmetry failure enters.
  • Kano model — separates protected from incremental value, in customer terms.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — adds cost of delay, which horizon ratios omit.
  • Buy-a-feature — forces a rivalrous budget, the section 4 condition.
  • User story mapping — shows what a horizon slice actually contains.
exp20v2-prio.portfolio.balance:
Balancing a Portfolio Across Horizons and Risk

Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making

1. A roadmap nobody chose

On Monday, 12 January 2026, Mridula Vengalil, chief product officer of Eranad, opened the draft roadmap for the year beginning 1 April. Eranad, a Kochi-based bill-payment and savings app, has 38 lakh monthly active users and earned ₹210 crore of gross profit in FY2024-25. Mahima Vettath, head of growth, had built the draft as the company always had: estimate each proposal's chance of working and fund them in descending order of confidence until the engineers ran out. Three squads of six engineers working fifty weeks give 900 engineer-weeks; eight proposals asked for 1,050.

The draft funded six: 500 weeks on four improvements to the existing app, 400 on two new products, and nothing on the two proposals whose chance of success was below one in three. Every line was defensible, but nobody had decided that mix; it had fallen out of the sorting rule.

Mathai Vayalil, the chief financial officer, expected the plan by Friday, 23 January. Safe bets alone would leave Eranad no better placed against larger rivals; moonshots could miss the revenue plan the board had seen. Her question was not whether each bet was good, but what the six added up to, and what was missing.

2. The idea

A portfolio view treats the roadmap as one holding rather than a list of independent items. Each proposal is a bet: it costs something certain (engineer-weeks) and returns something uncertain (added annual gross profit, if it works). Balancing means choosing deliberately how much capacity goes to bets of different risk and time to payoff, and naming what the mix leaves out.

The idea has three sources. In 1952 the economist Harry Markowitz argued that an investor should judge an asset by what it adds to the whole holding. In 1999 Mehrdad Baghai, Stephen Coley and David White of McKinsey proposed three horizons: Horizon 1 extends the core business, Horizon 2 builds emerging businesses, and Horizon 3 plants options on businesses that may matter later. In the 1990s Robert Cooper, Scott Edgett and Elko Kleinschmidt urged firms to set spending buckets for new products in advance rather than let project rankings decide. The popular 70/20/10 split is a rule of thumb, not a law.

Three terms recur. A sure thing is an improvement to something that exists, with probability of success of at least 0.60. A growth bet is a new offering with a probability from 0.30 up to, but not including, 0.60. An option is a small, capped purchase of the right to learn: probability of 0.20 or less, large payoff, and no more than a tenth of annual capacity per option. Expected value (EV) is probability multiplied by payoff. The sentence Mridula could repeat in a meeting: every roadmap is already a portfolio; the only question is whether anyone chose its mix.

3. How it works

First, put every proposal in a common currency: Eranad uses engineer-weeks for cost and rupee crore of added annual gross profit, in the year after launch, for payoff. Second, estimate probability and payoff separately and record who estimated them. Third, classify each bet against the written definitions before looking at any ranking.

Fourth, compute EV and EV per engineer-week. Fifth, the step the sorting rule skipped: decide the mix before filling it, in weeks per bucket and in tolerable variability, then fund each bucket in order of EV per week. Sixth, ask what is missing: which horizon or dependency is empty or overloaded.

Figure 1 shows the eight proposals on the two quantities that make up EV. The dashed curve joins every combination worth exactly ₹6 crore. Bets C, D, G and H lie on it: equal on average, yet C works three times in four and H once in ten.

Moving right buys certainty; moving up buys size. Dots above the curve (B, E, F) beat ₹6 crore of EV and A falls short. Nothing in the figure says which to fund: EV is one coordinate of a decision, and the mix is the other.

4. A worked example

Table 1 gives Mahima's inputs and two derived columns. EV per week is in ₹ lakh (1 crore = 100 lakh), so A's ₹4.8 crore over 120 weeks is ₹480 lakh over 120 weeks, or 4.0.

The draft ranks by p alone: A (0.80), C (0.75), B (0.70), D (0.60), E (0.40), F (0.35), then G and H. Cumulative cost is 120, 220, 370, 500, 720 and 900 weeks, so the budget runs out exactly after F. The two options hold 16.7 per cent of capacity (150 of 900 weeks) but 26.8 per cent of the rebalanced EV (12.0 of 44.7) and 72.8 per cent of its variance (528 of 725.01). The plan raises average return and also raises SD from 17.0 to 26.9 crore, and Mathai may rightly care about the second number.

Second pass: change one input. A partner's compliance review puts the remittance probe at 0.05, not 0.10. H's EV halves to 3.0 and its EV per week falls to 3.3 lakh, the lowest of the eight. The rebalanced plan still beats the draft, 41.7 against 39.7, since G and H together give 9.0 against F's 7.0. The margin shrinks from 5.0 to 2.0 crore and SD falls to 23.9. The conclusion survives, but thinly.

Figure 2 makes the draft's gap visible: no red segment. The rebalanced bar leaves the sure things untouched and pays for options by shrinking the growth block. Mridula is asking for a different division of capacity, not more.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Horizon and risk are different axes

Horizon asks when a payoff arrives; risk asks how likely it is. They correlate but differ. Migrating Eranad's ledger to a new database is near-certain, yet pays off in three years. Sort on one axis only and a bucket mixes unlike things.

Expected value is not what you get

No outcome of H equals its EV of ₹6 crore. It pays ₹60 crore or nothing, and nine times in ten nothing. EV is an average over many repetitions, and a company gets one year, so a spread measure belongs beside it.

Bets are not independent

The SD figures assume independence, which is generous. If a regulator changed how small UPI transactions may be charged for, A through F could suffer together, and the real spread is wider than Table 2 shows.

An option is priced by the cost of learning

Judged as a product, G looks poor: 85 per cent of the time it delivers nothing. Judged as an option, its 60 weeks buy a dated answer, so each option needs a kill review and a stop point.

The target mix is a hypothesis

Eranad's rebalanced plan is 55.6/24.4/16.7 with 3.3 per cent in reserve, not 70/20/10. The right mix depends on runway and on how fast the core is eroding; justify it, do not borrow it. Nor is a score such as RICE a mix: it ranks, and cannot see the whole.

What it cannot tell you

The method cannot make the inputs true. Every p and payoff is a judgement, mostly by the person asking for the weeks, and cost is treated as certain though estimates overrun. Ask who estimated each number and which single input would flip the answer.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In a consumer product such as Eranad, experiments revise probabilities within weeks. In B2B, bets are fewer and lumpier, and a large customer's custom request passes itself off as a sure thing. In a marketplace, success depends on both sides responding, so bets correlate more, usually through liquidity.

An early-stage company is itself an option; its question is how much variance its runway can survive. A large company faces the opposite danger: the core absorbs everything, so each bucket's budget should be ring-fenced.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the sorting rule as the strategy. Symptom: every funded item comes from one or two buckets, and nobody can say why. Misunderstanding: that a ranked list decides the mix. Diagnostic: total the weeks by class before approval.

Judging options as products. Symptom: a probe is cancelled for low odds, or scaled up before its first test reports. Misunderstanding: that a cheap bet must clear a large bet's bar. Diagnostic: ask what result, on what date, would end it.

Relabelling to hit the target. Symptom: the mix hits 70/20/10 exactly, yet the growth bucket holds core fixes. Misunderstanding: that the label is the property. Diagnostic: test every member against the written class definition.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Eranad's decision fits on one page. It states the mix in weeks and per cent, the EV and the spread, and the one input that would reverse the choice. Each option carries a budget, a review date and a kill criterion. It names what is missing: nothing hedges the shared payments dependency.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 23 January Mridula presented the rebalanced plan. Mathai pressed on the spread: ₹5.0 crore more EV for a rise in SD from 17.0 to 26.9 was not obviously a bargain. Mridula conceded the point, showed the H-at-0.05 pass, and committed to review points: G at week 20 of its 60, H at week 30 of its 90. Her reasoning: a year with no chance of a step change is also a decision, made by default. F was deferred, not rejected.

Next, study horizons and bet sizing, since staging turns options from a hope into a discipline. Then study calibration, since every figure above is only as good as its estimate.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of the eight probabilities would you most want evidence on before 23 January, and what is the cheapest evidence you could get? Second, in your own current roadmap, which bets share a dependency, so that one event could take several of them out together?
exp20v2-prio.platform.vs.feature:
Prioritising platform work against features

How do we fund the work customers never see?

1. A Monday in February

On Monday 9 February 2026, Kamalakshi Sreedharan, vice-president of product at Chempaka Commerce, opened the planning document for the quarter that would begin on Wednesday 1 April. Chempaka sold billing and point-of-sale software to mid-sized retailers in southern India, and its annual recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly value of subscriptions in force) stood at ₹42 crore. The plan had to be locked by Friday 13 February; the board would review it on Tuesday 12 May.

Forty engineers could each give ten productive weeks to the quarter, once leave and holidays were removed: 400 engineer-weeks. Kamalakshi reserved a quarter, 100, for bugs, support and keeping the system running. That left 300 for the roadmap, the work the company chooses to schedule.

Four visible features sat on the list, each backed by a salesperson who could name waiting merchants. Against them stood one item nobody outside engineering could see: a rebuilt billing-events layer, the internal service through which every invoice, payment and refund passes on its way to other systems. Krishnadas Sadanandan, who led platform engineering, estimated 90 engineer-weeks. He argued that the current layer caused four severity-one incidents a quarter and made every new integration cost 24 engineer-weeks.

Kannan Surendran, the chief revenue officer, had already promised a GST e-invoice export to eighteen prospects. Kumaresh Sivadasan, the finance chief, wanted every rupee tied to revenue he could point to in May. If Kamalakshi funded the platform and the integrations never came, she would have spent almost a third of her roadmap on an invisible asset. If she refused, she would pay in outages anyway.

2. The idea

Platform work is work whose value arrives through other work. A feature is valued by what customers do with it; a platform, whether infrastructure, shared tooling or an internal service, is valued by what it makes cheaper, faster or safer for the features and teams built on top of it. The two cannot be scored on one sheet without translation, because a platform has no end customers of its own and scores near zero on reach.

The logic has several origins. Ward Cunningham described technical debt in 1992 as a loan whose interest is paid in slower future work. Donald Reinertsen's 2009 book on product development flow ranked items by cost of delay, the value lost for each week of lateness. Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, in Team Topologies (2019), described the platform team whose product is other teams' speed. RICE, a scoring model associated with Intercom, supplied the arithmetic of reach, impact, confidence and effort.

The sentence Kamalakshi could say in the meeting without sounding glib was this: we fund a platform for the future work it makes cheaper, and we count only the future work we can name.

In Figure 1 the platform is a single box; its value is the six boxes on the right, and only those actually built.

3. How it works

The method has seven steps; the first three are usually left unsaid. First, fix capacity: 300 engineer-weeks after the reserve. Second, fix the horizon over which benefits count; Kamalakshi used the twelve months after delivery for every item. Third, name the exchange rate, what one engineer-week is worth, because a platform returns mostly engineer-weeks and these must become the same currency as feature revenue.

Fourth, score each feature as expected ARR: deals, times ARR per deal, times confidence that they close. Fifth, find the marginal item, the lowest-value feature the platform would displace. Its ARR per engineer-week is the exchange rate and its expected ARR is the opportunity cost, the value given up. Sixth, translate the platform's benefits into that currency. Seventh, compare, then change the most doubtful input and compare again.

All four features fit exactly: 60 + 90 + 50 + 100 = 300 engineer-weeks, worth ₹163.4 lakh. Feature B, the loyalty module, ranks lowest at ₹0.40 lakh per engineer-week, and removing it frees exactly the 90 the platform needs. The exchange rate is therefore ₹0.40 lakh per engineer-week and the opportunity cost ₹36.0 lakh.

4. A worked example, and what happens when one input moves

Table 2 sets out three benefit streams. Integration savings: six integrations at 15 engineer-weeks saved each is 90, and Kamalakshi judged a 0.6 probability that any one would be built within the horizon, so 54 are expected back. Incident time: four incidents a quarter at 3 engineer-weeks each is 12; Krishnadas's central estimate is a 75 per cent reduction, 9 a quarter or 36 over four quarters. Churn: two large accounts of ₹5.0 lakh ARR each had complained about outages, and she gave a 0.5 chance the platform keeps them. The result rests on one assumption: incidents are paid from the 100-week reserve, so valuing the freed 36 weeks at the roadmap rate assumes they can move to roadmap work. If they stay in the reserve, pass-1 value falls to 21.6 + 5.0 = 26.6, below B's 36.0.

Pass 1 compares two complete plans. The four features cost 300 engineer-weeks and yield ₹163.4 lakh. A, C, D and the platform also cost 300 (60 + 50 + 100 + 90) and yield 50.4 + 32.0 + 45.0 + 41.0 = ₹168.4 lakh, a lead of ₹5.0 lakh. Before celebrating, note that in engineer-weeks alone the platform returns 90 for the 90 it costs; its entire advantage is the churn line.

Pass 2 changes one input. Kannan, asked how many integrations were truly on the sales calendar, said perhaps half of what Kamalakshi assumed. At 0.3, integration savings fall to 27 engineer-weeks; with 36 from incidents, 63 come back, worth 25.2, and the total becomes 25.2 + 5.0 = ₹30.2 lakh. The platform plan yields 127.4 + 30.2 = ₹157.6 lakh, ₹5.8 lakh behind. Break-even is a probability of about 0.46: at least three of the six must really be built.

A gap of ₹5.0 lakh on ₹163.4 lakh is about three per cent, well inside the error of the inputs. The numbers cannot choose; they can only say which input must be defended.

5. What a newcomer must become aware of

Platform is defined by how value arrives

The test is whether payoff is realised through other work, not where the work sits in the stack. A shared service used by five teams is a platform; a deep new button is still a feature. Name the consumers.

It is not technical debt or refactoring

Debt is shortcuts whose cost recurs; refactoring repays it; a platform is a deliberate shared capability. They overlap in Table 2's incident line, but a platform case needs consumers while a debt case needs only a measured interest payment.

Timing is part of the answer

Platform benefits arrive after delivery, feature revenue often sooner. Kamalakshi counted both over twelve months, but discounting or a faster sales cycle would shift the tables. Choose one horizon and hold it for both sides.

Probabilities belong to product

The 0.6 was the most influential probability on the page, and the person best placed to challenge it was Kannan, who owns the sales calendar. Both sides must be weighted: features carry confidence factors, so the platform must carry probabilities too.

The exchange rate is an assumption

Valuing an engineer-week at ₹0.40 lakh holds only if freed weeks go to work of feature B's quality. If they would fund feature A at ₹0.84 lakh the platform is worth more; if they would produce nothing, less.

Some work is not a trade-off

Security patches and regulatory deadlines sit above any ranking; the method applies to the discretionary 300 weeks.

Benefits can be counted twice

If two streams draw on the same engineers' time, one week may be claimed twice. Every stream must be a different week or rupee.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot say whether the 75 per cent reduction is true, whether consumers will adopt the platform, or what an option on future capability is worth. It ranks assumptions; it does not validate them.

6. How the answer changes by setting

Table 3. The same logic, different evidence.

In a large company the consumers are other teams who can be interviewed and asked to commit, so probabilities rest on evidence. In a six-engineer start-up they are guesses, and the answer is usually features.

7. Common mistakes

The flat platform tax

Symptom: platform receives 20 per cent every quarter whatever is planned. Misunderstanding: platform is a category rather than a bet on named consumers. Diagnostic: ask for three consumers and their start dates.

Scoring a platform on reach

Symptom: platform items sit at the bottom of a RICE sheet. Misunderstanding: reach was defined as end customers. Diagnostic: re-score reach as dependent teams and see whether the rank moves.

The big-bang rebuild

Symptom: nine months in, nothing uses the platform. Misunderstanding: value arrives at completion. Diagnostic: ask which consumer goes live first, and when.

Forever benefits

Symptom: savings listed with no horizon or probability. Misunderstanding: a benefit is a fact, not an estimate. Diagnostic: halve the probability, as Kannan did, and see whether the decision flips.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the meeting opens with Table 1, not a debate: consumers named, probabilities owned by product, the doubtful input flagged. Krishnadas would split the 90 engineer-weeks so the first release served UPI AutoPay, the integration with the surest demand, within six weeks, with the rest unlocked on evidence.

9. The decision

Kamalakshi funded the platform on Friday 13 February, with one condition: by the following Friday, Kannan and the product managers must name at least three of the six integrations, each with an owner, a customer and a start date, because three built is where her own table breaks even. Feature A stayed, so Kannan's promise held; feature B moved to the next quarter. She wrote the break-even into the plan for the May board.

Her reasoning was not that the platform scored better; it scored ₹5.0 lakh better in one pass and ₹5.8 lakh worse in the other. It was that the cost of being wrong could be bounded: if fewer than three integrations were named, she would shrink the platform and restore feature B.

To learn next, study cost of delay and weighted shortest job first, which put timing into arithmetic this page held fixed, and platform-as-a-product thinking, which treats internal teams as customers.

Delivery & Technology · Prioritisation & Decision-Making

Prioritising platform work against features

How to fund the work customers never see — and why the standard scoring machinery returns the wrong answer by construction.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Wednesday 14 January 2026 in Bengaluru, Lakshmi Tharayil had ninety minutes to settle the FY27 plan for Daksham Logistics Cloud, which sells a transport management system to mid-sized Indian logistics firms: 46 customers, ARR of ₹38.4 crore and 26 months of runway, all at 31 December 2025. Every deal carries the same clause: the customer's carriers must be wired in, with e-way bill filing on the GSTN rails, telematics feeds and proof-of-delivery images. Daksham has built 23 of them by hand at a median of 19 engineer-days each; eleven more sit in FY27. Linesh Tonse, who runs platform engineering, wants 110 engineer-days for a Carrier Connector Framework — a normalised adapter contract, a sandbox, a self-serve carrier portal and a conformance suite — after which an integration costs 7 engineer-days rather than 19. Lambodar Thottungal, the revenue chief, wants those 110 days on the freight-audit module three deals are waiting on.

Three weeks later, on Tuesday 3 February, Lohita Thekkanath faced the same argument at Dhaanya Fresh, a subscription staples service in Pune, Mumbai and Nashik: 58,400 baskets delivered in December 2025, average basket ₹1,240, monthly GMV of ₹7.24 crore and contribution margin of 11 per cent, or ₹79.66 lakh a month. Lasith Talapady wanted 80 engineer-days, a four-engineer pod for four weeks, to replace the nightly catalogue upload with a Catalogue and Pricing Service; the growth team wanted the same pod for recipe baskets. Dhaanya's engineering group is 24 strong and a quarter about 1,440 engineer-days, so the service is 5.6 per cent of a quarter. Both arguments were conducted in the vocabulary of RICE, and both were unscoreable in it.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

Define platform work precisely. Work W is platform work with respect to a set S of future work items if the cost or the feasibility of the items in S changes conditional on W being done. Two consequences follow. Nothing is platform work in the abstract — the claim is relative to a named set, and a proposal that cannot name S has not made one — and the asset bought is S, not W. The platform is the receipt.

The framing predates software. Wheelwright and Clark's aggregate project plan (1992) separated platform from derivative projects and allocated capacity across the types rather than ranking them against each other. Baldwin and Clark's Design Rules (2000) made the sharper claim, that a modular design buys real options whose value rises with uncertainty. Reinertsen (2009) supplied the machinery most teams use, cost of delay and WSJF, in which platform work scores badly because its cost of delay is diffuse across a queue. Ward Cunningham's technical-debt metaphor (1992) is often folded in and should not be: debt removal lowers the cost of committed work, platform work of uncommitted work.

Four positions are genuinely held.

  • The annuity school. Signs: platform work must be underwritten by a named, dated set of items and a measured per-item saving. Will not sign: unnamed flexibility has value.
  • The options school. Signs: a platform's value rises with uncertainty about which features will matter. Will not sign: a committed roadmap justifies a platform — a known roadmap destroys the option premium.
  • The allocation school. Signs: platform work takes a protected share of capacity and is ranked only against itself. Will not sign: every platform item carries its own business case.
  • The customer-perceivable school. Signs: a platform ships inside the first feature that requires it. Will not sign: a platform may be built ahead of its first consumer.

3. Mechanics: what an expert actually computes

The procedure below separates a defensible case from an advocacy document. Steps 3, 5 and 6 are the ones usually skipped.

  1. Name the consuming set: items, owners, dates. Daksham's is 11 integrations, each attached to a named customer or prospect.
  2. Measure the per-item delta from history, build and recurring separately. Daksham: build 19 → 7 engineer-days; maintenance 1.4 → 0.5 per integration per quarter.
  3. Establish membership. Daksham's 110 days cover new integrations only. Migrating the 23 legacy ones costs about 4 engineer-days each and is out of scope, contributing to neither side.
  4. Integrate the benefit over its ramp. The framework lands 17 June 2026; four integrations follow in Q2, four in Q3, three in Q4. On the convention that an integration is maintained from the quarter after it ships, FY27 holds 12 integration-quarters of coverage, not 44.
  5. Probability-weight both sides alike. Six of the 11 are contractual at p = 0.95 and five late-pipeline at p = 0.55, so expected integrations are 6 × 0.95 + 5 × 0.55 = 8.45. Daksham's last four platform projects came in at 292 engineer-days against 225 quoted, a factor of 1.30, so a 110-day quote costs 143 expected days.
  6. Compute the break-even count, not an ROI: 143 ÷ 12 = 11.92, so the framework needs about 12 new integrations to repay its build saving.
  7. Name the leading indicator and kill criterion before building.
  8. Give the run cost an owner and a budget line.

Exhibit 1 is the number that loses the argument. Weighted symmetrically the framework costs Daksham 33.3 more engineer-days in FY27 than doing nothing; unweighted — 11 certain integrations against a 110-day quote at face value — it returns a net saving of 32.8. Either one-sided weighting lands on a wash: weight the savings only and the net is -0.3, weight the cost only and it is -0.2. Whichever asymmetry an advocate picks, the answer reads "too close to call" and gets settled by whoever speaks last.

Two things about Exhibit 2 should be said out loud. It carries the framework's run cost, which Exhibit 1 omits, so FY27's net there is -99.3 rather than -33.3, a difference of 66.0. And the FY28–29 figure of 9.00 is a run-rate, not a named set: Thottungal's plan carries ten requests a year at p = 0.90, against a history of 23 integrations in three years, or 7.7 a year. That is this page's own unnamed-set failure mode, and it decides the sign. Writing X for expected integrations a year in FY28–29, the three-year net is 30.3X - 214.5: -214.5 at X = 0, -32.7 at X = 6, crossing zero at X = 7.08 (at X = 9 the linear form gives 58.2 against the table's 58.3, on rounding). The FY27 cohort alone does not pay for the framework; only the run-rate does.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can fail

Six conditions, each testable, each applied to both protagonists.

C1 — the set reaches the break-even count. Daksham fails on FY27 alone (8.45 expected against 11.92 needed on build saving) and clears three years only if the FY28–29 run-rate holds: about 7.1 expected integrations a year once run cost is counted, against a planned 9.00, a margin of 21 per cent. Dhaanya has no effort break-even at all. Lohita's team had called six of its next eight items blocked by the catalogue; against the stated definition — unbuildable without effective-dated, city-scoped SKU versioning — three are blocked, two are merely slowed (buildable on workarounds costing 9 and 6 engineer-days) and three are independent. On the slowed two it is a 5.3-fold loss, 80 engineer-days to remove 15; the blocked three yield feasibility rather than days, so the five-member set yields no count and the case rests on them.

C2 — the per-item delta comes from history. Daksham passes, on 23 integrations. Dhaanya fails; Lasith's 80 days has no precedent.

C3 — both sides are weighted on the same basis. Daksham's set is largely contractual. Dhaanya's growth deck was the mirror failure: it priced recipe baskets at ₹5.14 lakh of incremental monthly GMV from an unweighted +₹22 lift on 40 per cent of baskets, while discounting the platform for delivery risk. At the team's own p = 0.45 the expected lift is ₹2.31 lakh a month, 45 per cent of the figure in the deck.

C4 — the first consumer ships within one planning cycle. Both pass. C5 — the run cost has an owner. Daksham passes; Tonse commits 0.4 of an engineer, the 88.0 engineer-days a year Exhibit 2 carries. Dhaanya does not. C6 — the constraint removed is the binding one. Daksham passes; Dhaanya fails the strong version, for reasons in section 6.

Three situations make the frame misleading: before product-market fit, when the set is a fiction and the exercise launders a preference; with one member, when the "platform" is that feature and the label hides its cost; and on a shrinking roadmap, where platform value falls with the set and debt value does not.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

In multi-product firms the set spans profit centres, so funding becomes transfer pricing; chargeback is observed to suppress adoption below the level that justified the platform, so mature firms more often levy a flat tax. In two-sided businesses half the set is supply-side tooling whose payoff appears as liquidity two or three quarters later, outrunning any quarterly planning cycle. In regulated products the recurring compliance surface, not the build saving, usually carries the case. In hardware-plus-software the set is hostage to a build plan the software organisation does not control, and families are cancelled more often than added. In AI-native products the platform is the evaluation layer and the constraint is measurement, not build.

At the seam, incentives diverge: a platform team measured on adoption is rewarded for breadth, a feature team measured on outcomes for forking. The symptom is a private copy of the platform's client library in a feature repository. What mature companies say they do is run a business case per platform item; what they more often do is run a protected allocation with an escalation path and write the case afterwards.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The set is the asset. The tell is a value section built on the verb "enable" with no object. An expert's first question is "name five consuming items and their owners." The obvious reading, that the deliverable is the platform, yields frameworks with no consumers.

Debt and platform are different instruments. The tell is a single "tech health" line. Ask: does this lower the cost of committed work, or of uncommitted work? Debt reduction pays off even if the roadmap stops and platform work does not, so firms that merge the two cut the wrong one in a downturn.

Uncertainty cuts both ways, and which way depends on which uncertainty. The tell is an advocate and a sceptic quoting the same sentence — "we don't know what we'll need next year" — as evidence. Uncertainty about which item will matter raises platform value, since optionality is the product; uncertainty about whether any happens destroys it.

Symmetry. The tell is a probability on one side of a comparison and not the other, and it is the commonest way a platform recommendation inverts: Daksham moves from +32.8 to -33.3 engineer-days on this alone. Weighting is not a courtesy extended to the side you doubt.

The dead zone. The tell is a case whose benefits begin in the delivery quarter. The quarter a platform ships is the quarter it produces nothing, and that gap is where credibility goes. Daksham's FY27 maintenance saving is 8.3 engineer-days against a steady-state 30.4 for the same expected 8.45 integrations.

Break-even counts, not returns. The tell is an expert asking "how many integrations before this pays?" rather than "what is the ROI?" A count is arguable by people who know the pipeline; a discounted return is arguable by nobody, which is why it survives review and then fails.

Legacy is out of scope and silently assumed in. The tell is a saving claimed across an installed base from a scope covering only new work. Daksham's 23 existing integrations would cost a further 92 engineer-days to migrate, and sit in Exhibit 1 at 128.8 on both paths so no claim can smuggle them in.

The constraint moves. The tell is doubled build capacity with an unchanged count of shipped experiments. Dhaanya's service would take the merchandising pod from 11.9 to 26.3 experiment slots a half-year, but the hypothesis backlog held 16 items in December 2025, so the ceiling is 16 attempts — which at the team's own rates, 5 of 9 attempted ship and 2 of 5 shipped validate, gives 3.6 validated wins, not 5.8.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The procedure in section 3 does not change across these; what changes is the unit the numerator is denominated in, and saying so beats inventing differences. For consumer products the unit is learning rate, because features are cheap and measurement is the bottleneck; rupees would need each experiment's share of GMV, which firms of Dhaanya's size do not track, so the throughput of validated experiments is the honest metric. For B2B and enterprise the unit is engineer-days and contractual commitments, and because the set is written into signed deals the annuity school is strongest there. For platforms and marketplaces the set includes third parties you cannot schedule, so the case belongs on its lower quartile. For AI products the unit is release cadence under a fixed quality bar.

By stage: pre-PMF, almost the only defensible platform investment is one where the platform is the product. In growth the annuity is real and large, as at Daksham. At scale the allocation school wins on administrative grounds, forty item-level cases costing more to referee than the variance they remove. Late on, platform work becomes consolidation and decommissioning, a different instrument whose benefit is run cost.

8. Three worked examples

Dakshinya Health Systems: the compliance surface. Dakshinya's hospital information system had to support health-ID linking under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission in seven modules. Module by module: 7 × 55 = 385 engineer-days and seven audit surfaces. As one consent-and-identity service: 150 days plus 7 × 12 = 84 of wiring, or 234, a build saving of 151. The decisive term was recurring: each audit surface costs 9 engineer-days an annual audit, so seven cost 63 a year against 9 for one, saving 54 a year. It shipped in June 2024 and two audits have since been observed, so 151 + 2 × 54 = 259 engineer-days are realised, reaching 313 at the FY27 audit. No RICE sheet in the building had a field for it.

Dhwaja Labs: the saving that never reached the budget. Dhwaja extracts fields from lending documents. Before January 2026 each model change was validated by hand on 40 documents at 2.5 engineer-days a release, six releases a quarter: 15.0 engineer-days a quarter. The harness cost 95 engineer-days: 1,200 labelled documents at 11 minutes each is 220 hours, or 27.5 person-days of labelling, plus 67.5 days of engineering. The per-release saving is flat at 2.5 - 0.3 = 2.2 engineer-days, so at the old cadence of six the harness returns 13.2 a quarter, 52.8 a year, repaying in 1.80 years; at the 19 releases a quarter Dhwaja reached by Q3 2026 it returns 41.8 a quarter, 167.2 a year, repaying in 0.57. Payback improved as cadence rose. The budget showed something else: the validation line fell only from 15.0 to 19 × 0.3 = 5.7, because the freed capacity bought 13 more releases rather than being handed back. Reading that 9.3 as the saving sets manual work at six releases against harness work at nineteen — the like-for-like breach C3 forbids, since 19 by hand would cost 47.5 — and understates the return 4.5-fold. Without the harness cadence would have stayed near six, so the gain is 13 releases a quarter, not recovered hours.

Deralakatte Instruments: the set that evaporated. In 2025 Deralakatte, which sells industrial flow meters with a cloud dashboard, built a device-ingest platform underwritten by a plan for nine meter families by 2027: the three then selling plus six new. Cost: six engineers for fourteen months at twenty working days a month, 1,680 engineer-days. Bespoke ingest runs 400 engineer-days a family against 180 on the platform, a saving of 220 net of migration, so nine families implied 1,980 days saved and a net of +300. By October 2026 four were on it: the three legacy ones, migrated, plus one new. Two had been cancelled when a sensor supplier exited and three deferred. Realised saving 4 × 220 = 880 against 1,680 spent, a net of -800 engineer-days. The recovery was not deletion. Deralakatte retired two of five abstraction layers, cutting maintenance from 1.8 engineers to 0.9 — ₹108 lakh a year to ₹54 lakh at ₹60 lakh fully loaded — and ruled that no platform may be underwritten on more than two quarters of committed roadmap.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The unnamed set. Warning: the value section has no objects. Diagnostic: name five consuming items and their owners. Caught late it costs what Deralakatte paid.

Asymmetric weighting. Warning: a probability on one side only. Diagnostic: what is the probability on the other side? Caught late, the recommendation was backwards and the approving review cannot be reconstructed.

The unbudgeted platform tax. Warning: a build line and no run line. Diagnostic: who maintains this in year three, out of whose headcount? Exhibit 2 is where Daksham answers it.

The allocation that became a quota. Warning: the share is met exactly every quarter and never contested. Diagnostic: what did we refuse inside the platform bucket last quarter? Caught late, the protected share stops buying leverage.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does uncertainty raise or lower platform value? The options school rests on real evidence: in modular systems the value of substituting a better component later grows with the spread of outcomes, and firms that built abstraction ahead of demand have captured markets that did not yet exist. It would be wrong if the distribution over the set were not merely wide but bimodal between "happens" and "does not happen at all" — and Deralakatte suggests hardware roadmaps are exactly that. The annuity school rests on platforms more often dying of no consumers than of insufficient generality, and would be wrong if the ones that paid off were those whose sets nobody could have named.

Should platform work be in the feature queue at all? The allocation school argues that item-by-item comparison imports a measurement regime platform work cannot satisfy, so the result turns on measurability rather than value, and a protected share removes the bias. It would be wrong if protected shares systematically funded low-value work, which the quota failure mode says they sometimes do. The annuity school replies that cost of delay through an unblocked queue is computable, as Exhibit 1 computes it.

Must a platform ship inside its first consumer? The customer-perceivable school rests on the same base rate as the annuity school, platforms dying of no consumers, plus one structural advantage: shipping inside the first consuming feature makes the set a fact rather than a forecast, so none of this page's errors can be committed. It would be wrong if that first feature were systematically too small to pay for the general version — Daksham's position precisely, since one integration saves 12 engineer-days and cannot carry 143.

A fourth disagreement changes what you do on Monday. The 120.7 engineer-days Tharayil's re-scoped framework nets over three years are, at ₹14,000 fully loaded, ₹16.90 lakh, or annualised ₹5.63 lakh a year — 0.15 per cent of a ₹38.4 crore ARR. The options school concludes the engineer-day ledger is the wrong frame and platform work belongs on feasibility and retention, where the stakes are an order of magnitude larger. The annuity school replies that feasibility arguments are unfalsifiable and the ledger is the only discipline available. Nobody has settled this.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the consuming set before the design and carries a break-even count rather than a return. They weight both sides by reflex and notice at once when only one side is weighted. They name the run-cost owner in the same breath as the build cost, say when a platform is not worth building this year and under what condition it would be, refuse a merged tech-health bucket, and measure a platform by its first consumer's ship date.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Tharayil approved the framework at a re-scoped 62 engineer-days. The 110 was adapter contract 34, sandbox 28, self-serve carrier portal 31 and conformance suite 17; she kept the first two and cut the last 48 days, on Tonse's note that a portal and a conformance suite change carrier self-onboarding and regression cost rather than the per-integration build, so the 19 → 7 delta and the 0.5 maintenance figure survive. At the 1.30 factor 62 becomes 80.6 expected days, moving break-even on build saving from 11.92 integrations to 6.72, below the 8.45 expected; FY27 then runs 29.1 engineer-days to the good before the framework's 66.0 of run cost and -36.9 after it, the three-year net rises to 120.7, and break-even arrives about thirty-one weeks into FY28 rather than twenty weeks into FY29. Her kill criterion: if fewer than three of the four Q2 integrations are live by Friday 31 July 2026, the pod stops. Thekkanath declined the 80-day service and bought the 31-day slice delivering effective-dated prices, deferring city-scoped overrides (34 days) and the ops console (15 days), and changed the pod's target from shipping a service to cutting median spec-to-live time from 31 days to 18 — the 14 above plus 4 for the surviving city workaround — by 30 June 2026.

Discussion questions.

  1. Daksham clears a three-year break-even only if FY28–29 deliver about 7.1 expected integrations a year against a planned 9.00. With 26 months of runway, which horizon should Tharayil plan on, and what would have to change in Thottungal's pipeline to flip the answer?
  2. Dhaanya's throughput case falls from 5.8 validated wins a half-year to 3.6 once idea supply is counted, against the two it banked on nine attempts in the half to December 2025. Is that worth 5.6 per cent of a quarter's engineering capacity, and what measurement would settle it?
  3. The options and annuity schools give opposite advice as roadmap uncertainty rises. Which of these two decisions is harder for the options school to defend, and what evidence in the next quarter would adjudicate?

13. Going deeper

  • Allocating capacity: features, debt, bugs, bets — where the protected share is set.
  • Platform-as-a-product thinking — the discipline that makes a set nameable.
  • Value vs effort — the frame whose numerator collapses here.
  • RICE scoring — reach is the term that mis-scores platform work.
  • Weighted scoring and WSJF — cost of delay through a queue, costed.
  • Kano model — why invisible work is under-demanded and over-needed.
  • Buy-a-feature — exposes what stakeholders will trade.
  • User story mapping — the cheapest route to step 1.
